The view is the symmetric opposite of Berys Gaut's ethicism: where Gaut holds moral defects always count as aesthetic defects, immoralism holds they can sometimes count as merits.

question: On a symposium, philosopher Rinaldo argues: 'The harmony of a Bach fugue or the proportion of a Doric column is not a fact ABOUT us. It is a fact about the work itself, which our responses succeed or fail in tracking.' Which view of aesthetic value is Rinaldo defending?
answer: Aesthetic realism - aesthetic properties are mind-independent features of works, and qualified responses succeed or fail by tracking those features, much as perception succeeds or fails.
choices: Aesthetic realism - aesthetic properties are mind-independent features of works, and qualified responses succeed or fail by tracking those features, much as perception succeeds or fails.
Response-dependent view - aesthetic properties are constituted by converging responses of qualified observers under suitable conditions; real but not independent of human sensibility.
Strict subjectivism - aesthetic 'properties' are sociological projections of taste; there is no independent fact about a fugue's harmony that critical agreement is tracking when they agree.
Kantian view - aesthetic judgments are responses (disinterested pleasure) claiming universal validity, but do not pick out mind-independent properties of the object in the realist's sense.
context: Aesthetic realism (Frank Sibley, 'Aesthetic Concepts,' 1959; Eddy Zemach, Real Beauty, 1997) holds aesthetic properties are real features of works. Response-dependent views (Hume, modern neo-Humeans) deny mind-independence but preserve objectivity through qualified-observer convergence. The dispute is ongoing.

question: An untrained recluse spends fifty years filling notebooks with extraordinary drawings, never shown to anyone. After her death they are discovered. Critic Wim says: 'These were art the whole time, with or without an artworld; the perceptual depth is intrinsic to the works themselves.' Which view of art is Wim defending?
answer: Aesthetic experience theory - works are art by their capacity to afford the distinctive aesthetic experience to attentive viewers, regardless of any institutional recognition ever received.
choices: Aesthetic experience theory - works are art by their capacity to afford the distinctive aesthetic experience to attentive viewers, regardless of any institutional recognition ever received.
Institutional theory of art - works become art only when conferred candidate-for-appreciation status by an artworld actor, so they become art on rediscovery, not in the recluse's lifetime.
Danto artworld theory - art-status requires an art-historical context and atmosphere of theory; works produced wholly outside such a context cannot count as art until context is supplied.
Tolstoyan expression theory - art requires successful transmission of feeling from artist to an audience, so works that never reached any audience in their making cannot have been art.
context: The outsider-art case (Henry Darger's discovered notebooks; the Vivian Maier photographs) is a standard test of institutional vs. aesthetic-experience accounts. Beardsley-style theorists say the works are art intrinsically; Dickie-style institutionalists say art-status is conferred, so the question becomes when the conferral occurred.

question: A novelist tells an interviewer: 'My books aim to do something no essay can - let the reader inhabit a kind of life and learn, from inside, what living that life is like. The value of literature, for me, is this distinctive knowledge.' Which view of art is the novelist defending?
answer: Cognitivism about art - art's distinctive value lies in the genuine understanding it gives us about the world, ourselves, or what living a particular kind of life is like from inside.
choices: Cognitivism about art - art's distinctive value lies in the genuine understanding it gives us about the world, ourselves, or what living a particular kind of life is like from inside.
Aesthetic experience theory - art's value lies in the unified, intense, complex experience the work affords an attentive perceiver; any knowledge gained is a byproduct rather than the value.
Tolstoyan expression theory - art's value lies in transmission of feeling from artist to audience through external signs, with knowledge claims a secondary effect rather than the chief aim.
Formalism - art's value lies in significant form (line, color, composition, dramatic shape) discernible by trained perception; didactic or cognitive content is incidental to aesthetic worth.
context: Cognitivism about art (Catherine Wilson, 'Literature and Knowledge,' 1983; Martha Nussbaum, Love's Knowledge, 1990) holds literature and other arts deliver distinctive understanding (perspectival, particular, imaginative) unavailable to argument. Anti-cognitivists (Jerome Stolnitz, Peter Lamarque) deny art has a special cognitive role.

question: On a panel, a defender of AI art argues: 'Cover the labels. If a viewer would judge an AI image and a hand-painted one identically on what is actually visible, the line, the color, the rhythm, then they have identical artistic value. Who or what made it is beside the point.' Which view is she using?
answer: Aesthetic empiricism — once the visible features match, the value matches; origin is irrelevant.
choices: Aesthetic empiricism — once the visible features match, the value matches; origin is irrelevant.
Intentionalism — a maker's intention is part of the work, so a mindless process only mimics art.
Institutional theory — art-status comes from the artworld's recognition, not from visible features.
Historical theory — a thing is art only if meant to be viewed as past art was viewed.
context: Aesthetic empiricism (Monroe Beardsley, Aesthetics, 1958; 'The Intentional Fallacy,' with W.K. Wimsatt, 1946) holds the work itself — its perceptible features — is the whole aesthetic object; the maker's biography and intention drop out. The AI-art debate sharpens it: intentionalists like Richard Wollheim reply that how a thing came to exist is part of what it IS.

question: An art critic argues: 'Picture two canvases that look exactly alike, one painted by a Renaissance master, one made by paint spilled at random. They are NOT the same artwork. What the maker did, meant, and answered to is part of what the work IS.' Which view is she using?
answer: Intentionalism — the maker's intent is part of the work, so look-alikes can be different works.
choices: Intentionalism — the maker's intent is part of the work, so look-alikes can be different works.
Aesthetic empiricism — identical visible features mean identical value; how each arose can't matter.
Institutional theory — whether the spill is art turns on the artworld's recognition, not intent.
Cluster theory — art has no single mark; intent is just one trait among many that may be present.
context: Intentionalism (Richard Wollheim, Art and Its Objects, 1968; Jerrold Levinson, 'Defining Art Historically,' 1979) makes the maker's intentional activity partly constitutive of a work, so two indiscernible objects can be different artworks. Beardsley's anti-intentionalist empiricism is the classic opposing view; Danto's Transfiguration of the Commonplace (1981) presses the indiscernibles puzzle too.

question: In 1917 Marcel Duchamp bought an ordinary urinal, signed it 'R. Mutt,' titled it Fountain, and submitted it to a New York show that had vowed to accept ANY entry. The jury hid it. By picking a mass-made object he hadn't even crafted, Duchamp meant to force which question?
answer: Whether art-status can come from an artist's choice and context, not from skill or beauty.
choices: Whether art-status can come from an artist's choice and context, not from skill or beauty.
Whether a sculpture can ever be as beautiful as a painting of the same subject.
Whether mass-produced goods were cheapening the craft of traditional sculptors.
Whether a hidden artwork can still count as having been publicly exhibited.
context: Duchamp submitted Fountain to the 1917 Society of Independent Artists, whose rules promised to show any work whose fee was paid; the board suppressed it and he resigned in protest. The readymade became the standard test case for George Dickie's institutional theory (Art and the Aesthetic, 1974): art-status as something conferred by choice and context rather than craft.

question: In 1964 the philosopher Arthur Danto walked into a New York gallery and saw Andy Warhol's Brillo Boxes: plywood boxes printed to look EXACTLY like the soap-pad cartons stacked in any grocery store. The puzzle that seized him: why is Warhol's box art when the grocer's identical box is not? What was Danto's answer?
answer: The difference is nothing you can see — it's the theory and art-history around the gesture.
choices: The difference is nothing you can see — it's the theory and art-history around the gesture.
Warhol's boxes were built from finer materials than the cardboard grocery cartons.
Warhol's boxes were beautiful in a way ordinary soap cartons simply are not.
There is no real difference — Warhol's boxes are not actually art either.
context: Seeing the Brillo Boxes at the Stable Gallery prompted Arthur Danto's essay 'The Artworld' (Journal of Philosophy, 1964), later The Transfiguration of the Commonplace (1981): the art/non-art line cannot be perceptual — it lies in 'an atmosphere of theory' and art-history. Danto's idea shaped Dickie's institutional theory, though the two split over whether the artworld is interpretive (Danto) or institutional (Dickie).

question: Borrowing Wittgenstein's image that games share no single trait—just a family of overlapping ones—Berys Gaut argues: 'Stop hunting for the ONE thing that makes art art. There isn't one. Art has a bundle of typical marks—skill, expression, imagination, form—and a work qualifies when enough show up.' Which view is he defending?
answer: Cluster view — no single feature is required; enough of a bundle of typical art-marks suffices.
choices: Cluster view — no single feature is required; enough of a bundle of typical art-marks suffices.
Institutional view — one thing settles it: the artworld conferring the status of art.
Intentionalist view — one thing settles it: the maker intending the object as art.
Formalist view — one thing settles it: significant form, the arrangement of line and color.
context: Berys Gaut's 'Art as a Cluster Concept' (2000, in Carroll's Theories of Art Today) adapts Wittgenstein's family-resemblance idea and abandons the hunt for necessary-and-sufficient conditions. Each rival here stakes everything on a single criterion; the cluster view's whole point is that none of them is required on its own.

question: Jerrold Levinson argues art is defined by an unbroken chain reaching back: 'A new thing counts as art when its maker means it to be approached the way earlier artworks were approached. Art is its link backward to the tradition of regard—not any timeless trait like beauty or expression.' Which view is he defending?
answer: Historical view — art is whatever is meant to be regarded as past artworks were regarded.
choices: Historical view — art is whatever is meant to be regarded as past artworks were regarded.
Institutional view — art is whatever the artworld today confers the status of art upon.
Formalist view — art is whatever has significant form, regardless of any past tradition.
Expressionist view — art is whatever expresses and transmits the maker's felt emotion.
context: Jerrold Levinson's 'Defining Art Historically' (1979) defines art recursively, anchoring each new work to the tradition of how earlier art was regarded. The three rivals fix art in something non-historical—present institutions, intrinsic form, or transmitted feeling—which is exactly what the backward-looking view rejects.

question: David Hume retells a tale: two kinsmen swore a wine had a faint taste of iron and of leather, and were mocked—until a key on a leather thong turned up at the cask's bottom. Beauty isn't simply in the object, Hume argues, nor is taste merely whatever pleases you. So where is its standard?
answer: Qualified-judges view — beauty's standard is the converging verdict of practiced, unbiased judges.
choices: Qualified-judges view — beauty's standard is the converging verdict of practiced, unbiased judges.
Realist view — beauty is a feature in the object; judges discover it but do not set the standard.
Subjectivist view — beauty is just what pleases each person; no judge ranks above any other.
Disinterested-pleasure view — beauty is whatever pleases apart from any interest in the thing.
context: David Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757) uses the wine-cask tale from Don Quixote to steer between pure subjectivism and realism: objectivity rests in the agreement of qualified judges—delicate, practiced, comparing widely, free of prejudice. The disinterested-pleasure rival is Kant's; the realist locates beauty in the object; the subjectivist denies any standard at all.

question: Immanuel Kant argues: 'Calling something beautiful claims everyone should agree—yet it tracks no property in the object. You can call a painting beautiful while wanting nothing from it, caring nothing for its use; that pleasure is free of all interest, so anyone with the same mind would feel it too.' Which view is he defending?
answer: Disinterested-pleasure view — beauty's universal claim rests on a pleasure free of all interest.
choices: Disinterested-pleasure view — beauty's universal claim rests on a pleasure free of all interest.
Qualified-judges view — beauty's standard is the agreement of practiced, unprejudiced critics.
Realist view — beauty is a feature in the object that the judgment simply reports.
Subjectivist view — beauty is just private response; the claim that all should agree is a mistake.
context: Kant's Critique of the Power of Judgment (1790) grounds beauty's claim to universal agreement not in a property of the object but in disinterested pleasure—delight that wants nothing from the thing's existence or use, and so is shareable by all. Hume's route runs through the convergence of trained judges instead; the realist and subjectivist take the two extremes Kant rejects.

question: Frank Sibley notes that an expert spots a painting's GRACE at a glance—yet hand them its every line, color, and measurement and no rule lets them DEDUCE that it is graceful. The aesthetic rides on those plain facts but follows from no rule. Which claim is he defending?
answer: Rides-on-but-no-rule — aesthetic qualities depend on the plain features yet follow by no rule.
choices: Rides-on-but-no-rule — aesthetic qualities depend on the plain features yet follow by no rule.
Rule-derivable — the right measurements simply entail that a work is graceful or balanced.
Pure projection — 'graceful' reports only the viewer's feeling, not anything in the work.
Form-only — just the formal structure matters; talk of grace adds nothing to that structure.
context: Frank Sibley's 'Aesthetic Concepts' (1959) argues aesthetic terms depend on non-aesthetic features without being condition-governed by them: spotting grace takes trained sensitivity, and no inference carries you from the bare facts to the verdict. The rule-derivable and pure-projection options are the two views Sibley is denying at once.

question: Kendall Walton points to a cubist painting: judge it as a normal portrait and it looks like a botched mess; judge it as cubist and it is a triumph. Whether a work is bold or clumsy depends on the CATEGORY you view it through—and the right category is set by its history, not your whim. Which view is he defending?
answer: Category-relative view — a work's aesthetic qualities depend on the historically right category.
choices: Category-relative view — a work's aesthetic qualities depend on the historically right category.
Visible-features view — only what the eye plainly sees counts; no category enters the judgment.
In-the-work view — boldness or clumsiness sits in the work itself, the same under any category.
Artworld-status view — what categories decide is whether a thing is art at all, not its merit.
context: Kendall Walton's 'Categories of Art' (1970) argues aesthetic properties are perceived relative to a category—cubism, impressionism, sonata-form—and the correct category is fixed by the artist's intention and historical context, not the viewer's choice. The rivals deny categories any role in perception, or confuse a question about merit with one about art-status.

question: Clive Bell insists every great work—a Persian carpet, a Giotto fresco, a Cezanne—shares one thing he calls SIGNIFICANT FORM: an arrangement of lines, colors, and masses that stirs a special aesthetic emotion. Subject, biography, history: none of it counts. Only the form, for its own sake. Which view is he defending?
answer: Form-only view — significant form alone makes art; subject, biography, and context are irrelevant.
choices: Form-only view — significant form alone makes art; subject, biography, and context are irrelevant.
Expression view — what makes art is the artist clarifying a felt emotion by giving it outward form.
Knowledge view — what makes art is the genuine understanding of life that the work delivers.
Artworld view — what makes art is the status the artworld confers on it, whatever its form.
context: Clive Bell's Art (1914) names 'significant form'—the combination of perceptual elements that stirs the aesthetic emotion—as the one essence shared by all art, with representation, subject, and context set aside. Each rival locates art's essence elsewhere: clarified feeling (Collingwood, who denied art merely transmits emotion to an audience), knowledge (the cognitivists), or institutional conferral (Dickie).

question: A urinal in a gallery and the same urinal in a restroom look identical. Nelson Goodman says only the gallery one can be art — because there it does a JOB the restroom one doesn't. What is that job?
answer: It works as a symbol — it points beyond itself, representing or expressing something.
choices: It works as a symbol — it points beyond itself, representing or expressing something.
It has been granted the status of art by the artworld that displays it.
It pleases the eye with a clean, well-shaped surface and nothing more.
It arranges line and form into a balance that stirs aesthetic emotion.
context: Nelson Goodman (Languages of Art, 1968; 'When Is Art?', 1978) shifted the question from 'what is art' to 'when does a thing function as art', analyzing works as symbols within structured systems — representation, expression, exemplification. The rivals answer with a different job: institutional status (Dickie), surface pleasure (the empiricist Beardsley), formal arrangement (Bell).

question: Plato warned that storytelling only breeds ignorance — pretty lies, two steps from the truth. A modern theorist fires back: great novels give REAL knowledge, moral and psychological, a sense of what other lives are like — and that knowing is PART of what makes them good art. Which view is this?
answer: Cognitivism — the knowledge a work delivers is part of its value as art.
choices: Cognitivism — the knowledge a work delivers is part of its value as art.
Autonomism — any truths are a bonus; they add nothing to its art-value.
Formalism — only the arrangement of parts matters; content is irrelevant.
Expressionism — art transmits the maker's feeling, not real knowledge.
context: Noel Carroll ('Art, Narrative, and Moral Understanding', 1998) and Gregory Currie (Narratives and Narrators, 2010) argue art's cognitive yield — moral, psychological, modal knowledge — is partly constitutive of its value, answering Plato's old charge in Republic X that mimesis only breeds ignorance. Autonomists (Lamarque, Stolnitz) reply that incidental truth is not art-value.

question: A reader gives Crime and Punishment five stars FOR teaching him real psychology. A philosopher of literature objects: even granting the psychology is true, that's the wrong reason to rate it as literature — true facts and art-merit are different kinds of value, and mixing them confuses the two. Which view is this?
answer: Autonomism — a work's art-value is separate from any knowledge it delivers.
choices: Autonomism — a work's art-value is separate from any knowledge it delivers.
Moralism — a work's moral failings count directly against it as art.
Institutional view — the artworld's verdict, not its content, makes it art.
Expressionism — a work's value is the feeling it transmits to the reader.
context: Peter Lamarque and Stein Haugom Olsen (Truth, Fiction, and Literature, 1994) defend the autonomist 'no-truth thesis': fiction may contain truths, but those truths are not what makes it literature. The cognitivist opponents (Carroll, Currie) hold the reverse. The dispute runs back through Sidney and Shelley to Plato's Republic X.

question: A novel is built to make readers ENJOY the torture of innocents — engineering that delight on purpose. A film scholar says this makes it worse AS ART, not merely morally worse: a moral flaw of that kind is an artistic flaw. Which view of art and morality is this?
answer: Moralism — a moral flaw of the right kind counts directly against the work as art.
choices: Moralism — a moral flaw of the right kind counts directly against the work as art.
Autonomism — moral and artistic merit are separate; a vicious work can be great art.
Institutional view — the artworld's verdict, not the morality, settles its art-status.
Formalism — only form matters; what a work asks you to feel is beside the point.
context: Noel Carroll ('Moderate Moralism', 1996) and Berys Gaut ('The Ethical Criticism of Art', 1998; his own term is 'ethicism') hold that ethical defects in the response a work elicits can be aesthetic defects. Autonomists (Lamarque, Olsen) deny any link; immoralists (Eaton, Jacobson) argue moral transgression is sometimes an artistic asset. The test cases are propaganda films.

question: In 1945 Han van Meegeren confessed he had FORGED the Vermeers that fooled Europe's experts — to escape execution for selling a Dutch treasure to the Nazis. An art historian grants the forgery looks identical to a real Vermeer, yet says it is worth LESS, because value rides on what the maker actually achieved. Which view is this?
answer: Achievement view — the maker's real achievement is part of the value, so a forgery is worth less.
choices: Achievement view — the maker's real achievement is part of the value, so a forgery is worth less.
Empiricism — identical look means identical value; how it was made is outside the work.
Institutional view — the forgery's worth turns on what status the artworld grants it.
Functionalism — if both afford the very same experience, then both have the same value.
context: The forgery debate (Alfred Lessing, 'What Is Wrong with a Forgery?', 1965; Goodman's Languages of Art, 1968; Denis Dutton on authenticity) tests whether value rides on perceptible features alone. The achievement (intentionalist) view makes the maker's achievement-history constitutive of value; the empiricist (Beardsley) denies it. Van Meegeren confessed in 1945 to escape a Nazi-collaboration charge.

question: A gallery hangs a blank canvas and calls it art; over the sea a sunset blazes that no one curated. A philosopher says the gallery CAN'T make the canvas art, and nothing stops the sunset from being art — all that matters is whether you get a certain attentive, unified experience. Which view is this?
answer: Functionalism — art is whatever performs the job of affording aesthetic experience.
choices: Functionalism — art is whatever performs the job of affording aesthetic experience.
Institutional view — art is whatever the artworld grants the status of art.
Cluster view — art has no one defining feature, just a bundle of typical traits.
Intentionalism — a thing is art only if its maker intended it as art.
context: Monroe Beardsley (Aesthetics, 1958) defines art as anything meant to afford aesthetic experience marked by unity, intensity, and complexity. Berys Gaut pursued related functionalist lines before moving to his cluster account (2000). Critics object the definition is too broad (rainbows, sports plays) and too narrow (avant-garde works built to unsettle).

question: Two friends sincerely clash over whether a song is beautiful. A philosopher says NEITHER is mistaken about any feature of the song — each is just reporting how it strikes them. 'Beautiful' picks out no shared property in the song at all. Which view of beauty is this?
answer: Subjectivism — 'beautiful' reports the listener's own response, not a property of the song.
choices: Subjectivism — 'beautiful' reports the listener's own response, not a property of the song.
Realism — beauty is a real feature of the song; one side here must be mistaken.
Expressionism — beauty is the feeling the composer poured in, recoverable in the song.
Cultural view — the song is beautiful if the listener's culture counts it so.
context: Pure aesthetic subjectivism, defended in readings from Hutcheson through Ayer's emotivism, makes aesthetic predicates express individual response rather than track shared properties. The rivals: realism (Mary Mothersill, Beauty Restored, 1984), expression theory, and culture-relative response-dependence — versus Hume's qualified-judges standard ('Of the Standard of Taste', 1757). The puzzle of sincere disagreement drives each.

question: A gallery hangs a single typed certificate: no image, no craft, nothing to look at. The artist insists the real work is the idea it states; the paper is just a receipt for it. Treated on its own terms, which theory of art does this defend?
answer: Conceptualism — the idea IS the work; the object is mere documentation.
choices: Conceptualism — the idea IS the work; the object is mere documentation.
Expressionism — the work is felt emotion passed from maker to viewer.
Formalism — the work is its arrangement of line, color, and shape.
Mimeticism — the work succeeds by faithfully depicting the world.
context: Sol LeWitt's 'Paragraphs on Conceptual Art' (1967): 'The idea becomes a machine that makes the art.' Conceptualism makes the proposition primary and the physical object secondary — exactly inverting formalism (Bell) and expressionism (Collingwood), which locate the art in something perceptible or felt.

question: A flawless pianist leaves a hall cold; a second, no more skilled, works a real grief through the same piece and the room weeps. A critic says only the second made ART, not mere craft — because feeling was clarified and handed to the listener. Which theory of art is that?
answer: Expressionism — art clarifies a real emotion and hands it to the listener.
choices: Expressionism — art clarifies a real emotion and hands it to the listener.
Formalism — art is its arrangement of pattern, perceived for its own sake.
Cognitivism — art's worth is the genuine knowledge it can deliver to you.
Conceptualism — the work just is the bare idea behind the performance.
context: R.G. Collingwood's The Principles of Art (1938) and Tolstoy's What Is Art? (1898): art is the imaginative expression of emotion — the maker clarifies a feeling in the making, and a successful work transmits it. The view splits sharply from Bell's formalism, where transmitted feeling is incidental to perceived form.

question: Before a coin flip, Owen blurts 'heads!' and grins. He has no reason — he just feels lucky. The coin lands heads. Did Owen actually KNOW it would?
answer: No — a guess that happens to land right isn't knowledge; he had no reason tracking the outcome.
choices: No — a guess that happens to land right isn't knowledge; he had no reason tracking the outcome.
Yes — his belief turned out true, and a true belief is what knowing something amounts to.
Yes — strong gut feelings ARE evidence, so a confident hunch should count as real knowledge.
No — knowledge needs a written proof or a tested rule; no everyday belief can ever count.
context: Knowledge is more than a true belief. Lucky guesses get the answer right by accident — the reason doesn't connect to the truth. JTB (justified, true, belief) names the missing piece: justification.

question: Your little brother insists there's a monster under his bed — he heard scratching. You look: it's a loose blanket rubbing the wall. Was his belief REASONABLE before you looked, even though wrong?
answer: Yes — the inference fit what he heard; reasonable beliefs can still turn out wrong on the facts.
choices: Yes — the inference fit what he heard; reasonable beliefs can still turn out wrong on the facts.
No — monsters don't exist, so any belief in one was unreasonable from the very start of his thought.
Yes — being right would have made it knowledge; being wrong means it was never reasonable at all.
No — without checking first, no belief about what's down there can count as reasonable to begin with.
context: A belief can be REASONABLE (well-supported by what someone knows) and still turn out wrong. Reasonableness is about the quality of inference, not whether the conclusion lands true.

question: A friend says, 'I just KNOW the test is Friday — I have a feeling.' She has not checked. Friday comes, and the test really is on Friday. Did she actually KNOW it would be?
answer: No — a feeling without reasons isn't knowledge, even when the prediction does turn out correct.
choices: No — a feeling without reasons isn't knowledge, even when the prediction does turn out correct.
Yes — her belief was true and she felt sure, which is what knowing something always comes down to.
Yes — strong feelings are themselves a kind of evidence about what is likely going to happen next.
No — knowledge requires a formal proof or an official document; daily beliefs can never count.
context: Knowledge calls for reasons that track the truth — not just a belief that happens to be true. A feeling that lands right is a lucky guess, not knowing. This is the JTB rule in everyday clothes.

question: Sara sees thick gray clouds rolling in and tells her dad it'll rain by afternoon. She is going by what the sky looks like. Was Sara's belief REASONABLE even before the weather proved her right?
answer: Yes — clouds like those reliably bring rain, so the inference fits her evidence and is reasonable.
choices: Yes — clouds like those reliably bring rain, so the inference fits her evidence and is reasonable.
No — a belief is only reasonable AFTER it turns out true; before the rain falls, it is just a guess.
Yes — any prediction about the future is reasonable; people can guess however they want, really.
No — only weather forecasters can have reasonable beliefs about rain; an ordinary kid simply cannot.
context: Reasonable belief depends on how well evidence supports the inference — not on the result. Sara is using a well-established pattern (dark heavy clouds bring rain), so the belief is reasonable now.

question: Before the game, Theo picks the Red team because red is his favorite color. He has no idea which team is better. The Red team wins. Did Theo KNOW the Reds would win when he picked them?
answer: No — picking by favorite color isn't a reason that tracks who wins; the right pick was just luck.
choices: No — picking by favorite color isn't a reason that tracks who wins; the right pick was just luck.
Yes — his belief was true, and any true belief about a game outcome counts as actually knowing.
Yes — fans pick teams all the time; a fan's confident pick should count as knowing the outcome.
No — sports outcomes can't be known at all by anyone, so no one ever knows who is going to win.
context: Knowledge needs reasons that connect to what makes a prediction come true. Favorite color has no link to a team's performance — a right pick from that reasoning is a lucky guess, not knowing.

question: Mia tells her brother, 'The cat is upstairs — I heard her meow.' The meow was actually the upstairs neighbor's cat. Mia's cat IS upstairs, in a closet. Did Mia really KNOW her cat was upstairs?
answer: No — her reason pointed at the wrong cat; being right by coincidence isn't really knowing.
choices: No — her reason pointed at the wrong cat; being right by coincidence isn't really knowing.
Yes — her belief about the cat's location is true, and a true belief just is what knowing means.
Yes — she had a reason (a meow) AND was right, so both pieces of knowing are clearly present.
No — she'd need to see the cat with her own eyes; only direct sight ever counts as knowing where.
context: This is a Gettier-style case: true belief plus a reason — but the reason doesn't actually connect to what makes the belief true. Mia got the floor right by accident, so it isn't real knowledge.

question: Leo is sure he ate roast venison at last winter's feast. The court chronicler shows him the kitchen ledger: it was mutton that night. He FELT certain. Before the ledger, was Leo's BELIEF reasonable, even though it turned out wrong?
answer: Yes — using your own memory IS a reasonable way to form beliefs, but memory can still be mistaken.
choices: Yes — using your own memory IS a reasonable way to form beliefs, but memory can still be mistaken.
No — strong feeling is never reasonable; you should not believe a memory unless someone confirms it.
Yes — Leo's feeling was strong, and any belief held strongly counts as reasonable for that reason.
No — memories are too unreliable for any belief based on one to ever be reasonable in the first place.
context: Memory is a reasonable source of belief and knowledge — we rely on it daily — but it is not infallible. A reasonable belief from a normally reliable source can still turn out wrong on the facts.

question: Sara hasn't seen the new movie. Her friend Ana, who already saw it, tells her the ending. Sara believes Ana and tells her brother. Was Sara's belief about the ending REASONABLE to hold?
answer: Yes — trusting a friend who actually saw it is a reasonable way to form a belief about the movie.
choices: Yes — trusting a friend who actually saw it is a reasonable way to form a belief about the movie.
No — you can never reasonably believe anything you haven't seen with your own eyes for yourself.
Yes — any belief a friend states is automatically reasonable; friendship makes claims true that way.
No — only experts can give reasonable testimony; an ordinary friend cannot, even about a movie ending.
context: Testimony from a witness who was actually there is a normal, reasonable source of belief — we use it constantly. The friend isn't an expert, but she was a witness, which is what counts here.

question: At the well, a fellow squire tells Jamie: 'I heard from someone who heard from someone that we feast tomorrow.' Jamie tells the steward we're feasting. Was Jamie's belief REASONABLE to hold?
answer: No — a chain of 'someone heard from someone' is weak evidence; the belief outruns what supports it.
choices: No — a chain of 'someone heard from someone' is weak evidence; the belief outruns what supports it.
Yes — if other squires are saying it, that is enough for a reasonable belief about the feast tomorrow.

context: Long testimony chains lose reliability with each step. A belief is reasonable only when the evidence behind it can actually hold the weight — a 'heard from someone' chain is too thin to carry much.

question: Asked how he knows the new kid wants to be friends, Eli shrugs: 'I just KNOW. I can tell.' He hasn't actually talked to him yet. The new kid does end up wanting to be friends. Did Eli KNOW?
answer: No — a feeling without any contact isn't real knowing, even when the prediction lands correct.
choices: No — a feeling without any contact isn't real knowing, even when the prediction lands correct.
Yes — his belief turned out true, and true belief is what knowing something always comes down to.
Yes — feelings about people are themselves evidence, so a confident social feeling is real knowing.
No — Eli would have to be a mind-reader, and since nobody is, no one EVER knows about other minds.
context: Even when a hunch about people lands right, a hunch isn't knowledge — there is no actual evidence linking the belief to the truth. Real knowing requires reasons that connect, not just a feeling.

question: Nina checks the live score on her phone: the home team is up 2-1. She tells her brother the home team is winning. The score really is 2-1. Was Nina's belief REASONABLE to hold?
answer: Yes — reading a live score from a normal phone app is a reasonable way to form a belief about it.
choices: Yes — reading a live score from a normal phone app is a reasonable way to form a belief about it.
No — apps can show wrong scores sometimes, so no belief from a phone can ever be reasonable at all.
Yes — any belief about a game in progress is automatically reasonable; sports are easy that way.
No — only watching the game live counts as reasonable; reading any score never counts at all.
context: Apps can fail, but a normally reliable source produces reasonable belief. Reasonableness doesn't require sources that NEVER err — it just requires they work well enough in normal conditions.

question: Ben's dog Rex always barks at strangers at the door. The doorbell rings — a stranger — and Ben tells his sister, 'Rex is about to bark.' Was Ben's belief REASONABLE before Rex actually barked?
answer: Yes — a strong pattern Ben has seen many times is good evidence; the inference fits what he knows.
choices: Yes — a strong pattern Ben has seen many times is good evidence; the inference fits what he knows.
No — animals can always surprise us, so no belief about a dog's next action can ever be reasonable.
Yes — any guess about a pet is reasonable; people know their pets too well for guesses to be wrong.

context: Past patterns are good evidence for future cases — that's how we form most of our reasonable beliefs about the world. Ben's belief might still be wrong, but the inference itself is sound.

question: Asked what 8 times 7 is, Mia confidently says 56 — because she remembers her teacher saying it. But her teacher had actually said 49 (and was wrong). 56 is correct. Did Mia really KNOW the answer?
answer: No — the reason she leaned on was wrong; being right with the wrong reason isn't really knowing.
choices: No — the reason she leaned on was wrong; being right with the wrong reason isn't really knowing.
Yes — her answer is correct and she gave it confidently, so it must count as actually knowing.
Yes — she had a reason (her teacher said so), so both belief and a reason are clearly present.
No — math facts can only be KNOWN by working them out from scratch every single time you say them.
context: Another Gettier-style case: true belief PLUS a reason, but the reason doesn't track the truth (the teacher was wrong). Mia got lucky. Real knowing wants the reason to actually connect to the answer.

question: A video on Theo's phone claims a famous singer is moving to his town. The video has no source — just a kid's voiceover. Theo plans to tell everyone at school. Was his belief REASONABLE to hold?
answer: No — an anonymous video with no source is too weak as evidence for a confident claim like that.
choices: No — an anonymous video with no source is too weak as evidence for a confident claim like that.

Yes — if it FEELS true and sounds exciting, that is enough reason to believe and share it widely.

context: Reasonable belief depends on the quality of the source. An unsourced video voiceover is too thin to support a confident claim — feeling-true and exciting-sounding aren't the same as actually-supported.

question: Coming back from school, Jules sees fresh puddles in the driveway. She tells her dad it rained while they were out. The puddles really did come from rain. Was Jules's belief REASONABLE?
answer: Yes — fresh puddles on a dry driveway are good evidence of rain; the inference fits what she saw.
choices: Yes — fresh puddles on a dry driveway are good evidence of rain; the inference fits what she saw.
No — puddles can come from many things, so no belief about rain from puddles can ever be reasonable.
Yes — any guess about the weather is automatically reasonable; weather guessing is just like that.

context: Inferring from what you see (fresh puddles) to a likely cause (rain) is exactly how reasonable beliefs work. Other causes are possible, but rain is the best explanation given what's available.

question: After her team loses, Ava says, 'I knew they were going to lose all along.' Before the game, she had told everyone the team would win. Did Ava actually KNOW the team would lose before the game?
answer: No — saying 'I knew it' after the fact isn't really knowing; her actual belief beforehand was wrong.
choices: No — saying 'I knew it' after the fact isn't really knowing; her actual belief beforehand was wrong.
Yes — if she truly felt it deep down, then in some way she did know it would happen, in her heart.

No — sports outcomes are never knowable by anyone in advance, so Ava could never have known.
context: 'Hindsight knowing' — claiming you knew it once you find out — is a common but mistaken move. Real knowing requires the belief to have been there, with reasons, BEFORE the answer was visible.

question: Lila — wrong about lunch half the time — confidently tells Theo it's pizza today. Sam — right nine times out of ten — quietly says it's salad. Theo believes Lila. Was his BELIEF reasonable?
answer: No — past track record is better evidence than volume; he leaned on the weaker witness's word.
choices: No — past track record is better evidence than volume; he leaned on the weaker witness's word.
Yes — loud confidence is strong evidence of truth, so believing the more confident friend is reasonable.

context: Past reliability — track record — is among the best clues for weighing testimony as evidence. Confidence and volume don't track truth. A reasonable belief weighs witnesses by past accuracy, not tone.

question: On a four-choice question, Hana doesn't recognize the answer and picks B at random. B turns out to be correct. Asked later if she knew the answer, did she really KNOW it before circling B?
answer: No — a random pick isn't knowing, even when chance lands you on the correct answer letter.
choices: No — a random pick isn't knowing, even when chance lands you on the correct answer letter.
Yes — her answer matches the right one, and any matching answer simply IS knowing, by definition.
Yes — she chose B confidently when she circled it, so her confidence in the moment turns it into knowing.
No — multiple-choice questions never really test knowledge anyway, so the issue can't come up at all.
context: Random guessing is the clearest case of accidental truth — pure chance, no reason. Even when the guess hits, the answer is right but unKNOWN. JTB: belief + truth + justification; the third is missing.

question: An older kid tells Marco the after-school club is canceled today. Marco repeats it as fact. The older kid was just guessing — but it really is canceled. Did Marco KNOW the club was canceled?
answer: No — the older kid was guessing, so Marco's reason didn't track the truth; he got lucky on it.
choices: No — the older kid was guessing, so Marco's reason didn't track the truth; he got lucky on it.
Yes — what Marco said matches reality, so his statement counts as knowing the fact about cancellation.
Yes — older kids generally know more; trusting them turns their guesses into knowledge for younger kids.

context: Trusting someone whose 'reason' is just their own guess passes the weakness right along. The belief lands true by accident — there is no real chain of reasons from belief back to the truth.

question: Ben's older sister says their younger brother broke the lamp. The younger brother says he didn't. Ben picks his sister's side just because she's older. Was Ben's belief REASONABLE to hold?
answer: No — picking by who is older isn't a reason that tracks truth; he ignored the conflict in stories.
choices: No — picking by who is older isn't a reason that tracks truth; he ignored the conflict in stories.
Yes — older siblings are usually right about household events, so age is enough to settle the question.
Yes — any belief Ben holds confidently about his own family is automatically reasonable to hold to.
No — Ben should never form ANY belief in a sibling dispute; only a parent's call ever counts as reason.
context: When two reports conflict, age alone doesn't track truth — outside evidence does. A reasonable belief in a conflict weighs evidence (broken pieces, witnesses, motive), not which speaker happens to be older.

question: A friend in the company of squires says: 'I just KNOW the captain's drill is tomorrow. I have a feeling.' The drill DOES turn out to be tomorrow. Did she really KNOW it was tomorrow?
answer: No — a feeling without reasons isn't knowledge, even when the lucky guess happens to land on the right answer.

Yes — if the quiz is really tomorrow, then her belief was true, and any true belief about it counts as real knowledge.

No — knowledge requires a written schedule or teacher's word; a feeling can never count as knowing anything at all.
context: Knowledge needs justified true belief — JTB. A feeling that happens to be right is a lucky guess, not knowledge, because the feeling didn't TRACK the truth. The friend would have had the same feeling whether the quiz was tomorrow or Friday.

question: After meeting one rude kid from the rival school, Theo announces: 'I KNOW everyone over there is rude — I met one of them.' Did Theo really KNOW everyone at the rival school is rude?
answer: No — one rude classmate is too small a sample to support a sweeping claim about every student at the entire school.
choices: No — one rude classmate is too small a sample to support a sweeping claim about every student at the entire school.
Yes — direct experience with even one student gives Theo a genuine reason that supports his wider claim about the school.
Yes — when his belief is based on something he saw firsthand, that personal experience is enough to count as knowing.
No — knowledge always requires a survey or a study; nothing a kid sees in person can ever count as evidence at all.
context: Knowledge needs a reason strong enough for the claim it supports. One rude kid supports 'I met a rude kid,' not 'everyone there is rude.' Generalizing from a single case is a known reasoning slip — hasty generalization — and it shows up here as a knowledge failure.

question: Hearing fourth-hand that Mia is mad at her, Lila tells everyone: 'I KNOW Mia hates me — Sara told Devon who heard from Jess.' Did Lila really KNOW Mia hates her?
answer: No — a long gossip chain is shaky evidence; each retelling can twist the message before it reaches the final listener.
choices: No — a long gossip chain is shaky evidence; each retelling can twist the message before it reaches the final listener.
Yes — when several people pass along the same message, that agreement among them is good evidence the message is true.
Yes — Lila heard it from a friend, and friends are reliable sources, so what comes through them counts as real knowing.
No — knowledge needs Mia herself to confirm it in person; nothing short of direct admission can count as evidence.
context: Testimony can give knowledge, but only when the chain is reliable. Each retelling adds room for distortion. A four-link chain like Lila's would need each link to be truthful AND accurate — and there's no reason to think that here. Justification fails before truth even gets tested.

question: Ben tells his class: 'I KNOW the school was built in 1962 — I remember a teacher saying it.' He's misremembering: the teacher actually said 1972. But the school WAS built in 1962. Did Ben really KNOW the year?
answer: No — his belief is true, but it traces back to a wrong memory; a guess that lands right isn't knowledge.
choices: No — his belief is true, but it traces back to a wrong memory; a guess that lands right isn't knowledge.
Yes — his belief turned out to be true, so the source doesn't matter; truth alone makes it count as knowing.
Yes — Ben remembered something that turned out right, and remembering is one normal way that people know things.
No — memory can never count as knowledge at all because memories are personal and can't be checked by others.
context: Classic Gettier shape: the belief is true (1962), and Ben has a reason (memory of a teacher), but the reason is broken — the teacher actually said something different. Ben got lucky. Justified true belief still fails when the justification doesn't actually connect to the truth.

question: Asked how he knows lightning never strikes the same place twice, Marcus shrugs: 'Everyone knows that. It's just one of those things people know.' Did Marcus really KNOW the claim?
answer: No — 'everyone says so' isn't a reason that tracks the truth; widespread belief can be wrong on questions of fact.
choices: No — 'everyone says so' isn't a reason that tracks the truth; widespread belief can be wrong on questions of fact.
Yes — when a saying spreads that widely, it must be based on something real, and that grounding is enough to know.
Yes — Marcus is repeating what a whole community believes, and shared knowledge is the most reliable kind of knowing.
No — Marcus could never know about lightning unless he had been struck or had seen the strike happen himself.
context: Appeals to 'everyone knows' don't transfer to knowledge. The lightning saying is in fact false — the Empire State Building gets hit dozens of times each year. Wide circulation tracks memorability, not truth. Knowing needs a reason that actually connects to how things are.

question: Before the tryouts, Riley insists: 'I just KNOW Coach will pick me — I can feel it.' Coach DOES pick her, but only because two other players got sick. Did Riley really KNOW she'd be picked?
answer: No — Riley's hunch and the actual reason for getting picked are unrelated; her belief lined up with truth by accident.
choices: No — Riley's hunch and the actual reason for getting picked are unrelated; her belief lined up with truth by accident.
Yes — her belief turned out exactly right; when prediction and outcome match like that, the prediction counts as knowing.
Yes — strong gut feelings often pick up real signals; the fact that she felt it shows her sense was working.
No — coaches' decisions are private, so no athlete can ever really know in advance who any coach will pick.
context: Riley's belief is true and she has a 'reason' (the hunch), but the hunch is causally disconnected from what actually decided the pick (two players being sick). When the justification doesn't track the truth, even a correct prediction is luck. JTB needs the J to do real work.

question: Owen sees the bus he takes every Tuesday morning roll past at 7:42 again. He plans his next Tuesday around catching it then. The route gets changed Sunday and he misses it. Was Owen's belief that the bus comes at 7:42 REASONABLE before the change?
answer: Yes — repeated firsthand observation is good evidence; a belief can be well-supported and still turn out wrong later.
choices: Yes — repeated firsthand observation is good evidence; a belief can be well-supported and still turn out wrong later.
No — since he ended up missing the bus, the belief he started with must have been faulty from the very beginning.
Yes — anything you experience yourself is automatically reasonable to believe, no matter what later happens.

context: Reasonableness is about quality of inference, not truth of the result. A belief well-supported by repeated observation can still turn out false when the world changes. Epistemology cares about whether your reasons WERE good given what you knew, not just whether you happened to be right.

question: Your little brother insists: 'Mom said I don't have to do chores tonight.' You're not sure he heard right. What's the most careful question to ask before believing him?
answer: Did he hear Mom say it himself, or did someone else tell him? — a check on whether his source was firsthand or secondhand.
choices: Did he hear Mom say it himself, or did someone else tell him? — a check on whether his source was firsthand or secondhand.
Does he WANT it to be true? — a check on his motives, since people who want a thing often believe it without much evidence.
Is he usually honest? — a check on his track record, since honest siblings tend to give claims you can rely on overall.
Could Mom even change her mind? — a check on the world, since rules vary night to night for many families this age.
context: Knowledge from testimony hinges on the source. Firsthand hearing leaves room for misunderstanding but is much stronger than a relayed message. Asking 'where did your information come from?' is the careful first move whenever someone reports a claim — it's the standard epistemic check.

question: On the guild meeting, a classmate links a the broadsheets and says: 'Did you know the lake by school has piranhas now? Crazy!' What's the most careful question to ask before believing the lake has piranhas?
answer: Where did the TikToker get this from? — a check on the source, since random video claims often spread without any real evidence.
choices: Where did the TikToker get this from? — a check on the source, since random video claims often spread without any real evidence.
Is the video popular? — a check on how many likes it has, since well-shared videos tend to be ones people find believable.
Does the classmate believe it? — a check on whether the friend who passed it on actually trusts what the post is claiming.
Could piranhas live there? — a check on the biology, since fact-checking the science settles whether the lake has them.
context: Online videos circulate without any reliability check. The careful epistemic move is to ask for the source: a state wildlife report, a local news story, a person who saw one. Without that, a viral claim is just gossip with better production. Popularity tracks shareability, not truth.

question: Jada is sure she returned the library book. 'I KNOW I did — I remember dropping it in the bin.' The book is found under her bed three days later, never returned. Did Jada really KNOW she had returned the book?
answer: No — knowledge needs a true belief; her memory of dropping the book in the bin doesn't match what actually happened.
choices: No — knowledge needs a true belief; her memory of dropping the book in the bin doesn't match what actually happened.
Yes — her memory felt vivid and specific, and a vivid memory always counts as enough reason to know what you did.
Yes — at the time she said it, she sincerely believed it, and sincere belief is enough for knowing your own actions.
No — people can never really know their own past actions; only outside witnesses can ever confirm what someone did.
context: Memory can fail: a vivid recollection of doing something can be entirely fabricated by the mind. The book under the bed proves the belief was false — and a false belief is never knowledge, however confident the believer feels. Truth is one of the three legs of JTB.

question: Before the midday meal, Ana announces in the great hall: 'I KNOW it's roast-venison day today — I just feel it.' The cooks bring out boiled cabbage. Did Ana really KNOW it was venison day?
answer: No — her belief turned out false, and a false belief can never count as knowing, no matter how sure she was at the time.
choices: No — her belief turned out false, and a false belief can never count as knowing, no matter how sure she was at the time.
Yes — Ana truly believed it, and sincere personal belief about your own school's menu is enough to count as knowing.
Yes — even false beliefs count as knowledge if they're held strongly enough, because the strength is what does the work.
No — students can never know the lunch menu without the official schedule; only the written list ever gives real knowing.
context: Knowledge requires truth. Even a strongly held belief, sincerely felt, fails as knowledge if the belief turns out false. Salisbury steak settles it. The 'truth' leg of JTB is non-negotiable: you can BELIEVE something untrue, but you can't KNOW something untrue.

question: Tess hears from her friend that the assembly is canceled. Her friend usually has the right info — she works in the office during free period. The assembly really is canceled. Did Tess KNOW the assembly was canceled, going by her friend's word?
answer: Yes — her friend has a reliable source (office work), the belief is true, and the chain from office to Tess actually connects.
choices: Yes — her friend has a reliable source (office work), the belief is true, and the chain from office to Tess actually connects.
Yes — any time a friend tells you something that turns out true, the friend's word makes it knowledge, source aside.
No — testimony can never be enough for knowledge, because everything important should be confirmed by official channels first.
No — Tess didn't see the announcement herself, and only firsthand experience can ever count as knowing anything for sure.
context: Reliable testimony from someone in a position to know IS a source of knowledge. The friend works in the office (the source); the assembly really is canceled (the truth); the message reached Tess intact (the connection). All three legs of JTB hold up, so Tess knows.

question: After tasting one cup at the new tavern in the realm, Devon declares: 'I KNOW that place is amazing. This is the best ale in the kingdom.' Did Devon really KNOW the new tavern was the best?
answer: No — one cup supports liking that cup, not a comparison; ranking all ale in the kingdom needs trying many taverns fairly.
choices: No — one cup supports liking that cup, not a comparison; ranking all ale in the kingdom needs trying many taverns fairly.
Yes — Devon's cup was good and he was honest about it, so his ranking is grounded in a real personal experience.
Yes — taste claims are about feeling, so if Devon felt the ale was the best, then for him that genuinely counts.
No — only royal tasters can ever really know about taverns; what apprentices think about ale never counts as actual knowing.
context: One sample doesn't ground a ranking claim. Devon could legitimately say 'I liked that cup,' but 'best in the kingdom' compares many taverns, and he's only been to one. The size of the evidence has to match the size of the claim — that's the basic epistemic match.

question: Your older brother says: 'You can't watch that movie — Mom said it's too violent.' You're not sure he's telling the straight story. What's the most careful question to ask before believing the rule?
answer: Did Mom actually use those words? — a check on whether your brother heard the rule himself or made up the 'too violent' part.
choices: Did Mom actually use those words? — a check on whether your brother heard the rule himself or made up the 'too violent' part.
Is the movie actually violent? — a check on the content, since if it isn't, then no parent could have ruled against it anyway.
Has Mom banned other movies? — a check on the pattern, since past bans suggest she would have banned this one too most likely.
Does your brother like the movie? — a check on his motives, since older siblings who like a film usually let you watch it.
context: Testimony is filtered by the messenger. Asking 'what were Mom's exact words?' separates what she actually said from what your brother is adding. The other questions check related things (content, pattern, motive) but don't get at the heart of whether the testimony is straight.

question: Looking at his messy desk, Marco insists: 'I KNOW my pencil is in the top drawer — I always put it there.' The pencil is in the top drawer, but it actually rolled there yesterday. Did Marco really KNOW where his pencil was?
answer: No — his reason for the belief (his habit) is broken in this case; the pencil being there is luck, not a tracked truth.
choices: No — his reason for the belief (his habit) is broken in this case; the pencil being there is luck, not a tracked truth.
Yes — his belief turned out true, and that match between belief and reality is what makes knowledge knowledge.
Yes — Marco gave a reason for his belief, so the belief is justified, and that's all knowing needs.
No — people can never really know where small objects are without looking; sight is the only path to that kind of knowing.
context: Classic Gettier puzzle: justified belief (the habit), true belief (pencil is there), but the justification doesn't connect to the truth (the pencil rolled there, not 'because' Marco always puts it there). Edmund Gettier (1963) showed that JTB needs more than the three pieces.

question: Convinced the new kid doesn't like her, Eva tells a friend: 'I KNOW he doesn't — I can just tell. It's a vibe.' She hasn't actually talked to him much. Did Eva really KNOW the new kid didn't like her?
answer: No — a 'vibe' without conversations or actions to point to isn't a reason that tracks the truth about what someone thinks.
choices: No — a 'vibe' without conversations or actions to point to isn't a reason that tracks the truth about what someone thinks.
Yes — Eva's social senses are her own, and what feels true to her in a room counts as enough reason for her to know.
Yes — vibes are a kind of pattern recognition, so trusting her feel of a person is a valid path to knowing what they think.
No — Eva can never know what someone thinks; only the person themselves can ever know their own opinion about anyone.
context: Feelings about other people can be real, but they aren't evidence about what those people actually think. To know the new kid's view, Eva would need observable signs — what he said, did, or how he behaved. Vibes track Eva's mood, not his opinion. JTB needs justification that connects.

question: In a watch-night debate by the gatehouse, Priya insists: 'I KNOW bats are blind — everyone knows that.' Bats actually see fine, though they often use echolocation in the dark. Did Priya really KNOW bats were blind?
answer: No — her belief is false, and a false belief can't be knowledge no matter how many people repeat the same saying.
choices: No — her belief is false, and a false belief can't be knowledge no matter how many people repeat the same saying.
Yes — the saying is so widespread that Priya was justified in believing it, and that justification makes it knowing.
Yes — common sayings get passed down because they're broadly true, so trusting them counts as a normal way to know.
No — Priya could never know about bats without studying biology; only specialists ever really know about animals at all.
context: 'Blind as a bat' is a common false saying. Bats are not blind — fruit bats see well, and even echolocating bats have functional eyes. Truth is one leg of JTB, so widely held false beliefs are never knowledge, however confident or popular they are. Knowledge can't be untrue.

question: Sam tells you: 'Mr. Owen HATES it when students email him at night. He'll mark me down for sure.' You're not sure Sam knows this for a fact. What's the most careful question to ask before believing it?
answer: Has Mr. Owen actually said this, or is Sam guessing? — a check on whether the claim has any direct source from the teacher.
choices: Has Mr. Owen actually said this, or is Sam guessing? — a check on whether the claim has any direct source from the teacher.
Does Sam often email teachers? — a check on his experience, since students who email a lot pick up on what teachers want.
Are other students worried too? — a check on the social signal, since teacher rules show up when many kids are nervous.
Does it matter to your grade? — a check on the stakes, since high-stakes rules tend to be the most enforced ones overall.
context: The key epistemic move is to separate evidence from rumor. Asking whether Sam heard this from Mr. Owen — or read it in a syllabus — gets at the source. The other questions look interesting but skirt the central issue: WHERE did this claim come from? That's the testimony check.

question: Looking at a family photo, Zoe insists: 'I KNOW that was the day we went to the zoo — I remember it.' Her mom shows the date stamp: it was actually a different trip entirely. Did Zoe really KNOW it was the zoo day?
answer: No — her belief turned out false once the date stamp showed the trip was different; a false belief can never be knowledge.
choices: No — her belief turned out false once the date stamp showed the trip was different; a false belief can never be knowledge.
Yes — the memory felt real to Zoe at the moment she spoke, and a vivid feeling is enough to ground a claim to knowing it.
Yes — memories of family events count as direct experience, and direct experience is always enough for genuine knowing.
No — children can never know which day a photo was taken; only adults with calendars can ever know that kind of detail.
context: Memory feels reliable from the inside but can be wrong. The date stamp is harder evidence and settles the truth — the zoo trip was not that day. False belief is never knowledge, so Zoe's confident recollection fails JTB on the truth leg, even though she sincerely believed it.

question: After winning his first chess game against a new opponent, Liam tells his friend: 'I KNOW I'm better than her — I beat her once already.' Did Liam really KNOW he was the better chess player?
answer: No — one game can be luck or one bad day; ranking two players needs more games to separate skill from random factors.
choices: No — one game can be luck or one bad day; ranking two players needs more games to separate skill from random factors.
Yes — Liam won fair and square, and beating someone in a real game is enough by itself to settle who is better at chess.
Yes — direct head-to-head is the gold standard in any game, so a single win gives a player real knowing about the rankings.
No — chess rankings can only ever be known from official tournaments; informal games can never count toward knowing skill at all.
context: One game doesn't separate skill from variance. A weaker player can beat a stronger one on any given day. To know skill order, you need enough games to see a pattern. Liam has a reason for his belief but not a reason that supports the size of the claim — that's where his knowing fails.

question: A debate-club captain glances at the school's wall clock and concludes it's 3:00 PM. It IS 3:00 — but the clock has been broken and frozen at 3:00 for weeks, only happening to match twice a day. Did she really KNOW the time?
answer: No — true belief isn't knowledge unless the reasons forming the belief actually track the truth, instead of coinciding with it by luck.
choices: No — true belief isn't knowledge unless the reasons forming the belief actually track the truth, instead of coinciding with it by luck.
Yes — she formed a confident belief from a clock and the belief turned out correct; that combination is what 'knowing the time' has meant.
Yes — her inference from a normally reliable clock was reasonable, and a reasonable inference that lands on the right answer is knowledge.
No — clocks can never deliver knowledge to anyone since they are mediated instruments; only direct sensory observation could ever count.
context: Bertrand Russell's stopped-clock case (1948) is a classic Gettier-style puzzle: justified true belief that misses knowledge because the justification and the truth came together by accident. Reliable reasons must TRACK the truth.

question: A monastery chronicle editor looks across a field and sees what appears to be a sheep, concluding 'there's a sheep in the field.' There IS a sheep — hidden behind a hill. What she SAW was a sheep-shaped rock. Did she actually KNOW there was a sheep in the field?
answer: No — her belief is true but only by luck; the rock that justified her has no connection to the real hidden sheep that makes it true.
choices: No — her belief is true but only by luck; the rock that justified her has no connection to the real hidden sheep that makes it true.
Yes — her belief that there was a sheep in the field is true, and she had visual evidence supporting it; that combination is knowledge.
Yes — visual perception is generally reliable for sheep-spotting, and reliable perception delivering a true belief is what knowing means.
No — knowledge requires absolute certainty no error is possible; any belief formed at a distance through fallible vision cannot count.
context: Roderick Chisholm's sheep case (1966) is a textbook Gettier example: the belief is justified, true, and yet fails to count as knowledge because the justification (the rock) is disconnected from what makes the belief true.

question: A wandering minstrel tells viewers a vitamin cures colds. Asked her source, she names a fitness pamphleteer. That pamphleteer, asked, cites a wellness a symposium. a symposium cites a tweet. The tweet cites no one. What's STILL the strongest reason to doubt this testimony chain?
answer: No link in the chain has actually inspected the original evidence, so the claim reduces to a single source no one in the chain has checked.
choices: No link in the chain has actually inspected the original evidence, so the claim reduces to a single source no one in the chain has checked.
The court poets may have misremembered which pamphleteer she got it from, so even a sound chain would still face an independent recall risk.
Fitness bloggers and wellness podcasters disagree with each other often, so the chain passes through people who would not agree at all.
Viewers may not hear the court poets carefully and may form mistaken beliefs about what she said; this is a separate transmission risk.
context: Testimony chains transmit warrant only as well as their weakest link. When no link has touched the original evidence, the whole chain reduces to one unchecked source — what Hume (1748) called the 'credulous transmission' problem.

question: A school newspaper covers a question on which two equally credentialed scientists publish OPPOSITE conclusions in peer-reviewed journals. The reporter wants to assert one as a settled fact. What's the most careful question to ask before believing one over the other?
answer: Whether either scientist's argument grounds its conclusion in evidence the OTHER has actually examined and engaged with directly.
choices: Whether either scientist's argument grounds its conclusion in evidence the OTHER has actually examined and engaged with directly.
Whether one of the scientists has more publications than the other; published output is a reliable proxy for likely correctness under disagreement.
Whether one scientist's institution is more prestigious; institutional ranking is the standard way readers sort competing scientific claims.
Whether one of the scientists agrees with what the reporter already believed; the more familiar conclusion is generally the safer one to report.
context: Expert disagreement is studied as a hard problem in social epistemology (Goldman 2001). When peers split, credentials cancel out; the careful reader asks whose argument actually engages the OTHER side's evidence and reasons.

question: A student is certain her favorite singer would never plagiarize lyrics, even after a court ruling and three independent musicologists conclude that she did. She says: 'I just KNOW she'd never do that.' What's STILL the strongest reason to doubt the student's knowledge claim?
answer: Her certainty tracks how badly she wants the singer innocent, not the court ruling and expert analysis; motivated belief isn't knowledge.
choices: Her certainty tracks how badly she wants the singer innocent, not the court ruling and expert analysis; motivated belief isn't knowledge.
Court rulings can be appealed and overturned in higher courts later, so the matter is not yet fully settled and her confidence is just premature.
Musicologists' analyses sometimes contradict each other on the same lyrics, so three independent ones agreeing is unusual but not yet final.
Plagiarism is a vague concept depending on which threshold of borrowing applies, and her disagreement may concern the threshold not the facts.
context: Motivated reasoning (Kunda 1990) is the pattern of believing what one wishes true while feeling sure one's reasoning is independent. The hallmark: evidence accumulates against the belief and confidence does not shift.

question: A wandering minstrel vividly recalls meeting a famous author at a bookstore signing as a child. Years later her mother shows tickets proving the family was on vacation that day, two states away. The memory feels vivid. Did she KNOW she had met the author?
answer: No — the vividness of a memory does not establish its truth; her belief tracked how clearly she remembered, not whether it occurred.
choices: No — the vividness of a memory does not establish its truth; her belief tracked how clearly she remembered, not whether it occurred.
Yes — at the time the memory was clear and undisputed, and a clear undisputed memory is what 'knowing what happened' has always meant.
Yes — adult recollection of childhood events is generally reliable, and knowledge is the natural product of generally reliable recall.
No — childhood memories can never count as knowledge regardless of accuracy; only adult experiences with full awareness could ever count.
context: False-memory research (Loftus 1997 and after) documents how vividness and confidence dissociate from accuracy. A vividly-felt memory can be wholly constructed; epistemic warrant requires the memory actually track the past.

question: A reporter for the school paper sees smoke pouring from the cafeteria and concludes there is a kitchen fire. She alerts the principal. It turns out a smoke machine was being tested for the school play. What's the most careful question to ask about whether she knew?
answer: Whether her belief was REASONABLE given what she knew at the time; reasonableness measures the quality of belief, not whether the result is true.
choices: Whether her belief was REASONABLE given what she knew at the time; reasonableness measures the quality of belief, not whether the result is true.
Whether the principal was annoyed by the false alarm, since the practical consequences of a wrong belief settle the knowledge question entirely.
Whether smoke machines are commonly used at her school, since how often this kind of scene arises is what settles whether knowledge was achieved.
Whether anyone else also believed the cafeteria was on fire, since shared belief among observers is what tips a personal impression into knowledge.
context: A belief can be REASONABLE (well-justified given what someone knew) and still turn out false. Reasonableness assesses the quality of belief; truth assesses match with the world. The distinction is fundamental to knowledge.

question: A brand markets its bottled water as 'scientifically proven' to improve focus, citing a study it funded itself, with no peer review, and a sample of twelve company employees told what the study aimed to find. What's STILL the strongest reason to doubt the brand's knowledge claim?
answer: Three independent flaws (funder ran it, no peer review, unblinded sample) each undermine warrant; together they leave essentially nothing.
choices: Three independent flaws (funder ran it, no peer review, unblinded sample) each undermine warrant; together they leave essentially nothing.
The bottled water industry has been embroiled in marketing controversies, so the public is justified in distrusting any brand in this industry today.
Twelve employees is a small sample for any psychological effect, so even a careful study with that size would deliver only weak evidence alone.
Improving focus is hard to measure objectively; reasonable disagreement about how to measure focus is enough on its own to block the claim.
context: Funder bias, missing peer review, and unblinded samples each independently undermine warrant. When all three converge, the claim has no real epistemic support left — the brand's certainty does not transfer to the consumer's belief.

question: A debate-club member is certain his teammate will win the tournament because the teammate showed him a pristine practice score sheet. The teammate does win — but on a different round, since the sheet was his brother's. Did he really KNOW his teammate would win?
answer: No — the practice sheet that justified him belonged to the wrong person, so his reasons had no real connection to the teammate's later win.
choices: No — the practice sheet that justified him belonged to the wrong person, so his reasons had no real connection to the teammate's later win.
Yes — he formed a confident prediction based on solid-looking evidence, and the predicted outcome did happen; that combination is knowing.
Yes — relying on a teammate's practice scores is a generally reliable method, and a reliable method delivering truth is what knowing means.
No — predictions about future tournament outcomes can never count as knowledge regardless of evidence; only past events can be known at all.
context: This is a classic Gettier pattern: justified true belief whose justification and truth are disconnected. The teammate did win, and the score sheet did justify expecting a win — but the sheet was about someone else entirely.

question: A student tells her friend the chemistry test will be on Friday. She knows because she overheard the teacher confirm it. The friend, trusting her, now believes the test is Friday. The test is Friday. Did the friend KNOW the test would be on Friday?
answer: Yes — knowledge transfers through reliable testimony when the speaker actually knew and the listener has no reason to doubt her account at all.
choices: Yes — knowledge transfers through reliable testimony when the speaker actually knew and the listener has no reason to doubt her account at all.
No — only the original observer can have knowledge of an event she overheard; testimony cannot deliver knowledge to a hearer regardless of source.
Yes — the friend believed a true claim about Friday, and ANY true belief rises to knowledge as long as the believer is sincere about it.
No — testimony delivers belief but never knowledge; only direct perception by the listener herself of the teacher's statement would count.
context: Testimony is widely treated as a legitimate source of knowledge when the speaker knows and the listener has no defeaters (Coady 1992). Most of what anyone knows about history, science, and current events comes through this route.

question: An online creator predicts every weather forecast by flipping a coin: heads for rain, tails for sun. On Tuesday she predicts rain. It rains. Did she KNOW it would rain on Tuesday?
answer: No — the process that produced her belief (a coin flip) is not reliably connected to the weather; the right answer is luck, not knowledge.
choices: No — the process that produced her belief (a coin flip) is not reliably connected to the weather; the right answer is luck, not knowledge.
Yes — she made a confident prediction about Tuesday's weather and the prediction was correct; that is what 'knowing what the weather will be' means.
Yes — coin-flip predictions about the weather are correct roughly half the time, and half-the-time correctness is sufficient for a flip to count.
No — short-range weather predictions can never count as knowledge regardless of how generated; only long-term climate facts are stable enough.
context: Reliabilism (Goldman 1979) says knowledge requires a belief-forming process RELIABLY connected to truth. A coin flip happens to land right sometimes, but its connection to the weather is random — so no flip yields knowledge.
