Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a sample of cases far too small or biased to actually support the broad claim being made from them.
context: Post hoc ergo propter hoc (Latin: 'after this, therefore because of this') treats sequence as proof of cause. The fix is asking what else changed alongside the app — the kind of student who downloads a study app is part of the cause story even before the app does anything.

question: A school newspaper reporter asks the principal why budget cuts hit the art program hardest. The principal answers: 'You know, our football team had its best season in twenty years, and that's something we should all be proud of.' The principal's reply commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Red herring — the principal drags the football team's strong season into the budget question to shift attention from the art-program cuts the reporter raised.
choices: Red herring — the principal drags the football team's strong season into the budget question to shift attention from the art-program cuts the reporter raised.
Straw man — distorting an opponent's argument into a weaker or wilder version so the easier-to-attack distortion can be knocked down in its place.
Tu quoque — deflecting criticism by pointing out the critic has the same fault, treating that hypocrisy as if it answered the original argument.
Appeal to emotion — substituting an emotional appeal for evidence, leaning on how the audience feels instead of on what the argument actually shows.
context: A red herring is an irrelevant point dropped into a discussion to redirect attention. The name comes from old fox-hunting lore: a smoked fish dragged across a trail to throw the hounds off-scent. The original question stays unanswered until someone reels it back in.

question: A teen explains why he tried a viral online challenge that left a kid hospitalized last week: 'Millions of people have done it without getting hurt, so the videos prove it must basically be safe.' His reasoning commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Bandwagon — the teen treats millions doing the viral challenge as evidence it must be safe, even after a hospitalization showed the videos hide what goes wrong.
choices: Bandwagon — the teen treats millions doing the viral challenge as evidence it must be safe, even after a hospitalization showed the videos hide what goes wrong.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a sample of cases far too small or biased to actually support the broad claim being made from them.
Appeal to popularity — treating widespread agreement, viewership, or sales as if it counted as evidence the underlying claim must actually be correct.
Post hoc — treating one event as the cause of another simply because the first happened before the second, with no real causal mechanism shown at all.
context: Bandwagon reasoning is especially dangerous with viral trends: the videos that go viral are filtered toward success, so the visible base rate is misleading. Popularity ranks spectacle, not safety. Last week's hospitalization is the kind of data the filter hides.

question: A nonprofit's fundraising email opens with a heartbreaking story about a single suffering child, then asks for monthly donations. The email never mentions what percentage of donations reach programs or how effective those programs are. The email's argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Appeal to emotion — the email substitutes a heartbreaking story for evidence on donation effectiveness, leaning on feelings instead of the program data needed.
choices: Appeal to emotion — the email substitutes a heartbreaking story for evidence on donation effectiveness, leaning on feelings instead of the program data needed.
Cherry picking — selecting only the evidence that supports the claim while quietly setting aside contrary data that would force a revision of the conclusion.
Red herring — dragging an irrelevant point into a discussion to shift attention away from the question that was actually on the table at the moment.
Loaded question — phrasing a question so any direct answer concedes a contested premise the questioner has quietly built into the wording itself.
context: Appeal to emotion isn't automatically a fallacy — feelings can be relevant evidence. It becomes fallacious when emotional content REPLACES the evidence that would actually settle the question. Giving wisely depends on outcomes; the story alone can't tell you what your dollar does.

question: A pundit predicts in January that the new policy will reduce inflation by July. By July inflation has risen. The pundit now insists: 'I always meant a multi-year effect — a single year was never going to be a fair test.' His response commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Moving the goalposts — the pundit changes the test from July to multi-year after his January prediction failed, so the failure no longer counts as one at all.
choices: Moving the goalposts — the pundit changes the test from July to multi-year after his January prediction failed, so the failure no longer counts as one at all.
No true Scotsman — redefining a sweeping category mid-argument to exclude any counterexample, preserving the claim by tightening the definition after the fact.
Equivocation — shifting the meaning of a key word partway through an argument so the conclusion only seems to follow because the word changed sense quietly.
Begging the question — assuming the very point in dispute as a premise, so the conclusion is presupposed instead of being independently established.
context: Moving the goalposts is the prediction-failure escape hatch. The original timeline becomes elastic the moment it's missed. The honest move is to acknowledge the prediction failed and explain why — not to redefine 'success' so failure becomes invisible.

question: A school newspaper reporter publishes a damaging claim about a teacher based on one anonymous student tip. Asked for corroboration, the reporter says: 'Nobody has come forward to deny it, so the silence itself confirms the story.' The reporter's argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Appeal to ignorance — the reporter treats the lack of public denial as proof the tip is true, moving from 'no one has spoken against it' to 'silence confirms.'
choices: Appeal to ignorance — the reporter treats the lack of public denial as proof the tip is true, moving from 'no one has spoken against it' to 'silence confirms.'
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a sample of cases far too small or biased to actually support the broad claim being made from them.
Bandwagon — treating widespread popularity or how many people agree as if it were evidence the underlying claim or product must therefore be true.
Circular reasoning — smuggling the conclusion into the premises so the argument loops back on itself instead of providing independent support for its claim.
context: Appeal to ignorance moves from absence of evidence to positive proof. Silence can mean many things — fear, indifference, ignorance of the story — none of which confirm the claim. Responsible reporting confirms with independent sources, not with the absence of denial.

question: A health blogger reports she took a new vitamin during her last three colds and felt better by day five each time. She concludes: 'The vitamin clearly cured my colds.' Most colds resolve within seven days regardless of treatment. Her argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: False cause — the blogger treats the vitamin as the cause of her cold recovery, ignoring that most colds resolve within a week on their own without treatment.
choices: False cause — the blogger treats the vitamin as the cause of her cold recovery, ignoring that most colds resolve within a week on their own without treatment.
Post hoc — treating one event as the cause of another simply because the first happened before the second, with no real causal mechanism shown at all.
Appeal to authority — treating a famous name's endorsement as proof the claim is true, even when the named source lacks the relevant subject expertise.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a sample of cases far too small or biased to actually support the broad claim being made from them.
context: False cause errors treat correlation as causation when the apparent effect would have happened anyway. The proper test is a control case: people taking nothing usually recover from a cold in the same window. The vitamin needs to beat that baseline to claim credit.

question: A self-help guru opens her seminar: 'Why trust me? Because everything I teach has been validated by thousands of people who became enlightened by my methods.' Asked who counts as 'enlightened,' she answers: 'Anyone who completed my methods.' Her argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Circular reasoning — the guru's evidence for trusting her methods is enlightenment she defines as completing her methods, so the argument loops on itself.
choices: Circular reasoning — the guru's evidence for trusting her methods is enlightenment she defines as completing her methods, so the argument loops on itself.
Begging the question — assuming the very point in dispute as a premise, so the conclusion is presupposed instead of being independently established.
Appeal to popularity — treating widespread agreement, viewership, or sales as if it counted as evidence the underlying claim must actually be correct.
No true Scotsman — redefining a sweeping category mid-argument to exclude any counterexample, preserving the claim by tightening the definition after the fact.
context: Circular reasoning happens when the supporting premise just IS the conclusion in different words. The argument never moves outside itself. The fix is finding independent evidence — testable predictions, outside benchmarks — that doesn't depend on the conclusion being true already.

question: A music-magazine columnist writes: 'Every musician in the new orchestra is a world-class soloist. Therefore this orchestra will be the greatest ensemble of the year.' The orchestra has only just formed and has never rehearsed. The columnist's argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Composition fallacy — the columnist infers from each musician being world-class that the orchestra is greatest, ignoring that ensemble play needs rehearsal.
choices: Composition fallacy — the columnist infers from each musician being world-class that the orchestra is greatest, ignoring that ensemble play needs rehearsal.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a sample of cases far too small or biased to actually support the broad claim being made from them.
Appeal to authority — treating a famous name's endorsement as proof the claim is true, even when the named source lacks the relevant subject expertise.
Bandwagon — treating widespread popularity or how many people agree as if it were evidence the underlying claim or product must therefore be true.
context: Composition fallacy moves from properties of parts to properties of wholes without showing the inference holds. An orchestra of soloists who haven't rehearsed can sound ragged; coordination is its own skill. Wholes have features parts don't carry by themselves.

question: A blogger writes: 'Evolution is just a theory. A theory is a guess. So evolution is just a guess.' In scientific usage 'theory' means a well-tested explanatory framework; in everyday usage 'theory' means a hunch. The blogger's argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Equivocation — the blogger swaps the scientific 'theory' (well-tested framework) for the everyday 'theory' (guess) so the dismissive conclusion seems to follow.
choices: Equivocation — the blogger swaps the scientific 'theory' (well-tested framework) for the everyday 'theory' (guess) so the dismissive conclusion seems to follow.
Straw man — distorting an opponent's argument into a weaker or wilder version so the easier-to-attack distortion can be knocked down in its place.
Genetic fallacy — judging an argument by where it came from or who said it rather than by what the actual content of the argument says about the issue.
Begging the question — assuming the very point in dispute as a premise, so the conclusion is presupposed instead of being independently established.
context: Equivocation slides a key word's meaning mid-argument so the conclusion sneaks through. 'Theory' is one of the most exploited equivocations in science discourse. A valid argument requires each key term to keep the same sense from premise to conclusion.

question: A podcast host interviews a school-board member and asks: 'When did your board decide to start ignoring parent feedback?' The board has not actually decided to ignore parent feedback. The host's question commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Loaded question — the host packs a contested premise (the board has decided to ignore parent feedback) into the wording, so any answer concedes the claim.
choices: Loaded question — the host packs a contested premise (the board has decided to ignore parent feedback) into the wording, so any answer concedes the claim.
Straw man — distorting an opponent's argument into a weaker or wilder version so the easier-to-attack distortion can be knocked down in its place.
Appeal to emotion — substituting an emotional appeal for evidence, leaning on how the audience feels instead of on what the argument actually shows.
Red herring — dragging an irrelevant point into a discussion to shift attention away from the question that was actually on the table at the moment.
context: Loaded questions hide contested premises inside the wording itself. The honest response is to reject the premise before answering: 'Your question assumes we've decided that — we haven't.' Interview ambushes lean on this device because the rejection feels evasive.

question: A school newspaper article concludes: 'Most students hate the new schedule.' The supporting evidence is a survey posted to a single hallway bulletin board near the drama room over one lunch period, with 14 responses. The article's argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Hasty generalization — the article draws a 'most students' conclusion from 14 responses at one bulletin board over one lunch period near the drama room.
choices: Hasty generalization — the article draws a 'most students' conclusion from 14 responses at one bulletin board over one lunch period near the drama room.
Cherry picking — selecting only the evidence that supports the claim while quietly setting aside contrary data that would force a revision of the conclusion.
Bandwagon — treating widespread popularity or how many people agree as if it were evidence the underlying claim or product must therefore be true.
Appeal to popularity — treating widespread agreement, viewership, or sales as if it counted as evidence the underlying claim must actually be correct.
context: Hasty generalization is the wrong-sample-size fallacy. Fourteen responses at one location during one lunch period isn't a base from which to read the whole student body. Sound surveys need scale and randomized sampling — the schedule survey has neither.

question: In a school newspaper debate, one writer argues: 'Either we ban phones in every classroom completely, or we accept that learning is over forever.' Middle-ground policies like lockers-during-class go unmentioned. The writer's framing commits which logical fallacy?
answer: False dilemma — the writer squeezes phone policy into either a total ban or learning ending forever, hiding middle-ground policies like lockers-during-class.
choices: False dilemma — the writer squeezes phone policy into either a total ban or learning ending forever, hiding middle-ground policies like lockers-during-class.
Slippery slope — claiming one small step must trigger a chain of much worse outcomes without showing why each link in the chain has to actually follow.
Appeal to emotion — substituting an emotional appeal for evidence, leaning on how the audience feels instead of on what the argument actually shows.
Straw man — distorting an opponent's argument into a weaker or wilder version so the easier-to-attack distortion can be knocked down in its place.
context: False dilemmas often hide their work behind dramatic stakes ('learning is over forever'). The cure is naming the unmentioned options aloud — lockers during class, designated breaks, age-graded policy. Once the alternatives are visible, the forced choice dissolves.

question: Podcast host Galen argues: 'Studies show our diet plan works — 87% of participants lost weight.' Pressed on the study, he admits participants were self-selected from his existing fanbase, and 'lost weight' meant any loss at all over 30 days. Galen's defense commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Cherry picking — Galen's self-selected fanbase sample and 'any-loss' success metric were both chosen in ways that practically guarantee the 87% result.
choices: Cherry picking — Galen's self-selected fanbase sample and 'any-loss' success metric were both chosen in ways that practically guarantee the 87% result.
Appeal to authority — treating an authority's say-so as decisive evidence even when the authority is outside their domain, paid, or speaking against the field's consensus.
Moving the goalposts — changing the success criterion after the original standard has been met, redefining 'success' so the current outcome no longer qualifies as a win.
False equivalence — treating two cases or sources as comparable when they differ in scale, evidence base, or kind, smuggling parity into the framing of the comparison.
context: Cherry picking covers both selection bias (which cases are included) and outcome-metric manipulation (what counts as success). Either alone seriously weakens a claim; together they let a 'study' tell whatever story the designer set out to tell from the start.

question: Columnist Vera demands triple-blind randomized trials before she will accept any claim that her favored policy raises hospital readmissions, but accepts a single op-ed anecdote as proof that the rival policy lowers them. Vera's framing commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Isolated demand for rigor — Vera applies triple-blind standards only to readmissions claims against her policy and accepts an anecdote on the same question for the rival.
choices: Isolated demand for rigor — Vera applies triple-blind standards only to readmissions claims against her policy and accepts an anecdote on the same question for the rival.
Cherry picking — presenting only the favorable data, cases, or quotations while quietly omitting the unfavorable ones that would change the overall picture.
False equivalence — treating two cases or sources as comparable when they differ in scale, evidence base, or kind, smuggling parity into the framing of the comparison.
Special pleading — claiming a general rule applies except in one's own case, without producing a principled reason why the case is genuinely different.
context: Isolated demand for rigor (named by Scott Alexander, 2014) is the asymmetric-skepticism move: one side gets a high evidentiary bar, the other a low one. The structural tell is that the bar moves with the conclusion, not with the question being asked.

question: On a talk show, pundit Roy points to a single dramatic airport-screening story and concludes: 'Clearly the new scanner is catching dangerous travelers — we need it everywhere.' He gives no figure for how many ordinary travelers the scanner also flags. Roy's argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Base rate neglect — Roy weighs the vivid airport-scanner catch without giving any weight to how often the same scanner flags innocent travelers in the underlying base rate.
choices: Base rate neglect — Roy weighs the vivid airport-scanner catch without giving any weight to how often the same scanner flags innocent travelers in the underlying base rate.
Anecdotal evidence — leaning on one or two memorable personal stories to support a general claim, when systematic data would be the relevant kind of evidence here.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a sample too small or too unrepresentative to license that scale of claim about the broader population.
Survivorship bias — drawing lessons only from the cases that survived a selection process, while ignoring the silent majority whose failure would change the conclusion.
context: Base rate neglect (Kahneman and Tversky, 1973) is the failure to weight a vivid individual case against the statistical background rate. For a rare threat, even a high-accuracy scanner produces overwhelmingly more false positives than true positives in absolute numbers.

question: After a star pitcher's worst-ever month, his team hires a famous mechanics coach. The next month, the pitcher's numbers bounce back toward his career average. Columnist Niko writes: 'The coach has clearly turned his career around — look at the data.' Niko's argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Regression to the mean — Niko reads the pitcher's natural drift from a worst-ever month back toward his career average as if the new coach were what caused the bounce.
choices: Regression to the mean — Niko reads the pitcher's natural drift from a worst-ever month back toward his career average as if the new coach were what caused the bounce.
Post hoc — treating one event as the cause of a later one simply because it happened first, without ruling out coincidence or a shared third cause.
False cause — treating a correlation between two variables as if it established that one of them is causing the other, with no mechanism or controls in evidence.
Cherry picking — presenting only the favorable data, cases, or quotations while quietly omitting the unfavorable ones that would change the overall picture.
context: Regression to the mean (Galton, 1886) is the structural fact that extreme observations tend to be followed by less extreme ones, with or without any intervention. Mistaking that drift for treatment effect is one of the commonest errors in sports, medicine, and education writing.

question: An op-ed notes that the wealthiest U.S. counties tend to vote Democrat and concludes: 'Therefore wealthy individuals are more likely than poorer ones to vote Democrat.' The author offers no individual-level data, only the county aggregates. The op-ed's reasoning commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Ecological fallacy — the op-ed reads a county-level pattern as if it told us how the wealthiest individuals within those counties personally voted on election day.
choices: Ecological fallacy — the op-ed reads a county-level pattern as if it told us how the wealthiest individuals within those counties personally voted on election day.
Composition — inferring that what is true of each part of a whole must therefore be true of the whole, with no argument that the property scales that way.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a sample too small or too unrepresentative to license that scale of claim about the broader population.
False cause — treating a correlation between two variables as if it established that one of them is causing the other, with no mechanism or controls in evidence.
context: Ecological fallacy (Robinson, 1950) is the structural error of inferring individual behavior from group statistics. A county can lean Democrat while its wealthiest residents lean the other way — the aggregate average says nothing direct about any particular person inside it.

question: A wellness brand markets supplements that 'rewire your immune system.' Pressed by a reporter, the founder retreats: 'We just mean: support overall wellness through vitamin C.' A week later, the marketing copy is back to 'rewire your immune system.' The brand's defense commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Motte-and-bailey — the brand sells 'rewire your immune system,' falls back to bland vitamin-C language when pressed, then quietly resumes the strong claim once the reporter is gone.
choices: Motte-and-bailey — the brand sells 'rewire your immune system,' falls back to bland vitamin-C language when pressed, then quietly resumes the strong claim once the reporter is gone.
Equivocation — shifting the meaning of a key term partway through the argument so the conclusion only goes through because two senses are quietly swapped.
Special pleading — claiming a general rule applies except in one's own case, without producing a principled reason why the case is genuinely different.
Moving the goalposts — changing the success criterion after the original standard has been met, redefining 'success' so the current outcome no longer qualifies as a win.
context: Motte-and-bailey (Nicholas Shackel, 2005) names a two-position rhetorical maneuver: the bailey is the bold profitable claim; the motte is a trivial defensible retreat. The brand alternates between them, banking the bailey's market value and the motte's deniability.

question: A debate show invites two guests on climate policy: a working climate scientist with 30 years of peer-reviewed publications, and a blogger with no relevant training. The host frames it as 'both sides of the science.' The host's framing commits which logical fallacy?
answer: False equivalence — the host treats a 30-year peer-reviewed climate scientist and an untrained blogger as comparable 'sides' of the same scientific question.
choices: False equivalence — the host treats a 30-year peer-reviewed climate scientist and an untrained blogger as comparable 'sides' of the same scientific question.
Appeal to authority — treating an authority's say-so as decisive evidence even when the authority is outside their domain, paid, or speaking against the field's consensus.
Bandwagon — treating widespread agreement or popularity as if it were itself evidence that the underlying claim is actually true on the merits.
Cherry picking — presenting only the favorable data, cases, or quotations while quietly omitting the unfavorable ones that would change the overall picture.
context: False equivalence smuggles parity into the framing of a comparison. Whether the two 'sides' are genuinely comparable is itself the contested question the framing has already answered. It is structurally distinct from ad hominem against the blogger — here the issue is the framing.

question: A bestselling business book profiles ten billion-dollar startups whose founders all dropped out of college. It concludes: 'Dropping out is a reliable path to founding a unicorn.' The book mentions no failed dropout founders. The book's argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Survivorship bias — the book draws lessons only from ten billion-dollar dropout founders, while ignoring the silent thousands of dropouts whose startups quietly failed.
choices: Survivorship bias — the book draws lessons only from ten billion-dollar dropout founders, while ignoring the silent thousands of dropouts whose startups quietly failed.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a sample too small or too unrepresentative to license that scale of claim about the broader population.
Cherry picking — presenting only the favorable data, cases, or quotations while quietly omitting the unfavorable ones that would change the overall picture.
Texas sharpshooter — drawing a target around a cluster of hits after the fact and treating the cluster as evidence of skill or pattern rather than chance arrangement.
context: Survivorship bias was made famous by Abraham Wald's WWII analysis of returning bombers: the planes that came back showed only the survivable hits. The relevant data was on the planes that did not return. Lessons drawn only from survivors systematically miss what kills.

question: Forecaster Mira surveys 200 stock predictions she made over five years, isolates the 14 that came true, and publishes a book titled 'How I Predicted the Market.' She omits the 186 misses. Mira's reasoning commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Texas sharpshooter — Mira draws her target around the 14 hits out of 200 forecasts after the fact and presents the cluster as evidence of predictive skill.
choices: Texas sharpshooter — Mira draws her target around the 14 hits out of 200 forecasts after the fact and presents the cluster as evidence of predictive skill.
Cherry picking — presenting only the favorable data, cases, or quotations while quietly omitting the unfavorable ones that would change the overall picture.
Survivorship bias — drawing lessons only from the cases that survived a selection process, while ignoring the silent majority whose failure would change the conclusion.
Post hoc — treating one event as the cause of a later one simply because it happened first, without ruling out coincidence or a shared third cause.
context: Texas sharpshooter (named for the joke about a shooter who fires at a barn and then paints targets around the densest holes) is the post-hoc-pattern move: any large random sample will contain clusters, and treating those clusters as designed is a category error.

question: On a debate stage, candidate Forrest rattles off 17 separate dubious claims about his opponent's record in under three minutes, then says: 'My opponent could not refute any of these.' His opponent had 90 seconds. Forrest's tactic commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Gish gallop — Forrest fires off 17 dubious claims in under three minutes, then treats the opponent's failure to address all of them in 90 seconds as if it confirmed each one.
choices: Gish gallop — Forrest fires off 17 dubious claims in under three minutes, then treats the opponent's failure to address all of them in 90 seconds as if it confirmed each one.
Red herring — introducing an irrelevant point to divert attention from the actual question, leaving the original challenge quietly unanswered in the meantime.
Straw man — distorting an opponent's claim into a wilder, easier-to-attack version, then refuting the distortion as though it were the original position.
Moving the goalposts — changing the success criterion after the original standard has been met, redefining 'success' so the current outcome no longer qualifies as a win.
context: Gish gallop (named by Eugenie Scott after creationist Duane Gish) exploits the asymmetry between asserting a claim and refuting it: a single false claim takes seconds, while a careful refutation takes minutes. Volume substitutes for quality of any individual point.

question: A supplement label reads: 'Made from 100% natural ingredients — therefore safe for daily use.' A pharmacist notes that hemlock, arsenic, and many poisonous mushrooms are also 100% natural. The label's framing commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Appeal to nature — the label slides from 'made from natural ingredients' to 'safe for daily use,' as though the descriptive label by itself settled the normative question.
choices: Appeal to nature — the label slides from 'made from natural ingredients' to 'safe for daily use,' as though the descriptive label by itself settled the normative question.
Equivocation — shifting the meaning of a key term partway through the argument so the conclusion only goes through because two senses are quietly swapped.
Appeal to tradition — treating long-standing practice as itself a reason the practice is correct, without examining whether the original justification still holds up.
Cherry picking — presenting only the favorable data, cases, or quotations while quietly omitting the unfavorable ones that would change the overall picture.
context: Appeal to nature (G. E. Moore framed the surrounding 'naturalistic fallacy' in 1903) treats 'natural' as automatically good. The label slides from descriptive ('grown in soil') to normative ('therefore safe') without any argument that the slide is licensed.

question: Asked why a college keeps a hazing ritual that has injured students, the dean replies: 'We've done it for 120 years — it's part of who we are.' He gives no current safety case for continuing. The dean's reply commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Appeal to tradition — the dean cites a 120-year practice as itself a reason to continue the hazing ritual, without examining whether the original justification still holds today.
choices: Appeal to tradition — the dean cites a 120-year practice as itself a reason to continue the hazing ritual, without examining whether the original justification still holds today.
Appeal to nature — treating 'natural' as automatically good and 'unnatural' as automatically bad, sliding from a descriptive label into a normative conclusion.
Genetic fallacy — judging a claim by its origin — who made it, where it came from, what motive it might serve — rather than by the substance of the argument itself.
Sunk cost — treating money, time, or effort already spent as a reason to continue, when the only rational question is whether further investment now still pays.
context: Appeal to tradition treats longevity as warrant. Genuinely good practices often survive a long time, but so do bad ones; the age of a practice is structurally separate from its current justification. The question 'should we keep doing this?' is not answered by 'we have.'

question: Music critic Hess writes: 'Every player in the new symphony is a virtuoso soloist, so this will be the finest ensemble performance of the season.' On opening night, the players keep stepping on each other's phrasing. Hess's pre-show argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Composition — Hess infers from each player being a virtuoso soloist that the whole symphony will be the season's finest ensemble work, with no argument that solo skill scales up.
choices: Composition — Hess infers from each player being a virtuoso soloist that the whole symphony will be the season's finest ensemble work, with no argument that solo skill scales up.
Division — inferring that what is true of a whole must therefore be true of each of its parts, with no argument that the property distributes that way.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a sample too small or too unrepresentative to license that scale of claim about the broader population.
Weak analogy — treating two cases as similar enough to share a conclusion when the relevant respects in which they differ are doing most of the actual work.
context: Composition is the structural error of moving from properties of parts to properties of the whole. Some properties scale up (every brick is red, the wall is red); many do not (every player is excellent at solo, the ensemble is excellent — ensemble skill is its own thing).

question: A financial paper notes that an investment fund averaged 12% returns over a decade. A reader concludes: 'Therefore every fund in their family must have returned 12% per year.' The reader has not looked at any individual fund's performance. The reader's reasoning commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Division — the reader infers from a fund-family average of 12% that each individual fund within the family must also have returned 12% per year, with no look at any individual fund.
choices: Division — the reader infers from a fund-family average of 12% that each individual fund within the family must also have returned 12% per year, with no look at any individual fund.
Composition — inferring that what is true of each part of a whole must therefore be true of the whole, with no argument that the property scales that way.
Ecological fallacy — inferring an individual-level conclusion from group-level statistics, when the group average says little about any particular member's case.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a sample too small or too unrepresentative to license that scale of claim about the broader population.
context: Division is composition's mirror image: inferring properties of parts from properties of the whole. A 12% average across many funds is consistent with wide dispersion among individual funds, including outright losers. The aggregate says nothing direct about any single member.

question: An editorial defending a failed urban rail project argues: 'We've already spent $3 billion on it — we have to finish it or the money is wasted.' The editorial offers no projection of whether further spending will produce its own returns. The editorial's reasoning commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Sunk cost — the editorial treats the $3 billion already spent on the rail project as a reason to keep spending, instead of asking whether further spending will still pay on its own.
choices: Sunk cost — the editorial treats the $3 billion already spent on the rail project as a reason to keep spending, instead of asking whether further spending will still pay on its own.
Appeal to tradition — treating long-standing practice as itself a reason the practice is correct, without examining whether the original justification still holds up.
Special pleading — claiming a general rule applies except in one's own case, without producing a principled reason why the case is genuinely different.
False dilemma — framing a situation as a forced choice between two options when several other real positions are available and equally on the table.
context: Sunk cost is the structural error of letting irrecoverable past spending dictate present choice. The rational question is always forward-looking: does the next dollar pay off? Past dollars are gone either way. Both psychology and political incentive resist this point.

question: Self-help guru Larkin tells his audience: 'Everyone who breaks a daily meditation streak loses their self-discipline.' Asked about his own three-week lapse last month, he says: 'My situation was different — I was building a new course.' Larkin's reply commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Special pleading — Larkin's rule that lapses destroy discipline applies to his audience but not to his own three-week lapse, with no principled reason his course-building case is different.
choices: Special pleading — Larkin's rule that lapses destroy discipline applies to his audience but not to his own three-week lapse, with no principled reason his course-building case is different.
Isolated demand for rigor — applying a much stricter evidentiary standard to one side of a debate than to the other, while leaving the other side's claims largely unchecked.
Moving the goalposts — changing the success criterion after the original standard has been met, redefining 'success' so the current outcome no longer qualifies as a win.
No true Scotsman — saving a sweeping claim from a counterexample by retroactively adding a purity qualifier so any contrary case is dismissed as not 'really' counting.
context: Special pleading invokes an unprincipled exception: the rule holds for everyone except me, for reasons that don't generalize. The structural tell is that the asserted difference would also exempt many of the cases the rule was meant to govern, if applied consistently.

question: An op-ed argues: 'A driver's license is required to operate a car, so a government license should be required to use a smartphone. Both are powerful tools with safety risks.' The op-ed lists no further point of comparison. The op-ed's argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Weak analogy — the op-ed treats a driver's license and a smartphone license as parallel, when the public-safety case for the car turns on features the smartphone doesn't share.
choices: Weak analogy — the op-ed treats a driver's license and a smartphone license as parallel, when the public-safety case for the car turns on features the smartphone doesn't share.
False equivalence — treating two cases or sources as comparable when they differ in scale, evidence base, or kind, smuggling parity into the framing of the comparison.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a sample too small or too unrepresentative to license that scale of claim about the broader population.
Slippery slope — claiming one modest step must inevitably trigger a chain of progressively worse outcomes, without showing why each link is genuinely required.
context: Weak analogy moves from 'two cases are alike in some respects' to 'they share the relevant consequence,' without showing the shared respects are doing the work. Two-ton machines on public roads and pocket devices differ in exactly the respects that license cars.

question: A respondent dismisses a peer-reviewed study showing modest benefits of a new drug-trial safety claim by saying: 'The lead author once consulted for the manufacturer — therefore the study cannot be trusted.' She does not engage the methodology. The respondent's argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Conflict of interest — the respondent treats the lead author's past consulting tie as itself decisive against the vaccine schedule study, never engaging the methodology on its own terms.
choices: Conflict of interest — the respondent treats the lead author's past consulting tie as itself decisive against the vaccine schedule study, never engaging the methodology on its own terms.
Genetic fallacy — judging a claim by its origin — who made it, where it came from, what motive it might serve — rather than by the substance of the argument itself.
Ad hominem — attacking the person making the argument — their motives, character, or background — instead of engaging the content of what they actually said.
Cherry picking — presenting only the favorable data, cases, or quotations while quietly omitting the unfavorable ones that would change the overall picture.
context: A conflict of interest is a real epistemic warning sign, but it raises a question — was the methodology compromised? — rather than answering it. Using affiliation as automatic refutation without engaging the methods is the fallacy; insisting on disclosure and audit is not.

question: On a panel, Senator Quill argues: 'The bill is good because it gives families the right to choose their own healthcare. Rights are sacred — therefore opposing the bill is opposing rights.' He shifts from legal permission to natural rights mid-argument. Quill's framing commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Equivocation — Senator Quill's argument depends on shifting 'rights' from legal permission to sacred natural rights mid-sentence, so the bold conclusion only seems to follow.
choices: Equivocation — Senator Quill's argument depends on shifting 'rights' from legal permission to sacred natural rights mid-sentence, so the bold conclusion only seems to follow.
Motte-and-bailey — advancing a strong, controversial claim, then retreating to a weak, defensible version when challenged, and treating the weak one as if it proved the strong.
Straw man — distorting an opponent's claim into a wilder, easier-to-attack version, then refuting the distortion as though it were the original position.
False dilemma — framing a situation as a forced choice between two options when several other real positions are available and equally on the table.
context: Equivocation trades on multiple meanings of a single word. The argument's apparent strength depends on the reader hearing one meaning when the premises were established and another when the conclusion is drawn. Untangling the senses usually deflates the inference.

question: Asked to explain why his political movement's members keep getting caught in financial scandals, columnist Vance replies: 'Those people aren't TRUE believers in the movement — a true believer would never do such things.' He revises the definition with each new case. Vance's defense commits which logical fallacy?
answer: No true Scotsman — Vance saves his movement from each new financial scandal by tacking on a 'true believer' qualifier so any embarrassing member is retroactively defined out of the group.
choices: No true Scotsman — Vance saves his movement from each new financial scandal by tacking on a 'true believer' qualifier so any embarrassing member is retroactively defined out of the group.
Special pleading — claiming a general rule applies except in one's own case, without producing a principled reason why the case is genuinely different.
Moving the goalposts — changing the success criterion after the original standard has been met, redefining 'success' so the current outcome no longer qualifies as a win.
Genetic fallacy — judging a claim by its origin — who made it, where it came from, what motive it might serve — rather than by the substance of the argument itself.
context: No true Scotsman (Antony Flew, Thinking About Thinking, 1975) saves a sweeping claim from counterexamples by adding a purity qualifier retroactively. The original claim was empirical; the revision makes it true by definition, which is a different and weaker kind of claim.

question: Senator Hollis argues: 'A clear majority of voters support the new energy bill, so it's the right policy.' Polls in fact show 62% support. Even if Hollis's conclusion that the bill is correct policy happens to be right, what fallacy does the ARGUMENT itself commit?
answer: Bandwagon — Hollis treats a 62% support figure for the energy bill as itself a reason the bill is correct policy, regardless of whether the policy turns out to be sound on the merits.
choices: Bandwagon — Hollis treats a 62% support figure for the energy bill as itself a reason the bill is correct policy, regardless of whether the policy turns out to be sound on the merits.
Appeal to authority — treating an authority's say-so as decisive evidence even when the authority is outside their domain, paid, or speaking against the field's consensus.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a sample too small or too unrepresentative to license that scale of claim about the broader population.
Appeal to tradition — treating long-standing practice as itself a reason the practice is correct, without examining whether the original justification still holds up.
context: A bad argument can reach a correct conclusion by accident — the truth of the conclusion doesn't repair the form. Hollis's claim about the energy bill could turn out to be right policy on the merits, but the structural move from 62% support to 'therefore correct policy' is still a bandwagon step regardless of how the bill performs.

question: Op-ed writer Marsh dismisses an economist's published forecast that inflation will rise by saying: 'He divorced his wife last year — he's hardly in a position to lecture anyone on careful planning.' Even if Marsh happens to be right that inflation will rise, what fallacy does the ARGUMENT commit?
answer: Ad hominem — Marsh's argument turns on the economist's divorce rather than on his inflation forecast's methodology, so the conclusion stands or falls independently of the dig.
choices: Ad hominem — Marsh's argument turns on the economist's divorce rather than on his inflation forecast's methodology, so the conclusion stands or falls independently of the dig.
Genetic fallacy — judging a claim by its origin — who made it, where it came from, what motive it might serve — rather than by the substance of the argument itself.
Tu quoque — deflecting a criticism by alleging the critic — or some third party — is guilty of the same fault, without addressing the original charge.
Red herring — introducing an irrelevant point to divert attention from the actual question, leaving the original challenge quietly unanswered in the meantime.
context: A correct conclusion does not rehabilitate a bad argument. Even if inflation does rise, the PATH to that conclusion via the economist's divorce is structurally an ad hominem move. Conclusions can be true accidentally; the form of the argument is what the fallacy names.

question: Theology blogger Reeves writes: 'The book is inspired because the book itself says it is inspired, and an inspired book would not lie about being inspired.' Even if Reeves's conclusion that the book is inspired turned out to be correct, what fallacy does the ARGUMENT itself commit?
answer: Circular reasoning — Reeves's argument that the book is inspired rests on the book's own claim plus a premise that already assumes inspiration, so no independent ground is given.
choices: Circular reasoning — Reeves's argument that the book is inspired rests on the book's own claim plus a premise that already assumes inspiration, so no independent ground is given.
Appeal to authority — treating an authority's say-so as decisive evidence even when the authority is outside their domain, paid, or speaking against the field's consensus.
Equivocation — shifting the meaning of a key term partway through the argument so the conclusion only goes through because two senses are quietly swapped.
Appeal to ignorance — treating the absence of disproof as if it were positive evidence for the claim, when in fact lack of evidence is not itself evidence either way.
context: Circular reasoning fails as inference even when the conclusion is in fact true. The job of an argument is to give a reader who does not yet accept the conclusion a reason to accept it. An argument that quietly assumes the conclusion gives that reader nothing to work with.

question: Editorialist Crane argues: 'If we let this surveillance bill pass, within ten years we'll be living under constant state monitoring.' He cites no mechanism for the steps in between. Even if Crane's prediction turns out right, what fallacy does the ARGUMENT commit?
answer: Slippery slope — Crane's argument moves from the surveillance bill to constant state monitoring without showing why each intermediate step is genuinely required to follow.
choices: Slippery slope — Crane's argument moves from the surveillance bill to constant state monitoring without showing why each intermediate step is genuinely required to follow.
False cause — treating a correlation between two variables as if it established that one of them is causing the other, with no mechanism or controls in evidence.
Appeal to ignorance — treating the absence of disproof as if it were positive evidence for the claim, when in fact lack of evidence is not itself evidence either way.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a sample too small or too unrepresentative to license that scale of claim about the broader population.
context: Slippery slopes can describe genuine causal chains; the question is whether the argument shows the links or just asserts them. Crane's prediction might turn out true while the argument is still structurally weak. Form and conclusion are independent dimensions.

question: Wellness influencer Pace claims: 'I took the new supplement on Monday and my migraine was gone by Friday, so the supplement works.' She runs no trial and reports no comparison case. Even if the supplement does happen to work, what fallacy does the ARGUMENT commit?
answer: Post hoc — Pace's argument that the supplement works rests on her Monday dose preceding her Friday recovery, with no comparison case showing the recovery wouldn't have happened anyway.
choices: Post hoc — Pace's argument that the supplement works rests on her Monday dose preceding her Friday recovery, with no comparison case showing the recovery wouldn't have happened anyway.
Anecdotal evidence — leaning on one or two memorable personal stories to support a general claim, when systematic data would be the relevant kind of evidence here.
Survivorship bias — drawing lessons only from the cases that survived a selection process, while ignoring the silent majority whose failure would change the conclusion.
Cherry picking — presenting only the favorable data, cases, or quotations while quietly omitting the unfavorable ones that would change the overall picture.
context: Post hoc ergo propter hoc treats sequence as proof of cause. The supplement may in fact work — that's a separate, testable question. The argument from one user's recovery to general efficacy does not show it, regardless of whether better evidence later might.

question: On her podcast, host Linnea says: 'My uncle smoked two packs a day, lived to 92, and was sharp till the end. Clearly the health establishment overstates smoking risk.' She cites no population data on smokers' lifespans. Linnea's argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Anecdotal evidence — Linnea's two-packs-a-day uncle is one memorable case used to override the population-level data on smoking that would actually settle the lifespan question.
choices: Anecdotal evidence — Linnea's two-packs-a-day uncle is one memorable case used to override the population-level data on smoking that would actually settle the lifespan question.
Survivorship bias — drawing lessons only from the cases that survived a selection process, while ignoring the silent majority whose failure would change the conclusion.
Cherry picking — presenting only the favorable data, cases, or quotations while quietly omitting the unfavorable ones that would change the overall picture.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a sample too small or too unrepresentative to license that scale of claim about the broader population.
context: Anecdotes serve well as illustrations and badly as evidence for claims about populations. One long-lived smoker is consistent with the population statistics on smoking, since the distribution of outcomes is wide. The relevant comparison is risk-adjusted, not memorable.

question: After a senator proposes raising the federal minimum wage by $1.50 over three years, a televised opponent responds: 'My colleague wants to destroy small business and force employers to pay teenagers $50 an hour.' The senator proposed neither. The opponent's reply commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Straw man — the opponent reshapes the senator's $1.50-over-three-years proposal into a $50-per-hour-for-teenagers demand that destroys small business, then attacks the distortion.
choices: Straw man — the opponent reshapes the senator's $1.50-over-three-years proposal into a $50-per-hour-for-teenagers demand that destroys small business, then attacks the distortion.
False dilemma — framing a situation as a forced choice between two options when several other real positions are available and equally on the table.
Slippery slope — claiming one modest step must inevitably trigger a chain of progressively worse outcomes, without showing why each link is genuinely required.
Ad hominem — attacking the person making the argument — their motives, character, or background — instead of engaging the content of what they actually said.
context: Televised straw-manning is especially common because the distortion is more dramatic than the real proposal, and the original speaker may not get rebuttal time. The honest standard is asking whether the response addresses the actual proposal or a worse-cousin caricature.

question: Asked at a press conference about an accounting scandal at his firm, CEO Boyd replies: 'You know, this country's real problem is the loss of manufacturing jobs — that's what I'm focused on.' He gives no answer about the accounting. Boyd's reply commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Red herring — Boyd shifts the press conference from his firm's accounting scandal to a national manufacturing-jobs topic, leaving the actual accounting question quietly unanswered.
choices: Red herring — Boyd shifts the press conference from his firm's accounting scandal to a national manufacturing-jobs topic, leaving the actual accounting question quietly unanswered.
Tu quoque — deflecting a criticism by alleging the critic — or some third party — is guilty of the same fault, without addressing the original charge.
Straw man — distorting an opponent's claim into a wilder, easier-to-attack version, then refuting the distortion as though it were the original position.
Gish gallop — burying a respondent under so many low-quality points at once that none can be addressed in the available time, then claiming the points stand.
context: A red herring is a deliberately introduced irrelevance — a topic chosen for its plausibility and emotional pull, not for its relation to the original question. Politicians and executives use it because the camera follows the new topic, not the unanswered one.

question: A wellness brand cites actor Tate Stein, who plays a doctor on a long-running medical drama, as their supplement's endorser: 'Tate believes in this product.' Stein has no medical training. The brand's framing commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Appeal to authority — the wellness brand treats actor Tate Stein's TV-drama endorsement as evidence its supplement works, when his expertise is in playing a doctor, not practicing it.
choices: Appeal to authority — the wellness brand treats actor Tate Stein's TV-drama endorsement as evidence its supplement works, when his expertise is in playing a doctor, not practicing it.
False equivalence — treating two cases or sources as comparable when they differ in scale, evidence base, or kind, smuggling parity into the framing of the comparison.
Genetic fallacy — judging a claim by its origin — who made it, where it came from, what motive it might serve — rather than by the substance of the argument itself.
Conflict of interest — treating a researcher's funding source or affiliation as itself decisive against the work, rather than examining the methods and evidence on the merits.
context: Appeal to authority is not always fallacious — citing a domain expert in their domain is legitimate. The fallacy is using authority outside the relevant field, ignoring conflict of interest, or treating a single name as decisive against the field's consensus. Acting is not medicine.

question: Op-ed columnist Diaz cites three viral incidents in two months and concludes: 'Clearly American workplaces have become uniformly hostile environments — there is no professional space safe from this anymore.' He cites no broader survey data. Diaz's argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Hasty generalization — Diaz extrapolates from three viral workplace incidents in two months to a universal claim that no American professional space is now safe from such hostility.
choices: Hasty generalization — Diaz extrapolates from three viral workplace incidents in two months to a universal claim that no American professional space is now safe from such hostility.
Anecdotal evidence — leaning on one or two memorable personal stories to support a general claim, when systematic data would be the relevant kind of evidence here.
Cherry picking — presenting only the favorable data, cases, or quotations while quietly omitting the unfavorable ones that would change the overall picture.
Survivorship bias — drawing lessons only from the cases that survived a selection process, while ignoring the silent majority whose failure would change the conclusion.
context: Viral cases are sampled by virality, not by representativeness. Three dramatic incidents spreading on social media tell us about the share-worthiness of those particular incidents; drawing a universal conclusion about millions of American workplaces requires survey data.

question: A cable pundit insists 'every serious economist agrees the tariff package is a disaster.' Confronted with several named PhD economists from major departments who endorse the package, he replies: 'Well, no SERIOUS economist would endorse that.' Diagnose the rhetorical maneuver.
answer: No true Scotsman — the pundit retroactively narrows 'serious economist' to exclude the named PhDs who endorse the tariff, preserving his sweeping claim by stipulation rather than evidence.
choices: No true Scotsman — the pundit retroactively narrows 'serious economist' to exclude the named PhDs who endorse the tariff, preserving his sweeping claim by stipulation rather than evidence.
Appeal to authority — leaning on the credentials or reputation of a source rather than engaging the substance of the dispute, as if institutional standing settled what the argument has to establish.
Cherry picking — selecting only the supporting cases, intervals, or metrics from a larger body of evidence while suppressing the contrary cases that would force a revision of the claim.
Genetic fallacy — dismissing or accepting an argument based on its origin, the motives of its source, or its funding, rather than evaluating the content of the argument on its own evidentiary terms.
context: Antony Flew named the No True Scotsman fallacy in Thinking About Thinking (1975): a sweeping claim survives a counterexample only because the category is redefined retroactively. The move looks like a clarification but functions as immunization against any disconfirming case.

question: A columnist writes that 'modern technology is destroying childhood' — citing teen depression data and demanding sweeping platform bans. Challenged, she retreats: 'I only meant smartphones have downsides for some kids.' Once unchallenged, she resumes the destruction-of-childhood framing. Diagnose the rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Motte-and-bailey — the columnist alternates between the modest defensible claim (smartphones have downsides for some kids) and the bold controversial claim (destruction of childhood) as she defends or asserts.
choices: Motte-and-bailey — the columnist alternates between the modest defensible claim (smartphones have downsides for some kids) and the bold controversial claim (destruction of childhood) as she defends or asserts.
Equivocation — shifting the meaning of a key term between premises so the argument's apparent validity rides on a hidden change of sense rather than on a stable inference.

Moving the goalposts — redefining the success criterion after a prediction has been met or disconfirmed, so the original test no longer counts and the position remains permanently unfalsifiable in practice.
Straw man — distorting an opponent's position into a wilder or weaker version that is easier to refute, then attacking the distortion as if the original argument had been engaged.
context: Nicholas Shackel coined the motte-and-bailey label (2005), drawing on medieval castle architecture: the bailey is the productive land you actually want, the motte the small fortified keep you retreat to under attack. The argumentative version trades on conflating the two claims as if they were one.

question: On a podcast, a commentator dismisses a peer-reviewed study contradicting his preferred policy: 'Replicate it ten times with pre-registration before I take it seriously.' Asked about a study supporting that same policy with methodology no stronger, he simply cites it as proven. Diagnose the rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Isolated demand for rigor — the commentator applies a near-impossible evidentiary standard to the contradicting study while granting the supporting study a free pass on the same methodology.
choices: Isolated demand for rigor — the commentator applies a near-impossible evidentiary standard to the contradicting study while granting the supporting study a free pass on the same methodology.
Cherry picking — selecting only the supporting cases, intervals, or metrics from a larger body of evidence while suppressing the contrary cases that would force a revision of the claim.

Moving the goalposts — redefining the success criterion after a prediction has been met or disconfirmed, so the original test no longer counts and the position remains permanently unfalsifiable in practice.
Genetic fallacy — dismissing or accepting an argument based on its origin, the motives of its source, or its funding, rather than evaluating the content of the argument on its own evidentiary terms.
context: Scott Alexander gave the move its current name in 'The Isolated Demand for Rigor' (2014). The tell is asymmetry: the same study design that disqualifies inconvenient findings is silently accepted when it produces convenient ones. Rigor is selectively, not consistently, applied.

question: In a televised debate, one candidate rattles off seventeen distinct dubious claims in ninety seconds — selective statistics, mangled quotes, dropped citations. The other candidate, with two minutes total, can only address three. Pundits afterward declare the second 'unable to rebut.' Diagnose the first candidate's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Gish gallop — the candidate buries the opponent under more dubious claims than can be refuted in the available time, so partial rebuttal of seventeen claims is misread by pundits as concession.
choices: Gish gallop — the candidate buries the opponent under more dubious claims than can be refuted in the available time, so partial rebuttal of seventeen claims is misread by pundits as concession.
Red herring — dropping an irrelevant but provocative point into the discussion so attention shifts off the original question and the substantive issue quietly goes unanswered in the diversion.
Burden-shifting — demanding the critic disprove a claim rather than the claim's defender support it, inverting the usual rule that the party asserting a positive thesis carries the case for it.
Straw man — distorting an opponent's position into a wilder or weaker version that is easier to refute, then attacking the distortion as if the original argument had been engaged.
context: Named for creationist Duane Gish, who deployed the technique routinely in 1970s-80s evolution debates. Eugenie Scott of the National Center for Science Education popularized the label. The asymmetry between production and refutation cost is what makes the maneuver work rhetorically.

question: An op-ed argues: 'Freedom requires limits — without traffic laws, no one is free to drive safely. Therefore restrictions on speech online actually expand freedom, just as traffic laws do.' The argument turns on the word 'freedom' carrying very different senses in its two halves. Diagnose the rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Equivocation — the word 'freedom' shifts between coordination-against-collisions (traffic laws) and political-liberty-from-state-action (speech) so the inference rides on a hidden change of sense.
choices: Equivocation — the word 'freedom' shifts between coordination-against-collisions (traffic laws) and political-liberty-from-state-action (speech) so the inference rides on a hidden change of sense.
False equivalence — treating two cases as morally or evidentially comparable when their relevant features differ in magnitude, kind, or causal role in ways the framing quietly suppresses.

Composition fallacy — inferring that what is true of the parts must be true of the whole, treating individually-true facts as if they automatically aggregated into a true claim about the system they compose.
Straw man — distorting an opponent's position into a wilder or weaker version that is easier to refute, then attacking the distortion as if the original argument had been engaged.
context: Equivocation has been catalogued since Aristotle (Sophistical Refutations). The move can be deliberate or accidental; what matters is that the apparent validity of the argument depends on a stable meaning for the key term, and the term is not stable. Naming the senses is the fix.

question: A wire-service report on a vaccine controversy reads: 'Critics and supporters disagree, with supporters citing fifteen large randomized trials and critics citing a documentary featuring two personal anecdotes.' The piece presents both as substantive sides of an open scientific debate. Diagnose the journalistic framing's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: False equivalence — the report treats fifteen large trials and a documentary of two anecdotes as comparable evidence simply because both exist, suppressing the gulf in their actual evidentiary weight.
choices: False equivalence — the report treats fifteen large trials and a documentary of two anecdotes as comparable evidence simply because both exist, suppressing the gulf in their actual evidentiary weight.
Appeal to popularity — treating widespread agreement, viewership, or follower counts as evidence the underlying claim is true, as if popular acceptance measured anything beyond popular acceptance.

Anecdotal evidence — treating a vivid individual case as if it overrode the systematic statistical pattern, as if one striking story outweighed the aggregate evidence the story is being used to dismiss.
Appeal to authority — leaning on the credentials or reputation of a source rather than engaging the substance of the dispute, as if institutional standing settled what the argument has to establish.
context: False equivalence (or false balance) is a recognized failure mode of both-sides journalism, documented across coverage of evolution, climate, and vaccines. The cost is hidden: by presenting asymmetric evidence as symmetric, the framing conveys uncertainty that the actual evidence does not.

question: Asked about credible reports of mass detentions in his country, an official responds: 'And what about the prisons in YOUR country? You have police shootings every week. How dare you lecture us.' He does not address whether the detentions occurred or were lawful. Diagnose the official's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Whataboutism — the official deflects the detention question by pivoting to alleged wrongs of the questioner's country, leaving the original charge about mass detentions entirely unanswered.
choices: Whataboutism — the official deflects the detention question by pivoting to alleged wrongs of the questioner's country, leaving the original charge about mass detentions entirely unanswered.
Tu quoque — deflecting a charge by alleging the critic is guilty of the same or worse conduct, as if symmetrical imperfection answered the substantive point at issue.
Red herring — dropping an irrelevant but provocative point into the discussion so attention shifts off the original question and the substantive issue quietly goes unanswered in the diversion.
Ad hominem — attacking the character, motives, or identity of the arguer in place of engaging the substance of the argument, as if a fault in the speaker disqualified what they actually said.
context: Whataboutism is the Cold-War-era English label for a Soviet press tactic: any criticism met with 'and you lynch Negroes.' It is closely related to tu quoque but distinguished by being deployed by states or institutions rather than between individuals, and by its purely deflective function.

question: A market guru promotes his service by highlighting twelve trades that produced spectacular gains over the past three years. He omits the ninety-three trades over that span that broke even or lost money. The chosen twelve become the 'predicted-it-all-along' track record. Diagnose the guru's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Texas sharpshooter — the guru draws the analytic target (his 'track record') around the twelve winning trades after the fact, presenting a cluster carved out of the data as if it had been predicted.
choices: Texas sharpshooter — the guru draws the analytic target (his 'track record') around the twelve winning trades after the fact, presenting a cluster carved out of the data as if it had been predicted.
Cherry picking — selecting only the supporting cases, intervals, or metrics from a larger body of evidence while suppressing the contrary cases that would force a revision of the claim.
Hindsight bias — treating an outcome as having been predictable from prior evidence only after the outcome is known, smuggling later knowledge into a reconstruction of what could have been foreseen.

Anecdotal evidence — treating a vivid individual case as if it overrode the systematic statistical pattern, as if one striking story outweighed the aggregate evidence the story is being used to dismiss.
context: The Texas sharpshooter fallacy is named for a marksman who fires at a barn first and then paints the target around the bullet holes. It differs from straightforward cherry picking by emphasizing the post-hoc target-drawing, common in epidemiology, finance, and parapsychology claims.

question: After a market crash, an analyst writes: 'The warning signs were obvious all along — anyone paying attention should have seen it coming.' He cites indicators that, before the crash, his own newsletter had dismissed as noise, and that pointed in conflicting directions at the time. Diagnose the analyst's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Hindsight bias — the analyst reconstructs the pre-crash signals as 'obvious all along,' smuggling knowledge of the outcome into a tidy story about indicators he himself read differently at the time.
choices: Hindsight bias — the analyst reconstructs the pre-crash signals as 'obvious all along,' smuggling knowledge of the outcome into a tidy story about indicators he himself read differently at the time.
Texas sharpshooter — drawing the analytic target around the clusters in already-collected data so a pattern that was carved out after the fact is presented as if it had been predicted in advance.
Cherry picking — selecting only the supporting cases, intervals, or metrics from a larger body of evidence while suppressing the contrary cases that would force a revision of the claim.
Post hoc — treating sequence as proof of causation: because B followed A, A must have caused B, with no account of confounders, base rates, or whether the link is mechanistic at all.
context: Baruch Fischhoff documented the hindsight bias experimentally in the 1970s, showing subjects consistently overestimate what they would have predicted before knowing the outcome. The bias is stable, robust, and especially common in financial and political post-mortems.

question: A self-help guru defends his unfulfilled prediction that his readers would 'all be millionaires by thirty': 'First, most of you didn't follow the program. Second, the program never promised that. Third, the ones who did follow it actually are millionaires — just not yet in cash terms.' Diagnose the rhetorical maneuver in this stacked defense.
answer: Kettle logic — the guru's three excuses (readers didn't follow, the program never promised, those who followed succeeded) undercut each other; the second contradicts the third, the first contradicts the second.
choices: Kettle logic — the guru's three excuses (readers didn't follow, the program never promised, those who followed succeeded) undercut each other; the second contradicts the third, the first contradicts the second.

Moving the goalposts — redefining the success criterion after a prediction has been met or disconfirmed, so the original test no longer counts and the position remains permanently unfalsifiable in practice.
Equivocation — shifting the meaning of a key term between premises so the argument's apparent validity rides on a hidden change of sense rather than on a stable inference.
Motte-and-bailey — switching between a defensible modest claim (the motte) and a controversial bold claim (the bailey) depending on whether one is asserting or defending the position.
context: Freud illustrated kettle logic with a man accused of returning a borrowed kettle damaged: 'I never borrowed it; it was already broken when I borrowed it; it was undamaged when I returned it.' Each defense if true refutes the others. Stacking them reveals motivated rather than truth-tracking reasoning.

question: A nutrition-influencer press release: 'Our study shows participants lost an average of fifteen pounds.' Buried details: participants were self-selected from the influencer's own paid program, had to complete all six months to count, and ninety-three percent of enrollees dropped out. Diagnose the rhetorical maneuver embedded in the press release.
answer: Cherry picking — the press release reports only the seven percent of paid program participants who completed all six months, treating that survivorship-selected slice as if it represented the program's typical effect.
choices: Cherry picking — the press release reports only the seven percent of paid program participants who completed all six months, treating that survivorship-selected slice as if it represented the program's typical effect.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a sample too small, too unrepresentative, or too self-selected to support the size of the claim being made about the general population.
Texas sharpshooter — drawing the analytic target around the clusters in already-collected data so a pattern that was carved out after the fact is presented as if it had been predicted in advance.

Moving the goalposts — redefining the success criterion after a prediction has been met or disconfirmed, so the original test no longer counts and the position remains permanently unfalsifiable in practice.
context: Cherry picking is a class of selection bias formally studied in clinical trial methodology and epidemiology; survivorship bias is its commonest form in commercial program evaluation. The fix is intention-to-treat analysis (counting everyone who started, not only those who finished).

question: Pressed on whether her wellness regimen actually works, an influencer with eleven million followers replies: 'If it didn't work, would I have eleven million followers? Would brands pay me what they pay me? The audience itself proves the regimen delivers.' Diagnose the influencer's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Appeal to popularity — the influencer treats eleven million followers and brand-deal volume as evidence that her wellness regimen produces results, conflating audience size with substantive efficacy.
choices: Appeal to popularity — the influencer treats eleven million followers and brand-deal volume as evidence that her wellness regimen produces results, conflating audience size with substantive efficacy.
Appeal to authority — leaning on the credentials or reputation of a source rather than engaging the substance of the dispute, as if institutional standing settled what the argument has to establish.
Genetic fallacy — dismissing or accepting an argument based on its origin, the motives of its source, or its funding, rather than evaluating the content of the argument on its own evidentiary terms.

Circular reasoning — smuggling the conclusion into the premises so the argument restates rather than supports its claim, with the result that whoever already accepts the conclusion is the only audience persuaded.
context: Appeal to popularity (ad populum) becomes especially dangerous in attention-economy contexts where audience metrics are themselves heavily engineered by platform algorithms tuned to engagement, not truthfulness. Follower counts measure something — just not what they are being asked to measure.

question: In 2018 a guru predicted civilization would collapse 'within five years.' In 2023 challenged to explain why this hadn't happened, he replies: 'Collapse is a process, not an event. We're in early collapse right now. The five-year window referred to onset, not completion.' Diagnose the guru's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Moving the goalposts — the guru redefines the original five-year collapse prediction after it failed, reinterpreting 'collapse' as 'early-stage onset' so no future state could ever falsify the claim.
choices: Moving the goalposts — the guru redefines the original five-year collapse prediction after it failed, reinterpreting 'collapse' as 'early-stage onset' so no future state could ever falsify the claim.
Equivocation — shifting the meaning of a key term between premises so the argument's apparent validity rides on a hidden change of sense rather than on a stable inference.
Motte-and-bailey — switching between a defensible modest claim (the motte) and a controversial bold claim (the bailey) depending on whether one is asserting or defending the position.
Burden-shifting — demanding the critic disprove a claim rather than the claim's defender support it, inverting the usual rule that the party asserting a positive thesis carries the case for it.
