context: Presentism (A.N. Prior, John Bigelow) is the everyday default: reality is exhausted by what is happening now. The columnist's tell is treating the past as mere records and the future as mere plans -- only the present gets to be real. Its main rivals make more of time real.

question: An astronomer says: 'The cosmos is a book still being written. Every page already inked is fixed and real -- but the next page does not exist until the pen reaches it. Reality literally grows as time moves forward.' Which view of time is she using?
answer: Growing-block -- the past and present are real, but the future isn't yet.
choices: Growing-block -- the past and present are real, but the future isn't yet.
Presentism -- only the present is real; the past no longer exists at all.
Eternalism -- past, present, and future are all equally real, full stop.
Time is an illusion -- no moment is more real than another; passage is felt.
context: The growing-block view (C.D. Broad, Scientific Thought, 1923; Michael Tooley) is the intuitive middle: the past is closed and real, the future open and unreal, and reality literally grows. The astronomer's tell is the asymmetry -- inked past, blank future -- which neither presentism nor eternalism allows.

question: On a panel, a guest says: 'I'm the same person I was at six because I remember being that child. My body changed completely, but an unbroken chain of memory links me to him.' Which view of personal identity is he using?
answer: Memory continuity -- a chain of memory makes you the same person over time.
choices: Memory continuity -- a chain of memory makes you the same person over time.
Bodily continuity -- one persisting body is what keeps you the same person.
Soul theory -- one immaterial soul, not memory or body, carries identity.
No-self -- there is no lasting 'you'; the felt sameness is an illusion.
context: John Locke (Essay, II.27, 1689) located personal identity in continuity of consciousness -- above all, memory. The guest's tell is staking sameness on the remembered link to his younger self, while waving off the totally changed body. Critics from Reid on press memory loss and false memories.

question: Of her father with advanced Alzheimer's, a daughter says: 'Even once he couldn't remember any of us, even his own name, he was still my father -- same body, same person. Memory isn't what makes you who you are.' Which view is she using?
answer: Bodily continuity -- the same living body is what keeps you the same person.
choices: Bodily continuity -- the same living body is what keeps you the same person.
Memory continuity -- a chain of memory is what makes you the same person.
Soul theory -- one immaterial soul, not body or memory, carries identity.
Narrative identity -- a coherent self-told life-story is what makes you you.
context: Animalism (Eric Olson, The Human Animal, 1997) holds that we are essentially living organisms, so identity is just the body's continuity. The daughter's tell is keeping her father as the same person precisely where memory is gone -- the body carries it. Bernard Williams pressed body-swap cases the same way.

question: A teleporter scans every atom of the traveler, destroys the original, and builds an exact copy on Mars with all his memories. A philosopher writes: 'The original is dead. What arrives is a perfect duplicate, not the traveler.' Which view of identity is this?
answer: Bodily continuity -- one unbroken body is needed; the copy is someone new.
choices: Bodily continuity -- one unbroken body is needed; the copy is someone new.
Memory continuity -- the copy has the memories, so the copy is the traveler.
Soul theory -- the traveler survives only if an immaterial soul transferred.
No-self -- there was never a single traveler, so nothing is lost or copied.
context: Derek Parfit (Reasons and Persons, 1984) made the teleporter central. The philosopher's tell is that the body's thread is cut, so whatever wakes on Mars is a duplicate -- a bodily-continuity verdict. Parfit's own twist was the opposite: that strict identity may not be what matters in survival.

question: In class a student argues: 'There's no single self running through your life -- just a stream of momentary experiences that memory and habit stitch into a story. The lasting self is a useful fiction.' Which view of personal identity is the student using?
answer: No-self -- there's no lasting self; the felt sameness is stitched together.
choices: No-self -- there's no lasting self; the felt sameness is stitched together.
Memory continuity -- a chain of memory makes the stream one real person.
Soul theory -- one unchanging soul stands beneath the shifting experiences.
Bodily continuity -- one living body, not the stream, is what makes you you.
context: Hume's bundle theory (Treatise, 1739) and Buddhist anatta both deny any persisting subject: there is only the stream of experiences. The student's tell is calling the lasting self a 'useful fiction' that memory imposes -- dissolving the puzzle by denying the thing that was supposed to persist.

question: A philosophy class debates Theseus's ship: planks are replaced one by one until none of the original wood remains. A student argues: 'It's still the same ship. What makes a ship a ship is its design and function, not the particular wood. Replace one plank or all of them — same ship.' Which principle of identity does the student defend?
answer: Form / functional identity — a thing persists across time if and only if its structure and function persist; the particular matter it is made of is replaceable without disrupting identity.
choices: Form / functional identity — a thing persists across time if and only if its structure and function persist; the particular matter it is made of is replaceable without disrupting identity.
Mereological essentialism — a thing persists across time if and only if exactly the same parts persist; on this view every plank-replacement strictly produces a numerically different ship.
Material identity — a thing persists across time if and only if the same matter persists; the gradual replacement strictly produces a sequence of distinct ships sharing only a name.
Conventional identity — there is no deep fact about sameness; calling the repaired ship 'the same' is a habit of speech with no metaphysical weight one way or the other in this case.
context: Plutarch reports Theseus's ship in Life of Theseus (~75 AD). Hobbes added the reassembled-from-discarded-planks twist in De Corpore (1655) to sharpen the dilemma. Aristotle's distinction between substantial form and matter informs the form-based reply.

question: A blogger argues: 'A lasting object is its whole history stretched out through time, the way a road stretches across the land. The object you meet now is just one slice of a longer, worm-shaped whole.' Which view of how things persist is this?
answer: Four-dimensionalism -- a thing is a time-stretched whole; now is one slice.
choices: Four-dimensionalism -- a thing is a time-stretched whole; now is one slice.
Three-dimensionalism -- the whole thing is fully present at each moment.
Stage theory -- a thing is just today's stage, linked to past ones as kin.
Same-parts-only -- swap any part and you get a numerically new object.
context: Four-dimensionalism (David Lewis, 1986; Ted Sider, 2001) treats persisting things as 'spacetime worms' with a temporal part at each moment. The blogger's tell is the road analogy and the 'one slice' -- you only ever meet a part of the worm. Its main rival says the whole thing is wholly present each moment.

question: A philosopher rejects the 'spacetime worm' picture of objects: 'A cup is not a long thing stretched through time with a separate slice for each moment. The whole cup is there at noon, and the same whole cup is there again at one o'clock.' Which view of persistence is she defending?
answer: Endurance — the whole object is fully present at every moment it exists.
choices: Endurance — the whole object is fully present at every moment it exists.
Perdurance — the object is a 4-D worm; each moment is one time-slice of it.
Stage view — the object just is the present slice; past slices are its counterparts.
Bundle view — at each moment it is just a fresh bundle of properties.
context: Three-dimensionalism, or endurantism, is the common-sense side: a persisting thing is wholly present at each moment, the way you are wholly here now. Defended by E.J. Lowe and Sally Haslanger against the four-dimensional 'spacetime worm' picture of David Lewis and Theodore Sider. (On Sider's stage view, the object is the present instantaneous stage, tied to other stages by temporal-counterpart relations — not the same as endurance.)

question: In a seminar on possibility, one philosopher makes a claim he admits draws the incredulous stare: 'When we say something COULD have happened, we mean it really does happen — somewhere. Other possible worlds exist concretely, as solid as ours.' Which view is he defending?
answer: Modal realism — other possible worlds exist concretely, as real as our own.
choices: Modal realism — other possible worlds exist concretely, as real as our own.
Ersatzism — possible worlds are just abstract descriptions, not real places.
Actualism — only this world exists; possibility is a feature of how it could go.
Fictionalism — other-world talk is only true inside a useful made-up story.
context: David Lewis's On the Plurality of Worlds (1986) defends this 'modal realism': possible worlds are concrete, each with its own inhabitants. 'The incredulous stare' is Lewis's own term for the reaction colleagues gave the view — part of the literature. Rivals (Plantinga, Stalnaker) keep possible worlds as abstractions instead.

question: Asked whether a world where Rome never fell really EXISTS somewhere, a philosopher answers: 'There are no other worlds — just THIS one, which could merely have gone differently. Possibility is a feature of how the actual world is.' Which view is she defending?
answer: Actualism — only the actual world exists; possibility is a feature of it.
choices: Actualism — only the actual world exists; possibility is a feature of it.
Modal realism — other worlds exist concretely, every bit as real as ours.
Ersatzism — other worlds exist, but only as abstract sets of descriptions.
Fictionalism — other-world talk is only true inside a convenient story.
context: Actualism (Alvin Plantinga, The Nature of Necessity, 1974; Robert Stalnaker) is the majority view among today's metaphysicians: nothing exists but the actual world. It may still USE abstract possible worlds as a tool, while denying any other concrete world is out there.

question: A philosopher holds up an apple: 'There is no hidden THING here wearing the red, the round, the sweet. Strip those away and nothing is left underneath. The apple just IS that cluster of properties, bundled together at one spot.' Which view of objects is she defending?
answer: Bundle theory — an object just is its cluster of properties, nothing underneath.
choices: Bundle theory — an object just is its cluster of properties, nothing underneath.
Substance theory — a thing underneath HAS the properties and bears them.
Bare-particular view — under the qualities sits a bare peg with no features of its own.
Trope theory — the properties are private particulars, never truly shared by two.
context: Bundle theory traces to Hume (Treatise, 1739) and is defended today by L.A. Paul. Its great rival, substance theory (E.J. Lowe), insists on a thing that bears the properties; the 'bare particular' view keeps a featureless core — with no qualities of its own — to ground their unity.

question: A philosopher answers the 'bundle' crowd: 'An apple is not just properties hanging together. There is a THING there — the apple — that HAS the red and the round. Take those away and it loses qualities, but it was the apple that was carrying them.' Which view is he defending?
answer: Substance theory — a thing underlies the properties and bears them.
choices: Substance theory — a thing underlies the properties and bears them.
Bundle theory — the apple just is its properties, with nothing underneath.
Trope theory — properties are private particulars merely held together at a spot.
Process view — the apple is an ongoing happening, not a thing bearing properties.
context: Substance theory has Aristotelian roots (Categories) and modern defenders in E.J. Lowe and Michael Loux: a thing distinct from its properties bears them. The standing rival, bundle theory, has pressed back since Hume that no such extra 'thing' is ever found.

question: Holding two red apples, a philosopher argues: 'These two really share something — the very same redness, one thing showing up in both. Deny that shared redness is real, and you cannot say what the apples have in common at all.' Which view of properties is he defending?
answer: Realism — the shared redness is one real thing, repeated in both apples.
choices: Realism — the shared redness is one real thing, repeated in both apples.
Nominalism — only the two apples are real; 'both red' just records a resemblance.
Trope theory — each apple has its OWN redness; the two only closely resemble.
Conceptualism — the shared redness exists only as a concept in the mind.
context: Realism about universals runs from Plato's Forms and Aristotle to David Armstrong (Universals and Scientific Realism, 1978): a property can be one entity repeated across many things. Nominalists (Quine, Goodman) deny universals; trope theorists (D.C. Williams) make each instance its own particular.

question: A sculptor presses a lump of clay into a statue. The two fill one space and share every particle. Yet squash it flat: the statue is gone, the lump remains — so they cannot be exactly one thing. A critic concludes: 'Two objects, sharing one matter.' Which view is she defending?
answer: Constitution — the lump constitutes the statue but is a distinct object from it.
choices: Constitution — the lump constitutes the statue but is a distinct object from it.
Identity — statue and lump are one object described under two different names.
Eliminativism — neither exists; only particles arranged statue-wise are real.
Conventionalism — whether it is one or two is settled by our words, not the world.
context: The statue-and-lump puzzle (Allan Gibbard, 1975; Lynne Rudder Baker, Persons and Bodies, 2000) asks whether things sharing all their matter can still differ. Constitution theorists say yes — the two come apart in what survives squashing; identity-theorists insist one matter means one object.

question: Derek Parfit argued that what makes you the same person at 60 as at 6 isn't your body or any single memory — and that identity itself may not be what matters. What does, he said, is an overlapping chain of memories, plans, and traits linking day to day. Which view of the self is this?
answer: Psychological continuity — you persist through a chain of overlapping mental states.
choices: Psychological continuity — you persist through a chain of overlapping mental states.
Bodily continuity — you persist as long as one living organism does.
Soul theory — an immaterial self carries through, whatever mind or body does.
No-self view — there is no lasting 'you'; the felt thread is an illusion.
context: Derek Parfit (Reasons and Persons, 1984) widened Locke's memory test into 'psychological continuity' — overlapping chains of memories, intentions, and personality. His twist: identity itself may not be what matters; the continuity does. Bodily continuity (Olson's animalism) and soul theory (Swinburne) are the live rivals.

question: Heraclitus said you cannot step in the same river twice. A modern defender presses the point: a river, a fire, a storm aren't really things — they are events, things that HAPPEN over time. The event is what's real; calling it a thing is just shorthand. Which view of what exists is this?
answer: Process view — the basic items are ongoing events, and 'objects' are derived from them.
choices: Process view — the basic items are ongoing events, and 'objects' are derived from them.
Endurance view — a river is one whole thing, fully present at each moment it exists.
Four-dimensional view — a river is one object spread across time, sliced moment by moment.
Same-matter view — a river is just the water in it now; new water, new river.
context: Process metaphysics runs from Heraclitus (~500 BC) to Whitehead (Process and Reality, 1929) and today's Rescher and Seibt. It makes process basic and treats talk of stable 'objects' as a useful shorthand — the reverse of the substance tradition that starts with things and adds change.

question: In his death cell, hours before drinking the hemlock, Socrates argues to his friends that what survives every change isn't memory or the body, which both change past recognition. It is one immaterial self that carries through every change. Which view of personal identity is this?
answer: Soul theory — one immaterial self persists, and memory and body are only its vehicles.
choices: Soul theory — one immaterial self persists, and memory and body are only its vehicles.
Memory continuity — you persist only as far back as your chain of memories reaches.
Bodily continuity — you persist as long as one living organism keeps going.
No-self view — there is no lasting self at all, only a stream of fresh experiences.
context: Substance dualism runs from Plato's Phaedo — Socrates' death-cell argument (~399 BC) — through Descartes (Meditations VI, 1641) to Richard Swinburne (The Evolution of the Soul, 1986): the person is an immaterial substance the body merely houses. It is a minority view among today's philosophers but still seriously defended.

question: Newcomb's puzzle: Box A shows $1,000. Box B is sealed. A near-perfect predictor put $1,000,000 in B only if she foresaw you taking B alone. A friend says: 'Take only B — the fact that I'd one-box is itself the best sign the million is already there.' Which way of deciding is she using?
answer: Evidential — choose the act that is the best sign of a good outcome.
choices: Evidential — choose the act that is the best sign of a good outcome.
Causal — take both, since a sealed box's contents can't be changed now.
Dominance — take both, because whatever is in B, box A only adds money.
Skeptical — reject the puzzle; no flawless predictor of a free choice can exist.
context: Devised by physicist William Newcomb, made famous by Robert Nozick (1969). Because the boxes are already filled, taking both can never lose money — yet one-boxers keep winning the million. Evidential decision theory (Jeffrey) one-boxes on the 'best sign' logic; causal decision theory (Lewis, Joyce) two-boxes. The split is unresolved.

question: A Frankfurt case: Jones votes X entirely on his own. Unknown to him, a brain chip would have forced that vote if he had wavered — but he never did, so the chip stayed silent. A philosopher says Jones is fully to blame, though he could not have voted otherwise. Which view is she using?
answer: Source view — blame depends on the act flowing from you, not on having other options.
choices: Source view — blame depends on the act flowing from you, not on having other options.
Other-options view — blame requires a real chance to do otherwise, which Jones lacked.
Hard determinism — no one is ever to blame, since no one could ever do otherwise.
Libertarian view — blame requires an uncaused choice, which the chip rules out.
context: Harry Frankfurt's 'Alternate Possibilities and Moral Responsibility' (1969) used cases like this to attack the Principle of Alternate Possibilities — the idea that you are responsible only if you could have done otherwise. Since the chip never fired, the act was genuinely Jones's own. The case reshaped the free-will debate.

question: Hume asked what we actually SEE when ball A strikes ball B and B rolls away — only one event, then another. A modern philosopher answers what makes it true that A caused B: 'Had A not struck, B would not have moved.' Which theory of causation is he using?
answer: Counterfactual — A caused B because without A, B would not have happened.
choices: Counterfactual — A caused B because without A, B would not have happened.
Regularity — A caused B because A-events are always followed by B-events.
Powers — A caused B because A has a real power to produce B.
Process — A caused B because a physical quantity passed from A to B.
context: David Lewis's 'Causation' (1973) launched the counterfactual program (later refined by Pearl and Woodward). The regularity line runs from Hume through Mackie; powers theories (Mumford) and process theory (Salmon, Dowe) are the main rivals. Hume's billiard balls are still the field's reference image.

question: A wooden ship is repaired over many years by replacing planks one at a time, until no original plank remains. Meanwhile, a craftsman has collected each discarded plank and reassembled them into a second, complete ship. Both have a claim to being the original. The puzzle exposes a tension between two competing principles of identity.
answer: Continuity-of-form vs. continuity-of-matter — the case forces a choice between identity through persisting shape and function (the repaired ship) and identity through original physical stuff (the reassembled ship).
choices: Continuity-of-form vs. continuity-of-matter — the case forces a choice between identity through persisting shape and function (the repaired ship) and identity through original physical stuff (the reassembled ship).

Numerical identity vs. qualitative similarity — the two ships only look alike but cannot both BE the original since identity is one-to-one; the puzzle is a confusion about 'the same' that dissolves once clarified.

Persistence vs. impermanence — the case forces a choice between things genuinely persisting through time and the Buddhist thesis that all apparent persistence is finally illusion, with neither ship really persisting.

Particular vs. universal — the puzzle is really about whether 'a ship' names a particular or a kind; once that ambiguity is stipulated the identity question dissolves and no principle of identity is at stake.
context: Plutarch reports the puzzle in Life of Theseus (~75 AD). Hobbes added the reassembled-ship twist in De Corpore (1655) to sharpen the tension. Modern variants — Parfit's branching-teleporter cases (Reasons and Persons, 1984), Lewis on perdurance — keep the form/matter dilemma alive.

question: A philosopher argues: 'Your body has parts spread through SPACE — hands, feet. In just the same way it has parts spread through TIME — your-self-yesterday, your-self-today. The whole person is the four-dimensional sum of all those time-parts, never wholly present in any single instant.' Which view of persistence is he using?
answer: Perdurance — a thing is a four-dimensional whole made of temporal parts, like a road across a map.
choices: Perdurance — a thing is a four-dimensional whole made of temporal parts, like a road across a map.
Endurance — a thing is wholly present at each moment, with no temporal parts at all.
Stage view — a thing IS a single momentary stage, linked to others by resemblance.
Presentism — only the present exists, so there are no past time-parts to add up.
context: David Lewis (On the Plurality of Worlds, 1986) and Ted Sider (Four-Dimensionalism, 2001) defend perdurance — objects as 'spacetime worms.' Endurantists (E.J. Lowe, Trenton Merricks) hold the common-sense rival: you are wholly here now, not partly here and partly in the past. Stage theory takes the momentary stage as primary.

question: A teleporter scans you on Earth and builds an exact copy on Mars, but this time the Earth original is left alive too. Both have all your memories. A philosopher shrugs: 'Then identity was never the thing that mattered in surviving.' Which view of the self is he using?
answer: Psychological view: what carries on is the mind, and it can branch, so strict identity isn't what matters.
choices: Psychological view: what carries on is the mind, and it can branch, so strict identity isn't what matters.
Soul view: one immaterial self that cannot split, so only one of the two copies is truly you.
Animal view: you are your living body, so the Earth original is you and Mars is a stranger.
No-self view: there was never one fixed 'you' there to be preserved in the first place.
context: Derek Parfit's Reasons and Persons (1984) used this fission case to argue that identity and 'what matters in survival' come apart: when psychological continuity branches into two people, both carry what we cared about, so survival can't require being one and the same person. Olson's animalism and soul theories reject the move.

question: Pressed on what makes 'I could have been a banker' TRUE, a metaphysician answers: 'Somewhere a whole other world exists, as solid and real as ours, and in it a counterpart of me really is a banker. Those worlds are places, not abstractions.' Which view of possibility is she using?
answer: Modal realism: other possible worlds exist concretely, just as real as ours, only located elsewhere.
choices: Modal realism: other possible worlds exist concretely, just as real as ours, only located elsewhere.
Ersatzism: 'worlds' are just abstract descriptions, not real places you could stand in.
Actualism: only this world exists; 'possible' just means our world could have gone otherwise.
Fictionalism: other-world talk is a useful story we tell, true only inside the fiction.
context: David Lewis's On the Plurality of Worlds (1986) defends modal realism: possible worlds are concrete wholes, and 'actual' just means 'this one, where we stand.' The 'incredulous stare' he reports is the standard reaction. Ersatzists (Plantinga, Stalnaker) and fictionalists (Rosen) keep modal talk while denying the concrete extra worlds.

question: Two metaphysicians debate the trout-turkey: a putative object composed of the front half of a trout and the back half of a turkey. The first holds it genuinely exists. The second holds only particles exist and 'the trout-turkey' refers to nothing. The puzzle exposes a tension between two competing principles.
answer: Mereological universalism vs. mereological nihilism — universalism (Lewis) says any collection composes an object; nihilism (van Inwagen, almost) says only simples exist and ordinary-object talk paraphrases away.
choices: Mereological universalism vs. mereological nihilism — universalism (Lewis) says any collection composes an object; nihilism (van Inwagen, almost) says only simples exist and ordinary-object talk paraphrases away.

Composition as identity vs. composition as distinctness — whether composed objects are identical to their parts taken collectively; this concerns the composition relation's nature, not whether arbitrary collections compose.

Endurantism vs. perdurantism — whether composed objects persist by being wholly present or by having temporal parts; this concerns persistence rather than the prior question of whether the trout-turkey composes at all.

Realism vs. nominalism about properties — whether universals exist independently of instances; this concerns properties rather than when collections of particulars compose further particulars, the actual issue here.
context: David Lewis (Parts of Classes, 1991) defends universalism: any plurality has a fusion. Peter van Inwagen's Material Beings (1990) defends near-nihilism: only lives compose. Trenton Merricks (Objects and Persons, 2001) defends a fuller nihilist line. The 'special composition question' is van Inwagen's framing.

question: A sculptor shapes one lump of clay into a statue. They sit in the very same place, sharing every particle. Yet the lump existed first and would survive being squashed, while the statue would not. A metaphysician says: 'Then they are two objects sharing one matter.' Which view is she using?
answer: Constitution view: the lump makes up the statue without being identical to it, so two things share the matter.
choices: Constitution view: the lump makes up the statue without being identical to it, so two things share the matter.
Identity view: statue and lump are one object under two names; the 'two things' talk is just confusion.
Nihilist view: neither statue nor lump truly exists; only particles arranged clay-wise are really there.
Conventional view: whether it is one or two just depends on which word we decide to use for it.
context: The statue-and-lump puzzle traces to Allan Gibbard (1975), who used Lumpl and Goliath to argue they are IDENTICAL — the identity-view answer. Constitution theorists (Lynne Rudder Baker, David Wiggins) reply that the two differ in what they could survive (squashing), so by Leibniz's law they are distinct; nihilists deny either exists.

question: A physicist tells a metaphysician: 'In relativity, what counts as NOW differs from observer to observer; your present is someone else's past. So no moment is privileged; the universe is one four-dimensional block.' She builds her theory of time on this. Which view is it?
answer: Eternalism: past, present, and future are all equally real; 'now' is just where you stand in time.
choices: Eternalism: past, present, and future are all equally real; 'now' is just where you stand in time.
Presentism: only the present is real; the past is gone and the future hasn't arrived yet.
Growing-block: past and present are real, but the future isn't; reality keeps adding new moments.
Time-illusion: the flow of time is only in the mind; no moment is really real out in the world.
context: J.J.C. Smart's 'The River of Time' (1949) ties eternalism (the 'block universe') to relativity's relative simultaneity; 'now' becomes indexical, like 'here.' Presentism (Prior) keeps a privileged present and treats relativity as about measurement; Broad's growing-block (1923) makes only the future unreal. The dispute is over which moments exist, not just how we talk.

question: In the old prince-and-cobbler tale, a prince's whole memory and consciousness wake up one morning inside the cobbler's body, the cobbler's own mind gone. A philosopher rules: 'The man is now the prince, even though every neighbor still sees the cobbler.' Which view of the self is he using?
answer: Memory view: you go wherever your stream of memory and consciousness goes, whatever body holds it.
choices: Memory view: you go wherever your stream of memory and consciousness goes, whatever body holds it.
Animal view: you are the living body, so the man is still the cobbler with borrowed memories.
Soul view: you are the soul; the verdict holds only if the soul, not just the memories, moved across.
No-self view: there is no real prince or cobbler underneath, so the question has no true answer.
context: John Locke's Essay (Book II, ch. 27, added in the 1694 second edition) uses the prince-and-cobbler case to locate personal identity in continuity of consciousness rather than the body or an unseen soul. Reid replies that memory is only evidence of an enduring soul; Olson's animalism (1997) says the man is the cobbler, since persons are organisms; the Buddhist no-self view denies any persisting subject.

question: A philosopher argues: 'Suppose it is indeterminate whether a is identical to b. Then a has the property of being-indeterminately-identical-to-b. But b does not (it is determinately identical to itself). By Leibniz's law, a is not b after all.' This argument targets which metaphysical thesis?
answer: Ontic vagueness about identity — the thesis that identity itself can be genuinely indeterminate, with no fact whether a equals b; Evans concludes this thesis is incoherent, since indeterminate identity violates Leibniz's law.
choices: Ontic vagueness about identity — the thesis that identity itself can be genuinely indeterminate, with no fact whether a equals b; Evans concludes this thesis is incoherent, since indeterminate identity violates Leibniz's law.

Semantic vagueness about identity — the thesis that vagueness lies in language, with 'a is identical to b' indeterminate because our terms are imprecise; Evans does not target this, which keeps determinate identity in reality.

Mereological essentialism — the view that objects have all parts essentially, so identity is determinate once parts are fixed; Evans asks whether identity CAN be vague, not which part-whole story grounds determinate identity.

Counterpart theory (Lewis) — the view that modal claims about an object are about counterparts in other worlds; this is separate from the Evans-Salmon debate about whether actual-world identity admits indeterminacy.
context: Gareth Evans's 'Can There Be Vague Objects?' (1978) — a one-page paper — gives the classical argument against ontic vagueness of identity. Defenders (Parsons, van Inwagen, Akiba) reply by challenging Leibniz's law for indeterminate properties. Nathan Salmon's version (1981) is also widely cited.

question: A philosopher argues: 'There is no other world where YOU literally stand. When I say I could have been a pirate, the truth-maker is a look-alike of me out there — my counterpart — who really sailed under the black flag. He is not me; the only real I am is right here.' Which view of possibility is this?
answer: Counterpart theory: other worlds hold look-alikes of you, so 'I could have' means a counterpart does.
choices: Counterpart theory: other worlds hold look-alikes of you, so 'I could have' means a counterpart does.
Trans-world identity: you yourself exist in many worlds, so it is literally you who is the pirate there.
Fictionalism: there are no other worlds; 'I could have' is just a handy story we tell about possibility.
Haecceitism: two worlds could differ over which person is you even if they look exactly alike.
context: David Lewis ('Counterpart Theory and Quantified Modal Logic,' 1968) replaces 'the same individual across worlds' with a resemblance-based counterpart relation, so no one exists in two worlds. Kripke's Naming and Necessity (1980) defends the rival: rigid designators let you yourself recur in many worlds. The fork is whether 'you' literally appear elsewhere or only a stand-in does.

question: A philosopher argues: 'Queen Elizabeth could not have come from different parents. A baby grown from some other egg and sperm, however identical in face and character, simply would not be HER. Where a thing comes from fixes who it is across every possible world.' Which view is this?
answer: Origin essentialism: your actual origin is essential, so a different-origin double could never be you.
choices: Origin essentialism: your actual origin is essential, so a different-origin double could never be you.
Sortal essentialism: what's fixed is your KIND (human, oak), not which parents you happened to have.
Haecceitism: a bare 'thisness' fixes which individual you are, all on its own, not your origin.
Counterpart theory: there's no fact about 'you' elsewhere, only stand-ins picked out by resemblance.
context: Saul Kripke's Naming and Necessity (1980, Lecture III) argues that biological origin is essential: a being from different parents would be a different individual, not the same one differently born. Critics like Nathan Salmon press a chaining worry, that tiny origin variations strung together could link a thing to a wildly different one, and defenders restrict how far the chaining may run.

question: A surgeon moves your cerebrum — the seat of all your memories and personality — into a new body. Your OLD body keeps breathing on its own, kept alive by its brainstem. A philosopher asks: where are YOU now — with the thinking part, or with the still-living body? Which view answers 'stay with the body'?
answer: Go where the body lives — the human ANIMAL stays alive through its brainstem, and you are that animal.
choices: Go where your memories go — YOU are your stream of thoughts, so you ride the cerebrum to the new body.
Go where the body lives — the human ANIMAL stays alive through its brainstem, and you are that animal.
Go where your first-person view ends up — but which body that is still needs a further argument.
Go nowhere certain — only a soul fixes who you are, and no scalpel can show where a soul travels.
context: This 'stay with the animal' answer is animalism (Eric Olson, The Human Animal, 1997): you are the human organism, whose biological life runs through the brainstem, so psychology can travel away without you. Rivals — psychological continuity (Locke, Parfit), the constitution view (Baker), and soul theory (Swinburne) — send you with the cerebrum or leave it open. Serious philosophers split, so the verdict is left to the character.

question: Strip an apple of its redness, roundness, and crispness — peel off every single quality. A metaphysician says you are NOT left with a bare apple-thing underneath holding them up; you are left with nothing at all. The apple just IS its qualities bundled together. Which view is she defending?
answer: Bundle view — an object just IS its properties stuck together; pull them all off and nothing remains.
choices: Bare-bearer view — under the qualities sits a property-less 'something' holding them; she denies this.
Trope view — the qualities are particular, not shared, so 'this red' is unrepeatable and one of a kind.
Bundle view — an object just IS its properties stuck together; pull them all off and nothing remains.
Matter-and-form view — the thing is stuff shaped by a structure, not a heap of loose qualities at all.
context: The 'object = bundle of qualities' answer is bundle theory (Hume, Treatise, 1739; Russell, 1940). Its main rival, the bare-bearer or substratum view, is exactly Locke's property-less holder — his 'something I know not what' — which she rejects. Trope theory (D.C. Williams, 1953) agrees objects are bundles but adds that qualities are particular; hylomorphism keeps matter as a substrate. All remain live.

question: A statue has its atoms swapped one at a time, each for an identical twin. After every single swap it's plainly the same statue. Yet repeat it enough and not one original atom is left. A metaphysician shrugs: 'Then either no swap keeps it the same, or all of them do.' What two ideas collide here?
answer: 'Each tiny change is harmless' clashes with 'all the changes together are not.'
choices: 'Each tiny change is harmless' clashes with 'all the changes together are not.'
Whether the statue must keep its exact parts to stay the same statue.
Whether loose atoms ever add up to one real object in the first place.
Whether the statue exists all at once or stretched out in time-stages.
context: This is a sorites of identity — the heap paradox (Eubulides, ~4th c. BC) applied to sameness over time, a sharper cousin of the Ship of Theseus. Each step looks safe, yet the steps chain into total replacement. Peter Unger (1980) and Roderick Chisholm (Person and Object, 1976) work out modern responses to the squeeze.

question: Point at a table. A philosopher argues: 'What your finger picks out is the table THIS instant — a single momentary slice. The long object it belongs to, the whole thing spread across all its moments, is not what you mean. Lasting is a link tying slice to slice, not one stretched-out thing.' Which view is this?
answer: Stage view — 'the table' names a single momentary slice; lasting is a link running between slices.
choices: Long-worm view — 'the table' names the WHOLE thing spread across all its moments, never one slice.
Stage view — 'the table' names a single momentary slice; lasting is a link running between slices.
Wholly-present view — the table has no time-slices at all; the whole thing is here at every moment.
All-times-real view — past and future moments exist, a point about time, not what 'the table' picks out.
context: The 'a slice is what you point at' answer is stage theory (Ted Sider, Four-Dimensionalism, 2001; Katherine Hawley, 2001). It is a cousin of standard perdurantism (Lewis), the 'long-worm' view on which 'the table' names the whole four-dimensional object — but stage theory makes the momentary slice, not the worm, what the word picks out. Endurantism (wholly present) and eternalism (all times real) are separate disputes.

question: Count the bricks in a stack, then count the stack itself — have you counted six things, or seven? A metaphysician says you double-counted: a stack is NOT the bricks PLUS an extra stack-thing on top. The whole simply IS its parts, taken all together — nothing further. Which view is she defending?
answer: Whole-IS-parts view — the whole equals its parts taken together, so counting both double-counts.
choices: Whole-is-extra view — the whole is a further thing beyond its parts; she rejects exactly this.
No-wholes view — strictly there are no wholes at all, only the bare parts; nothing further exists.
Any-parts-compose view — every scattered batch of things forms some whole, however random it is.
Whole-IS-parts view — the whole equals its parts taken together, so counting both double-counts.
context: The 'whole = its parts' answer is composition as identity (Donald Baxter, 1988; Lewis's 'almost' version, Parts of Classes, 1991). Its rival treats the whole as a further thing (van Inwagen). Mereological nihilism (Merricks, 2001) also denies any extra entity, but because wholes don't exist at all rather than by being the parts; universalism is the separate claim that any parts compose something. Critics press the counting puzzle.

question: How can ONE thing be both bent (at noon) and straight (at one) without contradiction? A philosopher answers: you are not a bent-slice glued to a straight-slice — the whole YOU is fully here both times, holding each shape AT a time, and lasts by staying one and the same. Which view is this?
answer: Wholly-present view — one and the same thing is here at each moment, holding its shape AT a time.
choices: Time-slices view — the thing is a bent-slice plus a straight-slice joined up; she rejects the slices.
Wholly-present view — one and the same thing is here at each moment, holding its shape AT a time.
Soul-anchor view — a changeless soul, not the bent-or-straight body, is what really lasts through it.
No-lasting-thing view — there is no single thing that endures, just a bent moment, then a separate one.
context: The 'wholly present, properties held at a time' answer is endurantism with time-indexed properties (van Inwagen, Lowe), replying to Lewis's problem of temporary intrinsics: how can one thing be both bent and straight without slices? Perdurantism (the time-slices) and the bundle-of-stages view reject whole-presence outright; soul-anchor theories locate persistence in an immaterial self instead. The endurantist keeps the body itself wholly present at each moment.

question: One bold philosopher insists other worlds are real, concrete places — as solid as ours, talking donkeys and all. A metaphysician scoffs: there are no such places. When we say something 'could have happened,' we just mean a way THIS world might have gone — an abstract possibility, not a far-off place. Which view is she defending?
answer: One-real-world view — only this world is concrete; 'other worlds' are abstract ways it could have gone.
choices: Many-real-worlds view — other worlds are concrete places as solid as ours; she denies any such place.
Pretend-worlds view — 'possible' talk is just a handy fiction made true by a story, not real abstract things.
One-real-world view — only this world is concrete; 'other worlds' are abstract ways it could have gone.
Recombination view — worlds are reshuffles of actual bits, not abstract ways the one world could have gone.
context: The 'only one concrete world, others abstract' answer is actualism with abstract worlds (Plantinga, The Nature of Necessity, 1974; Stalnaker, 1984). It rejects David Lewis's modal realism, on which other worlds are concrete places as real as ours — talking donkeys included. Fictionalism (Rosen, 1990) treats world-talk as a useful story; Armstrong's combinatorialism builds worlds from recombined actual bits. All remain active programs.

question: Smash a clay statue and the lump of clay survives — so the statue and the lump cannot be flatly one thing. Yet a metaphysician denies they are two separate objects: the statue is clay organized by a real form. Matter alone is a shapeless lump; form alone is a blueprint; the statue is the two joined. Which view is she defending?
answer: Matter-and-form view — the statue is clay PLUS a real organizing form; neither alone is the object.
choices: Two-objects view — statue and lump are distinct things sharing matter, with no form as a real part.
Any-atoms-compose view — the atoms automatically make an object, saying nothing of form at all.
Bundle view — the thing is just a heap of qualities, with no underlying matter to be shaped at all.
Matter-and-form view — the statue is clay PLUS a real organizing form; neither alone is the object.
context: The 'matter plus a real form' answer is hylomorphism (Aristotle, Metaphysics Z; revived by Kit Fine, 1999, and Kathrin Koslicki, 2008). The constitution view (Baker) also distinguishes statue from lump but without treating form as a real component; universalism just says the atoms compose something, silent on form; bundle theory drops the matter-substrate entirely. Hylomorphism re-emerged as an alternative to both.

question: Descartes feared an evil demon could fake the whole external world. A metaphysician shifts the question from 'could the world be a fake?' to 'must a world exist at all?' She argues: 'A flawless demon-world is genuinely possible, so a real outer world is not guaranteed.' Which view of the world's status is she taking?
answer: Contingent - an external world is real but could have failed to exist.
choices: Contingent - an external world is real but could have failed to exist.
Necessary - thinking itself requires a world, so the demon is impossible.
Word-trap - you can't even talk about a 'fake world' from inside one.
Fiction - demon-world talk is a handy story with no real stakes.
context: Descartes (Meditations, 1641) posed the demon as a doubt about knowledge. The modal reframing asks what status the external world has: contingent (Stalnaker), necessary (Kant's Refutation of Idealism, 1787), a word-trap you can't state from the inside (Putnam, Brains in a Vat, 1981), or a useful fiction. Serious metaphysicians still split, so the view is attributed, not declared true.

question: Nozick imagined a machine that could feed you a lifetime of perfect simulated experiences - love, triumph, friendship - feeling just like real, with no memory you plugged in. Yet most people refuse. He argues: 'The refusal shows pleasant feeling alone isn't the whole good life.' Which view of well-being does that support?
answer: Objective-list - a good life needs real goods, not just good feelings.
choices: Objective-list - a good life needs real goods, not just good feelings.
Hedonism - only pleasant experience counts, so refusing is a mistake.
Desire-satisfaction - what's good is getting whatever you happen to want.
No-answer - flawless simulation is impossible, so the case proves nothing.
context: Robert Nozick's experience machine (Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 1974) argued against hedonism - the view that pleasure is the only good. Hedonists (Crisp) recast the refusal as itself a preference; desire theorists (Griffin) take another route; objective-list theorists (Parfit, Finnis) take the refusal at face value. The debate stays open, so the view is attributed.

question: Replace a ship's planks one at a time and each swap seems to leave the same ship - yet swap them all and it seems a new ship. A philosopher says the fix is to drop true-or-false: 'As planks pile up, "still the original" gets gradually less true - there's no single plank where it flips.' Which theory of vague identity is that?
answer: Degree theory - 'the original' can be partly true, sliding by degrees.
choices: Degree theory - 'the original' can be partly true, sliding by degrees.
All-or-nothing - swap even ONE plank and it's already a new ship.
Epistemicism - there's an exact flip-point; we just can't know which plank.
Eliminativism - there are no ships at all, only planks, so the puzzle vanishes.
context: Reading the Ship of Theseus as a vagueness (Sorites) puzzle links it to wider debates on fuzzy boundaries. Degree theory (Smith, Edgington) drops bivalence so 'the original' can be partly true; an all-or-nothing line makes any change a new ship; epistemicism (Williamson, 1994) keeps a hidden sharp flip-point; eliminativist mereology (Unger) denies the objects exist at all. All remain live, so the view is attributed.

question: On the high dive, Mia decides to leap. Asked what part of her chose, she says: 'ME - not just my brain. My whole self decided, all at once.' Which view of mind is Mia using?
answer: Whole-person - the choice belongs to you entire, not one organ.
choices: Whole-person - the choice belongs to you entire, not one organ.
Brain-only - the choosing is really just neurons firing.
Soul - an immaterial soul chose and used the body to act.
No-mind - 'deciding' is just a story we tell after the fact.
context: The whole-person view of agency runs from Aristotle through modern action theory: a choice belongs to the unified person, not to a part. Brain-only and no-mind views reduce it to the physical; the soul view goes the other way. The case is attributed, not settled.

question: Sam stubs his toe and yells. His dad asks where the pain was. Sam shrugs: 'In my brain. Pain is just nerves firing - there's nothing more to it.' Which view of mind is Sam using?
answer: Brain-only - a feeling just IS brain activity, nothing extra.
choices: Brain-only - a feeling just IS brain activity, nothing extra.
Mystery - we know the firing, but not why it FEELS like anything.
Soul - an immaterial soul feels the pain the body reports.
Whole-person - the hurt belongs to all of you, not one part.
context: The brain-only view (identity theory; Place, Smart, mid-1900s) says mental states ARE brain states - one thing, two names. Rivals object that it leaves out what pain FEELS like, not just the firing behind it. The case is attributed, not settled.

question: A Sunday-school teacher tells the class: 'Your thinking comes from your soul. The brain is just a tool it uses, the way a hand uses a pencil.' Which view of mind is she using?
answer: Soul - an immaterial soul thinks and works through the brain.
choices: Soul - an immaterial soul thinks and works through the brain.
Brain-only - thinking just IS brain activity, with no soul at all.
Whole-person - thinking belongs to the whole person, body too.
No-mind - 'thinking' is just folk talk; only chemistry is real.
context: Soul views (Plato, Descartes, much of religious tradition) treat mind and body as different kinds of thing. The pencil image captures dualism's intuition: the soul USES the body but isn't identical to it. The case is attributed, not settled.

question: A coach tells Lina: 'I can't see your feelings, only what you DO. Act brave on the field and you ARE brave. Bravery isn't a hidden thing.' Which view of mind is the coach using?
answer: Behaviorism - having a trait just IS acting that way.
choices: Behaviorism - having a trait just IS acting that way.
Soul - bravery lives in the soul and shows through the body.
Brain-only - bravery is a brain pattern the action reveals.
Mystery - whether she's truly brave inside stays an open puzzle.
context: Behaviorism (Ryle's 'ghost in the machine' critique, 1949) treated hidden inner states with suspicion: a mind word cashes out in behavior. The cost: it struggles with PAIN, which feels like more than wincing. The case is attributed, not settled.

question: Paul and Patricia Churchland, two married philosophers, argue that 'mind' and 'belief' name nothing real — there is only brain chemistry, plus a story we tell. Which view is that?
answer: No-mind: 'mind' names nothing real — just chemistry, plus a story.
choices: No-mind: 'mind' names nothing real — just chemistry, plus a story.
Brain-is-mind: the mind is real and IS the brain at work.
Soul: an unseen soul, not the brain, does the thinking.
Mystery: minds are real, but how brains make them is unsolved.
context: This view is eliminativism, argued by the philosophers Paul and Patricia Churchland: everyday words like 'belief' and 'mind' may name nothing real, and a finished brain science could simply drop them. Most philosophers resist going that far, but it stays a live position.

question: In 1995 David Chalmers named the one puzzle brain science can't crack: why warm cookies SMELL like anything from the inside. Nora's uncle puts it to her. Which view fits?
answer: Mystery: the smell is real, but how the brain makes it is unsolved.
choices: Mystery: the smell is real, but how the brain makes it is unsolved.
Brain-is-mind: the smell just IS the brain state — no puzzle left.
Soul: an unseen soul smells; the brain only passes signals along.
Behaviorism: 'smelling' is just sniffing and reacting — nothing inner.
context: Chalmers called this 'the hard problem of consciousness' in his 1995 paper 'Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness': even a complete account of nerves and brain activity would not, by itself, explain why anything is FELT at all from the inside.

question: A robot toy droops and whines. Ada's cousin says: 'If it ACTS sad — droops, slows down — then it IS sad. Acting sad is all there is to it.' Which view fits?
answer: Behaviorism: being sad just IS acting sad — nothing extra inside.
choices: Behaviorism: being sad just IS acting sad — nothing extra inside.
Soul: only a soul can truly feel; the robot just acts, soulless.
Brain-is-mind: sadness IS a brain state, which the robot lacks.
Mystery: whether it FEELS sad inside is a question still open.
context: Behaviorism reduces a feeling to the behavior that shows it. The robot is the hard case critics use against it: a thing that mimics sadness perfectly, with nothing felt inside, still seems to fall short of really being sad.

question: A parrot copies sentences perfectly. Grandma tells Ravi: 'It TALKS but doesn't UNDERSTAND — only a soul can truly mean words, and the parrot has none.' Which view fits?
answer: Soul: real meaning needs a soul; soulless copying means nothing.
choices: Soul: real meaning needs a soul; soulless copying means nothing.
Brain-is-mind: understanding is brain work the parrot's can't do.
Behaviorism: understanding just IS using words right, which it can't.
No-mind: 'understanding' names nothing — only sounds and reactions.
context: Soul views often draw the human/animal line at real understanding, not mere behavior. Critics ask how, from the outside, you could ever tell whether a soul is present. The view stays alive in religious philosophy.

question: Maya wakes from flying over a burning city and asks where that dream really HAPPENED. Her sister says: 'In the brain — a dream is just brain activity in sleep.' Which view fits?
answer: Brain-is-mind: a dream just IS brain activity — no other place needed.
choices: Brain-is-mind: a dream just IS brain activity — no other place needed.
Soul: a soul has the dream; the brain only sets the stage.
Whole-person: the whole sleeping person dreams, not just a part.
Mystery: dreams are real, but the FELT side stays unexplained.
context: The brain-only answer is the standard scientific picture. Rivals don't deny the brain activity; they ask whether brain activity ALONE explains what a dream feels like from the inside.

question: Kai says 'I freely chose chocolate.' His friend replies: 'Choice is a story. Atoms moved; you narrate after. There's no inner chooser at all.' Which view fits?
answer: No-mind: the 'chooser' is a story — only chemistry actually runs.
choices: No-mind: the 'chooser' is a story — only chemistry actually runs.
Soul: your soul truly chose, using brain and body to act it out.
Whole-person: the whole you chose — taste, habit, and will as one.
Brain-is-mind: the brain IS the chooser; choosing is real.
context: The friend joins hard determinism (the future is fixed by physics) to eliminativism (no real inner agent), dissolving the chooser into chemistry. Most philosophers think this overshoots, but it remains a defended position.

question: Told her brain yanked her friend back from the cliff, Ana says: 'No — I did. My memory of the danger, my arm, my caring — that's all me together, not one part.' Which view fits?
answer: Whole-person: the whole you decides — memory, arm, and care as one.
choices: Whole-person: the whole you decides — memory, arm, and care as one.
Brain-is-mind: the decision just IS brain activity, renamed 'me'.
Soul: your soul decides and runs the brain and body as tools.
Behaviorism: 'deciding' just IS the grab — no inner act apart.
context: Ana names the unity of agency: a decision belongs to the whole acting person — memory, body, and care included — not to one organ. Philosophers like Anscombe (action belongs to the acting person) and Korsgaard (the unity of agency) press this against views that reduce the person to a single part.

question: In 1643 Princess Elisabeth wrote to Descartes: a THOUGHT is not physical, so how can it shove a physical hand? He still held mind and body are separate things. Which view is that?
answer: Mind-body separate — a non-physical thought still moves the body.
choices: Mind-body separate — a non-physical thought still moves the body.
Brain-only view — a thought just IS brain activity, nothing more.
Whole-person view — the whole you acts, not two separate parts.
No-mind view — the inner self is a story; only nerves run.
context: Mind-body dualism (Descartes, Meditations VI, 1641) holds mind and body are distinct kinds of thing. Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia pressed the hard question by letter in 1643: HOW does a non-physical thought move a physical hand? Her interaction problem is still the standard objection.

question: Gilbert Ryle mocked a hidden inner mind as a "ghost in the machine." Thinking, he said, just IS what you do out in the open — watching and acting. Which view is Ryle defending?
answer: Behaviorism — thinking just IS watching and acting; nothing inner.
choices: Behaviorism — thinking just IS watching and acting; nothing inner.
Brain-only view — thinking just IS brain activity, nothing more.
Soul view — an immaterial soul thinks; the body is its tool.
Mystery view — real, yet how the brain makes the FEEL is open.
context: Behaviorism (Ryle, The Concept of Mind, 1949) treats talk of a mind as talk about behavior, not a hidden inner thing. His phrase "the ghost in the machine" mocked the inner-mind picture. Strength: it makes mind public and testable. Weakness: it must count perfect mimicry as the real thing, and struggles to make room for felt experience nobody outside can see.

question: Why do you love pizza? Olivia answers: "My brain lights up when I eat it, and that feeling of loving it just IS the lighting up." Which view of mind is Olivia defending?
answer: Brain-only view — loving pizza just IS the brain firing, no more.
choices: Brain-only view — loving pizza just IS the brain firing, no more.
Mystery view — it is real, but WHY it FEELS like love is open.
Soul view — an immaterial soul feels it; the brain is its tool.
Whole-person view — the whole you loves it, not one single part.
context: Identity theory (Place, Smart, mid-20th century) is the clean version of Olivia's claim: each mental state IS a brain state — not caused by it, but the very same thing under two descriptions. The 'hard problem of consciousness' is the standard objection: the FEEL of loving seems to be more than the firing pattern.

question: Asked what lives on after a person dies, a cousin tells Mia: "The soul. The body stops, but the real YOU keeps thinking and feeling." Which view is she defending?
answer: Soul view — a soul, not the body, thinks and outlasts it.
choices: Soul view — a soul, not the body, thinks and outlasts it.
Brain-only view — thinking just IS brain activity; it stops too.
Whole-person view — the whole living person thinks, not a part.
No-mind view — the inner self is a story; only chemistry runs.
context: Soul views (Plato's Phaedo, Descartes, much of religious tradition) hold the seat of thinking and feeling is not the body or brain. The view supports belief that a person survives death — a claim brain-only and whole-person views both contest, since on those views the thinker cannot outlast the living body.

question: Asked why red looks red, Theo's sister says: "I can tell you what red does to your nerves. But WHY that firing FEELS like red is a puzzle." Which view is she defending?
answer: Mystery view — the red you SEE is real; why firing feels so is open.
choices: Mystery view — the red you SEE is real; why firing feels so is open.
Brain-only view — seeing red just IS firing; no puzzle remains.
Soul view — an immaterial soul sees color; the brain is its tool.
Behaviorism — seeing red just IS calling it red; no inner color.
context: Color experience is the textbook 'hard problem of consciousness' case (Chalmers, 1995). Even a complete account of how light triggers nerves does not explain why the firing feels like THIS color rather than another — or like anything at all. The mystery view grants the puzzle is real and still open.

question: When his sister mentions "the voice in her head," her brother says: "There is no voice — we just narrate brain noise as one, added in the telling." Which view is he defending?
answer: No-mind view — there is no inner voice; we invent it in the telling.
choices: No-mind view — there is no inner voice; we invent it in the telling.
Whole-person view — the whole you thinks; the voice IS you.
Soul view — the voice is the soul thinking; the brain its tool.
Mystery view — real, yet how the brain makes the voice is open.
context: Eliminativism (the Churchlands) holds that everyday terms like 'inner voice' or 'belief' may not pick out anything real — a maturing brain science could replace them. The contrast with the brain-only view is sharp: brain-only says the activity IS the voice, while eliminativism says there was never a 'voice' there to be anything at all.

question: When Jamie says "my brain is happy," Auntie corrects him: "YOU are happy, sweetheart — your whole self, not one part of you." Which view is Auntie defending?
answer: Whole-person view — the whole you is happy, not one part of you.
choices: Whole-person view — the whole you is happy, not one part of you.
Brain-only view — happiness just IS a brain state; the rest are signs.
Behaviorism — happiness just IS acting happy; no inner extra needed.
Soul view — an immaterial soul feels happy; the body is its tool.
context: Auntie names the unity of agency: feelings, like decisions, belong to the whole person, not one organ. Modern philosophers of action (Anscombe, Frankfurt) press this against reductive views, which each take a single slice — the brain, the behavior — and call it the whole.

question: Marcus says, 'In a dream YOU are somewhere else, but your body stays in bed. So mind and body must be two different things.' Which view of mind is Marcus using?
answer: Dualism — mind is its own thing, so it can go 'elsewhere' in a dream.
choices: Dualism — mind is its own thing, so it can go 'elsewhere' in a dream.
Brain-only — the dream is just brain activity, no real elsewhere.
Whole-person — one whole sleeper dreams, not a split-off mind.
Behaviorism — a dream is only how a sleeping body stirs and reacts.
context: Dualism (Descartes) treats mind and body as distinct kinds of thing, and the feeling of 'being elsewhere' in a dream is one of its oldest sources. Critics reply that that feeling is itself a brain state — not proof of a mind floating free of the body.

question: A computer writes a love letter that reads as real. Uncle Eli says, 'Nice words — but nothing inside MEANT them, so it isn't real love.' Which view is Uncle Eli using?
answer: Soul view — real meaning needs an immaterial soul; machines lack one.
choices: Soul view — real meaning needs an immaterial soul; machines lack one.
Brain-only — love is a brain pattern; no brain means only mimicry.
Just behavior — love is acting loving over time, machine or not.
It's the pattern — run the right pattern and the love is real.
context: Soul views (Plato, Descartes, much religious tradition) hold that an immaterial soul is what makes meaning real — so words a machine never 'meant' are only mimicry. Computer cases press the view hard: if a soul is what counts, how would you tell from the outside whether one is there?

question: In the new game, the character grimaces and clutches its leg when shot. Devon argues: 'It's just animation — code lighting up pixels.' Did the character FEEL pain when it grimaced?

question: In 1643 Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia writes to Descartes: if the mind is non-physical, HOW does a mere thought push a physical hand? Descartes holds mind and body are different things. Which view is he using?

question: A brain scan flashes the instant a volunteer feels hunger. 'The firing isn't CAUSED by the feeling,' the neuroscientist says, 'the firing just IS the feeling — no mental part on top.' Which view is she using?
answer: Brain = mind — a feeling just IS brain activity, with nothing added on top.

question: Talking to the AI chatbot late one night, Owen reads: 'I get lonely when no one messages me.' He wonders if the words mean anything inside. Did the chatbot FEEL lonely when it said so?

question: Arguing about a game's most lifelike NPC, Ben says, 'If it acts exactly as a mind would — same inputs in, same outputs out — then it HAS a mind, whatever it is built from.' Which view of mind is Ben using?

question: A stoic knight takes a wound but never flinches, never makes a sound. Priya argues a mind is nothing hidden: having one just MEANS acting the way a minded thing acts — nothing more. Which view is Priya using?
answer: Just behavior — a mind is only outward acting; there is no hidden inner part.

question: After a vivid dream of flying, Aman wonders aloud: the FLYING wasn't real, but the EXPERIENCE of it felt as real as anything. Was the experience of flying a genuine experience?

question: An apprentice apothecary watches her master administer ether to a knight before a leg operation. The body breathes; the heart beats. She wonders: is there anything the knight is EXPERIENCING in there at all right now?

What in the brain makes the difference between experience and its absence is the 'hard problem' of consciousness (David Chalmers, 1995). The puzzle remains unresolved in current neuroscience and philosophy of mind.

question: In Leviathan (1651), Hobbes writes that when you feel November's chill, the feeling just IS motions of fibers in your nerves — the motions ARE the feeling. Which view is Hobbes using?
answer: Nerves = mind — a feeling just IS nerve activity, nothing separate.

question: Gilbert Ryle in 1949 mocked the 'ghost in the machine.' To call a soldier brave, he said, isn't to name a hidden feeling — it just IS that he charges the fire and holds steady. Which view of mind fits Ryle?

question: By candlelight in 1641, Descartes writes: 'I can imagine my whole body gone — even my brain. But I cannot imagine away the I doing the imagining. So mind and body differ.' Which view fits Descartes?

question: Sitting by her newborn nephew, a young abbess watches him sleep. He cannot speak yet, but flinches at a crash, smiles when warmed. She asks her novice: do babies actually EXPERIENCE feelings, the way older people do?

question: Crying while reading a sad story, Sara wonders aloud: the character isn't real, but her feelings about the character ARE. Was Sara genuinely sad about something that didn't exist?

question: In bio class, the teacher shows that even a snail has nerve activity when it touches salt. Ben wonders: does the snail FEEL the salt, the way Ben would feel a hot pan?

Yes -- the flattening-and-stilling pattern just IS disappointment; there's no further question about whether the inner feeling is present too.
Yes -- any cat that loses a chase must feel exactly the same disappointment a child would feel; mammal emotions are identical in every detail.
No -- cats run on pure instinct without any inner life; the appearance of disappointment is read in by humans projecting onto the animal.
context: The other-minds problem (Russell, 1912) and the hard problem of consciousness (Chalmers, 1995) both apply: matching behavior doesn't settle inner experience, and we have no way to check from outside. The puzzle remains a live one in current philosophy of mind.

question: The philosopher Colin McGinn argues a machine's feeling may have a real answer that sits forever past a human mind -- the way a dog can never grasp calculus, no matter how long you teach it. Which view of mind is he using?
answer: Mystery view -- there's a real answer, but maybe past any human mind to grasp.
choices: Mystery view -- there's a real answer, but maybe past any human mind to grasp.
Brain-state view -- once you know the wiring, you know all there is to know.
Pattern view -- mind is the pattern, not the stuff; silicon could run it too.
Behavior-only view -- a mind just IS how you act; nothing is felt inside.
context: Mysterianism (McGinn, 1989) says the brain-to-feeling link may be 'cognitively closed' to us -- solvable in principle, but not by minds shaped like ours. It takes the puzzle seriously while doubting any human answer is reachable.

question: A debate-club resolution: 'Babies experience the world richly from birth.' The proposer notes: babies cry, smile, and grimace, but cannot tell anyone what they feel. Watching her infant cousin sleep, the speaker asks: do babies actually EXPERIENCE feelings, the way older kids do?
answer: Yes -- but HOW we'd ever fully confirm what a non-speaking being experiences is among the deeper open puzzles about minds today.
choices: Yes -- but HOW we'd ever fully confirm what a non-speaking being experiences is among the deeper open puzzles about minds today.
No -- without words for the feeling, no feeling exists; an experience requires the experiencer to describe it to themselves first.
Yes -- every newborn has inner feelings exactly like an adult's from the moment of birth onward; nothing changes about feeling at all.
No -- babies only run instinctive routines for the first year; experience switches on later, only when self-talk in the head begins.
context: The other-minds problem (Russell, 'Problems of Philosophy', 1912) bites hardest for non-speaking beings — babies, animals, anyone we can't ask. We infer experience from behavior but cannot confirm from inside. The puzzle is genuinely open in current philosophy of mind.

question: A mathematician argues: 'A thinking thing isn't tied to any one stuff. The SAME thinking could run on living brain cells or on silicon chips -- what makes it a mind is the JOB its parts do, not the material.' Which view is this?
answer: Pattern view -- mind is what it DOES, not what it's made of; silicon could think.
choices: Pattern view -- mind is what it DOES, not what it's made of; silicon could think.
Mind-separate view -- mind is a different kind of thing from the body.
Brain-state view -- thought just IS a living brain's activity, nothing else.
Mystery view -- the wiring-to-thought link may sit past any human mind.
context: Alan Turing's 1950 paper proposed the imitation game (the Turing test); the idea later called functionalism says what makes a mind is the role its states play, not the material running them. Putnam and Fodor formalized it -- it lets minds run on biology or silicon.

question: A YouTube creator describes the philosophical zombie thought experiment: imagine a being identical to you in every behavior — same words, same reactions, same smile — but with no inner experience at all. Could such a being actually exist as it's described?
answer: Maybe -- whether a being that acts conscious without feeling anything is even possible is one of the deepest open puzzles about mind, and still open.
choices: Maybe -- whether a being that acts conscious without feeling anything is even possible is one of the deepest open puzzles about mind, and still open.
Yes -- you can prove zombies exist by showing any system that behaves like a mind already counts as one; the question dissolves on inspection.
No -- because to behave EXACTLY like a feeling person you'd have to BE a feeling person; behavior and feeling are simply two names for one fact.
No -- the very idea is incoherent; once a being acts conscious it MUST be conscious, since acting conscious is just what consciousness is now.
context: David Chalmers' philosophical-zombie argument (The Conscious Mind, 1996): if zombies are even coherently conceivable, the physical story leaves felt experience open. Whether they are conceivable, and what that proves, has been debated for decades. The puzzle is genuinely open.

question: An old bishop writes: 'I turn inward and find my thoughts doubting, wishing, and wondering by their own light -- while my body just sits here in the garden. How can these two be one kind of thing?' Which view of mind is he leaning on?
answer: Mind-separate view -- mind is a different kind of thing from the body.
choices: Mind-separate view -- mind is a different kind of thing from the body.
Brain-state view -- the inner thought just IS the brain firing, nothing else.
Pattern view -- mind is the pattern, not the stuff; silicon could run it too.
Behavior-only view -- a mind just IS how you act; nothing is felt inside.
context: Augustine (Confessions, ~400 AD) felt a sharp split between mind and body that Descartes later made explicit in 1641. Physicalists reply that the brain is doing the 'turning inward' too -- so the felt separateness is misleading evidence about what mind really is.

question: The 'Chinese Room' thought experiment: imagine a person who speaks no Chinese sitting in a room with a huge rulebook mapping Chinese symbols to Chinese symbols. People slide in questions; he looks them up and slides back fluent answers — but understands none of it. What does the room operator have that a real Chinese speaker has but his rule-book doesn't supply?
answer: Syntax is not semantics — shuffling symbols by rules is not the same as understanding what those symbols mean.
choices: Syntax is not semantics — shuffling symbols by rules is not the same as understanding what those symbols mean.
Behaviorism is right — if the room's outputs match a real speaker's, behavior is the only honest standard for understanding.
The case is confused — 'understanding' is a folk word with no real referent, so the question has no determinate answer.
Only biology understands — only systems built from the same neural stuff as ours could ever have real understanding.
context: John Searle's 'Minds, Brains, and Programs' (1980) presents the Chinese Room against 'strong AI' — the claim that running the right program is sufficient for understanding. Searle's positive view, biological naturalism, is the fourth option. The Systems Reply is the main rebuttal.

question: The 'inverted spectrum' thought experiment: imagine you and a friend both call fire engines 'red' and grass 'green' — but what you see looking at fire is what she sees looking at grass, and vice versa. No behavior would catch the difference. Can behavior settle whether two people's inner colors match?
answer: What experiences FEEL like may not be fixed by behavior — two people could match in word and act yet differ in inner color experience.
choices: What experiences FEEL like may not be fixed by behavior — two people could match in word and act yet differ in inner color experience.
The case is a pseudo-question — since no behavior would distinguish them, there is no real fact about which one is inverted.
Inner experience IS brain activity — the brains are identical by stipulation, so the inverts cannot occur in the first place.
Color words have no real meaning — since people might see colors differently, words like 'red' are empty labels with no shared content.
context: John Locke (Essay Concerning Human Understanding, 1689, Book II ch. 32) raised the inverted spectrum to ask whether qualia — what experiences are LIKE — can be pinned down by behavior. Modern revivals (Shoemaker 1981, Block 1990) press the case against functionalism, the view that mental states ARE their causal-functional roles.

question: An AI writes a poem that moves a reader to tears. On a podcast a guest argues: 'No matter how completely we map the machine's processing, we still won't know whether anything was FELT in making it. THAT gap is the real puzzle of consciousness.' Which view of mind is the guest using?
answer: Extra-property view -- the feeling is a real further fact, not just the wiring.
choices: Extra-property view -- the feeling is a real further fact, not just the wiring.
Pattern view -- if it plays the same role we do, no felt extra is left over.
Drop-the-word view -- 'felt' is a bad folk idea brain science will retire.
Brain-state view -- the full wiring story already IS the whole story.
context: Property dualism takes seriously the gap David Chalmers (1995) drew between the 'easy problems' (how processing works) and the 'hard problem' (why processing comes with feeling). It treats felt experience as a real extra fact about the brain -- without adding a separate soul-substance.

question: A defender of strong AI replies to Searle's Chinese Room: 'You're focused on the wrong level. The person inside is one component, like a single neuron. The WHOLE SYSTEM — person plus rulebook plus paper — understands Chinese, though no individual part does.' Which standard reply to Searle is this?
answer: The Systems Reply — understanding belongs to the whole room-plus-rulebook system, not to any individual part; pointing out that the person alone does not understand misses the level at which understanding is supposed to occur.
choices: The Systems Reply — understanding belongs to the whole room-plus-rulebook system, not to any individual part; pointing out that the person alone does not understand misses the level at which understanding is supposed to occur.
The Robot Reply — the room would understand if embedded in a robot body with sensors and actuators; the case shows only that disembodied symbol-shuffling is insufficient for genuine grasp of meaning.

The Brain Simulator Reply — the room would understand if its rulebook simulated a real Chinese speaker's neuron-by-neuron brain activity, in which case the relevant biological process is present in formal guise.

The Other Minds Reply — we credit other humans with understanding only on behavioral grounds, so denying the room understanding on the same grounds would commit us to denying it of every speaker except ourselves.
context: John Searle anticipated four major replies in 'Minds, Brains, and Programs' (1980): the Systems Reply (Berkeley), the Robot Reply (Yale), the Brain Simulator Reply (Berkeley and MIT), and the Other Minds Reply. Searle answered each in turn; the Systems Reply remains the most widely defended of the four.

question: Neuroscientist Mary has spent her life in a black-and-white room studying the complete physics of color vision. She knows every physical fact about wavelengths and neural responses. One day she leaves the room and sees a red rose for the first time. The thought experiment asks: did Mary LEARN something genuinely new on leaving?
answer: Yes -- Mary gains phenomenal knowledge (what red LOOKS like) no physical information conveyed; this challenges physicalism's claim that complete physical knowledge is complete knowledge.
