choices: Yes -- Mary gains phenomenal knowledge (what red LOOKS like) no physical information conveyed; this challenges physicalism's claim that complete physical knowledge is complete knowledge.
No -- Mary already had complete physical knowledge by stipulation, so seeing red gives her only a new ability (to recognize, to imagine), not a new fact about the world that she lacked.
Yes -- but only because the stipulation is incoherent; no human could really possess complete physical knowledge of color vision, so the case shows nothing about the limits of physicalism.
No -- the framing presupposes a phenomenal/physical distinction, so any answer just restates whichever side one had already accepted before considering the thought experiment at all.
context: Frank Jackson's 'Epiphenomenal Qualia' (1982) presents Mary's Room as the knowledge argument against physicalism. The pro-physicalist 'ability hypothesis' (Lewis, Nemirow) is option B. Jackson himself later moved away from the argument, but the case remains a central debate.

question: A physicalist replies to Chalmers's zombie argument: 'Conceivability is not a reliable guide to possibility. People once conceived water that is not H2O — and were wrong. Coherent conceivability is no proof of metaphysical possibility.' Which reply to the zombie argument is this?
answer: Conceivability does not entail possibility — Kripkean a posteriori necessity (water = H2O is necessary but knowable only empirically) blocks Chalmers's premise.
choices: Conceivability does not entail possibility — Kripkean a posteriori necessity (water = H2O is necessary but knowable only empirically) blocks Chalmers's premise.
Zombies are conceptually incoherent — anything functionally identical to a conscious being must be conscious; the case is a hidden contradiction.
Phenomenal facts are over and above physical facts — Chalmers's zombie argument succeeds, refuting type physicalism in one step.
Functionalism is vindicated — once we explain cognitive functions, no consciousness-extra remains to explain; the zombie case asks about a non-thing.
context: The Kripkean conceivability-vs-possibility reply (Yablo 1993; Stoljar 2006; Dennett) is the leading physicalist response to Chalmers. Saul Kripke (Naming and Necessity, 1980) argued necessary identities can be discovered empirically — so coherent conceivability of their failure is no proof those failures are possible. Chalmers's reply (2002) refines the conceivability premise to dodge this objection.

question: A functionalist replies to inverted-spectrum cases: 'If the supposed inverts share every functional relation — same effects of red light on heart rate, sweating, aesthetic ratings — then there IS no fact about which one inverts. Talk of an inner 'what-it-is-like' that floats free of every functional relation is talk about nothing.' Which reply is this?
answer: Verificationist / eliminative reply — without any functional or behavioral difference, there is no fact of inversion; the alleged phenomenal residue is a non-existent entity.
choices: Verificationist / eliminative reply — without any functional or behavioral difference, there is no fact of inversion; the alleged phenomenal residue is a non-existent entity.
Type physicalist reply — the brain states of the supposed inverts would necessarily differ; the scenario is incoherent at the physical level and not genuinely possible.
Higher-order reply — what makes a quale the quale it is depends on its higher-order representation; identical functional roles guarantee identical qualia.
Property-dualist reply — the case shows qualia and functional roles can diverge, so any role-based theory is incomplete; consciousness is more than function.
context: Inverted-spectrum cases (Locke, Essay II.32; Shoemaker 1981; Block 1990) are the canonical pressure on functionalism. The eliminative reply (Dennett, 'Quining Qualia,' 1988) takes Wittgensteinian aim at the supposed phenomenal residue: if no functional or behavioral test could discriminate the inverts, the alleged phenomenal difference is a fiction.

question: Jackson's Mary has lived her life in a black-and-white room. She knows every physical fact about wavelengths and neural responses to red. The day she leaves the room and sees a red rose, she says: 'Oh — so THIS is what red is like.' What does the Mary case expose?
answer: The knowledge argument — physical knowledge does not include phenomenal knowledge; learning what red LOOKS like is gaining a fact no complete physical description contained.
choices: The knowledge argument — physical knowledge does not include phenomenal knowledge; learning what red LOOKS like is gaining a fact no complete physical description contained.
The ability hypothesis — Mary gains new abilities (to imagine, recognize, remember red) rather than new facts; the case shows know-how, not new propositional knowledge.
The acquaintance reply — Mary gains a new mode of access to a fact she already knew; the fact is the same, only the way of grasping it is new.
Eliminative materialism — 'what red looks like' is a folk-psychology category mature neuroscience will dissolve; the case shows the category fails.
context: Frank Jackson's 'Epiphenomenal Qualia' (1982) introduced Mary's room as the knowledge argument against physicalism. Jackson himself later (1998) abandoned the argument in favor of physicalism — the ability hypothesis (Lewis, Nemirow) was one of the considerations that moved him. Nagel's bat (1974) is in the same family of anti-reductive thought experiments.

question: Ned Block asks us to picture a billion people, each working a radio, together copying the exact firing pattern of a brain. The system behaves just like a mind, he says, yet surely no single feeling glows in the crowd. What does this aim to show against functionalism?
answer: A system can copy the full functional pattern and still feel nothing inside.
choices: A system can copy the full functional pattern and still feel nothing inside.
A mind needs a non-physical soul the radios could never supply.
Talk of 'feelings' is folk theory neuroscience will one day drop.
Behavior is all there is, so the crowd simply has no inner side.
context: Ned Block's 'Troubles with Functionalism' (1978) calls this the 'China brain' or 'nation of China' case. The worry is ABSENT QUALIA: if matching the functional role can leave felt experience missing, then a mental state cannot be just its functional role.

question: A defender of strong AI replies to Searle: 'You say only the right BIOLOGY could be conscious — but that's the old vitalist claim that only the right BIOLOGY could be alive, refuted by chemistry. You give consciousness the same special status with no better evidence.' Which standard objection is this?
answer: The neo-vitalism objection — biological naturalism marks consciousness as substrate-specific in the way vitalism marked life; chemistry refuted vitalism and consciousness deserves no different fate.
choices: The neo-vitalism objection — biological naturalism marks consciousness as substrate-specific in the way vitalism marked life; chemistry refuted vitalism and consciousness deserves no different fate.
The systems objection — Searle's Chinese Room tacitly assumes understanding belongs to the person not the system; his rejection of strong AI rests on a level-mistake.
The phenomenal-only objection — biological naturalism handles function but cannot explain phenomenal consciousness; it inherits the hard problem without solving it.
The eliminativist objection — 'consciousness' is a folk-psychology category neuroscience will replace; biological naturalism doubles down on a category that may not survive.
context: Searle's biological naturalism (The Rediscovery of the Mind, 1992) holds consciousness is a biological feature of the right kind of brain, not a substrate-independent computational pattern. Critics from Daniel Dennett onward press the neo-vitalism analogy: vitalism said only 'organic' chemistry could be alive, and was refuted. Why should consciousness be any different?

question: Churchland says future brain science will scrap 'belief' the way chemistry scrapped phlogiston. A critic shoots back: but to ASSERT that is to want you to BELIEVE it, so the claim leans on the very thing it tries to throw out. What kind of objection is the critic making?
answer: It is self-defeating: stating it already uses the category it says will vanish.
choices: It is self-defeating: stating it already uses the category it says will vanish.
Belief has predicted behavior for ages, so no theory beats its track record.
Belief should be reduced to brain states, not thrown out altogether.
Even if belief goes, raw felt experience would still be left unexplained.
context: This is the self-refutation objection (Lynne Rudder Baker, Saving Belief 1987; Jerry Fodor) to eliminative materialism. Churchland's reply: science will hand us a successor concept for belief-and-assertion too, just as it replaced phlogiston-talk. The dispute is still live.

question: One theory says a mental state turns conscious only when a SECOND state looks at it. A critic presses: then what makes THAT second state conscious - a third looking at it, then a fourth, with no end, like mirrors facing mirrors? Or does it just sit there, conscious yet unwatched? Which objection is the critic raising?
answer: The watching states form an endless chain that never bottoms out.
choices: The watching states form an endless chain that never bottoms out.
The theory predicts pairings the brain scans never actually show.
It still says nothing about what the conscious state FEELS like.
'Conscious' is folk theory that mature brain science will discard.
context: This is the regress objection to higher-order theories of consciousness, a standard worry pressed against them. David Rosenthal's higher-order-thought view replies that the higher-order state can itself be unconscious unless yet another state targets it; critics say that just concedes the puzzle.

question: Tononi's theory measures consciousness by a number, phi. A critic shows the math hands a giant grid of simple logic gates MORE phi than a wide-awake person, while a perfect brain simulation scores zero. He says a theory that ranks things so strangely should be doubted. Which objection is this?
answer: Its own formula credits the wrong systems and denies the obvious ones.
choices: Its own formula credits the wrong systems and denies the obvious ones.
Only living brains feel, so no number could ever capture it.
Consciousness is fixed by what a system DOES, not how it is wired.
'Consciousness' is folk theory mature brain science will replace.
context: Scott Aaronson ('Why I Am Not An Integrated Information Theorist,' 2014) showed simple grid and XOR networks score very high phi by IIT's own rules. Tononi answered by refining the theory's exclusion postulates; the objection is widely held to be still live.

question: A philosophy class reads Gilbert Ryle. One student summarizes: 'To say someone is intelligent is not to say there is a hidden inner thing in them. It is to say they ARE disposed to behave intelligently in the relevant kinds of situations. To look for the mind behind the behavior is to make a category mistake.' What view of mind is this?
answer: Logical behaviorism -- mental terms refer to dispositions to behave in characteristic ways; talk of inner mental states reduces to talk of behavioral and dispositional patterns in the agent.
choices: Logical behaviorism -- mental terms refer to dispositions to behave in characteristic ways; talk of inner mental states reduces to talk of behavioral and dispositional patterns in the agent.
Functionalism -- mental states are individuated by functional role, including internal causal transitions; behavior is one output of those inner roles, but the inner architecture is real.
Type physicalism -- every mental-state type is identical to a brain-state type; intelligence is a brain feature with characteristic behavioral effects, not reducible to dispositions alone.
Property dualism -- mental properties are non-physical features of physical systems; reducing intelligence to dispositions misses the phenomenal aspect of cognitive experience entirely.
context: Gilbert Ryle (The Concept of Mind, 1949) attacked the 'ghost in the machine' picture and defended logical behaviorism: mental talk is dispositional talk. The view has been largely displaced by functionalism (which keeps inner causal architecture) but Ryle's category-mistake critique remains influential.

question: On a panel a guest argues: 'Pain does not merely come from a brain firing - pain IS that firing, the very same thing under another name, the way water just IS H2O.' Which view of mind is the guest using?
answer: Identity theory - each mental state simply IS a brain state.
choices: Identity theory - each mental state simply IS a brain state.
Functionalism - a state is what it DOES, so other stuff could feel pain.
Property dualism - the felt side is an extra fact the brain story misses.
Behaviorism - pain is just the wincing, with nothing felt inside.
context: Type physicalism, or identity theory (U.T. Place 1956; J.J.C. Smart, 'Sensations and Brain Processes,' 1959), holds each mental-state TYPE is strictly identical to a brain-state type. Multiple-realizability arguments (Putnam, Fodor) pushed many toward functionalism instead.

question: A student sums up a theory of mind: 'What makes a feeling PAIN isn't the stuff it runs on — it's the job it does: damage triggers it, it makes you pull back and wince. Anything doing that job is pain, be it nerves, silicon, or an alien.' Which view of mind is this?
answer: Functionalism — a mental state is defined by the job it does, on any hardware.
choices: Functionalism — a mental state is defined by the job it does, on any hardware.
Mind-brain identity — pain just IS one brain event and nothing else.
Behaviorism — pain is only the outward wincing, with no inner state.
Dualism — pain is an extra non-physical thing beyond any brain event.
context: Hilary Putnam ('The Nature of Mental States,' 1967) launched functionalism. Its key claim is multiple realizability: the same mental state can run on very different physical systems, so pain need not be one specific brain event. Frank Jackson's Mary's Room and Ned Block's China-brain are the famous objections, pressing on what the job-description leaves out.

question: Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia writes to Descartes in May 1643 with the question that would haunt substance dualism for centuries: 'I beg you to tell me how the soul of a man — being only a thinking substance — can determine the bodily spirits to perform voluntary actions.' What objection is she pressing?
answer: The interaction problem — if mind is non-physical and body is physical, no coherent mechanism explains how mental events could cause physical motions; dualism postulates causation across a gap it cannot bridge.
choices: The interaction problem — if mind is non-physical and body is physical, no coherent mechanism explains how mental events could cause physical motions; dualism postulates causation across a gap it cannot bridge.
The conservation objection — physical conservation laws leave no causal room for non-physical influences on the brain; mental causation would violate physical conservation principles.
The simplicity objection — substance dualism doubles fundamental kinds without explanatory gain; methodological parsimony favors physicalism wherever a physical account is available.
The phenomenal-only objection — what dualists actually need is non-physical PROPERTIES of physical substances (property dualism), not a second kind of substance entirely.
context: Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia's letter of May 6, 1643 (and the five-year correspondence that followed) is the founding statement of the interaction problem. Descartes's responses — the pineal gland, the appeal to mind-body union as a 'primitive notion' — have struck most philosophers as unsatisfying. The problem remains the standard objection to substance dualism.

question: McGinn says consciousness has a normal explanation, but human minds are simply built wrong to grasp it. A critic answers: to KNOW we are walled off from the answer, you would need the very God's-eye view you say we lack. Which objection is the critic raising?
answer: Claiming we cannot know it already claims to know too much.
choices: Claiming we cannot know it already claims to know too much.
Brain science keeps making progress, so nothing is walled off.
A real gap this deep points to a soul, not just to our limits.
It is mere defeatism - a hard problem is no proof of a wall.
context: This is the self-defeat objection to McGinn's mysterianism (Can We Solve the Mind-Body Problem? 1989), pressed by Owen Flanagan and Daniel Dennett. McGinn replies that we can know our faculties are LIMITED without mapping exactly where the limit falls - as a color-blind person knows they miss something.

question: A philosopher discusses the Turing test: a judge sends text messages to a hidden human and a hidden machine and tries to tell them apart. Turing argued: if the machine reliably passes, the question 'can it think?' has effectively been answered. A critic responds: 'Passing settles only behavior, not understanding.' What does this expose?
answer: Behaviorist criteria are too thin for mind -- indistinguishable conversation could come from symbol-manipulation alone, leaving the question of inner understanding (semantics) unresolved.
choices: Behaviorist criteria are too thin for mind -- indistinguishable conversation could come from symbol-manipulation alone, leaving the question of inner understanding (semantics) unresolved.
The test is unfair to machines -- judges have a built-in bias that prevents fair adjudication; the critique would be answered if the test were properly redesigned to remove the prejudice.
Functionalism is vindicated -- since the machine plays the same role in conversation as a human, it must be in the same mental states; the critique misunderstands functionalism here.
Eliminative materialism handles the case -- 'thinking' is a folk-psychology term that will not survive mature theory, so the question of whether the machine 'really' thinks does not arise.
context: Alan Turing ('Computing Machinery and Intelligence,' 1950) proposed the imitation game as a behavioral criterion for thought. Searle's Chinese Room (1980) is the canonical version of the critique here: behavioral indistinguishability does not establish semantic understanding.

question: Panpsychism says even tiny bits of matter carry a faint speck of experience. A critic asks: so how do countless specks ADD UP into the one whole feeling you have watching a sunset? No one has shown how the bits combine. Which objection is this?
answer: It never shows how the specks merge into one whole feeling.
choices: It never shows how the specks merge into one whole feeling.
There is simply no evidence that matter feels anything.
Only living brains can feel, never plain bits of matter.
'Experience' is folk theory brain science will one day drop.
context: This is the combination problem, raised by William James himself (Principles of Psychology, 1890) and sharpened by Sam Coleman (2014). Galen Strawson, Philip Goff, and Hedda Hassel Morch offer answers (constitutive panpsychism, cosmopsychism, phenomenal bonding); none is yet settled.

question: A philosopher points out: a rock is not ABOUT anything. But a belief is always about something - a friend, a storm, even a unicorn that does not exist. He calls this 'aboutness' the one feature that marks minds off from mere matter. Which feature is he pointing to?
answer: Intentionality - a mental state is always directed AT some object, the way the belief is about a unicorn.
choices: Intentionality - a mental state is always directed AT some object, the way the belief is about a unicorn.
Consciousness - a mental state always has a felt, what-it's-like quality the rock lacks.
Behavior - a mind shows itself only in how a body outwardly acts, not in any inner trait.
Brain-basis - a mental state is just neural firing, so 'aboutness' adds nothing real.
context: Franz Brentano (Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint, 1874) revived the medieval term 'intentionality' for the directedness of mental states toward objects - their 'aboutness.' He argued this is the mark of the mental: physical things like rocks are not about anything; thoughts always are.

question: A thinker argues the mind feels things but causes nothing - it is mere 'steam off the engine,' a byproduct that pushes no levers. A critic shoots back: 'Then your own belief in this theory caused nothing either - so it could not have moved your hand to write the book defending it.' What is the critic's objection?
answer: It is self-undermining - if no belief can cause anything, his belief could not have caused the book he wrote.
choices: It is self-undermining - if no belief can cause anything, his belief could not have caused the book he wrote.
Evolution would not preserve a feeling that does no work, so the mind must do something useful.
It still never explains WHAT those feelings are like, only whether they push the levers at all.
Words like 'belief' are bad theory anyway and will be dropped entirely by future brain science.
context: Epiphenomenalism (T.H. Huxley, 1874; Frank Jackson, 1982, before he reversed) says mental events are caused by the brain but cause nothing. The self-stultification objection - pressed since William James - notes the theory undercuts its own defense: if belief moves nothing, it could not have moved anyone to assert the theory.

question: Donald Davidson's 'deviant causal chain': a climber holding a partner on a rope WANTS to drop her to save himself and BELIEVES letting go would do it. The very thought makes him so nervous his hand trembles and accidentally releases the rope. The desire and belief 'caused' the release — but did he genuinely ACT?
answer: No — action requires the right KIND of causal path from intention to movement; the climber's tremor was caused by his intention but did not execute it.
choices: No — action requires the right KIND of causal path from intention to movement; the climber's tremor was caused by his intention but did not execute it.
Yes — since the belief and desire produced the movement that fulfilled them, the causal theory of action counts this as a genuine action.
Yes — the climber wanted her to fall and she did, so morally he did the act; the inner pathway from thought to motion is a scientific detail.
No — no bodily movement is ever truly an action; 'action' is folk-psychology talk that mature science will replace with muscle and neural firing.
context: Donald Davidson ('Actions, Reasons, and Causes,' 1963; 'Freedom to Act,' 1973) developed the causal theory of action: actions are bodily movements caused IN THE RIGHT WAY by beliefs and desires. Deviant causal chains (climber, nervous assassin) show that 'caused by' is not enough; specifying the 'right way' has resisted clean solution.

question: In Sperry and Gazzaniga's 'split-brain' studies, patients whose two brain halves had been surgically separated could VERBALLY report only what the left hemisphere saw, while the left HAND (driven by the right hemisphere) reached correctly for objects the patient claimed not to see. What does it mean that the right hemisphere acts on visual information the patient denies seeing?
answer: Unity of consciousness is not guaranteed by having one body — the patient may host two streams of awareness, straining the picture of a single unified self.
choices: Unity of consciousness is not guaranteed by having one body — the patient may host two streams of awareness, straining the picture of a single unified self.
Personal identity reduces to body — the patient is plainly one person because one body persists, so the experimental quirks add nothing to identity.
There is no self at all — the case proves the everyday notion of personal identity is empty, since careful experiments dissolve any single thinking subject.
Consciousness is non-physical — since two streams cannot share one body, the case proves the mind is a substance separate from the brain entirely.
context: Roger Sperry's split-brain research (Nobel Prize 1981) on patients whose corpus callosum was severed to treat epilepsy revealed two streams of processing operating independently. Michael Gazzaniga ('The Bisected Brain,' 1970) developed the philosophical implications. The case is a linchpin in modern debates about personal identity and unity of mind.

question: An AI writes a poem that moves a reader to tears. A panelist argues: 'Even a COMPLETE wiring diagram of the machine would still leave one question open - whether anything was actually FELT as it wrote. That gap is metaphysics, not engineering.' Which view of mind is the panelist defending?
answer: Felt-extra view - it is all physical, but feeling is a further fact the full wiring story leaves open.
choices: Felt-extra view - it is all physical, but feeling is a further fact the full wiring story leaves open.
Pattern view - mind is what a system DOES, so matching the role leaves no extra question.
Brain-state view - the mind just IS the wiring, so the full diagram already settles everything.
Drop-the-words view - 'felt experience' is a bad category future science will simply discard.
context: David Chalmers ('Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness,' 1995) splits the 'easy problems' (explaining brain function) from the 'hard problem' (why any of it is FELT). Property dualism takes that gap seriously: the world is physical, but felt experience is an extra property no complete physical description captures.

question: Mary, a neuroscientist, has spent her entire life in a black-and-white room studying the science of color. She knows every physical fact about wavelengths, cone activation, and cortical processing. Stepping outside, she sees a red rose for the first time. The thought experiment asks: did Mary LEARN something genuinely new on stepping outside?
answer: Yes — Mary gains phenomenal knowledge (what red is LIKE) that no physical description conveyed; this challenges physicalism (the view that complete physical knowledge is complete knowledge).
choices: Yes — Mary gains phenomenal knowledge (what red is LIKE) that no physical description conveyed; this challenges physicalism (the view that complete physical knowledge is complete knowledge).
No — Mary had every physical fact by stipulation, and seeing red gives only a new ability (to recognize, to imagine), not a new fact about the world she previously lacked.
Yes — but only because the stipulation is incoherent; no human could really possess complete physical knowledge, so the case proves nothing about the limits of physicalism.
The question is malformed — 'experience' and 'knowledge' are distinct categories, and asking whether one yields the other commits a category mistake from the outset.
context: Frank Jackson's 'Epiphenomenal Qualia' (1982) is the canonical version. The pro-physicalist 'ability hypothesis' (Lewis, Nemirow) is choice B; Jackson himself later moved toward it. The knowledge argument remains a central test case for any reductive theory of mind.

question: A philosophy seminar reads Searle's Chinese Room: a person who speaks no Chinese sits in a room with an enormous rulebook mapping Chinese symbols to Chinese symbols. From outside, the answers look fluent. Searle concludes: 'The room passes the test but understands nothing.' What does the Chinese Room case expose?
answer: Functionalism faces a syntax/semantics gap — the room's behavior matches a Chinese speaker's, yet symbol-shuffling alone does not constitute understanding the meaning of the symbols.
choices: Functionalism faces a syntax/semantics gap — the room's behavior matches a Chinese speaker's, yet symbol-shuffling alone does not constitute understanding the meaning of the symbols.
Behaviorism is vindicated — since the room's outputs are indistinguishable from understanding, behavior is the only honest standard for crediting any system with comprehension.
Eliminative materialism is supported — 'understanding' is a folk-psychology term with no real referent, so the question of whether the room understands has no determinate answer.
Type physicalism is too narrow — only systems made of the same neural-state types as ours could understand, and the room's physical implementation is plainly the wrong stuff.
context: John Searle, 'Minds, Brains, and Programs' (1980), argues that syntax (formal symbol manipulation) is not sufficient for semantics (meaning). Searle's positive view is biological naturalism: only the right biology yields semantic content. The Systems Reply and Robot Reply contest the conclusion.

question: On a panel on integrated theories of consciousness, a guest describes the philosophical zombie: a being physically identical to you down to the last neuron, behaving exactly as you do, yet with no inner experience whatsoever. She argues: 'Even if no such creature could exist, it is coherently CONCEIVABLE, and that alone says something important.' What does the zombie case expose?
answer: Phenomenal facts are not entailed by physical facts — if zombies are coherently conceivable, the physical story leaves consciousness undetermined, counting against type physicalism.
choices: Phenomenal facts are not entailed by physical facts — if zombies are coherently conceivable, the physical story leaves consciousness undetermined, counting against type physicalism.
Conceivability tracks possibility unreliably — we can conceive impossibilities (water not H2O), so zombie-conceivability does not show consciousness is metaphysically extra at all.
Eliminative materialism is the natural conclusion — once 'phenomenal experience' allows such bizarre cases, we should suspect the category is incoherent and drop it from theory.
Functionalism is vindicated — since the zombie functions exactly as you do, it must be in the same mental states, so 'no inner experience' is a contradiction in terms here.
context: David Chalmers (The Conscious Mind, 1996) deploys the zombie argument: conceivability implies possibility, possibility entails non-entailment, and non-entailment refutes physicalism. The standard reply (Dennett, Yablo) is choice B — conceivability is a weak guide to metaphysical possibility.

question: A philosophy of mind workshop discusses inverted spectrum: two people raised identically, both calling fire engines 'red' and grass 'green,' yet one inwardly experiences what the other would call green when looking at fire, and vice versa. No behavioral test would distinguish them. What does the inverted spectrum case expose?
answer: Functional role does not fully fix phenomenal character — two systems can be functionally identical yet differ in what their experiences are LIKE; this counts against functionalism.
choices: Functional role does not fully fix phenomenal character — two systems can be functionally identical yet differ in what their experiences are LIKE; this counts against functionalism.
Behaviorism is vindicated — since no behavior would distinguish the two, there is no genuine fact about which inverts, and the case dissolves as a pseudo-question entirely.
Type physicalism handles the case — the brain states are identical by stipulation, so the inverts are impossible, and the conceivability of inversion is confused intuition.
Eliminative materialism is supported — 'what experience is like' relies on a folk category with no scientific anchor, so the case shows the category should be abandoned.
context: Inverted spectrum cases (Locke, Essay II.32; Sydney Shoemaker 1981; Ned Block 1990) press the gap between functional role and phenomenal quale. The case is designed to show that two systems can share all functional and behavioral properties yet differ phenomenally — a problem for any role-based theory of mind.

question: On a podcast on the limits of objective science, a philosopher summarizes Thomas Nagel: 'Bats navigate by sonar, a modality we lack. We can describe their neurology completely and STILL not know what their experience is like from the inside. The subjective is missed by the objective story.' The thought experiment asks: what does the bat case expose?
answer: Irreducibility of the subjective — phenomenal character (the 'what-it-is-likeness') is a property not captured by any third-person physical description of the system.
choices: Irreducibility of the subjective — phenomenal character (the 'what-it-is-likeness') is a property not captured by any third-person physical description of the system.
Higher-order theory — consciousness is a state's being the object of a higher-order representation; the bat is unknowable because we lack higher-order access to its states.
Functionalism vindicated — mental states are individuated by functional roles, so simulating the bat's functional architecture would give us full access to its experience.
Eliminative materialism — 'what it is like' relies on folk-psychological intuition mature neuroscience will discard; the bat case poses no problem once the category is dropped.
context: Thomas Nagel, 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' (1974), argues that the subjective character of experience cannot be captured by any objective, third-person account. The paper is an ancestor of Chalmers's hard problem and a foundational text for property dualism and related anti-reductive views.

question: A scientist argues: 'An octopus, a human, and a silicon alien could all feel pain. What makes a state pain is what it DOES - the alarm it raises, the avoiding it drives - not the stuff it runs on.' Which view of mind is she using?
answer: Pattern view - a state counts as pain by the ROLE it plays, so many different materials can run it.
choices: Pattern view - a state counts as pain by the ROLE it plays, so many different materials can run it.
Carbon-only view - only living tissue can feel, so the silicon alien is simply left out.
Brain-state view - pain just IS one human neural type, so octopus 'pain' cannot be the same.
Behavior-only view - pain is just wincing and fleeing, with no inner role doing any work.
context: Functionalism (Hilary Putnam, 'The Nature of Mental States,' 1967; Jerry Fodor, 1968) was driven by multiple realizability: the same mental state can run in different physical systems - octopus, human, or machine - because what fixes it is its causal role, not its material.

question: Summarizing Searle, a philosopher pictures a man sealed in a room, shuffling Chinese symbols by a rulebook - fluent replies slide out, yet nothing inside understands a word. REAL understanding, he says, takes REAL neurons; the same program in other stuff stays blind. Which view of mind is this?
answer: Brain-only view - real brains cause consciousness; a copy of the program in other stuff stays unconscious.
choices: Brain-only view - real brains cause consciousness; a copy of the program in other stuff stays unconscious.
Pattern view - run the right program in ANY stuff and you get the mind that goes with it.
Felt-extra view - it is all physical, but feeling is a further fact the brain story leaves open.
Drop-the-words view - 'consciousness' is a bad category future brain science will discard.
context: John Searle's Chinese Room ('Minds, Brains, and Programs,' 1980) and his biological naturalism (The Rediscovery of the Mind, 1992) hold that consciousness is caused by and realized in real brain processes, not by running a program. His other analogy - a simulated rainstorm is not wet - marks his split from any functionalism that lets minds run on any substrate.

question: Summarizing Churchland, a student says: 'Belief, desire, hope, fear - these come from an old folk theory for predicting people. As brain science matures, it will DROP them entirely, the way chemistry dropped "phlogiston" - not keep them under new names.' Which view of mind is this?
answer: Drop-the-words view - belief and desire are a failed theory that brain science will scrap, not relabel.
choices: Drop-the-words view - belief and desire are a failed theory that brain science will scrap, not relabel.
Reduce-the-words view - belief and desire are real and will be MATCHED to brain states, not dropped.
Useful-fiction view - belief talk predicts people well, so we keep it even if it names nothing deep.
Pattern view - belief and desire are real functional roles and survive as a higher-level science.
context: Paul Churchland ('Eliminative Materialism and the Propositional Attitudes,' 1981) argues folk psychology is itself a theory - and a poor one - that mature neuroscience will eliminate, not reduce, just as 'phlogiston' was scrapped. The rivals KEEP the categories: reductive physicalism matches them to brain states; Dennett's instrumentalism keeps them as a useful predictive stance.

question: A guest argues: 'A pain by itself is not yet conscious. It becomes conscious only when a SECOND state notices it. The moment you become aware of HAVING the headache - that awareness of it - is what lights the pain up.' Which view of consciousness is this?
answer: Watcher view - a state turns conscious only when a second, higher state represents it (you notice the headache).
choices: Watcher view - a state turns conscious only when a second, higher state represents it (you notice the headache).
Built-in view - the right state is already conscious by itself; no second state needs to notice it.
Broadcast view - a state is conscious when it is shared widely across the brain's many systems.
Drop-the-words view - 'conscious' is a bad category future brain science will simply discard.
context: Higher-order theories (David Rosenthal, 'Two Concepts of Consciousness,' 1986; Peter Carruthers) hold a state is conscious only when a distinct higher-order state represents it - you become aware of having it. First-order theorists (Dretske, Tye) disagree: the right first-order state is conscious on its own.

question: Neuroscientist Giulio Tononi defines consciousness as integrated information, a quantity he calls phi: a system is conscious to the degree its parts together hold more information than the parts apart. He grants this means even a thermostat has a faint flicker of it. Which view is Tononi defending?
answer: Integration view -- consciousness just IS integrated information, present to some degree in any system with phi.
choices: Integration view -- consciousness just IS integrated information, present to some degree in any system with phi.
Functionalism -- consciousness is the rich job a mind does, which a thermostat is far too simple to perform.
Biological view -- consciousness is a brain phenomenon, so no thermostat or chip could ever have any of it.
Higher-order view -- a state is conscious only when the mind notices it, which a thermostat can never do.
context: Giulio Tononi's Integrated Information Theory (2004; book Phi, 2012) identifies consciousness with integrated information. Its panpsychist edge -- positive phi anywhere means a flicker of consciousness -- is its most disputed feature; Scott Aaronson objects that simple grids then score absurdly high.

question: A cognitive scientist argues: 'Most of the brain runs in parallel, in the dark. One narrow stream wins the competition and gets BROADCAST to memory, planning, and speech all at once -- and that moment of wide broadcast just IS becoming conscious of it.' Which view of consciousness is this?
answer: Workspace view -- a state is conscious when it is broadcast widely to many systems at once.
choices: Workspace view -- a state is conscious when it is broadcast widely to many systems at once.
Higher-order view -- a state is conscious only when a separate thought turns to notice it.
Integration view -- a state is conscious by how tightly its parts weave information together.
Property dualism -- broadcast is just brain wiring and leaves the felt side wholly untouched.
context: Global Workspace Theory (Bernard Baars, 1988; Stanislas Dehaene, 2014) treats wide broadcast across cognitive systems as the conscious state. Critics grant it explains 'access' consciousness -- what we can report -- yet doubt it touches why the access is FELT at all.

question: A guest argues: 'Consciousness can't pop out of nothing. Either it appears by magic once matter gets complex enough, or it's already there in tiny amounts in matter's basic bits. The second is less spooky -- consciousness is fundamental and everywhere, like mass.' Which view of mind is the guest defending?
answer: Panpsychism -- consciousness is fundamental and present in tiny degree throughout all matter.
choices: Panpsychism -- consciousness is fundamental and present in tiny degree throughout all matter.
Strong emergence -- consciousness appears only at high complexity; basic matter has none of it.
Eliminativism -- 'consciousness' is a bad folk category that a mature science will discard.
Functionalism -- only systems complex enough to run the right roles are conscious at all.
context: Panpsychism (William James; Bertrand Russell; revived by Galen Strawson 2006, Philip Goff) takes consciousness as fundamental rather than emergent. Its central headache is the 'combination problem': how would countless micro-experiences fuse into the single unified experience you actually have?

question: A philosopher argues: 'Consciousness is real and non-physical -- but it does no work. Your choice to lift your arm FELT like the cause, yet the brain did all the real causing. Mind is like the steam above a train: real, but not what pulls the cars.' A critic pounces: if the feeling did nothing, how did your BELIEF in this view ever move a hand to write it down? Which view is the philosopher defending?
answer: Epiphenomenalism -- experience is a real byproduct of the brain but causes nothing itself.
choices: Epiphenomenalism -- experience is a real byproduct of the brain but causes nothing itself.
Interactionism -- the non-physical mind is real and genuinely pushes the body into action.
Eliminativism -- experience isn't a real thing at all; a mature science will drop the idea.
Functionalism -- a mental state just IS a causal role, so a powerless one is a contradiction.
context: Epiphenomenalism (T.H. Huxley, 1874; Frank Jackson, 1982, before he recanted) says brain events cause mental events that in turn cause nothing. Its sharpest worry is self-stultification: if experience does no work, how could a BELIEF in epiphenomenalism have moved anyone's hand to write the book defending it?

question: A guest argues: 'The brain DOES produce consciousness -- there's a real, natural answer for how. But our minds may be the wrong shape to ever grasp it, the way a dog can't grasp calculus. The truth exists; we just can't reach it.' Which view of mind is the guest defending?
answer: Mysterianism -- the answer is natural and real, but forever beyond our minds to grasp.
choices: Mysterianism -- the answer is natural and real, but forever beyond our minds to grasp.
Property dualism -- the gap is a real split in reality, not just a limit on our minds.
Eliminativism -- there's no real puzzle here; a mature science will drop the question.
Functionalism -- map the brain's machinery and nothing puzzling is left over to explain.
context: Colin McGinn ('Can We Solve the Mind-Body Problem?,' 1989) argued for what Owen Flanagan later dubbed new mysterianism: consciousness is natural, but human minds may be 'cognitively closed' to its explanation. The answer exists in nature, out of our reach.

question: Reading Donald Davidson, a student summarizes: 'Each mental event just IS some physical event -- no ghostly extra stuff. Yet no strict laws tie mental KINDS, like belief or desire, to brain kinds.' Jaegwon Kim presses: if no law links belief to any brain-kind, what work is the belief left to do? Which view is the student describing?
answer: Anomalous monism -- each mental event IS physical, but no rule ties mental KINDS to brain kinds.
choices: Anomalous monism -- each mental event IS physical, but no rule ties mental KINDS to brain kinds.
Type physicalism -- each mental KIND, like belief, reduces neatly to one specific brain-state kind.
Property dualism -- a physical event also carries extra mental properties not found in the physics.
Eliminativism -- belief and desire are a bad folk theory, so no reduction question even arises.
context: Donald Davidson's 'Mental Events' (1970) calls this anomalous monism: physical token by token, but with no psychophysical laws, so the mental stays irreducible as a kind. The balance is delicate -- Jaegwon Kim pressed that mental properties left with no lawful role risk doing no causal work.

question: On a panel responding to the Mary's Room argument, a physicalist replies: 'Mary gains a new CONCEPT of red, not a new FACT. Physical and phenomenal concepts refer to the same property under different cognitive modes — like "Hesperus" and "Phosphorus" both naming Venus. The gap is epistemic, not metaphysical.' Which physicalist move is the panelist defending?
answer: Phenomenal concepts strategy — physical and phenomenal concepts pick out the same underlying property; Mary acquires a new concept of an already-known property, so no new metaphysical fact is gained.
choices: Phenomenal concepts strategy — physical and phenomenal concepts pick out the same underlying property; Mary acquires a new concept of an already-known property, so no new metaphysical fact is gained.
Eliminative materialism — 'phenomenal' is a folk-psychology category mature neuroscience will discard; Mary's apparent learning is the surface of a confused concept, not new knowledge.
Property dualism — Mary really does learn a new non-physical property of experience; conceding that physicalism handles the case would give up the irreducibility of phenomenal character.
Functionalism — mental states are functional roles, so Mary already had every fact about red-experience that mattered; even the 'new concept' description misdescribes what occurs.
context: Brian Loar ('Phenomenal States,' 1990; 1997) and David Papineau (Thinking about Consciousness, 2002) developed the phenomenal concepts strategy: physicalism is true; the appearance of an explanatory gap is generated by the special cognitive mode of phenomenal concepts, not by extra properties.

question: When Descartes argued the mind is a non-physical, indivisible thing that could exist without the body, Princess Elisabeth shot back: how can something with no body or location PUSH a physical arm into motion? His critics still press it. Which view was Descartes defending?
answer: Substance dualism -- mind and body are two different kinds of stuff that can exist apart.
choices: Substance dualism -- mind and body are two different kinds of stuff that can exist apart.
Property dualism -- there's only physical stuff, but it carries irreducible mental properties.
Type physicalism -- the mind just IS the brain, named differently; no second substance exists.
Functionalism -- mind is a job a system does, runnable on brains or chips, not a special stuff.
context: Rene Descartes (Meditations, 1641) split reality into res cogitans (thinking stuff) and res extensa (extended stuff). Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia's 1643 letters pressed the interaction problem -- how a non-physical mind moves a physical body -- which keeps dualism a minority view today.

question: An octopus, a human, and a silicon alien can all be in pain, a thinker argues, yet each one's pain is just some physical event firing in that creature. So pain as a KIND is tied to no single brain-state, though every instance is physical. Which view is this?
answer: Token-physical -- each pain IS a brain event, but the kind 'pain' fits no one brain-state.
choices: Token-physical -- each pain IS a brain event, but the kind 'pain' fits no one brain-state.
Type-identity -- 'pain' just IS one brain-state, so octopus and human can't share it.
Two-substance -- pain is a non-physical event that no brain event could be.
No-such-state -- 'pain' is just a folk word real brain science will replace.
context: Token physicalism keeps materialism while granting that mental kinds need not carve nature at the same joints as physical kinds: every pain is a physical event, but 'pain' the type need not equal any one neural type. It is sustained by multiple-realizability arguments (Putnam, Fodor). Davidson's anomalous monism reaches the same token-identity by a different route -- the absence of strict psychophysical laws, not multiple realizability.

question: On a philosophy of mind seminar, a guest sharpens the case against type physicalism: 'Even granted that pain is correlated with C-fiber firing, WHY is C-fiber firing accompanied by anything felt at all? A complete physical story explains structure and function, but not why any of it is LIT UP from the inside.' What does the guest's argument expose?
answer: The explanatory gap — physical descriptions explain structure and function but leave unexplained why any of it is accompanied by phenomenal experience, which counts against type physicalism.
choices: The explanatory gap — physical descriptions explain structure and function but leave unexplained why any of it is accompanied by phenomenal experience, which counts against type physicalism.
Conceivability tracks possibility unreliably — we can conceive impossibilities, so the felt-gap intuition does not show consciousness is metaphysically extra; reductive theories survive.
Eliminative materialism is the proper response — 'lit up from the inside' relies on a folk category mature neuroscience will discard; the gap is generated by bad concepts, not reality.
Functionalism is vindicated — once we specify the functional role of pain, no further question about felt-ness remains; the explanatory gap is a confusion about what pain IS at the start.
context: Joseph Levine ('Materialism and Qualia: The Explanatory Gap,' 1983) coined the phrase; Chalmers (1995) sharpened it into the 'hard problem.' Type physicalists reply that all explanation has to bottom out somewhere; phenomenal-concepts theorists locate the gap in cognition, not metaphysics.

question: Otto, whose memory fails, writes every fact in a notebook he trusts and consults exactly as Inga trusts her memory. Andy Clark argues that when Otto reads 'the museum is on 53rd Street,' the notebook is literally PART of his belief -- mind isn't sealed inside the skull. Which view is Clark defending?
answer: Extended-mind -- a trusted notebook doing memory's job is literally part of the belief.
choices: Extended-mind -- a trusted notebook doing memory's job is literally part of the belief.
Inner-only -- real beliefs sit in the brain; the notebook is just a tool he reads.
Two-substance -- the mind is non-physical, so no object could ever be part of it.
No-belief -- 'belief' is a folk word brain science will drop, notebook or not.
context: Andy Clark and David Chalmers, 'The Extended Mind' (1998), argue the parity principle: if a process outside the head plays the same role as one inside, both count as cognition. Critics (Adams & Aizawa, Rupert) deny the parity and insist on a 'mark of the cognitive' that stops at the skin.

question: Putnam imagines a brain in a vat, wired to a computer feeding it a whole fake life. Surprisingly, he argues it could NOT truly think 'I am a brain in a vat' -- its word 'vat' was only ever caused by vat-fed images, never real vats. Which view of meaning does his reply need?
answer: Tracking -- a word means what caused it, so its 'vat' picks out the computer's vat-feed.
choices: Tracking -- a word means what caused it, so its 'vat' picks out the computer's vat-feed.
Meaning-in-head -- meaning sits wholly in the mind, so its words could reach real vats.
Convention -- a word means whatever the local community agrees to call things.
No-meaning -- 'meaning' is a folk idea cognitive science will one day drop.
context: Hilary Putnam (Reason, Truth and History, 1981) uses semantic externalism -- first defended in 'The Meaning of Meaning' (1975, Twin Earth) -- to defuse radical skepticism: if a word means whatever caused it in one's environment, the brain-in-a-vat's 'vat' only ever picks out the computer's feed, so the thought 'I am a brain in a vat' can't get a grip from inside.

question: Locke imagines a prince's whole consciousness -- every palace memory -- waking up overnight in a cobbler's body, while the cobbler's old body now thinks and remembers as the prince. Locke says the person who wakes IS the prince, in a cobbler's body. Which view of personal identity is this?
answer: Memory-link -- you persist as long as your consciousness reaches back in memory.
choices: Memory-link -- you persist as long as your consciousness reaches back in memory.
Same-body -- you persist as the same living organism, whatever you remember.
Same-soul -- you persist as one immaterial soul behind every change of body.
No-self -- no one truly endures; each is just a run of passing experiences.
context: John Locke (Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book II ch. 27, added in the 1694 second edition) uses the prince-and-cobbler case to ground personal identity in consciousness: a person is whoever can extend consciousness back to earlier experience -- gaps like sleep allowed. Derek Parfit (1984) later widened this into psychological-continuity theory and pressed the hard branching cases.

question: Harry Frankfurt's 'unwilling addict' case: a drug addict desires heroin and uses it, but at a deeper level desires NOT to desire heroin — he wishes his cravings did not move him. Frankfurt contrasts this with a 'wanton' addict who simply has the craving and acts on it with no inner objection. What distinction does the case expose, on Frankfurt's view?
answer: First-order vs. higher-order desires — genuine agency requires desires ABOUT one's desires (wanting-not-to-want); the unwilling addict has them, the wanton lacks them, and that is the mark of a free will.
choices: First-order vs. higher-order desires — genuine agency requires desires ABOUT one's desires (wanting-not-to-want); the unwilling addict has them, the wanton lacks them, and that is the mark of a free will.

Reasons vs. causes — the addict is unfree because his action is caused, not reasoned; only desires backed by reasons constitute genuine agency, and any craving (higher-order or not) just disqualifies him.
Compatibilism vs. libertarianism — the case is meant to show that determinism is incompatible with freedom; the addict is unfree because his desires were caused by prior states he did not control.
Mental causation vs. epiphenomenalism — the addict's higher-order wish does no causal work in the world; the case shows that mental states are inert byproducts of brain events, not real causes.
context: Harry Frankfurt's 'Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person' (1971) introduces second-order desires — desires about which first-order desires move us. A 'person' is a creature who has, and acts from, second-order volitions. Critics (Watson, Wolf) press the question of what makes a higher-order desire AUTHORITATIVE without an infinite regress.

question: Before sailing, every sailor signed the ship's articles by hand. The bosun says the no-grog-on-watch rule binds because they all signed. Which view of authority is he using?
answer: Consent -- the rule binds because everyone signed on to it.
choices: Consent -- the rule binds because everyone signed on to it.
Tradition -- it binds because the ship has always done it.
Strength -- it binds because the captain can enforce it.
Merit -- it binds because the ablest sailor chose it.
context: Consent theory (Locke, Rousseau) holds that rules bind only those who agreed to them. A ship's articles, signed by every hand before sailing, were a real consent device on merchant and pirate crews alike: the signature is what turns a captain's order into a rule the crew owes. The bosun's tell is 'they all signed.'

question: Coach Reeves keeps the same pre-game huddle. He says: 'Every team since 1962 has done it this way -- that's what makes us this team.' Which view of authority is Coach using?
answer: Tradition -- it binds because the team has always done it.
choices: Tradition -- it binds because the team has always done it.
Consent -- it binds because the players agreed to it.
Strength -- it binds because the coach can enforce it.
Merit -- it binds because the best player chose it.
context: Tradition theory (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790) grounds authority in continuity: long-standing practice carries knowledge no single person could design from scratch. Coach's tell is 'since 1962.'

question: On the playground the biggest sixth-grader announces who gets the swings. He tells Ana: 'Rules are whatever I say -- try to stop me.' Which view of authority is he using?
answer: Strength -- it binds because he can make you obey.
choices: Strength -- it binds because he can make you obey.
Consent -- it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition -- it binds because it's always been done.
Anarchism -- no rule really binds anyone at all.
context: Strength theory is what Thrasymachus defends in Plato's Republic: 'justice is the advantage of the stronger.' Socrates rejects it -- force can compel, but compulsion alone does not make a rule just. The boy's tell is 'try to stop me.'

question: Navigator Priya alone sets the ship's heading by the stars. She tells them: 'I'm the one trained to read the sky -- so the heading is mine to set.' Whose reasoning fits Priya's?
answer: Merit -- it binds because the most-qualified one decides.
choices: Merit -- it binds because the most-qualified one decides.
Consent -- it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition -- it binds because the group always has done it.
Strength -- it binds because the strong can enforce it.
context: Priya grounds authority in being best-qualified -- the idea behind Plato's 'philosopher-kings' in the Republic: those who know best should rule. The hard part, critics note, is agreeing on who actually knows best.

question: A sailor refuses to sign the ship's articles: 'No captain truly owns my obedience -- I haul the rope when I choose to, never because I'm bound.' Whose reasoning fits the sailor's?
answer: Anarchism -- no rule truly binds; obeying is your choice.
choices: Anarchism -- no rule truly binds; obeying is your choice.
Consent -- it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition -- it binds because the group always has done it.
Merit -- it binds because the most-qualified one decides.
context: The sailor's claim -- that no rule has real hold on you, so obeying is always a free choice -- is the anarchist view (from Greek 'anarkhia', no ruler). Tolstoy and Henry David Thoreau (Civil Disobedience) argued obedience is chosen, never owed.

question: The scout troop votes on which lake to camp by. Leon says: 'We voted, so the winning pick binds everyone -- even the kids who wanted the other lake.' Whose reasoning fits Leon's?
answer: Consent -- it binds because everyone agreed to it.
choices: Consent -- it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition -- it binds because the group always has done it.
Strength -- it binds because the strong can enforce it.
Merit -- it binds because the most-qualified one decides.
context: Leon grounds the rule in agreement: even those who lost the vote are bound, because they agreed in advance to settle it by voting. Locke called this 'tacit consent' to the rules of the game.

question: A senior knight defends the night-watch rotation: 'The company has kept it for seven generations. Custom holds knowledge no captain could write down.' Whose reasoning fits his?
answer: Tradition -- it binds because the group always has done it.
choices: Tradition -- it binds because the group always has done it.
Consent -- it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Strength -- it binds because the strong can enforce it.
Anarchism -- no rule truly binds; obeying is your choice.
context: The knight grounds authority in inherited custom -- Edmund Burke's argument (Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790): long practice carries collective knowledge no single person could design from scratch.

question: Big brother Sam grabs the remote: 'Take it from me if you can -- whoever holds it picks the show. That's the only rule that actually counts here.' Whose reasoning fits Sam's?
answer: Strength -- it binds because the strong can enforce it.
choices: Strength -- it binds because the strong can enforce it.
Consent -- it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition -- it binds because the group always has done it.
Merit -- it binds because the most-qualified one decides.
context: Sam's 'might makes right' is the view Thrasymachus defends in Plato's Republic: justice is just the advantage of the stronger. Socrates rejects it -- force can compel, but compulsion alone doesn't make a rule just.

question: As the wounded are carried in, the field surgeon decides who is treated first: 'I'm the one trained to read these wounds -- so the call is mine to make.' Whose view is she using?
answer: Merit -- it binds because the most-qualified one decides.
choices: Merit -- it binds because the most-qualified one decides.
Consent -- it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition -- it binds because the group always has done it.
Anarchism -- no rule truly binds; obeying is your choice.
context: The surgeon grounds authority in expertise -- the pilot flies the plane, the navigator reads the sky. It echoes Plato's philosopher-kings; the standing challenge is how a group picks who really is the expert.

question: When the curfew bell rings, old Mara keeps her lamp lit in the window: 'No town council owns my obedience -- I keep their rules only when I please.' Whose view is Mara using?
answer: Anarchism -- no rule truly binds; obeying is your choice.
choices: Anarchism -- no rule truly binds; obeying is your choice.
Consent -- it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition -- it binds because the group always has done it.
Merit -- it binds because the most-qualified one decides.
context: Mara's 'I obey only when I please' is the anarchist view: genuine cooperation can't be commanded, only chosen. Kropotkin and Emma Goldman argued obedience is always a free choice, never a duty owed to an institution.

question: Before sailing, a ship's crew met and elected their captain by open vote. When a sailor resents an order, a mate reminds him: 'We all chose him — that vote is why his command binds us.' Which view of authority is the mate using?
answer: Consent — it binds because everyone agreed to it.
choices: Consent — it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition — it binds because crews always have.
Strength — it binds because the captain enforces it.
Merit — it binds because the captain knows the sea.
context: Consent theory grounds authority in agreement. Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau all argued the legitimate state begins with a 'social contract' — a moment, real or implied, when free people agree to be bound, turning raw power into rightful command.

question: A student tells the principal: 'Even if you vote to ban our paper, you can't — the right to read stands whether the school votes for it or not.' Which view is she using?
answer: Natural rights — some rights stand above any rule.
choices: Natural rights — some rights stand above any rule.
Consent — it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition — it binds because the school always has.
Strength — it binds because leaders enforce it.
context: Natural-rights theory (Locke, Aquinas before him) holds some rights belong to people by virtue of being human. A school or state can recognize or violate them, but cannot create or vote them out of existence.

question: A clan elder explains the standing-stones vigil: 'We keep it because our people always have. Generations of practice know what words can't capture.' Which view is she using?
answer: Tradition — it binds because the group always has.
choices: Tradition — it binds because the group always has.
Consent — it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Strength — it binds because the powerful enforce it.
Merit — it binds because the wisest member set it.
context: Burke argued reforms should respect what generations of practice have shown to work, even when no one can fully explain WHY it does. Long-running customs carry collective wisdom — 'the latent wisdom that prevails in them' (Reflections, 1790).

question: A newcomer never signed the village's founding oath, yet lives by its rules. When he protests one, an elder answers: 'By staying and sharing our wells, you accepted them — that's why they bind you.' Which view is the elder using?
answer: Consent — it binds because everyone agreed to it.
choices: Consent — it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition — it binds because the village always has.
Strength — it binds because leaders enforce it.
Anarchism — no village rule really binds you at all.
context: Locke distinguished express consent (you sign or vote) from tacit consent — the newcomer's case: by enjoying a community's roads and protection, you accept its rules even without signing. Both turn raw power into authority by tying the rule back to agreement.

question: In Plato's Republic, Thrasymachus snaps at Socrates: 'Justice is the advantage of the stronger — a rule binds only because the powerful enforce it.' Which view is he defending?
answer: Strength — it binds only because the powerful enforce it.
choices: Strength — it binds only because the powerful enforce it.
Consent — it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition — it binds because the group always has.
Merit — it binds because the wisest one decides.
context: Thrasymachus states the strength theory in Republic I (Plato, ~380 BC). Socrates replies that if might alone made right, a powerful thief would be just — an absurdity that refutes the theory. The exchange has shaped political philosophy for 2,400 years.

question: The guild raised hands to vote on how to forge the king's blade. The old master overruled them: 'I've forged swords for forty years — the one who knows the craft decides, not a show of hands.' Which view is the master using?
answer: Merit — it binds because the expert knows best.
choices: Merit — it binds because the expert knows best.
Consent — it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition — it binds because the guild always has.
Strength — it binds because the king demands it.
context: Authority-by-merit (technocracy) grants decision-power to demonstrated expertise — here, the master overruling the vote. It can be efficient, but raises a hard question: who certifies the expert, and what happens when the experts disagree?

question: A monitor refuses a hungry kid lunch over a forgotten ticket. Theo objects: 'Some basic things can't be taken away — feeding a hungry child is one.' Which view is Theo using?
answer: Natural rights — some rights stand above any rule.
choices: Natural rights — some rights stand above any rule.
Consent — it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition — it binds because the school always has.
Strength — it binds because the monitor enforces it.
context: Natural-rights philosophers from Aquinas to Locke argued some duties hold prior to any rule — feeding the hungry, sheltering the homeless. The Declaration of Independence calls these rights 'unalienable.'

question: Rousseau opened his most famous book with a thunderclap: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.' What did he say could ever make those chains legitimate?
answer: Consent — the free agreement of the governed
choices: Consent — the free agreement of the governed
Tradition — the long custom of the elders
Strength — the power of whoever rules now
Merit — the judgment of the wisest one
context: Rousseau (The Social Contract, 1762), building on Locke (1689), argued that legitimate rule begins only when free people agree to it — not from force or inherited custom. The chains bind justly only where the governed have, in some real sense, said yes.

question: Since no one is born another's master, the printer Proudhon argued, no king or majority can set its commands above your own judgment. What did he conclude about every government?
answer: No ruler holds real authority over you
choices: No ruler holds real authority over you
Only the elected hold real authority
Only the wisest hold real authority
Only the strongest hold real authority
context: In 1840 Pierre-Joseph Proudhon became the first person to call himself an anarchist on purpose. Anarchism (later Bakunin, Kropotkin) denies that any state holds legitimate authority at all; order, it argues, should grow from free cooperation, never from a power that can command and punish you.

question: In Plato's ideal city, only those who truly KNOW the good may rule — he called them philosopher-kings. What is his basis for who should hold power?
answer: Merit — the one who truly knows should rule
choices: Merit — the one who truly knows should rule
Consent — those who agreed should rule
Tradition — those who always ruled should rule
Strength — the one who can enforce should rule
context: Authority-by-merit traces to Plato (Republic, ~375 BC): rule belongs to those with real knowledge of the good. It fits fields like medicine or piloting, but raises a hard question elsewhere — who certifies the expert, and what happens when the experts disagree?

question: A new market-fair rule passes the council of squires. Maya tells a doubter: 'Every councilor voted yes. That vote itself — not custom, not the captain — is what binds us.' Which view is Maya using?
answer: Consent — the vote itself is what binds us
choices: Consent — the vote itself is what binds us
Tradition — the council has always voted so
Merit — the ablest councilor drafted it
Strength — leaders can punish those who dodge
context: Consent theory (Locke, 1689; Rousseau, 1762) grounds authority in the agreement of the governed. Maya makes the democratic move exactly: the vote is not merely how the rule passed — the agreement itself IS the whole claim to legitimacy.

question: As revolutionary France tore down its ancient institutions in 1790, Edmund Burke wrote a famous warning against sweeping them away. Why did he say a centuries-old custom deserves the benefit of the doubt?
answer: It carries lessons learned over many lifetimes
choices: It carries lessons learned over many lifetimes
It was chosen by today's majority vote
It was designed by a single expert mind
It is backed by whoever holds power now
context: Burke (Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790) argued that a practice surviving many generations holds tested wisdom no lone planner can replace, so the burden falls on the reformer to justify the change. The reply to Burke: custom can also entrench injustice.

question: Plato's ideal city is ruled by philosopher-kings — those who alone truly know the good. A captain echoes him to squires: 'The master studied this for years. She knows what we don't.' Which view is he using?
answer: Merit — her hard-won expertise is what binds
choices: Merit — her hard-won expertise is what binds
Consent — the company voted the rule in
Tradition — warriors have long eaten this way
Strength — she can bench any squire she likes
context: Authority-by-merit (Plato's philosopher-kings, Republic) grounds rule in superior knowledge of the good. Critics answer that knowing best is not the same as the right to bind — even a wise doctor cannot force her diet on you without your say.

question: Without government, Hobbes warned, life is 'nasty, brutish, and short.' So people trade some freedom for safety. Sara invokes that trade to defend her guild's rules. Which view is she using?
answer: Social contract — a trade is what binds us
choices: Social contract — a trade is what binds us
Tradition — guilds have long had such rules
Merit — the sharpest member wrote them
Strength — leaders can kick out rule-breakers
context: Social contract theory (Hobbes, Leviathan, 1651; later Locke and Rousseau) says people would rationally trade some liberty for shared benefits like peace. Sara's 'trade' is that move: plain consent needs only agreement, while the contract adds the mutual gain that motivates it.

question: In Plato's Republic, Thrasymachus snaps at Socrates: 'Justice is just the advantage of the stronger — whoever can shove the rest sets the rules.' Which view of authority is he voicing?
answer: Might-makes-right — raw power to enforce is itself the authority.
choices: Might-makes-right — raw power to enforce is itself the authority.
Consent — the weaker agreed in advance to follow the stronger.
Tradition — the city has long let the strongest rule it.
Merit — the strongest has earned the right to rule the rest.
context: Thrasymachus makes this claim in Plato's Republic I (~380 BC). Socrates' reply lands the point: then a powerful thief who can enforce his will would count as 'just' — which shows that what power CAN do and what is RIGHT are not the same thing.

question: Priya tells the principal the dress code must bind every student alike, no exemptions by background: 'We're all created equal — a fair school treats us as equals.' Which idea of justice is Priya appealing to?
answer: Equal treatment — justice means no group gets favored or exempted.
choices: Equal treatment — justice means no group gets favored or exempted.
Liberty — justice means students pick their own clothes, code or not.
Greatest good — justice means whatever outcome helps the most kids.
Custom — justice means keeping the dress code the school always had.
context: Egalitarianism holds that justice requires treating people as moral equals. The line 'all men are created equal' runs from Rousseau through the American founding to Rawls's A Theory of Justice (1971), which built fairness on equal standing.

question: The chess-club president wants tournaments made mandatory. Pablo refuses: 'A club can't CONSCRIPT you — it binds you only if you freely chose to join.' Which idea of authority is Pablo defending?
answer: Liberty-first — rules may not override a free choice to take part.
choices: Liberty-first — rules may not override a free choice to take part.
Equal treatment — a rule is fine so long as it binds every member alike.
Greatest good — a rule is fine if mandatory play helps the club most.
Power — the president runs the club, so she may simply require it.
context: Libertarianism (Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 1974) makes individual liberty the primary political value: a group may not conscript your participation, and any rule that overrides a free choice needs strong justification. The clash with equal-treatment and greatest-good views runs through modern debates.

question: The captain made everyone 'agree' to extra practice by threatening to bench non-signers. Aiden later objects: 'That signature wasn't real consent.' Why is 'they all signed' NOT enough to make the rule legitimate?
answer: Consent under threat isn't consent — agreement that flows from fear fails the voluntariness that makes consent bind.
choices: Consent under threat isn't consent — agreement that flows from fear fails the voluntariness that makes consent bind.
Tradition still grounds it — established practice carries authority; that the captain insisted is an incidental fact.
Expertise still applies — the captain knows the sport better; her superior judgment justifies the schedule anyway.
Equal fairness still holds — every player faced the same threat; equal treatment is enough to give legitimacy here.
context: Consent theory requires VOLUNTARY agreement — coerced consent ('sign or be punished') fails the precondition. Locke's Second Treatise (1689) requires real freedom to dissent; threatened signatures don't supply it.

question: Eight kids on the bus vote to exclude one quiet kid from the back-row seats. Asked why it's wrong though it won the vote, Layla pushes back. Why is 'majority approved' NOT the same as 'justly decided'?
answer: Majorities can violate basic rights — a vote stripping one kid's fair access doesn't become just by counting more hands.
choices: Majorities can violate basic rights — a vote stripping one kid's fair access doesn't become just by counting more hands.
Tradition outranks votes — bus seating has long followed first-come rules; the vote overrode that established custom.
Experts should decide such matters — drivers and teachers know seating better; their judgment beats the eight kids' vote.
Stronger kids set real rules — eight kids voted because they had numbers; the vote just describes power, nothing binding.
context: Tyranny of the majority — Tocqueville (Democracy in America, 1835) and Mill (On Liberty, 1859) warned that bare-majority votes can crush minority rights. Procedure (a vote) and substance (justice) are different things.

question: The principal moves to shut the school paper. Reese answers: 'Free speech isn't the school's to GRANT — we already have it. They can recognize the right, never invent it.' Which view of rights is Reese using?
answer: Natural rights — some rights exist before any rule and are only recognized.
choices: Natural rights — some rights exist before any rule and are only recognized.
Rights-from-rules — a right is real only once a rulebook lists it.
Rights-from-custom — a right holds because the school long allowed it.
Rights-from-deal — a right comes from a bargain students struck with staff.
context: Natural-rights theory (Locke, 1689; Aquinas's natural law before him) holds some rights — life, liberty, free conscience — belong to people simply as humans, prior to any government. Legal positivism denies any rights before law writes them.

question: Asked if a right can exist before the law names it, a positivist insists: 'A right exists only when valid law creates it — so an enslaved person in 1850 had NO right to liberty.' Which view of rights is this?
answer: Rights-from-rules — a right exists only because a rulebook creates it.
choices: Rights-from-rules — a right exists only because a rulebook creates it.
Natural rights — a right exists before any rulebook and is only recognized.
Rights-from-custom — a right holds because the law long allowed it.
Rights-from-deal — a right comes from a bargain people struck with rulers.
context: Legal positivism (Bentham, 1789; H.L.A. Hart, The Concept of Law, 1961) denies natural rights: a legal right exists only because valid law creates it. The 1850 case is the classic challenge — if the slave had no right to liberty merely because the law denied one, the view seems to lose the ground from which to call that law unjust.

question: VP Adams bans phones at lunch over Mara's protest that it's her choice: 'A few lose out, but lunch ends up better for the most students — so the rule is just.' Which idea of justice is Adams using?
answer: Greatest good — a rule is just if it helps the most people on balance.
choices: Greatest good — a rule is just if it helps the most people on balance.
Liberty — a rule is just only if it leaves the phone choice to each student.
Natural rights — a rule is just only if it respects a right held beforehand.
Equal treatment — a rule is just only if it binds every student alike.
context: Utilitarian justice (Bentham, 1789; J.S. Mill, Utilitarianism, 1861) judges rules by the total good they produce — Bentham's 'greatest happiness.' Critics object that the sum can run over an individual's choice or right when the numbers favor it, exactly as it runs over Mara here.
