question: Imagine choosing society's rules before birth, blind to whether you'll be rich or poor, gifted or struggling, devout or skeptic. A thinker says the rules you'd pick from behind that 'veil' are the only fair ones. Which school is she using?
answer: Rawlsian liberalism — fairness is what we'd agree to behind a veil hiding our own advantages
choices: Rawlsian liberalism — fairness is what we'd agree to behind a veil hiding our own advantages
Hobbesian absolutism — any rule a strong sovereign enforces beats the chaos of no rule at all
Burkean conservatism — good rules are inherited and time-tested, not picked by blank-slate strangers
Marxism — talk of fair 'agreement' just hides which class the rules are quietly built to serve
context: John Rawls's A Theory of Justice (1971) built the 'original position': parties behind a veil of ignorance, knowing only general facts, would choose equal basic liberties plus the difference principle (inequality allowed only when it helps the worst-off). Critics: Nozick, Sandel, Cohen.

question: A basketball star draws huge crowds; each fan happily drops a quarter in his box to watch, and he ends up rich while the rest stay as they were. A critic says no one was wronged — every step was freely chosen, so the lopsided result is just, and forcing a tidy spread would trample what people gave. Which tradition backs him?
answer: Entitlement libertarianism — just steps make a just result, whatever its shape.
choices: Entitlement libertarianism — just steps make a just result, whatever its shape.
Rawlsian liberalism — gaps are fair only if they help the worst-off.
Utilitarianism — the just spread is whatever yields the most welfare.
Capability approach — justice is each person reaching core capabilities.
context: Robert Nozick (Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 1974) splits historical from end-state principles: just holdings come from fair acquisition and transfer, not from matching any preferred pattern. This is his own Wilt Chamberlain example — fans freely pay to watch, he gets rich — arguing that locking in a pattern would demand endless meddling with people's free choices.

question: A constitutional scholar argues: 'The case against comprehensive economic planning is not that planners have bad intentions but that the knowledge needed for rational allocation is dispersed across millions of actors and largely tacit — no central authority could ever assemble it.' Which tradition most directly grounds this argument?
answer: Hayekian classical liberalism — the knowledge problem (dispersed, tacit information no central agent can assemble) makes spontaneous order through prices a discovery procedure no central plan can match.
choices: Hayekian classical liberalism — the knowledge problem (dispersed, tacit information no central agent can assemble) makes spontaneous order through prices a discovery procedure no central plan can match.

Marxism — the difficulties of planning are real but historically conditioned; the historical-materialist view treats them as dissolvable through better information systems and the transformation of class relations.

Rawlsian liberalism — economic institutions are evaluated against principles chosen behind a veil of ignorance; the planning question turns on fair-choice conditions, not on a claim about dispersed knowledge.

Burkean conservatism — established economic practice carries the wisdom of generations; the objection to planning stems from disrupting inherited institutional knowledge, not from in-principle aggregation limits.
context: Friedrich Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945) frames the knowledge problem: economic knowledge is dispersed and largely tacit, and the price system aggregates it without anyone needing to assemble it centrally. The Mises-Hayek calculation debate (1920s-40s) launched the position; Lange and Lerner are the leading socialist replies.

question: A slave serves a kind master who, by luck of temperament, never once interferes with her. A panelist insists she is STILL unfree — what freedom needs is not non-interference but security against arbitrary power. Which school is she using?
answer: Republicanism — you're free only when no one HOLDS arbitrary power over you, used or not
choices: Republicanism — you're free only when no one HOLDS arbitrary power over you, used or not
Classical liberalism — you're free as long as no one actually interferes, kind master included
Marxism — real freedom waits on ending the class power of one person over another's labor
Hobbesian absolutism — you're free wherever the sovereign's law happens to stay silent
context: Philip Pettit's Republicanism (1997) and Quentin Skinner's Liberty Before Liberalism (1998) recover the neo-Roman idea of freedom as non-domination: a status of being secured against arbitrary power, not merely the absence of actual interference. Berlin's negative-vs-positive liberty maps onto it only loosely.

question: A political theorist argues that liberal frameworks 'presuppose an unencumbered self that chooses its ends from a standpoint prior to all attachments' — and that this picture distorts moral and political life, since people are partly constituted by ties they did not choose: family, community, tradition, and faith. Which tradition grounds her critique?
answer: Communitarianism — the constitutive-ties view (Sandel, Taylor, MacIntyre) holds that identities are partly made by unchosen attachments, so liberalism's chooser-prior-to-ends picture misdescribes the self.
choices: Communitarianism — the constitutive-ties view (Sandel, Taylor, MacIntyre) holds that identities are partly made by unchosen attachments, so liberalism's chooser-prior-to-ends picture misdescribes the self.

Rawlsian liberalism — political principles can be chosen by parties bracketing their particular conceptions of the good; the critique mistakes a political device for a metaphysical thesis about the self.

Anarcho-capitalism — what matters is whether institutions rest on voluntary consent; the metaphysical debate over how the self is constituted has no bearing on whether enforcement of those institutions is just.

Marxism — talk of constitutive ties masks underlying class relations; the relevant attachments are determined by material position rather than by communal narratives the framework treats as superstructure.
context: Michael Sandel's Liberalism and the Limits of Justice (1982) launched the communitarian critique of Rawls. Charles Taylor (Sources of the Self, 1989) and Alasdair MacIntyre (After Virtue, 1981) develop allied lines. Rawls's Political Liberalism (1993) reframed his project in part as a response to these criticisms.

question: Writing during a civil war that made life feel 'nasty, brutish, and short,' a theorist argues that any sovereign who keeps the peace beats the war of all against all — so a regime that holds order is legitimate, rights-talk and all. Which school is she using?
answer: Hobbesian absolutism — any sovereign that keeps the peace beats the war of all against all
choices: Hobbesian absolutism — any sovereign that keeps the peace beats the war of all against all
Lockean liberalism — a ruler who keeps order but tramples rights has forfeited its legitimacy
Marxism — 'order' is never neutral; it quietly locks in whichever class already holds power
Republicanism — bare order isn't freedom if the ruler's power over you stays arbitrary
context: Thomas Hobbes wrote Leviathan (1651) during the English Civil War: from a 'state of nature' that is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' he argues only an absolute sovereign can secure the peace that makes any social life possible. Legitimacy rests on the covenant that founds that sovereign. Locke's Second Treatise (1689) is the canonical liberal reply.

question: Edmund Burke had cheered the American colonists, so Europe expected him to cheer the French Revolution too. Instead, in 1790, he wrote a furious warning against it. His core objection was about how to change a society. What was it?
answer: Tearing institutions down to rebuild them from pure theory throws away wisdom built up over centuries.
choices: Tearing institutions down to rebuild them from pure theory throws away wisdom built up over centuries.
Any revolution is wrong because rebellion against a lawful king is always a sin against God.
Ordinary people can never be trusted to govern themselves and always need a strong ruler.
All change should be blocked, because the old order is already as good as it could be.
context: Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790) is the founding text of modern conservatism. He did not oppose all reform, he backed the colonists and Catholic relief, but argued inherited institutions carry hard-won practical wisdom ('prescription') that remaking everything from first principles destroys.

question: A theorist argues that rights and consent are just the painted upper floor of a building whose real load-bearing base is who-owns-what — until you change the base, 'equal rights on paper' only ratifies the inequalities it won't look at. Which school is she using?
answer: Marxism — the economy is the base; rights are surface dressing over the real class relations
choices: Marxism — the economy is the base; rights are surface dressing over the real class relations
Rawlsian liberalism — fair rules come first; who-owns-what is then settled within them
Republicanism — the worry is domination by any arbitrary power, not class ownership as such
Hayekian liberalism — no planner can reshuffle ownership without hitting the knowledge problem
context: Marx and Engels's The German Ideology (1845-46) and Marx's 1859 preface frame the base/superstructure picture: economic relations are the 'base', and law and politics the 'superstructure' resting on it. G.A. Cohen's Karl Marx's Theory of History (1978) gives the canonical analytic reconstruction. Critics: Berlin, Popper.

question: A panelist points at the two things that make a state a state — it forbids any rival police and it makes you pay for it — and argues both are theft dressed as protection; calling it legitimate 'because it has always been so' just begs the question against everyone who never consented. Which school is she using?
answer: Anarcho-capitalism — even the state's police monopoly and taxes violate the rights it claims to guard
choices: Anarcho-capitalism — even the state's police monopoly and taxes violate the rights it claims to guard
Nozickian minimal state — a tiny state may still hold that monopoly, grown fairly by an invisible hand
Lockean liberalism — a state may hold that monopoly so long as it secures everyone's natural rights
Hobbesian absolutism — a single monopoly on force is the very thing that makes any order possible
context: Murray Rothbard's For a New Liberty (1973) and The Ethics of Liberty (1982) develop anarcho-capitalism: the state's two defining marks — a territorial monopoly on force and compulsory taxation — both violate the rights it claims to protect. David Friedman's The Machinery of Freedom (1973) gives a consequentialist cousin of the argument.

question: A development scholar who studied famines where food still sat in the markets argues you measure a society not by average income, nor by the pile of goods each person holds, but by what each can actually DO and BE — the real freedoms to live a full human life. Which school is she using?
answer: Capability approach — measure the real freedoms people have to do and be, not their income
choices: Capability approach — measure the real freedoms people have to do and be, not their income
Rawlsian liberalism — measure each person's bundle of primary goods: rights, chances, income
Utilitarianism — measure the total well-being added up across everyone in the society
Libertarianism — ask only whether people's holdings were acquired and traded fairly
context: Amartya Sen's Commodities and Capabilities (1985) and Martha Nussbaum's Women and Human Development (2000) built the capability approach as a rival to both welfare-counting and Rawls's primary goods. Sen's famine work showed people starving amid full markets. Nussbaum lists ten central capabilities; Sen leaves the list more open. The UN Human Development Index draws on the framework.

question: You want a law banning Sunday work because your faith commands rest. A theorist replies: that conviction may move YOU, but the state may coerce a neighbor who shares none of it only on grounds every reasonable citizen could accept. Which school is she using?
answer: Public-reason liberalism — coercive law needs reasons every reasonable citizen could share
choices: Public-reason liberalism — coercive law needs reasons every reasonable citizen could share
Communitarianism — a community may rightly govern by the shared goods its tradition already holds
Hobbesian absolutism — the sovereign's job of keeping peace is what licenses its use of force
Natural-law view — just law should track moral truth, not pass a test of public acceptability
context: John Rawls's Political Liberalism (1993) recasts justice as a 'freestanding' political idea rather than one comprehensive moral doctrine. Public reason limits the basis of coercive law to reasons all reasonable citizens can share. Critics: Sandel and MacIntyre (communitarian), Wolterstorff (religious objection), Habermas (from within liberalism).

question: A policy analyst argues: 'Decisions should be made by the smallest competent body — family, local community, regional association — and only delegated upward when the lower body cannot handle the matter; this is not merely an efficiency claim but a principle about the proper structure of social authority.' Which tradition most directly grounds this principle?
answer: Subsidiarity — Catholic social teaching treats subsidiarity as a structural principle: authority belongs to the smallest competent body and only delegates upward, as right not efficiency.
choices: Subsidiarity — Catholic social teaching treats subsidiarity as a structural principle: authority belongs to the smallest competent body and only delegates upward, as right not efficiency.

Hayekian classical liberalism — the case for local decision rests on the knowledge problem; the locus of authority tracks where dispersed information lives, but this is an epistemic point, not a structural one.

Republicanism — decentralization may serve non-domination by limiting concentrated power, but the framework accepts whatever institutional level best secures freedom, not a structural preference per se.

Communitarianism — local community has thicker moral resources than the state; the picture overlaps but treats the principle as procedural-structural rather than as following from substantive shared goods.
context: Pope Pius XI's Quadragesimo Anno (1931) gives the canonical formulation of subsidiarity: matters should be handled by the smallest competent authority. The principle is foundational in Catholic social teaching and shapes EU constitutional law (Maastricht, Lisbon). Treats devolved authority as a matter of right, not efficiency.

question: Max Weber asked NOT whether a ruler is just, but why people accept his commands as binding — and named three sources of that authority: tradition, charisma, and written law. A new king rules by terror alone. Which of the three does his hold lack?
answer: All three — naked force is none of them; lasting rule needs people to accept the ruler's RIGHT to command.
choices: All three — naked force is none of them; lasting rule needs people to accept the ruler's RIGHT to command.
Only tradition — a throne taken by force is always retaken by force within a single reign.
Only written law — he broke the law to seize power, and a lawbreaker can never rule lawfully.
Only charisma — subjects obey solely rulers they personally like, and terror makes a king unlikable.
context: Max Weber (Economy and Society, 1922) distinguished three types of legitimate authority: traditional ('we have always obeyed this line'), charismatic (devotion to an extraordinary leader), and legal-rational (rules and office). Bare coercion is none of these — which is why a regime resting on force alone must keep spending it.

question: John Stuart Mill wrote that the only purpose for which power may rightly be used over a citizen against his will is 'to prevent harm to others' — never for 'his own good.' A council wants to stop a harmless hermit drinking wine alone, purely for his own sake. May it?
answer: No — by Mill's harm principle the state may coerce an adult only to protect others, never merely for his own good.
choices: No — by Mill's harm principle the state may coerce an adult only to protect others, never merely for his own good.
Yes — guarding a citizen from ruining himself is among the first duties any government has.
No — but only because one quiet hermit is far too small a case for any law to bother with.
Yes — the wider community is always harmed when any one of its members lives a wasted life.
context: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty (1859): 'the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilised community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others. His own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant.' This is the anti-paternalist core of classical liberalism. Critics (Patrick Devlin) argued law may also enforce shared morality.

question: Two villages live in peace. One serves a gentle king who could tax or jail them at any whim but never does; the other governs itself by laws it makes. A historian says only the second village is truly FREE. Which idea of freedom is she using?
answer: Freedom as non-domination — being under no arbitrary power, even a kind one.
choices: Freedom as non-domination — being under no arbitrary power, even a kind one.
Freedom as non-interference — being free so long as no one actually stops you right now.
Freedom as raw license — being free to do whatever you want with no rules at all.
Freedom as inner mastery — being free once reason rules over your own passions.
context: Quentin Skinner (Liberty Before Liberalism, 1998) and Philip Pettit recovered the neo-Roman idea, running from Rome through Machiavelli: a person living at the mercy of a master is UNFREE even if the master is kind and never interferes, because he depends on another's arbitrary will. Only a self-governing free state secures the standing of a free citizen. This rivals Berlin's 'negative liberty' as mere absence of interference.

question: Hegel rejected the idea that the state is a deal we strike for protection or a tool we may scrap at will. He called it Sittlichkeit — 'ethical life' — the shared world in which freedom takes on real shape. On this view, how does a person become free?
answer: Not by joining a contract as a finished self — you become free only THROUGH family, work, and institutions.
choices: Not by joining a contract as a finished self — you become free only THROUGH family, work, and institutions.
By signing a contract that merely guards the natural rights you fully possessed before it.
By seizing the state machinery the ruling class wields to hold down everyone beneath it.
By escaping a monopoly on violence that the people never truly consented to obey at all.
context: G.W.F. Hegel (Philosophy of Right, 1821) rejected the social-contract picture: the state is not built by individuals who exist fully formed before it, but is Sittlichkeit ('ethical life') — the institutions of family, civil society, and state in which a person's freedom gains concrete content. Locke is the contract rival; Marx (1843) answered that Hegel had reality upside down.

question: A policy analyst defends a tax-and-transfer scheme: 'Permitting an unequal distribution is justifiable only when the inequality actually benefits the least advantaged members of society — equality is the baseline against which deviations must be defended, not the other way around.' Which tradition most directly grounds this principle?
answer: Rawlsian liberalism — the difference principle (inequalities permitted only when they maximize the position of the least advantaged) makes equality the baseline and treats deviations as needing justification.
choices: Rawlsian liberalism — the difference principle (inequalities permitted only when they maximize the position of the least advantaged) makes equality the baseline and treats deviations as needing justification.

Entitlement libertarianism — the relevant test is whether holdings arose by just acquisition and transfer, not whether their pattern benefits the worst-off; treating equality as baseline begs the question.

Welfare utilitarianism — the right policy is whichever maximizes aggregate welfare regardless of distribution; privileging the worst-off is at most a proxy for welfare-maximization, not a deep commitment.

Capability approach — the test is whether each person reaches central capability thresholds; framing in terms of advantaged-vs-disadvantaged groups misses the focus on each person's functional life directly.
context: John Rawls's A Theory of Justice (1971) frames the difference principle as one of two principles chosen behind the veil of ignorance. Equality of basic liberties is lexically prior; economic inequalities are permitted only when they maximize the position of the worst-off. Nozick's Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) is the canonical libertarian reply.

question: The thinker Michael Oakeshott compared political life to seamen on 'a boundless and bottomless sea' — no harbor, no chart, no appointed destination; the task is only 'to keep afloat on an even keel.' What is he claiming about political knowledge?
answer: It is practical skill learned within a tradition, not a blueprint deduced from abstract principles.
choices: It is practical skill learned within a tradition, not a blueprint deduced from abstract principles.
It is impossible — since no one can steer the sea, politics is mere drift and teaches nothing.
It is a fixed science whose correct rules, once found, settle every question in advance.
It belongs to experts alone — only a trained few should ever be trusted to hold the helm.
context: Michael Oakeshott (Rationalism in Politics, 1962) attacked 'rationalism' — the belief that politics can be run from a book of abstract principles. The seamanship image is his: knowing how to govern is like knowing how to sail, a practical skill carried in a living tradition, not a doctrine you apply from outside. Kindred to Burke and Hayek's distrust of central blueprints.

question: A constitutional scholar argues: 'When a government systematically violates the rights it was constituted to protect, those subject to it are released from their obligation to obey — they may resist, and may constitute a new government, because legitimacy was conditional on the protection it has now forfeited.' Which tradition most directly grounds this argument?
answer: Lockean liberalism — the Second Treatise grounds revolution in conditional consent: legitimacy rests on protection of natural rights, so systematic violation dissolves the obligation to obey the ruler.
choices: Lockean liberalism — the Second Treatise grounds revolution in conditional consent: legitimacy rests on protection of natural rights, so systematic violation dissolves the obligation to obey the ruler.

Hobbesian absolutism — the obligation to obey survives all but the absolute breakdown of the sovereign's capacity to maintain order; rights-violation grounds presuppose conditions only the sovereign sustains.

Burkean conservatism — change should be incremental and within established forms, since the abstract right of revolution invites disasters that destroy the institutional inheritance from which the rights came.

Marxism — talk of natural rights and constitutional violation abstracts from the underlying class question; revolution is the transformation of production, not the restoration of pre-political rights.
context: John Locke's Second Treatise of Government (1689) develops the right of revolution as conditional on the ruler's protection of natural rights. The framework is the philosophical backbone of the American Declaration of Independence (1776) and the early French revolutionary documents. Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651) is the contemporary opposite pole.

question: Russell Kirk was asked to write 'the five rules of conservatism' so it could be taught like a creed. He refused, saying that to freeze it into fixed doctrine would betray the thing itself. Why would writing the rules betray it?
answer: Conservatism is a disposition — prudence and care for what endures — not a checklist of rules.
choices: Conservatism is a disposition — prudence and care for what endures — not a checklist of rules.
Its real rules are kept secret on purpose, shared only with insiders the movement fully trusts.
It has no actual content at all, so any list would just invent beliefs that no one really holds.
Each nation needs its own private rules, so one shared list could never fit every country at once.
context: Russell Kirk (The Conservative Mind, 1953) insisted conservatism is not an ideology but a temperament: prudence, attachment to 'the permanent things,' suspicion of grand utopias, respect for the variety of human communities. To reduce it to a rigid program would make it the very abstract system it distrusts. He sketched 'canons' as a sensibility, never a creed.

question: Milton Friedman argued in 1970 that a firm's one job is profit; critics said it should serve everyone affected. The public-choice founders Buchanan and Tullock replied: SOMEONE decides which interests count, and people use power for themselves, so judge a rule by its incentives, not its noble reason. What move is that?
answer: Judge a rule by how the people running it will actually behave, not by its stated good intentions.
choices: Judge a rule by how the people running it will actually behave, not by its stated good intentions.
No planner could ever gather the scattered facts needed to weigh so many interests at once.
Agencies built to police an industry slowly drift into shielding the very firms they oversee.
Small organized groups quietly pull gains away from large groups too scattered to push back.
context: This is the public-choice move (Buchanan and Tullock, The Calculus of Consent, 1962): treat officials and managers as self-interested actors, not neutral guardians, and predict outcomes from their incentives. Friedman's 1970 essay on the social responsibility of business raises the same warning about stakeholder mandates.

question: Iyer proposes a new agency to oversee a complex industry, citing public-interest expertise. Critic Vora replies: 'Agencies created to regulate an industry come to serve that industry — regulated firms supply the expertise, the revolving door routes personnel, the agency's survival comes to depend on a healthy industry. Predict from the structure.' Which reasoning move is Vora making?
choices: Regulatory capture — agencies come over time to serve the interests of the industry they regulate; predict outcomes from the structural relations (information asymmetry, revolving door) between them.
Public choice — policymakers are self-interested actors rather than neutral planners; the agency's outcome should be predicted from the incentives of legislators who created it, not its mandate.
Knowledge problem — dispersed information required to regulate a complex industry cannot be assembled by a centralized agency; the resulting failures are about information, not loyalty.
Dispersed costs — small organized industry groups extract from large diffuse consumer groups when the math is negative-sum, because organized beneficiaries out-mobilize unorganized payers.
answer: Regulatory capture — agencies come over time to serve the interests of the industry they regulate; predict outcomes from the structural relations (information asymmetry, revolving door) between them.
context: George Stigler's 'The Theory of Economic Regulation' (Bell Journal, 1971) gave the canonical formal treatment of regulatory capture, building on Bernstein. The move predicts outcomes from the structural relations (information asymmetry, revolving door, agency dependence on industry) rather than from formal mandates.

question: Renn proposes a universal basic income (UBI) to ensure a floor under poverty. Critic Pell replies: 'The interesting question is not whether the rationale is appealing but whether the policy delivers what it promises. The pilot data, second-order labor-market effects, inflation pass-through to recipients — these are the test, not the framing.' Which reasoning move is Pell making?
choices: Judge by results — a policy's standing depends on outcomes it actually produces (pilot data, labor-market and price effects), not on the moral framing when it was proposed.
Knowledge problem — information needed to set an optimal UBI level is dispersed across households and labor-market decisions, so any centrally-set figure miscarries the coordination it attempts.
Public choice — UBI designers are self-interested actors rather than neutral planners; predict outcomes from the incentives of those who set the level and the administrative apparatus.
Compared-to-what — every UBI proposal must be measured against realistic alternatives (negative income tax, earned-income credits, in-kind transfers), not against the imagined zero-poverty world.
answer: Judge by results — a policy's standing depends on outcomes it actually produces (pilot data, labor-market and price effects), not on the moral framing when it was proposed.
context: Milton Friedman's 'judge by results, not intentions' summarizes the move and applies cleanly to UBI: the empirical record is the test, not the rationale. The other three choices are real critiques applied to UBI elsewhere. Friedman himself proposed a negative income tax as the compared-to-what alternative.

question: Bastiat warned in 1850 to count not just what you SEE but what you do not. Thomas Sowell aimed it at admissions quotas: the balanced numbers are what everyone sees, but unseen is the rumor that standards dropped, cheapening the credential even for those the rule meant to help. What move is that?
answer: Weigh the hidden later cost of a policy, not only the visible result it puts on display.
choices: Weigh the hidden later cost of a policy, not only the visible result it puts on display.
Compare the policy to real alternatives, not to a perfect world that was never on offer.
Expect the officials running the policy to bend it toward their own interests over time.
Doubt that any planner could gather the scattered facts the targets would really need.
context: This is Bastiat's seen-versus-unseen (1850): the visible effect is easy to count, the unseen effect is what the policy also causes but no one tallies. Sowell applies it to preferences (Affirmative Action Around the World, 2004): a policy can hit its visible target while degrading the credential's signal for its intended beneficiaries.

question: A policy seminar defends a redistributive scheme: 'Social justice requires reallocation.' A Hayek-influenced critic replies: 'Social JUSTICE only makes sense where an agent acts unjustly. Market outcomes are no one's decision — they emerge from countless exchanges. Talking of injustice without an actor is a category error.' Which distinction is the critic drawing?
answer: Catallactic order vs designed order — Hayek's distinction between spontaneous outcomes (no actor, so 'injustice' misapplies) and designed outcomes (which can genuinely be unjust).
choices: Catallactic order vs designed order — Hayek's distinction between spontaneous outcomes (no actor, so 'injustice' misapplies) and designed outcomes (which can genuinely be unjust).
Just law vs legal plunder — Bastiat's distinction between law as a restraint on aggression and law used as an instrument for taking from one party to give the proceeds to another party.
Procedural legitimacy vs substantive justice — a procedurally regular vote can produce outcomes failing tests of substantive fairness; procedural legitimacy does not entail substantive justice.
Sovereign immunity vs ordinary moral reasoning — whether the state is subject to the same moral constraints individuals respect or operates under standards exempt from those constraints.
context: Hayek's The Mirage of Social Justice (Law, Legislation and Liberty Vol. 2, 1976) argues 'social justice' as applied to spontaneous market outcomes commits a category error — only agents can be just or unjust. Critics (Sen, Cohen, Nussbaum) reply that institutional choices that shape distributions ARE agent-acts. The bank flags the distinction; the verdict is open.

question: A campaign ad announces: 'Public servants are working in your interest.' A political economist responds: 'PREDICT politicians the way you predict anyone else — from their incentives. Treating elected officials as benevolent voices of an aggregate interest imports an assumption economists abandoned for businesspeople a century ago.' Which distinction is she drawing?
answer: Public choice vs benevolent planner — Buchanan and Tullock: politicians should be modeled from their own incentives, not from a presumed benevolent voicing of an aggregate public interest.
choices: Public choice vs benevolent planner — Buchanan and Tullock: politicians should be modeled from their own incentives, not from a presumed benevolent voicing of an aggregate public interest.

Specific actors vs abstract collective — naming 'the public' as agent obscures which particular people are deciding policy and which other particular people are being made to comply with their decisions.

Catallactic order vs designed order — Hayek's distinction between spontaneous coordination through prices and centrally designed coordination through deliberate command of allocations across the economy.

Conditional vs unconditional cooperation — market exchanges both parties can walk away from versus state commands no individual party can decline once a rule has been formally adopted by the legislature.
context: Public-choice economics — Buchanan and Tullock's The Calculus of Consent (1962), Buchanan's later Nobel-laureate work — treats politicians, bureaucrats, and voters as ordinary self-interested agents, applying to political actors the framework long applied to market actors. Critics ask whether asymmetric skepticism is warranted; the distinction itself is real.

question: A constitutional-law lecturer concludes: 'The state's monopoly on force is just how things have to be.' A student responds: 'Locke and Spooner raise the obvious question — is the state subject to the same moral constraints as individuals, or exempt? Acts called ROBBERY between persons get other names when the state performs them.' Which distinction is the student drawing?
answer: Sovereign immunity vs ordinary moral reasoning — Locke and Spooner: whether the state is subject to the same moral constraints as individuals, or operates under a moral exemption.
choices: Sovereign immunity vs ordinary moral reasoning — Locke and Spooner: whether the state is subject to the same moral constraints as individuals, or operates under a moral exemption.
Just law vs legal plunder — Bastiat's distinction between law functioning as a restraint on aggression and law used as an instrument for taking from one party and giving the proceeds to another.
Original vs ongoing consent — whether the consent given by founding-era parties transfers to people who did not personally consent to live under the arrangements those earlier parties established.
Procedural legitimacy vs substantive justice — even a procedurally regular legislative vote can produce outcomes that fail any plausible independent test of substantive fairness in their effects.
context: Locke's Second Treatise (1689) treats rulers as ordinary moral agents under the same constraints as everyone else. Lysander Spooner's No Treason (1867-70) sharpens the question with the asymmetric-naming critique: identical acts get different names depending on who performs them. The student names the distinction the 'has to be' move presupposes is resolved.

question: A friend believes in God because she prayed and felt at peace. Her cousin says: 'A calm feeling isn't proof — people feel calm for many reasons.' What's his point?
answer: One feeling can have many causes, so it cannot show which one is real.
choices: One feeling can have many causes, so it cannot show which one is real.
Feelings are never any evidence at all for what a person believes.
Her friend must be wrong, since calm proves nothing either way.
Only a lab test could ever count as a real reason to believe.
context: This is evidentialism, argued by W.K. Clifford ('The Ethics of Belief,' 1877): a private feeling can't settle a public claim, because shareable reasons are needed to tell true beliefs from false ones. Note the cousin's careful limit — he doesn't say feelings never matter or that the friend is wrong; only that ONE feeling can't by itself pick out its own cause. William James (1896) pushed back.

question: Grandma tells Lily: 'When I prayed during your grandpa's surgery, I felt God right there with me. That feeling itself is why I believe.' What kind of reason is Grandma giving?
answer: The experience itself is her evidence.
choices: The experience itself is her evidence.
No reason is needed; faith stands alone.
Only proof others can check would count.
It works for her, so it's worth holding.
context: This is experientialism (William Alston, Perceiving God, 1991): a vivid religious experience can justify belief much as ordinary seeing does, unless there's reason to doubt it. Evidentialists like W. K. Clifford reject private feeling as a reason; fideists say faith needs no reason at all.

question: Soren Kierkegaard called real faith a 'leap' — a trust that reaches past what any argument can prove. So Uncle Sam tells his niece: 'Asking me to prove my faith misses what faith even is.' What is he claiming about faith?
answer: Faith needs no proof; that's not what it is.
choices: Faith needs no proof; that's not what it is.
A strong feeling counts as his evidence.
Belief needs reasons others can check.
It steadies his life, so it's worth it.
context: This is fideism (Latin for 'faith-ism'). Soren Kierkegaard described faith as a 'leap' that reaches beyond proof, and Tertullian argued some claims are credible precisely because they are unexpected. Critics like Thomas Aquinas held that reason and faith work together rather than standing opposed.

question: David Hume argued every proof FOR God runs into serious problems — and every proof AGAINST runs into them too. So Mira tells Theo: 'Both sides fall short. I just don't know.' What is Mira's position?
answer: It can't be settled, so suspend judgment.
choices: It can't be settled, so suspend judgment.
There is no God; the silence proves it.
Belief needs reasons others can check.
A felt experience would be reason enough.
context: This is religious skepticism, older than atheism. Hume's Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779) argues that every proof for God has serious problems — and so does every proof against. Note the difference from atheism: the skeptic suspends judgment rather than denying that God exists.

question: Coach Reyes tells the chaplain: 'I can't prove any of it. But my faith makes me a better dad and a kinder neighbor. That's reason enough.' What is Coach's test of his faith?
answer: What it does in his life.
choices: What it does in his life.
A felt encounter with God.
Reasons others can check.
Faith needs no test at all.
context: This is pragmatic faith (William James, The Will to Believe, 1896): a belief that genuinely improves a life can be reasonable to hold even without proof. The Gospels offer a pragmatic test too: 'by their fruits you shall know them' (Matthew 7:16). Critics warn a belief can be useful yet still false.

question: Sam tells his sister: 'Believing in God without absolute proof isn't crazy. We trust big things we can't prove that way — like that our friends love us.' What is Sam's argument?
answer: No proof is fine; many beliefs we trust lack it.
choices: No proof is fine; many beliefs we trust lack it.
No claim should be held without hard proof.
A felt experience is what backs his belief.
It helps his life, so it's worth believing.
context: This is reasonable faith (Alvin Plantinga, Richard Swinburne): religious belief can be rational without proof, since many everyday beliefs — about other minds, the past, the future — lack proof too. Strict evidentialists like W. K. Clifford reject the comparison and demand sufficient evidence for every belief.

question: Sam asks: 'If God is good, why let people do mean things?' Her dad answers: 'Real choice means real wrong has to be possible.' Which reply to the problem of evil is this?
answer: Free choice is worth the wrong it allows.
choices: Free choice is worth the wrong it allows.
The hardship serves a greater good.
We're too small to judge God's reasons.
The cruelty shows no good God is there.
context: This is the free-will defense (Alvin Plantinga, God, Freedom, and Evil, 1974). It doesn't deny suffering; it argues that moral evil is the price of genuine freedom, which is itself a great good. It's one of several classic theistic replies to the problem of evil.

question: Lila asks why Grandpa got so sick. Grandma says: 'Some good comes only THROUGH the hardship — courage, patience, a family pulled close.' Which reply to the problem of evil is this?
answer: Suffering can buy goods reachable no other way.
choices: Suffering can buy goods reachable no other way.
Wrong is the price we pay for real freedom.
Nobody can judge God's hidden reasons here.
The pain shows no good God is there at all.
context: This is the greater-goods view (Augustine, Aquinas, classical theodicy): suffering may be permitted only when it is tied to a good that could not come any other way, like courage or compassion. Critics point to gratuitous suffering — cases that seem to serve no purpose at all.

question: Epicurus poses it bluntly: if God could stop suffering but won't, He isn't good; if He wants to but can't, He isn't all-powerful. Which view does this defend?
answer: Such suffering rules a good, all-powerful God out.
choices: Such suffering rules a good, all-powerful God out.
God allows it as the price of real human freedom.
It serves some good we can't yet see, like courage.
We're too small to judge God's reasons for this.
context: This is the problem of evil. The dilemma is credited to Epicurus (~300 BC) and sharpened in modern form by J.L. Mackie (1955): the scale of suffering is offered as evidence against a good, all-powerful God. The three rivals here are the free-will defense, the greater-goods view, and skeptical theism. The debate is ancient and still live.

question: W.K. Clifford tells of a shipowner who silenced his doubts, called his rotten ship sound, and watched it sink with all aboard. His verdict? Which view is this?
answer: Only shareable evidence, not private faith, can settle it.
choices: Only shareable evidence, not private faith, can settle it.
The felt experience itself is reason enough to believe.
Faith needs no reasons at all; proof misses the point.
What matters is whether the belief makes your life better.
context: This is evidentialism. W.K. Clifford's 'The Ethics of Belief' (1877) opens with the shipowner parable and draws the hard line: it is wrong, always, to believe anything on insufficient evidence — a private feeling can't settle a claim. William James replied that some beliefs can't wait for proof, so the debate stays live.

question: After forty days in the desert, an anchorite tells her novice: 'I felt His presence beyond any argument. That experience itself is why I believe.' Which view is she defending?
answer: The felt experience itself is reason enough to believe.
choices: The felt experience itself is reason enough to believe.
Only shareable evidence, not private faith, can settle it.
Faith needs no reasons at all; proof misses the point.
Neither side can settle it; suspend judgment instead.
context: This is experientialism. William Alston (Perceiving God, 1991) argued some religious experiences work like ordinary perception — they justify belief unless there's reason to doubt them. Mystics across traditions (al-Ghazali, Teresa of Avila, the bhakti poets) rely on this kind of ground; evidentialists reject it.

question: A flood takes a child's home. Stephen Wykstra answers: not seeing God's reason is like not spotting a flea on a far wall — unseen isn't absent. Which view is this?
answer: We're too small to judge God's reasons for this.
choices: We're too small to judge God's reasons for this.
God allows it as the price of real human freedom.
It serves some good we can't yet see, like courage.
Such suffering rules a good, all-powerful God out.
context: This is skeptical theism (Stephen Wykstra, Michael Bergmann). Wykstra's 'noseeum' point: if there is a God, His reasons would often outstrip ours, so failing to see a reason is not evidence there isn't one. It differs from the greater-goods view, which claims to name the good. Critics worry the move proves too much.

question: In Carthage around 200 AD, Tertullian writes that the Son's death is 'wholly credible because it is unfitting' — the harder for reason, the more it is faith. Which view is this?
answer: Faith needs no reasons at all; proof misses the point.
choices: Faith needs no reasons at all; proof misses the point.
Only shareable evidence, not private faith, can settle it.
The felt experience itself is reason enough to believe.
What matters is whether the belief makes your life better.
context: This is fideism — faith resting where reasons run out. Tertullian's real line in De Carne Christi (~206 AD), 'credibile est, quia ineptum est,' was an argument about the Incarnation; it was later sharpened into the famous (and not-quite-his) tag 'credo quia absurdum,' 'I believe because it is absurd.' Aquinas held the opposite — that reason and faith complement each other.

question: A student says: 'I can't prove other minds exist, or that my memories are real, yet I reasonably believe both. Belief in God can be basic the same way.' Her view?
answer: Like other minds or memory, it can be reasonable with no proof.
choices: Like other minds or memory, it can be reasonable with no proof.
Such suffering rules a good, all-powerful God out.
Only shareable evidence, not private faith, can settle it.
What matters is whether the belief makes your life better.
context: This is reformed epistemology, or proper basicality. Alvin Plantinga (Warranted Christian Belief, 2000) argued belief in God can be 'properly basic' — held without argument, like our belief in other minds or the past. It differs from fideism: the student offers a reason (the analogy), she doesn't reject reasons. Strict evidentialists disagree.

question: Pressed to prove her faith, a believer answers with the old line: 'By their fruits you shall know them' — judge it by whether it makes you patient and brave. Her view?
answer: What matters is whether the belief makes your life better.
choices: What matters is whether the belief makes your life better.
Only shareable evidence, not private faith, can settle it.
The felt experience itself is reason enough to believe.
Faith needs no reasons at all; proof misses the point.
context: This is pragmatic faith. William James (Pragmatism, 1907) judged a belief by its effects on a real life. The Gospels offer their own version — 'by their fruits you shall know them' (Matthew 7:16). Critics answer that a belief can be useful and still be false.

question: Reyna has just sat through two campus talks — a believer's and a skeptic's. She tells her youth group: 'Each one had a hole. I'd rather just say I don't know.' Which view is she taking?
answer: Suspend judgment — neither side proves it, so withhold.
choices: Suspend judgment — neither side proves it, so withhold.
Faith alone — belief needs no reasons at all.
Show me — only checkable evidence justifies belief.
No good God — the world's suffering rules one out.
context: Reyna takes the line of religious skepticism (Hume's Dialogues, 1779): if the case for God and the case against both fall short, suspending judgment is the honest response. It differs from atheism, which asserts God does not exist; skepticism only withholds.

question: A man brushes off your private peace as proof of God: 'It is wrong, always and everywhere, to believe anything on insufficient evidence — and a feeling only you can see is not evidence.' Which view is he taking?
answer: Show me — only checkable evidence justifies a belief.
choices: Show me — only checkable evidence justifies a belief.
The feeling counts — the experience is itself a reason.
Faith alone — belief needs no reasons at all.
By its fruits — judge it by what it does in a life.
context: This is evidentialism. The man echoes W.K. Clifford's maxim from 'The Ethics of Belief' (1877): 'It is wrong always and everywhere to believe anything upon insufficient evidence.' William James's 'The Will to Believe' (1896) is the famous reply — some beliefs can't wait for proof.

question: A Sufi master tells his student: 'In prayer I came to know Him beyond any argument. That knowing was my reason — not a step toward one.' Which view is the master taking?
answer: The experience counts — it is itself the reason, not a path to one.
choices: The experience counts — it is itself the reason, not a path to one.
Show me — only evidence others can check justifies belief.
Faith alone — belief needs no reasons; proof misses the point.
Suspend judgment — neither side proves it, so just withhold.
context: This is experientialism. William Alston (Perceiving God, 1991) argued a religious experience can justify belief much as seeing a color does — informative, even if you can't hand it to someone else. Mystics across traditions rely on it: al-Ghazali, Teresa of Avila, the bhakti poets.

question: Augustine writes: 'God could have made beings who could not sin — but they would not really CHOOSE the good. Real freedom needs the real possibility of going wrong.' Which response is Augustine defending?
answer: Free-will defense — God permits human freedom; without the real possibility of wrong, freedom isn't real.
choices: Free-will defense — God permits human freedom; without the real possibility of wrong, freedom isn't real.
Greater-goods view — some hardship serves real goods (courage, patience) that wouldn't otherwise come to be.
Skeptical theism — humans lack the perspective to judge whether God has any reason for a given hardship.
Atheist reply — the cruelty is evidence no good God exists; a good God would not allow this kind of harm.
context: Augustine framed the free-will defense in the 5th century (City of God; On the Free Choice of the Will). Alvin Plantinga gave its sharpest modern form in God, Freedom, and Evil (1974). It is a 'defense' not a 'theodicy' — it shows belief is logically possible, not that we can name God's actual reasons for any given evil.

question: A man can't argue you into his faith: 'But watch what it did — my work, my students, my choices at 3 a.m. Judge it by the fruit.' Which view is he taking?
answer: By its fruits — judge it by what it does in a life.
choices: By its fruits — judge it by what it does in a life.
Show me — only checkable evidence justifies belief.
The feeling counts — the encounter is itself the reason.
Suspend judgment — neither side proves it, so withhold.
context: This is pragmatic faith. William James (Varieties of Religious Experience, 1902) judged a belief by its effects on a real life, borrowing the Gospel line 'by their fruits you shall know them' (Matthew 7:16). Critics like W.K. Clifford reply that a useful belief and a true one can come apart.

question: On the bus Naomi tells her seatmate: 'Believing in God without knockdown proof is fine. We believe plenty of big things — that our friends love us — without that kind of proof.' Which view is Naomi defending?
answer: Reasonable trust — belief without proof can be rational, as everyday trust is.
choices: Reasonable trust — belief without proof can be rational, as everyday trust is.
Show me — no belief is justified unless strict evidence backs it.
Faith alone — belief needs no reasons; proof-talk misses the point.
By its fruits — what it does in a life, not its truth, is the test.
context: Reformed-epistemology thinkers (Alvin Plantinga, God and Other Minds, 1967) hold belief in God can be rational without conclusive proof — like belief in other minds or the past, which we also can't strictly prove. Strict evidentialists reject the comparison.

question: Asked why she left church, Hannah tells her brother: 'A belief is only worth holding with real evidence. Without proof we can both check, you can't sort the true from the false.' Which view is Hannah's?
answer: Show me — no belief is justified unless shareable evidence backs it.
choices: Show me — no belief is justified unless shareable evidence backs it.
Reasonable trust — belief without strict proof can still be rational.
Faith alone — belief needs no reasons; proof-talk misses the point.
By its fruits — judge a belief by what it does in a life.
context: Strict evidentialism (W.K. Clifford, 'The Ethics of Belief,' 1877): it is always wrong to believe anything on insufficient evidence. William James and modern reasonable-faith defenders reject the standard as too demanding.

question: Asked why she keeps her faith, Lila tells her sister-novices: 'I don't need to prove it. My belief makes me kinder, calmer, more honest — what it DOES in my life is what matters.' Which view is Lila defending?
answer: By its fruits — judge a belief by what it does in the believer's life.
choices: By its fruits — judge a belief by what it does in the believer's life.
Show me — only the evidence backing a belief can justify it.
Faith alone — belief needs no reasons; effects and proof both miss it.
Reasonable trust — belief without strict proof can still be rational.
context: Pragmatism in religion (William James, Varieties of Religious Experience, 1902) shifts the test from evidence to consequences: does the belief make a livable, honest life possible? Critics worry a useful belief can still be false.

question: Kierkegaard called faith a leap over a chasm reason cannot cross. Caleb takes that side: faith doesn't NEED proof, and asking for evidence misses the point of trusting God. Which view is Caleb defending?
answer: Fideism - faith needs no proof; asking for evidence misreads it
choices: Fideism - faith needs no proof; asking for evidence misreads it
Evidentialism - no belief is justified without shareable evidence
Pragmatism - what matters is whether the belief works in life
Reasonable faith - unproved, yet rational like trusting a friend
context: Fideism, illustrated by Kierkegaard's 'leap of faith,' treats religious belief as trust that runs deeper than argument. The slogan 'I believe because it is absurd' is popularly tied to it, though that is a later misreading of Tertullian, not his actual words. Most Christian philosophers reject pure fideism - Aquinas held reason and faith are compatible, not opposed.

question: After youth group, Mira tells her cousin: 'Last night the room went still and I felt a presence I could no more doubt than the floor under my feet. That encounter itself is my reason.' Which view is this?
answer: Experientialism - the felt encounter itself counts as a reason
choices: Experientialism - the felt encounter itself counts as a reason
Evidentialism - a private feeling can never be a reason to believe
Pragmatism - what matters is whether the belief works in life
Fideism - faith leans on nothing at all, not even experience
context: Experientialism (William Alston, Perceiving God, 1991) argues that religious experience, like ordinary perception, can give real but non-conclusive grounds for belief. Critics ask why conflicting experiences across rival faiths shouldn't cancel each other out.

question: Hume's rule was blunt: a wild claim needs evidence as wild as itself. A viral video shows a doctor-defying healing; Owen won't believe it yet, not without records and exams. What is his most careful reason?
answer: A surprising claim needs evidence as strong as itself - one video isn't
choices: A surprising claim needs evidence as strong as itself - one video isn't
Miracles are flatly impossible, so any report of one has to be a lie
If the video moves you, that feeling alone is reason enough to believe
Whether to believe it turns only on whether believing helps his life
context: Hume's 'Of Miracles' (1748) gave the classic case: extraordinary claims need extraordinary evidence, and lone testimony cannot outweigh the steady uniformity of nature. Note Owen does not say miracles are impossible - only that the bar of evidence is high. Defenders of miracles like Swinburne reply that Hume sets the bar too high.

question: Ava tells her science teacher why she still believes: 'I can't prove my parents love me with a lab test either - but I have good reasons. Religious trust can work the same way.' Which view is Ava defending?
answer: Reasonable faith - belief can be rational without lab-proof, like trust in kin
choices: Reasonable faith - belief can be rational without lab-proof, like trust in kin
Evidentialism - no lab-style proof means the belief should be dropped
Pragmatism - believe it only if it actually works out well for you
Fideism - faith needs no reasons or everyday comparisons at all
context: Reformed epistemology (Alvin Plantinga, Warranted Christian Belief, 2000) argues belief in God can be 'properly basic' - rational without argument, like belief in other minds or the past. Ava's 'I trust my parents' move runs the same line. Strict evidentialists reject the standard.

question: In Hume's Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, a believer and a skeptic argue God's existence to a standstill - neither lands a knockout. Devon draws the same conclusion: suspend judgment. Which view is this?
answer: Skepticism - neither side proves it, so suspend judgment
choices: Skepticism - neither side proves it, so suspend judgment
Atheism - lack of proof for God shows that God is not real
Fideism - proof is just not needed; simply hold the faith
Reasonable faith - belief is fair even without any proof
context: Theological skepticism (Hume's Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, 1779) holds the case for and against God is undecidable by argument, so suspending judgment is the honest move. It differs from atheism, which asserts God's non-existence. James's 'Will to Believe' is a direct reply.

question: After a heated cafeteria argument, Jonah tells his table: 'I sincerely believe my religion is true — that's enough, right?' His friend Mira gently disagrees. Why is 'I sincerely believe it' NOT enough to make a religious claim true?
answer: Sincerity isn't truth — believing hard doesn't make it so; rival believers feel just as sure with conflicting religions.
choices: Sincerity isn't truth — believing hard doesn't make it so; rival believers feel just as sure with conflicting religions.
Tradition isn't truth — long practice settles nothing; whether a religion is true is separate from how old it happens to be.
Experience isn't truth — feeling God in prayer settles nothing on its own; the experience could happen and still mean less.
Popularity isn't truth — many believers don't add up to truth; whether a religion is true is unconnected to its head count.
context: The 'sincere belief' move slides between two questions: whether someone holds a belief, and whether the belief is true. Sincere believers across rival traditions can't all be right — so sincerity alone never adjudicates which one is the case.

question: William James argued a belief proves itself by its payoff in a life, not by proof on paper. Eli says the same of prayer: 'It steadies me, keeps me kind, holds the family together.' Which view is Eli defending?
answer: Pragmatism - the practice earns its place by its real-life effects
choices: Pragmatism - the practice earns its place by its real-life effects
Evidentialism - good effects in a life do not make a claim true
Fideism - faith rests on trust alone, not on any of its results
Experientialism - a directly felt encounter is the real reason
context: Pragmatic religion (William James, The Will to Believe, 1896) judges a belief by its lived effects rather than by proof. Christian thinkers push back: a religion that 'works' but isn't true is in trouble - Paul's I Corinthians 15 makes truth primary.

question: Trying to settle an argument at the watch-night fire, Marcus says: 'Two billion people are Christians — that has to mean it's true.' Sara pushes back. Why is 'lots of people believe it' NOT enough to make the religious claim true?
answer: Popularity isn't truth — billions of believers across rival traditions can't all be right; headcounts don't settle which is true.
choices: Popularity isn't truth — billions of believers across rival traditions can't all be right; headcounts don't settle which is true.
Sincerity isn't truth — believers being earnest doesn't establish a religion; what each sincerely feels can be honestly mistaken.
Tradition isn't truth — long practice can encode error; the age of a religion is unrelated to whether it tracks how things are.
Experience isn't truth — many people feeling peace in prayer settles nothing; the experience can happen and still tell us little.
context: Counting believers across rival religions illustrates the limit of headcount arguments: Christianity, Islam, Hinduism each have hundreds of millions, but they make incompatible truth-claims about God. Popular numbers can't decide which is right.

question: C.S. Lewis went from hardened atheist to believer. Talia tells her friends: 'He met God directly - and that firsthand encounter, not any outside proof, is itself his evidence.' Which view is this?
answer: Experientialism - the encounter itself, not its results, is the evidence
choices: Experientialism - the encounter itself, not its results, is the evidence
Evidentialism - only public, repeatable proof can ever count
Pragmatism - what matters is only whether believing helps you live well
Fideism - belief needs no evidence or experience of any kind
context: Alston's Perceiving God (1991) and the broader Reformed tradition argue religious experience can ground belief much as sense perception does - the encounter itself, not its later fruits, doing the work. C.S. Lewis and many converts make this move in their testimonies. Critics worry that rival experiences across faiths undercut it.

question: Tertullian wrote of Christian belief: 'I believe because it is absurd.' Reasons, he held, are not even the right tool for faith — asking for them misses the point. Whose view of religious belief is this?
answer: Faith needs no reasons — asking for them misses what faith is.
choices: Faith needs no reasons — asking for them misses what faith is.
Faith is reasonable — like trusting other things we can't see.
Faith proves itself by what it does for your life.
Only shared evidence everyone can check should settle it.
context: This is fideism: reasons sit outside faith's domain, so demanding them mistakes what faith is (Kierkegaard's 'leap of faith' is the classic version). The famous slogan 'I believe because it is absurd' (credo quia absurdum) is loosely attached to Tertullian but is an Enlightenment-era sharpening of his actual line, 'it is certain because it is impossible.' Aquinas, Plantinga, and Swinburne reject fideism — they hold that Christian belief can offer reasons too.

question: After her aunt felt peaceful praying for the first time, she tells everyone: 'I felt peace, so God must be real.' Mara — kindly — challenges her. Why is 'I felt peace in prayer' NOT enough on its own to prove God exists?
answer: Other things give the same feeling — meditation, music, deep breaths produce peace; the experience can't pick its own source.
choices: Other things give the same feeling — meditation, music, deep breaths produce peace; the experience can't pick its own source.
Sincerity isn't truth — sincerely feeling something doesn't make a belief true; the feeling can be sincere yet still mistaken.
Tradition isn't truth — that prayer is an old practice doesn't make any one prayer connect with God; longevity is unrelated here.
Popularity isn't truth — that millions feel peace while praying settles nothing; head counts don't bear on which religion is true.
context: The 'argument from religious experience' has a parallel problem: peace, awe, and comfort can come from many sources. Religious-experience defenders (Alston) respond that pattern across many believers, not one feeling, is what matters.

question: Asked how she can believe in an unseen God, Esme says: 'I believe in infinity, and no one has seen that either. Believing in real unseen things is normal for thoughtful people.' Whose view is Esme using?
answer: Faith is reasonable — like trusting other unseen things we accept.
choices: Faith is reasonable — like trusting other unseen things we accept.
Faith needs no reasons — a comparison like that misses the point.
Faith proves itself by what it does for the life you live.
Only shared evidence everyone can check should settle it.
context: Esme uses the unseen-realities argument: belief in real things we cannot see — numbers, other minds — can be rational, and faith may fit the same pattern. Reformed epistemologists like Alvin Plantinga develop versions of this. Critics answer that infinity is tested in proofs, not merely accepted unseen — a disanalogy.

question: Talking through which religion is true, Felix says: 'You can't go by who feels most sincere — sincere believers fill every faith. Only evidence anyone can check could pick the right one.' Whose view is Felix using?
answer: Only shared evidence everyone can check should settle it.
choices: Only shared evidence everyone can check should settle it.
A personal experience can itself count as real evidence.
Faith is reasonable without that kind of strict proof.
Faith needs no reasons — it isn't decided that way at all.
context: Felix uses strict evidentialism (W.K. Clifford, 'The Ethics of Belief,' 1877): with sincere believers across rival faiths, only shareable evidence could pick the true one. Plantinga and Alston reply that a person's own experience may still leave room for warranted belief.

question: Asked why she believes, Carla shrugs: 'It's what my family always believed.' Her school friend Diego asks her to think about it. Why is 'my family always believed it' NOT enough to settle whether it's true?
answer: Family sets exposure, not truth — kids of rival religions inherit different ones; family background can't pick the true religion.
choices: Family sets exposure, not truth — kids of rival religions inherit different ones; family background can't pick the true religion.
Sincerity isn't truth — believing what parents believed sincerely doesn't make it so; sincerity does no work to verify a claim.
Popularity isn't truth — large religions have many family lines; wide hand-down doesn't settle which religion is the right one.
Tradition isn't truth — long practice can encode error; the age of a family religion is unrelated to whether it tracks reality.
context: The 'genetic-of-belief' worry: people in Riyadh raised Muslim, in Chennai raised Hindu, in Atlanta raised Baptist. Family of origin shapes who believes what but can't be the reason a religion is true — competing families can't all be right.

question: Losing the argument, Greta says: 'I don't need a tight proof. My faith holds my whole life together — that's what matters, and that's why I keep it.' Whose view of religious belief is Greta using?
answer: Faith proves itself by what it does for your life.
choices: Faith proves itself by what it does for your life.
Faith needs no reasons — what it does for you isn't the point.
Faith stands on reasons, not on how it makes life feel.
Only shared evidence everyone can check should settle it.
context: Greta uses pragmatism about belief (William James): what matters is the 'cash value' a belief has for living. James coined that phrase in Pragmatism (1907); his earlier 'The Will to Believe' (1896) defended holding such beliefs. Christian thinkers push back — Paul's letters insist truth comes first and comfort second.

question: After something she prayed for came true, Selena tells Theo: 'That answered prayer is a real reason to believe — not a proof, but more than a coincidence I can wave off.' Whose view is Selena using?
answer: A personal experience can itself count as real evidence.
choices: A personal experience can itself count as real evidence.
Only shared evidence everyone can check should settle it.
Faith proves itself by what it does for your life.
Faith needs no reasons — answered prayers aren't the point.
context: Selena treats religious experience as evidence: the prayer plus the matching outcome serves as a real (not absolute) reason. Critics point to confirmation bias — the prayers that go unanswered get forgotten. Defenders reply that the pattern, not one case, is what counts.

question: In a debate-club round, Mason quotes a religious text to settle whether the text is reliable. His opponent objects. Why is 'the book says it's true' NOT enough — in this kind of debate — to prove the book is true?
answer: Self-citation isn't proof — using the book to vouch for the book begs the question; outside reasons must do that job here.
choices: Self-citation isn't proof — using the book to vouch for the book begs the question; outside reasons must do that job here.
Sincerity isn't truth — Mason sincerely trusting the book doesn't establish it; what one earnestly cites can still be plain wrong.
Popularity isn't truth — many people quoting the same book settles nothing; headcounts of citers don't bear on whether it's true.
Experience isn't truth — feeling moved by the book settles nothing; emotions while reading don't supply a reliable reason at all.
context: Begging the question (Latin: petitio principii) when arguing for a text's reliability with the text itself is a familiar problem in debates between religious and non-religious thinkers. The reply: appeals must extend to shared ground.

question: Leibniz pressed a question that haunts metaphysics: why is there something rather than nothing? A chain of dependent things, however long, never explains why anything exists - something undependent must ground it. Which argument for God is this?
answer: First-cause: the chain of dependent things needs an undependent ground.
choices: First-cause: the chain of dependent things needs an undependent ground.
Fine-tuning: the universe is set too precisely for life to be chance.
Moral law: real right and wrong must rest on a lawgiver beyond us.
Pure logic: the very idea of a perfect being forces it to exist.
context: This is the cosmological (first-cause / contingency) argument: Aquinas's Five Ways (c. 1265) and Leibniz's 'why is there something rather than nothing?' (1697). The Kalam version (al-Ghazali, revived by Craig) adds that the universe began. The other three choices name the design, moral, and ontological arguments.

question: Paley said a watch found on a heath implies a watchmaker. The constants of physics, defenders add, sit in a razor-thin window for life - nudge gravity a hair and no stars form. That precise setting points to a setter. Which argument for God is this?
answer: Fine-tuning: the universe is set too precisely for life to be chance.
choices: Fine-tuning: the universe is set too precisely for life to be chance.
First-cause: the chain of dependent things needs an undependent ground.
Moral law: real right and wrong must rest on a lawgiver beyond us.
Pure logic: the very idea of a perfect being forces it to exist.
context: Fine-tuning is the modern heir of Paley's watchmaker (Natural Theology, 1802); defenders include Robin Collins and John Polkinghorne. Critics answer with the multiverse and anthropic selection. The other choices name the first-cause, moral, and ontological arguments.

question: C.S. Lewis argued: without a moral law beyond us, calling a thing evil just means you dislike it. But torturing a child for fun is really wrong, not merely disliked - a fact that comes from beyond human opinion. Which argument for God is this?
answer: Moral law: real right and wrong must rest on a lawgiver beyond us.
choices: Moral law: real right and wrong must rest on a lawgiver beyond us.
First-cause: the chain of dependent things needs an undependent ground.
Fine-tuning: the universe is set too precisely for life to be chance.
Pure logic: the very idea of a perfect being forces it to exist.
context: The moral argument runs from Kant's moral postulate (Critique of Practical Reason, 1788) to, in modern form, C.S. Lewis (Mere Christianity, 1952): binding obligation needs a personal ground that mere preference can't supply. The other choices name the first-cause, design, and ontological arguments.

question: A friend asks a debate-club captain: 'If God is all-good and all-powerful, why let people do terrible things?' The captain replies that God values real freedom, and freedom must include the genuine possibility of doing wrong. Which response to the problem of evil is she defending?
answer: Free-will defense — God permits moral evil because removing wrong choice would also remove the genuine freedom that makes moral agency meaningful.
choices: Free-will defense — God permits moral evil because removing wrong choice would also remove the genuine freedom that makes moral agency meaningful.
Skeptical theism — humans lack the capacity to judge whether God has good reasons for permitting evils; absence of seen reason is not absence of reason.
Soul-making theodicy — suffering builds virtuous character; a world without challenge could not develop the moral souls a good God intends to form here.
Mystery move — divine reasons exceed our understanding entirely; the puzzle is beyond our ability to address and should be set aside rather than engaged.
context: The free-will defense was developed by Augustine and given modern form by Plantinga (God, Freedom, and Evil, 1974). It targets the logical problem of evil — the claim that God and evil are logically incompatible — and aims to show their joint possibility.

question: 'A child dying of cancer,' a friend says - 'free will can't explain that. If God had a reason, we'd see it.' A reviewer replies: 'Why expect to see God's every reason? Our view is tiny.' Which reply to the problem of evil is the reviewer making?
answer: Limited view: we're too small to judge whether God has good reasons.
choices: Limited view: we're too small to judge whether God has good reasons.
Free will: real choice means God must allow people to do harm.
Soul-making: hardship is the only thing that grows real virtue.
Hidden good: there IS a greater gain the suffering secretly buys.
context: This is skeptical theism (Wykstra, Alston, Bergmann), aimed at the evidential problem of evil: from 'I see no reason' it does not follow that 'there is no reason' - a beginner can't always see the master's reasons. Note the contrast with the greater-good reply: the reviewer makes only the modest epistemic move ('we can't see the reasons'), not the bolder claim that a hidden good is definitely there. The other choices name the free-will, soul-making, and greater-good replies.

question: Plantinga argued: belief in God needn't be reasoned out from evidence the way science is. It can be basic - held directly, the way you just trust your memory or that other people have minds. Which view of religious belief is this?
answer: Basic belief: trust in God can start directly, like trusting your memory.
choices: Basic belief: trust in God can start directly, like trusting your memory.
Evidentialism: a belief is only fair if the evidence backs it up.
Faith alone: belief rests on commitment, not on reasons at all.
Testing rule: a claim is empty unless some observation could check it.
context: This is Reformed epistemology (Plantinga, 'Reason and Belief in God,' 1983; Alston, Perceiving God, 1991): belief in God can be 'properly basic,' not inferred from argument, much like belief in other minds. The other choices name evidentialism, fideism, and verificationism.

question: A.J. Ayer argued: a sentence means something only if some observation could in principle confirm or deny it. 'God loves us' predicts nothing you could check - so it isn't really saying anything. Which view of religious language is this?
answer: Testing rule: a claim is empty unless some observation could check it.
choices: Testing rule: a claim is empty unless some observation could check it.
Evidentialism: the claim has meaning but needs evidence to believe.
Basic belief: trust in God can stand on its own without a test.
Pluralism: each tradition catches part of one truth too big to test.
context: This is verificationism (Ayer, Language, Truth and Logic, 1936): untestable religious and ethical statements were called literally meaningless. The famous reply: the verification principle fails its own test - no observation could confirm IT - so most philosophers dropped it. The other choices name evidentialism, Reformed epistemology, and pluralism.

question: John Hick compared the great religions to blind men touching one elephant - each describes the same reality from a different angle, each catching part of the truth, none simply right, none simply wrong. Which view of religious diversity is this?
answer: Pluralism: every tradition glimpses part of one reality none fully owns.
choices: Pluralism: every tradition glimpses part of one reality none fully owns.
Exclusivism: one tradition is right where the others conflict with it.
Inclusivism: one tradition has the full truth; others only echoes.
Naturalism: the experiences are just psychology, with no reality beneath.
context: This is religious pluralism, associated with John Hick (An Interpretation of Religion, 1989) and his blind-men-and-the-elephant image, drawing on Kant's noumenon/phenomenon split: traditions are culture-shaped responses to the same ultimate 'Real.' Exclusivism, inclusivism, and naturalism are its rivals.

question: A peer-review reader replies to a classmate who says she believes in God because she felt peace during prayer: 'Lots of people feel peace for many reasons. The feeling can't settle whether the belief is true.' Why is 'I sincerely feel it' not enough, on this account, to justify belief?
answer: Evidentialism — sincere feelings don't track truth reliably enough; justifying any belief requires evidence beyond the feeling itself.
choices: Evidentialism — sincere feelings don't track truth reliably enough; justifying any belief requires evidence beyond the feeling itself.
Reformed epistemology — religious experience can ground belief directly without external evidence; the reader misapplies evidentialism to basic belief.
Fideism — religious belief is justified by faith and stands outside the demand for evidence; the reader assumes the wrong framework for the claim.
Religious pluralism — many traditions touch the same reality through experience; the feeling is meaningful even without pinning down which tradition.
