context: Evidentialism (W.K. Clifford, 'The Ethics of Belief' 1877: 'It is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence.') sets a uniform evidence standard for any belief. Plantinga's reformed epistemology is the standard reply.

question: Tertullian declared the gospel certain BECAUSE it is impossible — the more reason recoils, the truer it rings. Kierkegaard later called faith a leap past anything reason can settle. Which view of faith is this?
answer: Fideism — faith stands beyond reason; demanding proof mistakes what faith is.
choices: Fideism — faith stands beyond reason; demanding proof mistakes what faith is.
Evidentialism — believe only as far as the evidence allows, never further.
Reformed epistemology — belief in God is basic, like trusting your memory.
Natural theology — plain reason can prove God exists before faith begins.
context: Tertullian's real line (De Carne Christi 5.4) is 'certum est, quia impossibile' — it is certain because it is impossible (the popular 'I believe because it is absurd' is a later Enlightenment distortion). Kierkegaard's 'leap of faith' (Fear and Trembling, 1843) carries the same spirit. Critics like Aquinas hold reason and faith cooperate rather than divide — the contrast that makes the other three options real rivals here.

question: A peer-review reader writes about a natural disaster: 'The suffering is real. But we can imagine allowing it serves goods we don't fully see — the structure of a world where choices matter, character formed through hardship.' Which response to the problem of evil is she defending?
answer: Greater-goods defense — apparent evils may be permitted to serve unseen goods that could not otherwise be obtained; the evil is real but serves a real good.
choices: Greater-goods defense — apparent evils may be permitted to serve unseen goods that could not otherwise be obtained; the evil is real but serves a real good.
Free-will defense — God permits moral evil because removing wrong choice would also remove the genuine freedom that makes moral agency meaningful.
Skeptical theism — humans lack the capacity to judge whether God has good reasons for permitting evils; absence of seen reason is not absence of reason.
Deflection — the responsibility for evil lies entirely with human choosers; natural-disaster cases dissolve once all suffering is attributed to human agency.
context: The greater-goods defense (Augustine, Aquinas, classical theodicy) claims apparent evil may serve goods otherwise unobtainable. Critics (Mackie) note it must show the goods are actually unobtainable without the evil — a stronger claim than the bare possibility.

question: Blaise Pascal, the gambler-turned-believer, argued: bet on God and win, you gain everything; bet against and lose, you lose everything. So belief is the smart wager. What kind of move is this?
answer: Treating belief as a bet — choosing by the payoffs when proof runs out.
choices: Treating belief as a bet — choosing by the payoffs when proof runs out.
Demanding hard evidence before accepting any claim at all.
Claiming to perceive God directly, the way one sees a tree.
Insisting faith needs no reasons, because reasons miss the point.
context: This is Pascal's Wager (Pensees, 1670): belief framed as a decision under uncertainty with lopsided stakes. Critics raise the 'many gods' problem (bet on which God?) and ask whether a bet-driven belief is real faith at all — a strategy isn't trust.

question: Asked why a good God allows suffering, a thinker answers that the world is no finished paradise but a vale of soul-making — hardship is the very stuff courage, patience, and mercy are forged from. Which response to evil is this?
answer: Soul-making — hardship is the workshop where strong character is forged.
choices: Soul-making — hardship is the workshop where strong character is forged.
Free-will defense — real freedom must include the power to choose wrongly.
Skeptical theism — we can't see God's reasons, but that doesn't mean none exist.
Mystery move — the question is beyond us, so it should simply be set aside.
context: The phrase 'a vale of soul-making' is John Keats's (1819); the theodicy is tied to John Hick (Evil and the God of Love, 1966), reaching back to Irenaeus. The world is not a finished paradise but a place where character is actually built.

question: Thomas Aquinas split truths in two: preambles plain reason can prove — that God exists, is one — and deeper articles only revelation reveals. The two, he held, can never clash. Which view is this?
answer: Natural theology — reason proves the basics; revelation supplies the rest.
choices: Natural theology — reason proves the basics; revelation supplies the rest.
Fideism — faith alone reaches God; asking reason to help misses the point.
Reformed epistemology — belief in God is basic and needs no proof at all.
Verificationism — only testable claims mean anything, so God-talk says nothing.
context: Aquinas (Summa Theologiae, c. 1265) split 'preambles' reason can reach (that God exists, is one) from 'articles' needing revelation (the Trinity, the Incarnation). On his view faith presupposes reason where reason can reach.

question: A peer-review reader replies to a miracle claim at a healing service: 'Sincere reports, even from honest people, can't settle whether the cause was supernatural. Ordinary causes produce surprising recoveries too.' Why is 'sincere eyewitnesses reported it' not enough to establish a miracle?
answer: Humean evidentialism — extraordinary claims need evidence stronger than testimony usually provides; ordinary causes remain a live alternative for recoveries.
choices: Humean evidentialism — extraordinary claims need evidence stronger than testimony usually provides; ordinary causes remain a live alternative for recoveries.
Reformed epistemology — religious experience grounds belief directly without external evidence; the reader misapplies evidentialism to a properly basic belief.
Fideism — faith neither requires nor benefits from evidence; the reader assumes the wrong framework for assessing what kind of claim a miracle report is.
Verificationism — only statements verifiable in principle are meaningful; the reader's complaint is about meaning, not evidence, and misses what miracles do.
context: Hume's argument against miracles (Enquiry, X, 1748): 'No testimony is sufficient to establish a miracle unless its falsehood would be more miraculous than the fact it endeavours to establish.' Critics (Earman, Hume's Abject Failure 2000) dispute the probabilistic framing.

question: William Alston argued that someone who experiences God is in the same position as someone who sees a tree — a direct perception that counts as real evidence, until you have reason to doubt it. Which view is he defending?
answer: Perception model — sensing God works like seeing, so it counts as evidence.
choices: Perception model — sensing God works like seeing, so it counts as evidence.
Evidentialism — private experience proves nothing unless others can check it.
Reformed view — belief in God is basic, needing no evidence at all.
Verificationism — only testable claims mean anything, so it shows nothing.
context: William Alston (Perceiving God, 1991) frames religious experience as a 'doxastic practice' on a par with ordinary sense perception: both yield prima facie evidence, and both are circular if you demand they justify themselves from outside.

question: In Plato's dialogue, Socrates traps the priest Euthyphro: is an act holy BECAUSE the gods command it, or do they command it because it is already holy? One horn says the command itself makes it right. Which view of right and wrong is that?
answer: Divine command — what is right is fixed by what God commands.
choices: Divine command — what is right is fixed by what God commands.
Natural law — what is right is fixed by how human nature is built.
Moral realism — moral facts are simply out there; God at most reveals them.
Relativism — what is right is fixed by each culture's say-so.
context: The dilemma is Plato's Euthyphro fork: is an act right because God commands it, or commanded because it is already right? Robert Adams' modified divine command theory (Finite and Infinite Goods, 1999) is a careful modern reply to the first horn.

question: A school newspaper editor replies to a claim that God must exist because most cultures have religions: 'That many people across history believed in something doesn't settle whether what they believed in is real.' Why is 'most cultures have believed it' not enough to establish God exists?
answer: Individualist evidentialism — widespread belief doesn't track truth reliably; the question is what evidence the cultures had, not how many cultures believed.
choices: Individualist evidentialism — widespread belief doesn't track truth reliably; the question is what evidence the cultures had, not how many cultures believed.
Religious pluralism — different traditions touch one reality partially; the consensus across cultures supports a shared reality the editor's reply misreads.
Reformed epistemology — religious belief can be properly basic, grounded in experience; the consensus across cultures is then evidence of a shared faculty.
Fideism — religious belief is justified by personal faith not cultural counting; the editor rejects consensus rightly but for the wrong sort of reason here.
context: The 'common consent' argument (consensus gentium) appears in Cicero and lingers as background warrant. Critics note that wide belief tracks human cognitive tendency, not the truth of the object — many false beliefs have also been near-universal across cultures.

question: The monk Anselm claimed God is a being greater than which none can be thought — and since a real God beats one that exists only in the mind, God MUST exist. What does this argument reason from?
answer: From the very definition of God, using no facts about the world.
choices: From the very definition of God, using no facts about the world.
From things that begin or change, which need a first cause behind them.
From the fine-tuned constants that make a life-bearing universe possible.
From binding moral duties that only a lawgiver could ground.
context: Anselm's ontological argument (Proslogion, c. 1078) reasons from the concept of God to God's existence. The monk Gaunilo mocked it with a 'perfect island' that would have to exist by the same logic; Kant objected that existing isn't a real property. Modal versions (Plantinga, 1974) revive it.

question: A friend asks a youth-group leader: 'If God is all-good and all-powerful, why does evil exist?' The leader replies: 'You shouldn't ask that — it's disrespectful to question God's ways.' Which response actually engages the problem of evil rather than refusing it?
answer: Free-will defense — God permits moral evil because removing wrong choice would also remove the genuine freedom that makes moral agency meaningful.
choices: Free-will defense — God permits moral evil because removing wrong choice would also remove the genuine freedom that makes moral agency meaningful.
Suppression move — questioning is disrespectful, so the issue should not be raised at all; the puzzle dissolves once the questioner is told to stop asking.
Verdict move — God exists despite the evil, so any reasoning that troubles this conclusion must be mistaken; the puzzle is settled by conclusion not argument.
Motive impugning — atheists must want evil to keep happening, so the objection is self-defeating; the puzzle dissolves once motives are reframed badly.
context: The free-will defense engages the actual structure of the problem of evil — it accepts the question's premise (evil exists) and offers a candidate reason (free agency requires possibility of wrong). Refusing to ask or impugning motives does not engage it.

question: An op-ed columnist writes: 'If God is all-good and all-powerful, creatures who could only do good would still be possible - so why permit moral evil?' A theologian replies: 'A world with genuine moral agents requires the real possibility they choose wrongly; rigged goodness is not goodness.' Which response is the theologian giving?
answer: Free-will defense - moral evil is the cost of creating genuine moral agents, since rigged goodness in creatures who never went wrong would not be moral agency at all.
choices: Free-will defense - moral evil is the cost of creating genuine moral agents, since rigged goodness in creatures who never went wrong would not be moral agency at all.
Greater-goods defense - apparent evil is permitted only when it serves higher goods we cannot fully see, without denying the evil or weakening any divine moral attribute.
Sceptical theism - humans simply lack the cognitive capacity to judge whether God has good reasons for any specific permitted evil; agnosticism about divine reasons is the honest move.
Soul-making theodicy - evil is the necessary occasion for moral growth, since souls develop virtue only by working through suffering they could not face in a frictionless world.
context: Alvin Plantinga's God, Freedom, and Evil (1974) develops the free-will defense against Mackie's logical problem of evil. Plantinga shows it is logically possible that God could not actualize a world containing free creatures who never sin - blocking the Mackie inconsistency proof.

question: On a religion-and-philosophy podcast, host Camille presses: 'Surely we can SEE that some sufferings serve no greater good.' Theologian Dwight responds: 'A finite mind isn't well-placed to rule out reasons an infinite mind might have; not-seeing-a-reason isn't the same as seeing-no-reason.' Which response is Dwight giving?
answer: Sceptical theism - finite minds aren't well-placed to canvass an infinite mind's reasons, so 'we see no good' falls short of 'there is no good'; agnosticism about specifics is honest.
choices: Sceptical theism - finite minds aren't well-placed to canvass an infinite mind's reasons, so 'we see no good' falls short of 'there is no good'; agnosticism about specifics is honest.
Free-will defense - the suffering in question is the price of genuine moral agency, since a world in which wrong choices were impossible would not contain real moral agents at all.
Greater-goods defense - the suffering serves identifiable goods (moral growth, the stability of natural law, structures of meaningful choice) that justify permitting the evil in this case.
Soul-making theodicy - the suffering is the necessary occasion for character development, since souls grow into virtue only through facing trials they could not face in a frictionless world.
context: Sceptical theism (Stephen Wykstra, 1984; Michael Bergmann, 2001) blocks the evidential problem of evil at the inferential step: our failure to see God-justifying reasons for some evil doesn't license the inference that no such reasons exist. The position is logically modest and widely discussed in contemporary philosophy of religion.

question: Philosophy podcaster Bex summarizes an argument: 'Whatever begins to exist has a cause. The universe began to exist. Therefore the universe has a cause - and a cause that is itself uncaused, beyond time, and immensely powerful.' At its sharpest, what does this argument claim?
answer: Kalam cosmological argument - because the universe began to exist, it requires a cause; the argument concludes to a timeless, immensely powerful cause as the source of the universe.
choices: Kalam cosmological argument - because the universe began to exist, it requires a cause; the argument concludes to a timeless, immensely powerful cause as the source of the universe.
Thomistic First Way - every motion requires a prior mover, and the regress of movers must terminate in an unmoved mover; the argument turns on causal series here and now, not beginnings.
Ontological argument - the very concept of a maximally great being entails its existence, since a being that exists in reality is greater than one that exists in the mind alone here.
Fine-tuning design argument - the physical constants are calibrated so precisely for life that brute chance is a poor explanation; the conclusion is intelligent design, not first cause.
context: The kalam version (William Lane Craig, The Kalam Cosmological Argument, 1979) is distinguished by its reliance on the universe's temporal beginning - philosophical arguments against actual infinites plus cosmological evidence. Aquinas's cosmological arguments do not turn on a temporal beginning; they reason from causal dependence.

question: On a panel, theologian Aleksy presents an argument: 'In every chain of contingent beings, each one depends on another for existing right now. The whole chain of dependent existers cannot itself be the explanation; there must be a non-contingent ground.' At its sharpest, what does Aleksy's argument claim?
answer: Thomistic argument from contingency - dependent existers cannot collectively ground their own existing; an explanatorily ultimate non-contingent being is required as the ground of all.
choices: Thomistic argument from contingency - dependent existers cannot collectively ground their own existing; an explanatorily ultimate non-contingent being is required as the ground of all.
Kalam cosmological argument - whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began, so its cause is timeless and powerful; the argument turns on a temporal beginning of the cosmos.
Design argument - the fitting arrangement of natural things for ends presupposes an ordering intelligence; the argument turns on apparent purpose, not on dependent existence's ground.
Moral argument - objective moral obligations exist and are best explained by a moral lawgiver; the argument turns on the existence of binding ethical norms, not contingent existence.
context: Aquinas's Third Way (Summa Theologiae I.2.3) reasons from contingency: things that can fail to exist could not all be contingent, since then at some point nothing would have existed. Modern readers (Edward Feser, Five Proofs of the Existence of God, 2017) distinguish this Thomistic argument sharply from Craig's kalam, despite shared 'cosmological' label.

question: On a podcast on classical arguments, host Reza summarizes a medieval move: 'God is THAT than which no greater can be conceived. Such a being must exist in reality - because one existing only in the mind would be less great than one existing in fact.' At its sharpest, what does this argument claim?
answer: Ontological argument - existence is built into the concept of a maximally great being; the very coherence of the concept entails its instantiation, by analysis of the idea alone.
choices: Ontological argument - existence is built into the concept of a maximally great being; the very coherence of the concept entails its instantiation, by analysis of the idea alone.
Cosmological argument - contingent things require a non-contingent cause; the argument here moves from the actual world's dependence outward to its ground, rather than from any concept.
Design argument - the regularities and apparent purposes of nature presuppose an ordering intelligence; the argument moves from features of the world outward, rather than from any concept.
Moral argument - the binding character of objective moral obligations is best explained by a moral lawgiver; the argument moves from ethical features of reality, not from any concept.
context: Anselm's Proslogion (1078) is the classical ontological argument. Kant's standard objection holds that 'existence is not a predicate' the way 'great' is. Plantinga's modal ontological argument (1974) recasts it using modal logic: a maximally great being possibly exists, so necessarily exists. Critics dispute the possibility premise.

question: Science writer Pell summarizes the case for cosmic design: 'The physical constants are calibrated within tolerances so narrow that shifting any one slightly would forbid stars, chemistry, or life. Brute chance is a remarkably poor explanation; design is a better inference.' At its sharpest, what does this argument claim?
answer: Fine-tuning design argument - the precise calibration of physical constants for life is better explained by intelligent design than by chance, even with multiverse hypotheses in view.
choices: Fine-tuning design argument - the precise calibration of physical constants for life is better explained by intelligent design than by chance, even with multiverse hypotheses in view.
Paley's watchmaker argument - the integrated functional complexity of organisms presupposes a designer; the argument turns on biological adaptation, not on physical constants of the cosmos.
Kalam cosmological argument - whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began, so its cause is timeless and powerful; the argument here is about the cosmos beginning, not its laws.
Anthropic principle - we shouldn't be surprised to find ourselves in a life-permitting universe since only such universes contain observers; the move undercuts inference to design.
context: Modern fine-tuning arguments (Robin Collins, John Polkinghorne) build on physical-constants data developed since the 1970s. Paley's earlier watchmaker (Natural Theology, 1802) reasons from biological complexity. Hume's Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779) anticipates objections, and the anthropic principle is the standard rebuttal.

question: On a campus debate, philosopher Renault argues: 'Objective moral obligations are real - the wrongness of torturing innocents isn't a feeling we have. But objective obligations need a ground, and natural facts do not deliver oughts. A moral lawgiver is the best explanation.' At its sharpest, what does this argument claim?
answer: Moral argument - the reality of objective moral obligations points to a transcendent moral lawgiver as their best explanation, since natural facts alone do not yield genuine oughts.
choices: Moral argument - the reality of objective moral obligations points to a transcendent moral lawgiver as their best explanation, since natural facts alone do not yield genuine oughts.
Ontological argument - the concept of a maximally great being entails its existence, since a being that exists in reality is greater than one that exists in the mind alone here.
Cosmological argument - the existence of contingent things requires a non-contingent cause; the argument moves from the actual world's dependence outward, not from binding moral norms.
Pragmatic Pascalian wager - given uncertain stakes about God's existence, the expected utility of belief outweighs unbelief; the argument here is decision-theoretic, not about morals.
context: The moral argument has classical roots (Kant treats God as a postulate of practical reason) and modern defenders (C. S. Lewis, Mere Christianity, 1952; William Lane Craig). Critics (J. L. Mackie, Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong, 1977) accept the conditional but reject moral realism. Naturalist moral realism is a further rival.

question: Reporter Sina presses a philosopher: 'People report encounters with the divine, but feelings aren't evidence.' The philosopher answers: 'Perception generally confers prima facie warrant on experience-based belief. If religious experience is perception-like, the same default applies.' Which response engages the reporter's challenge?
answer: Religious experience as evidence - if such experience is genuinely perception-like, the standard epistemic default treating perception as prima facie warranting applies to it directly.
choices: Religious experience as evidence - if such experience is genuinely perception-like, the standard epistemic default treating perception as prima facie warranting applies to it directly.
Fideism - religious belief requires no evidence at all, since demanding evidence misunderstands what faith is; the appropriate posture is trust prior to and apart from any argument.
Reformed epistemology - belief in God can be properly basic, formed in basic conditions without inference from other beliefs; the response should bypass the evidence framing altogether.
Strict evidentialism - the reporter is right that feelings alone aren't evidence; serious religious belief requires shareable arguments and external evidence in the standard public sense.
context: William Alston (Perceiving God, 1991) develops religious experience as a doxastic practice on a par with sense perception. Richard Swinburne's principle of credulity (The Existence of God, 1979): in the absence of defeaters, experiences are evidence for what they seem to be experiences of. Critics dispute the perception-like claim.

question: An evidentialist insists: 'No belief is rational without a supporting argument; belief in God is no exception.' Philosopher Tess responds: 'Many basic beliefs - that there is a past, that other minds exist - have no supporting argument yet are perfectly rational; belief in God may sit among them.' Which response engages the challenge?
answer: Reformed epistemology - belief in God can be properly basic, formed in appropriate conditions without inference, like our basic beliefs about the past and about other minds.
choices: Reformed epistemology - belief in God can be properly basic, formed in appropriate conditions without inference, like our basic beliefs about the past and about other minds.
Religious experience as evidence - the warrant for belief in God comes from perception-like religious experience that confers prima facie warrant on its content under epistemic defaults.
Pragmatic Pascalian wager - the relevant warrant is decision-theoretic: under uncertainty about God's existence, the expected utility of belief outweighs that of unbelief on the stakes.
Strict evidentialism - the challenger is right; rational belief requires sufficient public argument, and any move to 'basic belief' is special pleading for one belief no other belief enjoys.
context: Alvin Plantinga's 'Reformed Objections to Natural Theology' (1980) and Warranted Christian Belief (2000) develop properly-basic theistic belief on the model of basic beliefs about the past, other minds, and the external world. The position rejects classical evidentialism (Clifford) at the level of foundational epistemology, not theology.

question: A blog post defends religion by Pascal's wager: 'Either God exists or doesn't. If you believe and He exists, you win infinitely; everything else is finite. So believe.' Theologian Aaron objects: 'A bet driven by payoff cannot deliver real faith - mere expected utility isn't belief.' Why is the wager not enough, on Aaron's view?
answer: Belief-from-utility objection - faith is a relational stance toward God, not a bet on expected utility; reasoning oneself into belief from payoff alone does not produce real belief.
choices: Belief-from-utility objection - faith is a relational stance toward God, not a bet on expected utility; reasoning oneself into belief from payoff alone does not produce real belief.
Many-gods objection - the wager assumes a binary choice, but rival religions offer rival infinite payoffs; without a way to choose between them the decision matrix does not yield a verdict.
Infinite-utility math objection - decision theory breaks down once any option has infinite expected utility, since any positive probability of belief yields the same infinity as any other.
Evidentialist objection - one shouldn't believe anything without sufficient evidence regardless of stakes; using prudential reasons to fix one's beliefs is a violation of intellectual duty.
context: Pascal's Pensees (1670) presents the wager as practical reasoning under uncertainty. Standard objections include the many-gods problem (William James), infinite-utility breakdown (Alan Hajek), and the belief-from-utility objection: utility doesn't produce belief, only intention to acquire belief, which is a different mental state.

question: Philosopher Mira presents a classic argument: 'An all-powerful, all-good being could and would prevent any evil. Evil exists. So an all-powerful, all-good being does not. The three claims are STRICTLY inconsistent.' At its sharpest, what does Mira's argument claim?
answer: Logical problem of evil - traditional divine attributes plus the existence of any evil at all are strictly logically inconsistent, so no being matching the description can exist.
choices: Logical problem of evil - traditional divine attributes plus the existence of any evil at all are strictly logically inconsistent, so no being matching the description can exist.
Evidential problem of evil - particular evils of certain types provide strong probabilistic evidence against God, even if the relevant claims are not strictly logically inconsistent here.
Hume's argument against miracles - reports of miraculous events should never be believed since the evidence for the regularity violated is always stronger than testimony for the violation.
Divine hiddenness argument - a perfectly loving God would not allow nonresistant nonbelief to occur; widespread nonresistant nonbelief therefore tells against the existence of such a being.
context: J. L. Mackie's 'Evil and Omnipotence' (Mind, 1955) is the canonical statement of the logical problem of evil. Plantinga's free-will defense (God, Freedom, and Evil, 1974) is widely taken to have shown the logical version unsuccessful: it is logically possible that God could not create free creatures who never sin. The debate then shifted.

question: Op-ed philosopher Drest writes: 'A fawn dies slowly after a forest fire, alone, with no human to learn from or be ennobled by it. Suffering of THIS kind - intense and apparently pointless - is EVIDENCE against the existence of an all-good, all-powerful God, even if not strict proof.' At its sharpest, what does Drest claim?
answer: Evidential problem of evil - particular instances of apparently pointless intense suffering are probabilistic evidence against traditional theism, even without strict logical inconsistency.
choices: Evidential problem of evil - particular instances of apparently pointless intense suffering are probabilistic evidence against traditional theism, even without strict logical inconsistency.
Logical problem of evil - traditional divine attributes plus the existence of any evil at all are strictly logically inconsistent, so no being matching the description can exist whatsoever.
Argument from divine hiddenness - a perfectly loving God would not allow nonresistant nonbelief, so widespread nonresistant nonbelief is evidence against the existence of such a being.
Argument from religious diversity - the deep disagreement of sincere people about religious matters tells against any one tradition's claims to deliver knowledge of the divine reliably.
context: William Rowe's 'The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism' (American Philosophical Quarterly, 1979) introduced the fawn case and the evidential framing. Standard theistic replies (Wykstra's sceptical theism; Stump's soul-making theodicy) target the inference from 'no good we see' to 'no good there is.'

question: Op-ed columnist Inez argues: 'Real suffering exists, and appealing to mystery is intellectually weak.' Theologian Yara responds: 'Goods like genuine moral growth, meaningful choice, and stable natural law cannot be obtained without permitting some evils we see; the evils are not denied, only contextualized.' Which response is Yara giving?
answer: Greater-goods defense - apparent evil is permitted only when it serves identifiable greater goods (moral growth, meaningful choice, lawful nature); the evil is not denied, only situated.
choices: Greater-goods defense - apparent evil is permitted only when it serves identifiable greater goods (moral growth, meaningful choice, lawful nature); the evil is not denied, only situated.
Sceptical theism - finite minds aren't placed to canvass an infinite mind's reasons, so 'we see no good' falls short of 'there is no good'; agnosticism about specifics is the honest move.
Free-will defense - the evil at issue is the cost of creating genuine moral agents, since rigged goodness in creatures whose choices never went wrong would not be moral agency at all.
Soul-making theodicy - the evil at issue is the necessary occasion for soul-development, since souls grow toward virtue only by working through trials they could not face in a soft world.
context: The greater-goods defense has classical roots in Augustine (Confessions VII) and Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I.49), and is elaborated in modern theodicy (Richard Swinburne, Providence and the Problem of Evil, 1998). It is broader than the free-will defense and overlaps with John Hick's soul-making theodicy (Evil and the God of Love, 1966).

question: A pastor cites eyewitness testimony for a miracle. Sceptic Niall answers: 'A miracle would be a violation of a regularity confirmed by countless cases. Testimony, no matter how earnest, is supported by much weaker regularity than the law it would overturn. The rational man rejects testimony.' Which response is Niall giving?
answer: Humean argument against miracles - testimony for a miracle is always supported by weaker evidence than the regularity the alleged miracle would violate, so the rational stance is rejection.
choices: Humean argument against miracles - testimony for a miracle is always supported by weaker evidence than the regularity the alleged miracle would violate, so the rational stance is rejection.
Evidential problem of evil - apparent gratuitous suffering is probabilistic evidence against an all-good, all-powerful God; the argument here is against theism through evil, not testimony.
Logical problem of evil - the attributes of God are strictly logically inconsistent with the existence of any evil at all; the argument here proceeds through inconsistency, not testimony.
Argument from religious diversity - deep disagreement of sincere people about religion tells against a tradition's claim to divine knowledge; the move isn't specifically about miracles.
context: Hume's 'Of Miracles' (Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, 1748) argues that the evidence for the law violated is always stronger than the evidence of testimony for the violation. Modern Bayesian replies (John Earman, Hume's Abject Failure, 2000) press the case that strong, independent multiple testimony can in principle suffice.

question: Podcast guest Helga argues: 'If I sincerely believe my religion, that's all the warrant I need.' Philosopher Olen pushes back: 'Sincerity is consistent with believing anything; sincere people believe contradictory things. Whatever sincerity is, it cannot be what makes a religious claim true.' Why is sincerity not enough, on Olen's view?
answer: Evidentialism - sincerity is consistent with believing contradictory things, so sincerity alone cannot make a religious claim true; reasons external to the believer's stance are required.
choices: Evidentialism - sincerity is consistent with believing contradictory things, so sincerity alone cannot make a religious claim true; reasons external to the believer's stance are required.
Religious experience reply - sincerity isn't enough because the relevant warrant comes from genuine perception-like experience of the divine, not from the subjective feeling of sincerity.
Reformed epistemology - sincerity isn't enough; the property is being formed in appropriate basic conditions, which a properly working faculty might supply where mere sincerity does not.
Pragmatic objection - sincerity isn't enough because religious practice requires action under genuine commitment, which is shown by what one does rather than by inner subjective assurance.
context: W. K. Clifford's 'The Ethics of Belief' (1877) is the classical statement of evidentialism: 'It is wrong, always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence.' William James's 'The Will to Believe' (1896) and modern Reformed epistemology offer the leading replies to Clifford's strict standard.

question: An atheist columnist writes: 'Faith is belief without reasons; reasoned inquiry is its opposite.' Theologian Marlin replies: 'On the classical view, faith and reason address overlapping matters and ultimately cannot contradict, since the same God is the source of both natural light and revelation.' Which response is Marlin giving?
answer: Faith-and-reason concord (Thomistic) - faith and reason address overlapping subject matters and cannot ultimately contradict, since both natural inquiry and revelation have the same source.
choices: Faith-and-reason concord (Thomistic) - faith and reason address overlapping subject matters and cannot ultimately contradict, since both natural inquiry and revelation have the same source.
Fideism - faith and reason are separate domains; religious truth lies wholly outside the reach of reason, and demanding reasons misunderstands what faith requires of the believer.
Evidentialism - faith is rational only as it rests on sufficient public argument; absent such argument the columnist is right that faith is belief without reasons in the relevant sense.
Reformed epistemology - faith is rational because belief in God can be properly basic without argument, much as belief in other minds is properly basic; the columnist mistakes the model.
context: Aquinas (Summa Contra Gentiles I.7) holds that since truth cannot contradict truth, what is delivered by faith and what is delivered by reason cannot ultimately conflict. Vatican I (1869-70) and Fides et Ratio (John Paul II, 1998) reaffirm the concord. Tertullian's 'credo quia absurdum' is the fideist counter-tradition within Christianity.

question: Reader Phin worries: 'If God knows now what I'll choose tomorrow, my choice is fixed - so how is it free?' Philosopher Selene answers: 'God's knowledge isn't a forecast in advance. He sees all of time at once. Knowing what I freely choose doesn't make me unfree, any more than a friend's seeing it does.' Which response is Selene giving?
answer: Boethian eternalism - God knows time-bound events from outside time as a single eternal present, so foreknowledge isn't prior forecasting and doesn't compromise creaturely freedom.
choices: Boethian eternalism - God knows time-bound events from outside time as a single eternal present, so foreknowledge isn't prior forecasting and doesn't compromise creaturely freedom.
Open theism - the future of free choices isn't yet a fact, so even God doesn't know in advance what creatures will do; freedom is preserved by limiting the scope of divine foreknowledge.
Molinist middle knowledge - God knows what each possible free creature would choose in each possible circumstance, and uses that in providence without overriding the creature's choice.
Hard theological compatibilism - foreknowledge fixes future actions, but freedom is compatible with this since freedom means acting on one's own desires, not enjoying metaphysical openness.
context: Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy (524) offers the eternalist solution: God's knowledge is timeless rather than temporally prior, so the analogy to forecasting fails. Molinism (Luis de Molina, 1588) and open theism (Pinnock et al., 1994) are the two major rivals. The issue remains live in contemporary philosophical theology.

question: Philosopher Cale presses an argument: 'A loving God would not allow open-hearted seekers to remain without belief. But such seekers exist. So no such God exists.' Theologian Riva replies: 'Forming a loving relationship may require kinds of epistemic distance that overwhelming presence would foreclose.' Which response is Riva giving?
answer: Epistemic-distance reply to hiddenness - loving relationship may require cognitive openness that overwhelming divine presence would foreclose, making hiddenness consistent with divine love.
choices: Epistemic-distance reply to hiddenness - loving relationship may require cognitive openness that overwhelming divine presence would foreclose, making hiddenness consistent with divine love.
Sceptical theism - finite minds aren't placed to canvass the reasons an infinite mind might have for hiding from some seekers; agnosticism about the specific reasons in hiddenness is honest.
Free-will defense - the hiddenness in question is the cost of creating creatures whose belief is genuinely free; overwhelming evidence would coerce belief and undercut its freedom and merit.
Reformed epistemology - the hiddenness is illusory; seekers who appear blameless actually fail to form belief because the sensus divinitatis is damaged, not because evidence is lacking.
context: J. L. Schellenberg's Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason (1993) developed the modern hiddenness argument. The epistemic-distance reply traces to John Hick (Faith and Knowledge, 1957) - genuine love between persons requires a measure of non-coercive distance. Free-will and sceptical-theism replies are also live in the literature.

question: Columnist Reza writes: 'Given how many sincere people disagree about religion, no tradition can claim privileged knowledge.' Philosopher Tova replies: 'Sincere disagreement occurs in every contested domain, including ethics and politics. It doesn't show no tradition is right; only that the question is hard.' Which response is Tova giving?
answer: Exclusivist response to diversity - sincere disagreement occurs in every contested domain without showing no view is right, so religious diversity alone doesn't undercut a tradition's claim.
choices: Exclusivist response to diversity - sincere disagreement occurs in every contested domain without showing no view is right, so religious diversity alone doesn't undercut a tradition's claim.
Religious pluralism - all major traditions are independently valid responses to the same transcendent reality; the disagreement is real but compatible with each being a path to that reality.
Religious inclusivism - one tradition is uniquely true but salvation isn't restricted to its adherents; sincere followers of other paths participate in the truth without recognizing it.
Sceptical theism - finite minds aren't well-placed to judge whether God has reasons for permitting diversity; the disagreement of sincere people doesn't tell against any tradition's claim.
context: Religious pluralism (John Hick, An Interpretation of Religion, 1989) treats traditions as equally valid responses. Exclusivists (Alvin Plantinga, 'Pluralism: A Defense of Religious Exclusivism,' 1995) press that disagreement in contested domains is normal and does not undercut a particular view's claim to be the right answer.

question: On a panel, theologian Maren defends a theodicy: 'The world is a vale of soul-making. Virtues like courage and compassion only develop where there is danger and need; a frictionless paradise could not contain the creatures we are MEANT to become.' Which response is Maren giving?
answer: Soul-making theodicy - evil is the necessary occasion for moral and spiritual growth, since virtues like courage and compassion develop only by working through trials in a difficult world.
choices: Soul-making theodicy - evil is the necessary occasion for moral and spiritual growth, since virtues like courage and compassion develop only by working through trials in a difficult world.
Free-will defense - moral evil is the cost of creating genuine moral agents, since the real possibility of doing wrong is required for the real possibility of doing right under accounts.
Greater-goods defense - apparent evil is permitted only when it serves identifiable goods, including the stability of natural law and structures of meaningful choice that the world embeds.
Sceptical theism - humans simply lack the cognitive capacity to canvass an infinite mind's reasons for permitting any specific evil; agnosticism about divine reasons is the honest move here.
context: John Hick's Evil and the God of Love (1966) develops the soul-making theodicy from an Irenaean tradition (against the Augustinian perfect-and-then-fallen frame). Virtues that distinguish mature moral character are response-dependent on difficulty. Critics press that some sufferings are too severe for soul-making to plausibly explain.

question: A philosopher of religion argues on a seminar panel: 'If it is even possible that a maximally great being exists, then by the logic of necessity such a being exists in every possible world, including ours — the premise carries the conclusion once we grant the possibility.' Which argument is the philosopher defending?
answer: Modal ontological argument — Plantinga uses possible-worlds logic to argue that maximal greatness, if possibly instantiated, must be instantiated necessarily, so the conclusion follows.
choices: Modal ontological argument — Plantinga uses possible-worlds logic to argue that maximal greatness, if possibly instantiated, must be instantiated necessarily, so the conclusion follows.

Kalam cosmological argument — the universe began to exist; whatever begins to exist has a cause; so the universe has a cause, traditionally identified with God, but the move here uses causation rather than modality.

Anselmian classical argument — God is that than which nothing greater can be conceived; existence in reality is greater than existence in the mind alone, so God exists in reality, but Anselm's form predates modal logic.

Fine-tuning argument — the physical constants are improbably calibrated for life; design is the best explanation of the calibration, but the argument turns on probability and physical evidence rather than possibility-necessity.
context: Alvin Plantinga's modal ontological argument (The Nature of Necessity, 1974) reformulated Anselm's argument in modal logic: if a maximally great being (omnipotent, omniscient, morally perfect in every possible world) is possibly instantiated, then by S5 modal logic it is necessarily instantiated. Critics dispute the possibility premise itself.

question: The medieval Islamic theologian al-Ghazali sharpened an argument his tradition called kalam, "speech." Revived by William Lane Craig in 1979, it rests on one bold claim: the universe BEGAN to exist, so it has a cause beyond itself. Several God arguments exist; which one rests on the universe having a BEGINNING?
answer: Kalam argument: the universe began, and whatever begins to exist must have a cause.
choices: Kalam argument: the universe began, and whatever begins to exist must have a cause.
Contingency argument: things that could fail to exist need a necessary being to ground them.
Fine-tuning argument: the constants are set so precisely for life that design beats chance.
Ontological argument: the very idea of a greatest possible being implies it must exist.
context: Al-Ghazali (d. 1111) was the great critic of the falasifa, and advanced the kalam in that fight; the temporal premise, that the universe has a finite past, is its distinctive feature. The contingency, design, and ontological arguments do not use a beginning. Standard rival: a beginningless universe on some cosmological models.

question: Aquinas argued each thing might never have existed, so a world of only such things would explain nothing -- something that CANNOT fail to exist must ground them. Aldo counters that the universe BEGAN, and whatever begins needs a cause. Whose reasoning is the contingency argument?
answer: Aquinas's, since it runs from things that might not have existed, not from a beginning in time.
choices: Aquinas's, since it runs from things that might not have existed, not from a beginning in time.
Aldo's, since it turns on the universe having a first moment when it began to exist.
Both, since each one reasons purely from the order and design found in nature.
Neither, since both only define a perfect being into existence from its concept.
context: Aquinas's line is the contingency argument (here in Leibniz's 'sufficient reason' form, the move his Third Way is famous for): from beings that could fail to exist, to one whose existence cannot. Aldo gives the Kalam argument (al-Ghazali, revived by William Lane Craig), which turns instead on the universe BEGINNING in time. Both differ from the design and ontological arguments.

question: An atheist philosopher argues: 'An omnipotent and wholly good God could and would prevent all evil; evil exists; so the existence of such a God is logically impossible.' A theistic philosopher replies, offering a possibility-claim about why God might permit some evils. Which reply is the theistic philosopher giving?
answer: Free-will defense — Plantinga (God, Freedom, and Evil, 1974) argues that if creating genuinely free agents is possibly a great good, then God's permitting moral evil is logically compatible with omnipotence and goodness.
choices: Free-will defense — Plantinga (God, Freedom, and Evil, 1974) argues that if creating genuinely free agents is possibly a great good, then God's permitting moral evil is logically compatible with omnipotence and goodness.

Soul-making theodicy — Hick (Evil and the God of Love, 1966) argues evil is the necessary environment for moral and spiritual growth, but the move is a positive theodicy of why evil exists, not a possibility defense.

Skeptical theism — Bergmann argues humans lack the cognitive resources to judge whether God has good reasons for any specific evil, but the move sidesteps the logical problem rather than answering its compatibility claim.

Privation theory — Augustine treats evil as the absence or corruption of good rather than a positive thing in itself, but the metaphysics of evil-as-privation does not by itself settle the logical compatibility question.
context: J.L. Mackie's 'Evil and Omnipotence' (1955) formulated the logical problem of evil. Alvin Plantinga's God, Freedom, and Evil (1974) developed the free-will defense, arguing it is possible that God could not actualize a world with morally significant freedom and no moral evil. Most philosophers treat the logical problem as defused; the evidential problem remains live.

question: A theologian on stage argues: 'Evil and suffering, distressing as they are, can be the necessary environment for the development of moral and spiritual qualities — courage, compassion, mature love — that could not be formed in a frictionless paradise.' Which theodicy is the theologian advancing?
answer: Soul-making theodicy — Hick argues God permits evil because the world is a vale of soul-making where moral and spiritual character is forged, not a hedonic paradise of frictionless ease.
choices: Soul-making theodicy — Hick argues God permits evil because the world is a vale of soul-making where moral and spiritual character is forged, not a hedonic paradise of frictionless ease.

Free-will defense — Plantinga argues that if creating free agents is possibly a great good, God's permitting moral evil is logically compatible with goodness, but the move is a possibility defense, not a positive account.

Skeptical theism — Bergmann argues humans lack the cognitive resources to judge whether God has good reasons for specific evils; the position grants the puzzle but counsels agnosticism rather than offering a positive theodicy.

Augustinian privation theory — evil is the absence of good rather than a positive thing in itself; the metaphysics describes what evil is, not the divine purpose for permitting the suffering people actually experience.
context: John Hick's Evil and the God of Love (1966) develops the soul-making (Irenaean) theodicy, drawing on the second-century theologian Irenaeus rather than Augustine. The Augustinian theodicy attributes evil to the Fall; the Irenaean treats this world as an environment designed for moral-spiritual development. Critics: Rowe, Plantinga (different routes).

question: An evidentialist atheist argues: 'Some particular evils — the slow death of an animal in the forest from untreated injury — appear gratuitous; no good we can identify justifies them; so they probably are gratuitous, and gratuitous evil counts against theism.' A theistic philosopher gives a specific reply. Which is it?
answer: Skeptical theism — Bergmann argues that the move from 'we see no good justifying this evil' to 'there is no such good' presupposes we would see it if it existed, which our cognitive limits relative to God do not warrant.
choices: Skeptical theism — Bergmann argues that the move from 'we see no good justifying this evil' to 'there is no such good' presupposes we would see it if it existed, which our cognitive limits relative to God do not warrant.

Free-will defense — Plantinga argues that if creating free agents is possibly a great good, moral evil is logically compatible with God's goodness, but forest-animal suffering is not moral evil generated by free choice.

Soul-making theodicy — Hick argues evil is the environment for moral-spiritual growth, but animal suffering with no soul present to be made does not fit the theodicy's account of why suffering serves character formation.

Privation theory — Augustine treats evil as the corruption of good rather than a positive thing in itself, but the metaphysics does not address whether particular sufferings are gratuitous on the evidence we actually have.
context: William Rowe's 'The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism' (1979) formulated the modern evidential problem of evil, using the example of a fawn dying slowly in an unobserved forest fire. Skeptical theism (Wykstra, Bergmann, Howard-Snyder, Alston) replies by challenging the noseeum inference: from 'we see no justifying good' to 'there is none.'

question: A philosopher says belief in God can be reasonable even if you never argue your way to it from evidence, the way you reasonably believe other people have minds, or that the world did not pop into being five minutes ago. You don't prove those; they are starting points. Which claim is she making about belief in God?
answer: It can be a rational starting point, not a conclusion you must infer from arguments.
choices: It can be a rational starting point, not a conclusion you must infer from arguments.
It must be built up from a cumulative case of evidence, design, and experience.
It rests entirely on religious experience counting as a kind of evidence.
It lies beyond reason itself, so asking for reasons just misses the point.
context: This is Alvin Plantinga's reformed epistemology (Warranted Christian Belief, 2000): belief in God can be 'properly basic', warranted directly, like belief in other minds, not derived from arguments. He distinguishes it from natural theology (which infers), from Alston's experience-as-evidence, and from fideism (which abandons warrant).

question: A thinker presses an objector: 'You trust your eyes that a tree is there, yet you cannot prove your eyes are reliable without already using them. Perceiving God works the same way.' If the parallel holds, what follows for the doubter?
answer: Then doubting the God-experience needs its own reason, not just the lack of outside proof.
choices: Then doubting the God-experience needs its own reason, not just the lack of outside proof.
Belief in God is a basic starting point, so no perception is even needed here.
Nothing is really known by perception, so the tree case collapses the same way.
Only shared, repeatable evidence counts, so the experience by itself proves nothing.
context: William Alston (Perceiving God, 1991): 'Christian mystical practice' is a doxastic practice on a par with ordinary sense perception, both circular if you demand outside proof, so neither can fault the other. Perception is innocent until shown guilty, which shifts the burden onto the doubter. This differs from Plantinga's basicality route, which needs no perception; Swinburne's 'principle of credulity' is kin.

question: A physicist on a panel argues: "Constants like the cosmological constant sit in a band so narrow that nudging them even slightly leaves a dead universe with no stars or life. On blind chance that is wildly unlikely; design explains it better." Several God arguments exist; which one rests on the VALUES of the constants?
answer: Fine-tuning argument: life-permitting constants are far likelier under design than under chance.
choices: Fine-tuning argument: life-permitting constants are far likelier under design than under chance.
Kalam argument: the universe began to exist, so it must have a cause beyond itself.
Design-in-nature argument: plants and animals act toward goals, implying a directing mind.
Moral argument: real duties that bind everyone point to a lawgiver standing above us.
context: Robin Collins, John Leslie, and William Lane Craig develop the fine-tuning argument as a modern design argument: it weighs the probability of the constants on design against chance or necessity. Unlike the kalam (which turns on a beginning) it turns on the calibrated VALUES of physics. The multiverse is the leading rival reply.

question: Socrates' puzzle: is a good act good BECAUSE God commands it (so God could command cruelty), or does God command it because it is ALREADY good (so goodness outranks God)? A philosopher answers: 'Neither. God commands it because it flows from God's loving character, which just IS goodness.' What does his move do to the puzzle?
answer: It dissolves both horns: God's character settles goodness, so commands are neither arbitrary nor outside-ruled.
choices: It dissolves both horns: God's character settles goodness, so commands are neither arbitrary nor outside-ruled.
It takes the first horn: whatever God happens to command becomes thereby right, even cruelty.
It takes the second horn: goodness exists on its own and God only reports it to us here.
It drops God altogether: goodness comes from human nature aiming at its own proper ends.
context: This is the Euthyphro dilemma (Plato, Euthyphro 10a). Robert Adams's modified divine command theory (Finite and Infinite Goods, 1999): wrongness is being contrary to a loving God's commands, while goodness is grounded in God's character, so the two horns are dissolved, not chosen between. Natural-law theory (Aquinas) is the human-nature rival.

question: A scholar says every religion is like blind men touching one elephant -- each grabs a different part of one Reality that lies beyond all human concepts, so none is simply right and none simply wrong. Which view of religious difference is this?
answer: Pluralism: all are partial cultural views of one reality beyond concepts, none uniquely right.
choices: Pluralism: all are partial cultural views of one reality beyond concepts, none uniquely right.
Exclusivism: one tradition is right where they conflict, the rest mistaken.
Inclusivism: one tradition holds the fullest truth, others a partial share of it.
Naturalism: there is no reality behind the experiences; it is all human psychology.
context: The blind-men-and-elephant image is the classic picture of John Hick's pluralism (An Interpretation of Religion, 1989), which borrows Kant's noumenon/phenomenon split: the religions are culturally-shaped responses to one 'Real' that none grasps as it is in itself. Plantinga and Alston defend exclusivism against it; Karl Rahner is the leading inclusivist.

question: A believer says her religion's central claims are true, so the conflicting claims of other faiths are false. 'How arrogant to think only you are right,' a classmate scoffs. 'But saying every religion is equally valid is itself a claim the rest got wrong,' she answers. Which is her defense?
answer: Calling any claim true already treats whatever contradicts it as false; that is normal, not arrogant.
choices: Calling any claim true already treats whatever contradicts it as false; that is normal, not arrogant.
She cannot be blamed at all, because no one can really know which religion is right.
Each religion is only a different window on one same reality, so in truth no one is wrong.
Her certainty is just a private feeling, so it owes no defense or explanation to anyone.
context: Alvin Plantinga, 'A Defense of Religious Exclusivism' (1995): holding substantive claims about reality just does commit you to thinking incompatible claims false, no more arrogant than any other belief. His sharpest turn, the one the believer throws back here: pluralism is itself an exclusive claim about religious truth, so it cannot escape the charge it presses.

question: Blaise Pascal helped invent the mathematics of probability - how to bet wisely when an outcome is uncertain. Late in life he turned that tool on the question of God: granting that reason cannot settle whether God exists, he asked which way it is smarter to bet. What is distinctive about his argument?
answer: It treats belief as a bet: weigh the payoff of being right or wrong, not the evidence.
choices: It treats belief as a bet: weigh the payoff of being right or wrong, not the evidence.
It claims the order and design of nature prove some maker must have arranged it.
It argues the very idea of a perfect God already implies that God must exist.
It says faith is a leap into the dark that reason can never reach or judge.
context: This is Pascal's Wager, from his Pensees (1670). Blaise Pascal co-founded probability theory with Fermat, then applied expected-value reasoning to faith: if God exists the gain is infinite and the cost of believing finite, so the bet favors belief. Famous objections: which God do you bet on, and can belief be chosen for payoff at all?

question: Kierkegaard pointed to Abraham, the knife raised over his own son Isaac on God's command -- obeying with no proof and no calculation, only a passionate leap held in total uncertainty, reaching what reason and odds cannot. What picture of faith is this?
answer: Faith as a leap beyond reason, embraced in uncertainty, not reached by argument.
choices: Faith as a leap beyond reason, embraced in uncertainty, not reached by argument.
Faith as a smart bet: believe because the possible payoff is huge.
Faith as a basic belief: a rational starting point needing no argument.
Faith as a conclusion: the reasonable end of weighing the evidence.
context: Soren Kierkegaard built Fear and Trembling (1843) around Abraham at Mount Moriah; the Concluding Unscientific Postscript (1846) names faith a passionate inwardness held in objective uncertainty, the 'leap.' He sets it apart from Pascal's wager (a calculation), Plantinga's basic belief, and natural theology's evidence, though critics press whether a leap can still be told apart from arbitrary belief.

question: Richard Swinburne argued in 1979 that no single proof settles whether God exists, but the universe existing, its order, fine-tuning, consciousness, and reports of religious experience each nudge the odds up a little, and stacked together they tip the balance toward God. What is the SHAPE of his case?
answer: A cumulative case: many weak clues that add up to more than any one alone.
choices: A cumulative case: many weak clues that add up to more than any one alone.
A single knockdown proof: one airtight argument meant to settle it by itself.
A leap of faith: a choice made past reason, where no evidence is needed.
A basic belief: trust in God that stands firm with no argument behind it.
context: Swinburne (The Existence of God, 1979) builds the cumulative case with Bayesian probability: cosmological, design, moral, and experiential arguments each raise the probability of God a little, and he argues the joint result passes one-half. It contrasts with a single deductive proof, Kierkegaard's leap, and Plantinga's properly-basic belief.

question: The mathematician W.K. Clifford asked you to picture a shipowner who sends an old, leaky vessel to sea full of emigrants. He talks himself into trusting it without inspecting it; it sinks, and all aboard drown. Clifford says he is guilty of their deaths. What broader rule did Clifford draw from this?
answer: It is always wrong to believe anything on evidence you have not honestly checked.
choices: It is always wrong to believe anything on evidence you have not honestly checked.
He is guilty only because the ship happened to sink, not for believing it.
Believing whatever helps you act is fine, since hesitation costs lives too.
Owners answer for ships, but ordinary beliefs carry no such duty of care.
context: Clifford's 'The Ethics of Belief' (1877) uses the shipowner parable to argue that believing on insufficient evidence is itself a moral fault, even when things happen to turn out fine. William James's 'The Will to Believe' (1896) is the classic reply: some choices we must make before the evidence is in.

question: An atheist argues: 'Some suffering an all-good, all-powerful God could prevent serves no greater good. So PROBABLY no such God exists — not that it's impossible, just unlikely given all this needless pain.' Which form of the argument from evil is this?
answer: Evidential — needless suffering makes God improbable, not outright impossible.
choices: Evidential — needless suffering makes God improbable, not outright impossible.
Logical — any evil at all is flatly incompatible with such a God.
Natural-evil — only suffering from nature, not human wrong, tells against God.
Evidentialist duty — believing without enough evidence is itself wrong.
context: William Rowe's 'The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism' (1979) gave this its canonical form — the fawn dying unseen in a forest fire — arguing apparently pointless suffering makes theism improbable (inductive), not impossible. That contrasts with Mackie's 1955 LOGICAL problem (any evil is incompatible with God), which Plantinga's free-will defense answered. Theists reply with skeptical theism: we may not see the goods that justify a given evil.

question: The Jesuit Karl Rahner startled fellow theologians with a phrase: a sincere Hindu who never heard the gospel might still be saved as an "anonymous Christian." He wants one faith to be uniquely true AND its grace to reach sincere outsiders. Which move lets him hold both?
answer: Truth can be fully present in one faith, yet its grace still reach those who never met it.
choices: Truth can be fully present in one faith, yet its grace still reach those who never met it.
Outsiders cannot share that grace at all, so only the visible faithful are ever saved.
No faith is uniquely true; each is one equal window onto the same divine reality.
Talk of salvation names nothing real, since religion is only a human invention.
context: This resolution is inclusivism. Karl Rahner coined 'anonymous Christian' in the 1960s (Theological Investigations) and helped shape the Second Vatican Council (Lumen Gentium, Nostra Aetate). It sits between exclusivism (deny outsiders share the grace — Plantinga) and pluralism (deny any one faith is uniquely true — Hick), keeping one tradition central while extending its reach.

question: Augustine, who once believed evil was a dark force at war with good, later changed his mind. He pointed to blindness: it is not some object added to the eye, but simply sight that is — missing where it ought to be. On his new view, what is evil?
answer: Not a thing at all — it is the absence or spoiling of a good that ought to be there.
choices: Not a thing at all — it is the absence or spoiling of a good that ought to be there.
A real force of darkness, equal to good and locked with it in unending war.
An illusion — nothing is truly bad; we only judge things good or evil by habit.
Whatever a community forbids — evil is just the rules a given culture lays down.
context: Augustine spent his early years a Manichaean, holding evil to be a positive substance; after his conversion he argued instead for privation (Confessions VII; Enchiridion, 421): evil has no being of its own, only the corruption of a created good. Aquinas carried the view into medieval thought.

question: You have never been to Antarctica, yet you know it is there — you trust reliable reports handed down to you. The philosopher C.A.J. Coady argues a Christian believes the same way: on testimony from scripture, church, and centuries of community. What is his claim about where that belief gets its warrant?
answer: From trusting reliable testimony — the everyday route by which we know most of what we know.
choices: From trusting reliable testimony — the everyday route by which we know most of what we know.
From an argument each believer must work out alone before being entitled to hold it.
From a private inner experience that no outside report could ever stand in for.
From a built-in instinct for God that needs no reasons and no reports at all.
context: C.A.J. Coady (Testimony, 1992) showed that testimony is a basic source of knowledge in general: most of what anyone knows rests on trusting others. Mavrodes and Plantinga extend this to religious belief — scripture and tradition can justify belief without each person re-deriving every argument.

question: Galileo argues the Earth moves, but nearly every scholar of 1610 agrees the Sun circles a still Earth. 'Everyone holds the old view, so the matter is closed.' He is near-friendless, yet objects. His best reply?
answer: How many hold a view is no evidence it is true; whole ages have been wrong.
choices: The old view must be right, since so few now dare defend the new one.
How many hold a view is no evidence it is true; whole ages have been wrong.
No claim is ever settled, so 'the matter is closed' is always a mistake.
Only the loudest scholar present, not the crowd, can decide who is right.
context: This is the bandwagon fallacy (appeal to popularity): a head-count is treated as proof. Agreement can track fashion or pressure rather than truth. For centuries nearly everyone agreed the Earth sat motionless at the center of the cosmos — and they were wrong.

question: Urging a yes vote, a speaker says: 'Be on the right side of history — the future will see we were right.' A councillor wants the plan but distrusts that reason. What is her best objection?
answer: What later ages think is no evidence the plan is right now; the future errs too.
choices: Whatever wins out in the end is right, so the speaker simply cannot be doubted.
What later ages think is no evidence the plan is right now; the future errs too.
No one can foresee the future, so every plan is exactly as good as any other.
Only tonight's vote, never history, can make a plan right or wrong at all.
context: This is appeal to novelty (and to posterity): 'the right side of history' treats the future's supposed verdict as proof now. But later ages also held views we reject, so their imagined agreement settles nothing today.

question: A petitioner warns a wavering signer: 'If you will not sign with us, you stand with the harm.' The signer backs the cause but doubts the petition will work. What is his best objection?
answer: Sharing the goal while doubting one tactic is not the same as siding with harm.
choices: Since so many have signed already, refusing now is clearly the wrong call.
A lone signature could never matter, so 'complicit' makes no sense here.
Sharing the goal while doubting one tactic is not the same as siding with harm.
No one is ever to blame for harm they merely allowed and did not cause.
context: This is a false dilemma: 'sign or you stand with the harm' offers two boxes, ally or enemy, erasing everyone who shares the aim but questions the method. The honest middle (back the goal, doubt the tactic) is the option it hides.

question: Vienna, 1847: Semmelweis shows hand-washing stops doctors killing mothers with fever. 'No respected physician believes it, so we drop it.' A colleague grants the idea is unpopular, yet objects. His best reply?
answer: A view having few believers is not the same as the view being shown false.
choices: A view having few believers is not the same as the view being shown false.
Since most physicians reject it, dropping the idea is clearly the safe course.
An idea is true only while unpopular, so dropping it proves it was right.
Ideas can never be judged at all, so the doctors have no ground to drop any.
context: This is the bandwagon fallacy in reverse (appeal to the majority): a view shedding believers is treated as a refutation. But popularity tracks mood, not truth — Semmelweis was mocked in his lifetime and vindicated long after.

question: An apprentice shipwright scorns the old hull: 'That shape is old-fashioned; ours is the modern one, so ours is the better ship.' A boatwright likes the new hull but distrusts that reason. Her best reply?
answer: Newer does not mean better; a design's age says nothing about whether it floats.
choices: The older hull must be stronger, since it has stayed afloat far longer.
No two designs can really be compared, so picking either is just arbitrary.
Newer does not mean better; a design's age says nothing about whether it floats.
Only what most shipwrights favor this season can decide which hull is best.
context: This is appeal to novelty: treating 'newer' as 'better.' Novelty and merit are independent — the real question is whether the design works, not when it was drawn. Its mirror image, 'older is wiser,' is the appeal to tradition.

question: An activist tells a student who wrote a harsh op-ed: 'Words are violence — your essay assaulted us as surely as a fist would.' The student agrees words can wound, but says this goes too far. Her best objection?
answer: A blow removes your choice; a sentence only tries to change your mind — force is not offense.
choices: A blow removes your choice; a sentence only tries to change your mind — force is not offense.
Only a count of who was hurt could settle this, never a person's heated wording now.
One short op-ed has no real reach at all, so the charge cannot stick to it here.
Words can never carry any harm whatever, so the whole worry here is simply hollow.
context: The slogan equivocates on 'violence,' sliding from a physical attack to speech that offends. The line it blurs is force versus persuasion: a punch removes your choice, an argument appeals to it. Even people who think cruel words can be wrong resist 'violence,' since it would let any offended listener claim self-defense.

question: A campaigner tells a man who skipped a charity drive: 'Not giving is the same as killing — every coin you kept let a child die.' He grants giving is good, but says the charge overreaches. His best reply?
answer: Letting a child die is not the same as taking a life — it collapses omission into murder.
choices: Letting a child die is not the same as taking a life — it collapses omission into murder.
Only a tally of who survived could ever settle this, not some stranger's guilt-trip.
One man's few spare coins are far too small to save anyone, so it cannot apply here.
Skipping a single drive can carry no blame whatever, so the whole charge is empty.
context: The slogan equivocates on 'killing,' sliding from causing a death to merely not preventing one — the act/omission distinction. Peter Singer presses this hard; most ethicists still hold that killing and letting-die differ in kind, even if both can be wrong, since otherwise everyone alive is a murderer.

question: A councillor warns: 'Ban one violent book and you may as well burn the library — soon every novel that offends someone will be gone.' A clerk grants the risk is real but says the leap is too fast. Her best objection?
answer: One narrow ban need not trigger the rest — the end is asserted, never shown to follow.
choices: One narrow ban need not trigger the rest — the end is asserted, never shown to follow.
Only a count of books actually pulled could settle this, not a vivid warning.
One small council has no power to empty a library, so the fear cannot apply.
Banning a book can never do any harm at all, so the whole worry is hollow.
context: This is the slippery-slope fallacy: a small first step is treated as if it must slide to a disastrous end, with no reason given for why each link pulls the next. The dread does the work the missing argument should. A slope is only valid if each step genuinely forces the following one.

question: A knight argues: 'Let the king tax us one copper and he will not stop — next half our gold, then our very lands.' A scribe agrees taxes can grow but says the chain is assumed, not earned. His best reply?
answer: A small tax need not lead to seizing everything — the ruin is feared, never shown to follow.
choices: A small tax need not lead to seizing everything — the ruin is feared, never shown to follow.
Only a ledger of what the king took could settle this, not a grim prophecy.
One knight's lone copper is far too little to matter, so the fear cannot apply.
A small tax can never cause any harm whatever, so the whole worry is hollow.
context: This is the slippery-slope fallacy: each step is presumed to drag the next toward catastrophe, with no mechanism given for why it must. A real chain argument has to show each link forces the following one; here only the dread of the ending supplies the push.

question: Challenged that her budget numbers don't add up, a leader fires back: 'How dare you nitpick when children are starving?' — then moves on without fixing the math. A page sees the dodge. His best objection?
answer: Starving children are real, but they don't make the budget add up — she swapped the question.
choices: Starving children are real, but they don't make the budget add up — she swapped the question.
Only her own staff's word could settle the figures, never an outsider's doubt.
One page's small objection has no weight at all, so the math need not be met.
Budget numbers can never truly be checked, so the whole challenge is pointless.
context: This is the red herring: a stirring but irrelevant point (starving children) is dropped in to pull attention off the live question (do the numbers work?). The emotion is genuine; it is simply not an answer. The repair is to set the distraction aside and return to the claim actually under fire.

question: A columnist defends a sweeping new mandate: 'It's just being kind to people who are suffering.' Pressed on whether the mandate actually helps or only feels good, he repeats, 'It's about kindness — who could be against that?' and moves on. Why is this a bad argument?
answer: He defends a mood nobody attacks (kindness) to avoid defending the mandate itself.
choices: He defends a mood nobody attacks (kindness) to avoid defending the mandate itself.
He treats his own good intentions as proof his actual policy must work.
He assumes one small kind act must scale up to every situation alike.
He counts the mandate's popularity as if being liked proved it worked.
context: A motte-and-bailey hides a contested claim (the 'bailey' — this mandate works) behind an unassailable one (the 'motte' — kindness is good), sliding to the safe claim when challenged. Nicholas Shackel named the move in 2005. The tell: the disputed policy is never argued for, only relabeled as kindness.

question: A dean defends hiring targets tied to applicants' ancestry. Asked how that squares with judging each person on merit, she says, 'Diversity just means everyone belongs here — surely you want that?' and returns to the targets. Why is this a weak argument?
answer: She retreats to a slogan all sides accept to avoid defending the ancestry targets.
choices: She retreats to a slogan all sides accept to avoid defending the ancestry targets.
She assumes her own good aim guarantees the targets produce fair results.
She takes one campus case as settling how every workplace ought to hire.
She paints the questioner as against belonging rather than truly answering.
context: Motte-and-bailey (Nicholas Shackel, 2005): an easy, agreeable claim (the 'motte' — everyone belongs) shields a contested one (the 'bailey' — ancestry-based targets), and the speaker swaps them under fire. 'Diversity' carries both meanings, so the disputed claim rides along untested.
