question: A guest closes the debate: 'Ninety-seven percent of experts agree, so the question is closed — stop asking.' Even granting the ninety-seven percent, why does this fail as an argument?
answer: How many experts agree isn't the same as why they're right, and inquiry doesn't close on a head-count.
choices: How many experts agree isn't the same as why they're right, and inquiry doesn't close on a head-count.
It assumes the experts are concealing every study that happens to point the other way.
It treats just two possible positions as the only ones a careful person could take.
It brands the lone doubter dishonest rather than ever meeting the doubt being raised.
context: Appeal to authority. Consensus is real evidence, but a tally of who agrees is not the reasons behind the claim — and 'stop asking' inverts how knowledge grows, since open questions are re-examined, not sealed by vote. The error is mistaking a count of agreers for the argument.

question: On air, an anchor waves off every rival network: 'Any reasonable viewer can SEE we're the only honest one — that's just what being reasonable means.' A guest presses him for proof. Why does his argument fail?
answer: His one reason, that reasonable people agree, is built so any disagreement makes you unreasonable.
choices: His one reason, that reasonable people agree, is built so any disagreement makes you unreasonable.
He leans on his own network's fame as though being popular proved it always told the truth.
He offers only two possible camps, his one honest network and every other dishonest one.
He attacks the doubters as secretly biased instead of facing the actual point they raised.
context: Begging the question (petitio principii): the conclusion is smuggled into the premise. 'Reasonable people agree with us' defines anyone who disagrees as unreasonable, so the claim can never lose — and an argument that no one could possibly counter proves nothing. The circularity is self-sealing: the premise is rigged to include the conclusion.

question: A herald nails a fresh decree to the city gate, its motto carved beneath: 'This law is just, because it is the law -- and the law is what is just.' A scribe is ordered to copy it as proof the decree is fair. Why is the motto empty as an argument?
answer: It calls the decree fair by assuming the decree is fair, so its reason just restates the claim.
choices: It calls the decree fair by assuming the decree is fair, so its reason just restates the claim.
It leans on the lawmaker's high office as if rank alone could make a decree fair.
It allows only two verdicts: a perfectly just law or an utterly worthless one.
It brands anyone who objects a mere lawbreaker instead of offering a reply.
context: Circular reasoning: the premise and the conclusion are the same claim in different words, so the argument never moves forward. Whether THIS decree is truly just is exactly what was in question, and the motto settles it only by helping itself to the answer.

question: Shown that the communes she championed left behind roughly 100 million dead -- by famine, purge, and gulag -- a thinker replies: 'Those were never REAL socialism; true socialism has not yet been tried.' She grants the record is grim. Why does this rescue fail as an argument?
answer: It rules out every actual case in advance, so no result could ever count against the idea.
choices: It rules out every actual case in advance, so no result could ever count against the idea.
It blames the failures on the leaders rather than on the system they installed.
It assumes anything that failed before is fated to fail in every future as well.
It leans on how noble the dream feels instead of on what the record shows.
context: The no-true-Scotsman move (named by Antony Flew, 1975) saves a claim by redefining its terms so no counterexample can ever count. A belief that no possible evidence could refute is not invincible -- it is empty. The death toll cited: roughly 65-100 million (Black Book of Communism).

question: A guru teaches that a hidden field guides all events. A student notes that nothing ever seems to disprove it. 'Exactly,' the guru beams, 'doubters just prove the field is testing their faith.' Why does turning every objection into support weaken the claim?
answer: If both proof and doubt are counted as evidence for it, no observation could ever show it false.
choices: If both proof and doubt are counted as evidence for it, no observation could ever show it false.
The guru attacks the doubters' sincerity rather than answering the point they raise.
The guru assumes a claim is true simply because no rival has yet disproved it.
The guru leans on his standing as a teacher instead of on any actual finding.
context: A claim is only meaningful, Karl Popper argued (1934), if some possible observation could refute it -- this is falsifiability. When a theory absorbs every result, including its own apparent failures, it explains everything and therefore predicts nothing.

question: A columnist demands triple-blind trials before believing crime rose under her favored policy, yet cites one neighbor's story as proof crime fell under it. Pressed, she says, 'I just hold claims to a high standard.' Why does this defense fail?
answer: The hard bar is aimed only at the claim she dislikes, so it tracks her side, not the truth.
choices: The hard bar is aimed only at the claim she dislikes, so it tracks her side, not the truth.
She rejects the trials over who funded them rather than on anything in their method.
She treats two rival studies as equal when their methods differ sharply in quality.
She points only to the figures that flatter her policy and buries all the rest.
context: Scott Alexander named the isolated demand for rigor (2014): one side faces a near-impossible bar while the other passes on a whisper. The tell is asymmetry -- the bar shifts with the conclusion, not with the question, so skepticism becomes a weapon rather than a discipline.

question: At a town hall, a speaker recounts the night her shop burned, then concludes: 'I lived through it, so my account of WHO set the fire cannot be questioned.' A listener grieves the loss but balks at the leap. What is the listener's sharpest objection?
answer: That the fire truly happened to her does not place her theory of who lit it beyond challenge.
choices: That the fire truly happened to her does not place her theory of who lit it beyond challenge.
Her single case is far too small a sample to support any sweeping conclusion.
Only a controlled study, never a personal account, can reveal what is really true.
Strong feeling about an event has no bearing at all on what we should believe.
context: This slides from a report of experience (which has real authority) to an interpretation of it (which does not get the same immunity) -- the testimony/inference distinction. Honoring someone's account of WHAT happened is not the same as accepting their theory of WHY, which is open to evidence like any other.

question: Defending a sweeping speech code, an organizer says: 'All we mean by violence is anything that makes a person feel unsafe.' Challenged that words then equal assault, she repeats the wide definition. Why does this redefinition mislead?
answer: Stretching 'violence' to cover discomfort lets a grave word smuggle in harm that was never shown.
choices: Stretching 'violence' to cover discomfort lets a grave word smuggle in harm that was never shown.
She retreats to a mild claim whenever she is pressed, then advances the bold one again later.
She assumes only two options exist here: a feeling of total safety or open cruelty to others.
She treats the intentions of her own side as plainly purer than the intentions of her critics.
context: This is a loaded redefinition (a persuasive definition, named by C. L. Stevenson, 1938): a word's emotional charge is kept while its meaning is quietly widened, so feelings owed to real violence transfer to things that are not. The fix is to ask whether the new sense still earns the old word's weight.

question: Thales, the first Greek philosopher, walked along gazing up at the stars. Lost in thought, he tumbled straight into a well. A servant girl burst out laughing. Why?
answer: He was so set on the sky that he missed the hole at his own feet.
choices: He was so set on the sky that he missed the hole at his own feet.
He had foretold the weather, yet failed to predict his own fall.
He claimed to know the gods, yet they let him stumble anyway.
He was the richest man in town, brought low into the mud.
context: Plato's Theaetetus (~369 BC) tells it: a Thracian maid mocked Thales for chasing knowledge of the heavens while blind to what lay right before him. The jab became the model joke about thinkers lost in abstraction.

question: In broad daylight, the philosopher Diogenes walked the crowded Athens market holding up a lit lamp, peering into every face. Asked what he sought, what did he say?
answer: An honest man — and he had yet to find a single one.
choices: An honest man — and he had yet to find a single one.
A thief who had just stolen the lamp from his hand.
The road back to his home, long after dark had come.
The richest man in Athens, to beg a coin from him.
context: Diogenes Laertius records the Cynic Diogenes (~4th c. BC) carrying a lamp by day, saying he sought a true human being (anthropon) — popularly retold as a search for one honest man. Searching at noon was living theater: as if integrity were so rare you needed a light to find it in daylight. The Cynics taught by such stunts, not lectures.

question: Diogenes owned almost nothing but a wooden cup for drinking. One day he saw a boy scoop water to his mouth with bare cupped hands. Diogenes threw his own cup away. Why?
answer: The boy showed he could live with even less than he had.
choices: The boy showed he could live with even less than he had.
The cup had cracked, so it could hold no water at all.
He wished to hand the cup to the thirsty boy as a gift.
He feared the boy would steal the cup if he kept it.
context: Diogenes the Cynic (~4th c. BC) taught that true freedom is needing as little as possible. A child outdoing him in simplicity was a lesson, not a loss — so the cup had to go.

question: The philosopher Heraclitus stood by a flowing river and said you can never step into the same river twice. The water looks the same to the eye. What did he mean it was not?
answer: The water is always new, so it is never the very same river.
choices: The water is always new, so it is never the very same river.
A river is too wide for one person to ever cross it twice.
Stepping in once makes the water dirty for the next time.
Only the gods may step into the same sacred river twice.
context: Heraclitus of Ephesus (~500 BC) taught that everything flows — the world is constant change. The water you stepped in a moment ago has already swept past; fresh water has taken its place, so it is never quite the same river.

question: On trial for his life, the philosopher Socrates was told he could go free if he simply stopped asking his probing questions in the streets of Athens. He refused. Why?
answer: An unexamined life, with no questions asked, was to him not worth living.
choices: An unexamined life, with no questions asked, was to him not worth living.
He was sure the jury would never truly dare to vote for his death.
He had sworn an oath to the gods never to fall silent while alive.
He thought exile from Athens would be a fate far worse than death.
context: Plato's Apology (~399 BC) records Socrates' defiance: offered acquittal if he gave up philosophy, he answered that 'the unexamined life is not worth living,' and chose the hemlock over a silent old age.

question: As his weeping friends looked on, the condemned philosopher Socrates calmly drank the cup of hemlock poison. He told them their grief was misplaced. Why did he not fear death?
answer: To fear death is to act sure it is bad — but no living person knows that.
choices: To fear death is to act sure it is bad — but no living person knows that.
The poison would be painless, so there was simply nothing left to dread.
A famous man's death is remembered, and such fame outlasts the body.
His accusers, not he, would carry the guilt for the killing forever.
context: In Plato's Apology and Phaedo (~399 BC), Socrates argues that to fear death is to presume you know it is an evil, when no living person knows what death holds — so dread mistakes ignorance for knowledge. He drank the hemlock calmly while his friends wept.

question: Aristotle tutored the teenage Alexander, drilling him in Homer's Iliad. Marching across Asia years later, Alexander kept the poem under his pillow and called it his guide to war. Why would a conqueror treat an old war poem that way?
answer: Its heroes model how to lead and hold honor under pressure -- a rehearsal for command.
choices: Its heroes model how to lead and hold honor under pressure -- a rehearsal for command.
It listed the exact routes and supply lines an army would need to cross into Asia.
Reciting old verse each night was thought to keep a soldier safe from harm in war.
A famous tutor's gift was a charm whose worth lay in who gave it, not in its words.
context: Plutarch reports Alexander carried Aristotle's edited 'casket copy' of the Iliad under his pillow with his dagger, calling Homer a guide to the art of war. The deeper move: great literature works as a rehearsal for conduct, letting a reader practice courage and judgment before the real test.

question: To defend his teacher Parmenides, who claimed motion is illusion, Zeno set a trap: swift Achilles can never catch a tortoise given a head start, since he must first reach where it WAS, by which time it has crept on. What kind of argument is this?
answer: A reductio: assume motion is real, derive an impossibility, conclude the assumption is false.
choices: A reductio: assume motion is real, derive an impossibility, conclude the assumption is false.
An appeal to the senses: what we plainly see in a footrace must be how the world truly is.
A generalization: because one slow tortoise wins, every race must work the same way.
An analogy: a footrace resembles a flying arrow, so both must obey one shared rule.
context: Zeno of Elea (~450 BC) defended Parmenides with paradoxes built as reductio ad absurdum -- proof by contradiction. Calculus later showed an infinite sum of shrinking gaps can total a finite distance, but the puzzle about completing infinitely many steps is still debated.

question: In Plato's tale, a prisoner chained to face a cave wall is freed, climbs to the surface, and sees the sun. He goes back down to tell the others the shadows they watch are not real. Plato warns the returning man is in danger. Why?
answer: The shadows are the only world they trust, so the man unsettling it seems a threat, not help.
choices: The shadows are the only world they trust, so the man unsettling it seems a threat, not help.
His eyes, still adjusting to the dark, leave him too blind to defend himself below.
The keepers of the cave fear him most and move first to silence the freed prisoner.
The others would simply ignore him, too absorbed in the passing shadows to listen.
context: Plato's cave (Republic VII, ~375 BC) ends in a warning: at 517a the prisoners would kill anyone trying to drag them up, since they take the shadows for the whole of reality. Plato, whose teacher Socrates was executed by Athens, knew that those who report a larger reality are often resented, not thanked.

question: Condemned to death and writing in his cell, Boethius pictures Lady Philosophy scolding him for grieving his lost honors and wealth. She points to Fortune's turning wheel. What is her core consolation to a man about to die?
answer: Goods that Fortune can spin away were never truly his, so losing them takes nothing real.
choices: Goods that Fortune can spin away were never truly his, so losing them takes nothing real.
The gods will reward his suffering with a far better life beyond this one.
His accusers will face justice in time, so his bitter anger is well earned.
Death itself is swift and painless, so a brave man has no cause to dread it.
context: Boethius wrote The Consolation of Philosophy around AD 523 in prison, awaiting execution under the Ostrogothic king Theodoric. Lady Philosophy's lesson on Fortune's wheel: peace anchored to gifts Fortune merely loans you will spin away with them, so the wise tie their happiness to what cannot be taken.

question: On campaign at the Danube frontier, the emperor Marcus Aurelius fills a private notebook he titles only 'To Himself' and never means anyone to read. Knowing his reader was himself alone, what was he chiefly doing in it?
answer: Drilling himself each night in the Stoic habits he wanted to act on by day.
choices: Drilling himself each night in the Stoic habits he wanted to act on by day.
Recording orders and battle plans for his frontier generals to follow.
Drafting a public defense of his reign to be read out across the empire.
Composing letters of advice to the young son he hoped would succeed him.
context: The Meditations (Greek 'Ta eis heauton', 'To Himself') were written ~170-180 AD during the Marcomannic Wars and never meant for publication. Marcus wasn't teaching an audience; he was rehearsing Stoic discipline on himself, which is why the book reads as reminders, not lectures.

question: Ordered by Nero to take his own life, the Stoic Seneca opened his veins but bled slowly. His will long settled, he stayed calm and called for scribes. What did he have them do as he was dying?
answer: Take down his final words, making his composed death itself a last lesson.
choices: Take down his final words, making his composed death itself a last lesson.
Record a written confession admitting the plot Nero had charged him with.
Carry an urgent plea for mercy back to Nero before it was too late.
Draft new bequests dividing his vast fortune among his grieving friends.
context: Tacitus records Seneca's death in AD 65: forced to suicide for an alleged conspiracy against Nero, he dictated to scribes as he bled. For a Stoic who had written for years that death holds no terror, dying calmly on command was the final demonstration of the philosophy.

question: Cicero spent his last months hurling speeches called the Philippics at Mark Antony to rally the dying Republic. Antony's men hunted him down and killed him. Which grim detail marked how Antony answered those speeches?
answer: His head and the very hands that wrote the speeches were nailed up in the Forum.
choices: His head and the very hands that wrote the speeches were nailed up in the Forum.
His every book and speech was gathered up and burned in the public square.
His name was struck from all the Republic's records, as if he had never lived.
His grand estate was seized and his heirs were driven into exile from Rome.
context: Cicero was proscribed and killed in December 43 BC after the Second Triumvirate formed. On Antony's order his head and his hands, the hands that had penned the Philippics, were displayed on the Rostra in the Forum, the very platform from which he had spoken against Antony.

question: Russell and Whitehead spent ten years and three volumes trying to derive ALL of mathematics from pure logic. In 1931 a 25-year-old, Kurt Godel, proved their dream was impossible. What did his proof show?
answer: Any system big enough for arithmetic holds true statements it can never prove.
choices: Any system big enough for arithmetic holds true statements it can never prove.
Their three volumes hid a single contradiction that wrecked every proof.
Arithmetic itself is contradictory, so its theorems are all worthless.
Pure logic is too weak to express even the simplest sum correctly.
context: Kurt Godel's 1931 incompleteness theorems sank the Russell-Whitehead 'Principia Mathematica' program: no consistent formal system rich enough for arithmetic can prove every truth it can express. The truths exist; the system just cannot reach them all. He was 25.

question: Ludwig Wittgenstein wrote one short book and declared he had solved all of philosophy: words mean by PICTURING facts in the world. Years later he came back and tore down his own masterpiece. What did the older Wittgenstein decide meaning really was?
answer: How a word is actually used among people, not a picture it paints of facts.
choices: How a word is actually used among people, not a picture it paints of facts.
A private feeling in the speaker's mind that no outsider can ever share.
A fixed label pinned to one object, settled once and never shifting again.
Whatever a strict committee of logicians rules that the word shall denote.
context: Wittgenstein's early 'Tractatus' (1921) held that language pictures reality. His later 'Philosophical Investigations' (published 1953) reversed it: meaning is use, learned in shared 'language-games.' Few thinkers ever publicly demolished their own great work.

question: In 1656 Amsterdam's Jewish community hit the 23-year-old Baruch Spinoza with its harshest curse, the herem: a total excommunication, never once lifted, that forbade anyone to speak to him or even stand near him. They first offered to cancel it, plus a yearly pension, if he would keep quiet. Why did he take the curse instead?
answer: Following where reason led mattered more to him than keeping his whole community.
choices: Following where reason led mattered more to him than keeping his whole community.
He had already secretly joined a rival church that promised him higher rank.
He expected the curse to be lifted quietly once the elders had cooled down.
He wanted revenge, and his exile would shame the elders who had judged him.
context: The 1656 herem was the severest excommunication the Amsterdam community ever issued, and it was never rescinded. Offered reinstatement and a pension to recant his views on God and Scripture, Spinoza calmly declined and lived on grinding lenses, free to think.

question: In a Soviet labor camp, where paper was forbidden and a single hidden page meant death, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn still composed thousands of lines of poetry about his years behind the wire. How did he keep the whole poem without writing a single word?
answer: He memorized it, counting the lines on a bread-pellet rosary of beads.
choices: He memorized it, counting the lines on a bread-pellet rosary of beads.
He carved the verses in code on the underside of his wooden bunk.
He dictated it nightly to a guard who was secretly on his side.
He buried inked pages in the prison yard and dug them up later.
context: Solzhenitsyn memorized roughly 12,000 lines of verse in the camps (1947-1952), telling them off on a knotted bread-pellet rosary so no paper could betray him. He dared write them down only after his release. His later prose epic, 'The Gulag Archipelago,' reached the West in 1973.

question: A guildmaster catches one apprentice stealing and bars the whole guild from the market: 'One rotten apple proves the barrel is spoiled.' Why is that a weak claim?
answer: One thief can't show what the others are like — one case can't judge them all.
choices: One thief can't show what the others are like — one case can't judge them all.
It condemns the guild for its rank, not for what any member truly did.
It points to the sheer size of the guild as the reason to distrust it.
It treats catching one thief as proof that no honest trade can exist.
context: This is hasty generalization: leaping from a single instance to a sweeping claim about a whole group. One sample says almost nothing about thousands; the repair is to ask how many cases the conclusion actually rests on. The proverb's 'one bad apple' hides the leap.

question: Robbed on his first night in Constantinople, a traveler warns every caravan he meets: 'That whole city is full of thieves — I saw it with my own eyes.' Why is his warning a weak claim?
answer: One bad night out of thousands of people is far too little to judge them all.
choices: One bad night out of thousands of people is far too little to judge them all.
His own fear, not the city, is really what is doing the talking here.
A city can never be honest or dishonest, since only people can be.
He felt wronged, so he wants the whole city to share in his blame.
context: Hasty generalization in its 'one bad experience' form: a single encounter is treated as a representative sample of a whole population. 'I saw it with my own eyes' feels strong, but one event can't fix the rate for thousands. The fix is to weigh how typical the case really is.

question: Pushing a new law, a councilor cries: 'Think of the children — picture how they suffer!' Even if children matter deeply, why is this a weak argument?
answer: Caring about children does not show the law itself would actually help them.
choices: Caring about children does not show the law itself would actually help them.
It leans on how worthy the cause sounds rather than on the law's actual terms.
It rests on how loud the plea is rather than on who proposed the law.
It treats one councilor's word as enough to settle the matter alone.
context: This is appeal to emotion (argumentum ad passiones): a strong feeling is offered in place of a reason the policy would work. The pity is real and the cause may be worthy, but moving the crowd is not the same as showing the law does any good. Ask for the evidence the feeling skips.

question: A merchant on trial weeps about his sick mother and ruined shop until the jury, moved to tears, clears him of the theft. Even so, why was that a weak basis for the verdict?
answer: Pity for his hardship is not evidence about whether he took the goods.
choices: Pity for his hardship is not evidence about whether he took the goods.
It clears him on his low standing rather than on what the proof showed.
It assumes a man in tears must have purer motives than his accuser.
It assumes a man who weeps in court must be telling the truth.
context: Appeal to pity (argumentum ad misericordiam) is appeal to emotion aimed at sympathy: the merchant's suffering, however real, bears on his hardship, not on the facts of the theft. A verdict tracks what the evidence shows; a moving story is not evidence either way.

question: A hunter is told his sport is cruel. He shoots back: 'You eat meat yourself, so you have no right to object to my hunting.' Why does that reply miss the point?
answer: The critic's own habits do not show the hunting is right or wrong.
choices: The critic's own habits do not show the hunting is right or wrong.
It assumes a meat-eater could never sincerely care about cruelty.
It assumes hunting and eating meat must be exactly the same act.
It treats one shared fault as proof the whole worry is empty.
context: This is tu quoque ('you too'), a form of ad hominem: pointing at the critic's own inconsistency. Even a hypocrite can be right — whether the hunting is cruel is settled by reasons about the hunting, not by the accuser's diet. The charge of hypocrisy changes the subject.

question: Shown that his favored regime starved millions, a debater shoots back: 'But what about all the people THEIR side killed?' and moves on. His rival grants the other crimes are real, but says this dodges the point. Why?
answer: Pointing at someone else's wrongs does not make your own regime's deaths any less real.
choices: Pointing at someone else's wrongs does not make your own regime's deaths any less real.
Only a full body count from both sides, not sharp words, could ever settle the matter.
The other side's larger crimes prove his regime was the gentler of the two evils.
No regime can ever be blamed for a famine, since hunger has natural causes too.
context: This is whataboutism, a form of red herring (tu quoque): meeting a charge by pointing at an opponent's sins changes the subject instead of answering it. Even if the other side's crimes are real and worse, that has no bearing on whether YOUR regime's deaths happened.

question: A squire spurns a battlefield remedy that stops a festering wound from killing: 'A cruel, treacherous lord brewed it first, so the whole cure is poisoned at the root.' His teacher agrees the lord was wicked, but says the dismissal fails. Why?
answer: Where an idea first came from says nothing about whether it is true or works.
choices: Where an idea first came from says nothing about whether it is true or works.
A wicked man's remedy should always be trusted, since cruelty and skill go together.
Only the lord who brewed it could judge the cure, so no outsider may question it.
A cure works precisely when a popular, well-liked person is the one to offer it.
context: This is the genetic fallacy: judging a claim by its origin rather than its merits. A good remedy from a villain still heals; a useless one from a saint still fails. The cure either closes the wound or it does not, regardless of who first brewed it.

question: A market herbalist presses a root on a knight: 'It's wholly natural, straight from the earth, so it must be safe and good for your health.' The knight is tempted, but recalls his training. What is his sharpest reply?
answer: Being natural does not make a thing safe or healthy — hemlock and nightshade are natural too.
choices: Being natural does not make a thing safe or healthy — hemlock and nightshade are natural too.
Nothing on this earth is truly natural, so the seller's whole promise is meaningless.
A root is safe only once a royal physician has stamped his approval upon the jar.
Whatever grows from the soil is always gentler than any tonic mixed by human hands.
context: This is the appeal to nature: treating 'natural' as a stand-in for 'safe' or 'good.' But hemlock, nightshade, and arsenic are perfectly natural and deadly, while many lab-made medicines save lives. Whether the root helps depends on what it DOES, not on where it grew.

question: Cornered for a hole in his argument, a court advocate suddenly cries: 'And think of the poor orphans who will suffer if you doubt me!' The judge feels for the orphans, yet says the outburst proves nothing. Why?
answer: Pity for the orphans is real but beside the point — it does not patch the hole in his argument.
choices: Pity for the orphans is real but beside the point — it does not patch the hole in his argument.
Orphans plainly do not exist, so the advocate has simply invented them out of thin air.
Strong feelings always signal a strong case, so his passion shows that he must be right.
A judge must always rule for whichever speaker manages to sound the most deeply moved.
context: This is a red herring: dragging in a vivid but irrelevant point to pull attention off the real question. The orphans may be genuinely worth pity, yet their plight has nothing to do with whether the advocate's argument actually holds together.

question: A village elder waves off the tonic that broke a fever no garden herb could touch: 'It was brewed in an alchemist's flask, not grown in honest soil, so it can only be poison.' The healer grants it is man-made, but says the elder errs. Why?
answer: Being made by human hands does not make a cure harmful — what matters is what it does in you.
choices: Being made by human hands does not make a cure harmful — what matters is what it does in you.
Anything an alchemist brews is sure to outperform whatever a humble garden can ever grow.
Only the alchemist who mixed the tonic is fit to say whether it truly heals or harms.
A cure works just when the village happens to trust the person who is handing it over.
context: This is the appeal to nature run in reverse — the 'appeal to the unnatural': treating 'man-made' as a synonym for 'harmful.' Synthetic does not mean toxic any more than natural means safe; the tonic either lowered the fever or it did not, whatever flask it came from.

question: A debate coach asks his rival across the table: 'Have you stopped rigging your team's scrimmages yet?' Either answer admits past cheating. The rival objects. What is his sharpest reply?
answer: The question smuggles in an unproven charge, so any yes-or-no answer concedes what was never shown.
choices: The question smuggles in an unproven charge, so any yes-or-no answer concedes what was never shown.
A real judge would never let two opponents question each other during a formal debate round.
Coaches are too invested in winning to be trusted as honest witnesses about their own teams.
Whether scrimmages were rigged cannot matter, since only the official match results are counted.
context: This is the loaded (or complex) question, named by logicians at least since the medieval 'fallacia plurium interrogationum.' It hides an unproven premise so that any direct answer grants it. The honest reply rejects the question itself: 'I never rigged anything, so there is nothing to have stopped.'

question: Shown a study linking smoking to lung disease, a knight scoffs: 'My grandfather smoked a pipe daily and lived to ninety, so the danger is clearly overblown.' Why does his reply fail?
answer: One survivor cannot overturn a pattern across many cases; he treats a lucky exception as if it set the rule.
choices: One survivor cannot overturn a pattern across many cases; he treats a lucky exception as if it set the rule.
He attacks the researchers' funding rather than addressing the actual findings of their study.
He insists the claim is false only because a smoke-free world would feel unbearably dull.
He assumes that what was once true of pipes must stay true of every tobacco product forever.
context: This is anecdotal evidence used against statistics: a single vivid case is offered to refute a trend measured across thousands. A risk is a probability over a population, so one survivor is fully compatible with real danger. The grandfather is the rare winner the odds always leave standing, not proof the odds are wrong.

question: A scholar lays out the Ukrainian Holodomor of 1932-33 — millions starved under a regime the council reveres. A councilman waves the figures away: 'If that were true, our cause would be monstrous, so it cannot be true.' Why does his reply fail?
answer: How dreadful a fact would be has no bearing on whether it happened; comfort is not a test of truth.
choices: How dreadful a fact would be has no bearing on whether it happened; comfort is not a test of truth.
He points to an unrelated error the scholar once made instead of facing the figures.
He treats one disputed source as if it settled a question that needs far wider proof.
He demands the scholar disprove the famine rather than offering any evidence himself.
context: This is the appeal to consequences: judging a claim true or false by how welcome its implications are, rather than by the evidence. Reality is indifferent to whether a fact is bearable. The Holodomor — the man-made famine that killed millions in Soviet Ukraine in 1932-33 — is documented precisely because the deaths were counted, however unwelcome the count.

question: A merchant swears his lucky charm cures illness: 'Three buyers wore it and recovered!' He never mentions the dozens who wore it and stayed sick. A physician objects. What is her strongest point?
answer: Counting only the recoveries and ignoring the failures rigs the verdict before the test even begins.
choices: Counting only the recoveries and ignoring the failures rigs the verdict before the test even begins.
A charm cannot work by any mechanism we know, so the recoveries must be outright lies.
The merchant profits from each sale, so nothing he claims about the charm can be trusted.
Calling it a cure would be cruel to the sick, so the claim should be ruled false at once.
context: This is cherry-picking: reporting only the cases that fit the claim while hiding the ones that do not. A fair test counts hits and misses alike, since without the failures the recoveries say nothing. This is why medicine compares a treated group against a control group rather than collecting testimonials.

question: An inquisitor demands of a scribe: 'Why did you hide the forbidden book you stole?' The scribe stole nothing and hid nothing. He refuses to answer as asked. Why is his refusal the right move?
answer: The question bundles two unproven claims as settled, so any direct answer hands the inquisitor both at once.
choices: The question bundles two unproven claims as settled, so any direct answer hands the inquisitor both at once.
An inquisitor holds too much power over the scribe to ever count as a fair questioner here.
A single accusation can never outweigh the scribe's years of loyal service to the library.
Theft of a book matters little, since the text itself was never truly his to begin with.
context: This is the loaded question in its compound form, stacking two unproven premises (that he stole it and that he hid it) into one demand. Answering 'why' concedes both. The repair is to separate and challenge each premise before any explanation is owed.

question: In a debate, one side rattles off thirty quick claims against the bridge plan in two minutes. The engineer answers the one real flaw, but the crowd booms: 'She only rebutted ONE point — the other twenty-nine stand!' Why is that unfair?
answer: Throwing out many weak claims faster than anyone can check them is not the same as a strong case.
choices: Throwing out many weak claims faster than anyone can check them is not the same as a strong case.
The plan must be sound, since the crowd clearly sided with the engineer's single short reply.
Whatever has failed for older bridges is surely bound to doom this new bridge plan as well.
Her answer should be trusted here only because she is the trained expert in the room today.
context: This is the Gish gallop (named for creationist Duane Gish, who used it against evolutionary biologists): drowning a debate in a flood of small claims so no one can refute them all in the time given, then treating each unanswered scrap as if it scored. Volume of assertions is not weight of evidence.

question: A scholar accepts dozens of ancient battles on a single old chronicle, yet rejects one famous siege: 'We have three sources, but until we have flawless proof, I cannot grant it.' He keeps every other battle. Why is his stance unfair?
answer: He sets an impossible bar for the one claim he dislikes while waving the rest through on far less.
choices: He sets an impossible bar for the one claim he dislikes while waving the rest through on far less.
Ancient history can never be known at all, so no battle on his list belongs there.
A few written sources always settle a question, so doubting the siege makes no sense.
He must be right about the siege, since he is the careful expert on these records.
context: This is the isolated demand for rigor (named by Scott Alexander, 2014): applying a crushing standard of proof to one disfavored claim while letting everything you already believe pass on ordinary evidence. The unfairness is the double standard, not the high standard itself.

question: Pressed to back up his claim, a man waves the question away: 'I'm not spoon-feeding you — do your own research.' He never names a source. Why does this dodge the burden of proof?
answer: The one making the claim owes the reasons for it; 'go look' shifts that job onto the doubter.
choices: The one making the claim owes the reasons for it; 'go look' shifts that job onto the doubter.
His claim must be false, since a man who won't explain himself is hiding something.
Only a published study could ever settle this, so talking about it is pointless.
He is surely right, because plenty of people online already believe the same thing.
context: 'Do your own research' can be a genuine invitation — but here it works as a thought-stopper that shifts the burden of proof onto the listener. Whoever asserts a claim carries the duty to support it (onus probandi); 'go find it yourself' is a refusal dressed as advice.

question: A girl raises a flaw in the school's grading. A boy shuts her down: 'Kids are starving in the world and you're upset about GRADES?' She agrees famine is worse. Why is his reply still a bad argument?
answer: That a worse problem exists somewhere doesn't make a real but smaller one not worth fixing.
choices: That a worse problem exists somewhere doesn't make a real but smaller one not worth fixing.
Her grading complaint must be right, since he could not actually answer it.
Only the single worst problem on Earth is ever worth anyone's time to discuss.
He is the one who decides which complaints count, so hers can be set aside.
context: This is the fallacy of relative privation (a form of 'appeal to worse problems'): dismissing a concern merely because something more serious exists elsewhere. By that logic no problem but the very worst could ever be addressed — which would freeze almost all useful action.

question: A young knight thanks the cook for a fine meal. An older squire sneers: 'Peasants beyond the wall have nothing — how dare you ENJOY supper?' The knight grants their hunger is a graver wrong. Why is the squire's rebuke still hollow?
answer: Joy here is no debt owed to suffering far off; gratitude for a real good is not theft from the hungry.
choices: Joy here is no debt owed to suffering far off; gratitude for a real good is not theft from the hungry.
The meal must be undeserved, since the knight had no ready answer to give the squire.
No one may ever enjoy a single supper until every last hunger in the world has ended.
The squire alone gets to decide which joys are allowed, so the knight's thanks do not count.
context: Another face of relative privation, aimed at enjoyment rather than complaint: treating any gratitude or pleasure as forbidden while greater suffering exists somewhere. But refusing every small good until the largest evil is gone helps no one — it only adds one more joyless person to the world, with no extra bread reaching the hungry.

question: Archimedes sank into a full bath and watched the water spill over the rim. He leapt up shouting 'Eureka!' — 'I found it!' What had he just realized?
answer: A sinking body pushes aside its own bulk of water — its exact volume.
choices: A sinking body pushes aside its own bulk of water — its exact volume.
Cold water makes gold gleam brighter than any jeweler's cloth.
Hot water heals a tired body better than a court doctor can.
A morning bath keeps a busy thinker's mind sharp and clear.
context: Vitruvius (1st c. BC) tells it: a goldsmith may have swapped silver into King Hieron's gold crown. In the bath Archimedes (Syracuse, ~250 BC) saw that a submerged body displaces its own volume of water, letting him measure the crown's volume, and so its density, without melting it.

question: A king feared his gold crown was secretly cut with cheap silver. He told Archimedes to test it unbroken. Archimedes solved it in his bath. What did the bath reveal?
answer: Silver is bulkier than gold, so the crown shoved aside more water.
choices: Silver is bulkier than gold, so the crown shoved aside more water.
Gold and silver weigh the same, so a plain scale would expose it.
A deep scratch would show the cheaper silver hidden under the gold.
An honest goldsmith would swear an oath before the royal court.
context: King Hieron II of Syracuse set the puzzle (~250 BC). Archimedes leapt from the tub crying 'Eureka!' ('I have found it!'): silver is bulkier than gold for the same weight, so a silver-laced crown displaces MORE water than equal-weight pure gold. He had turned a cheating problem into a measurement, the birth of what we now call density testing.

question: Fleeing killers, old Pythagoras ran until a field of beans blocked his path. His own rule forbade trampling them. What did he do?
answer: He refused to cross, and his pursuers caught and killed him there.
choices: He refused to cross, and his pursuers caught and killed him there.
He crawled through on his belly to keep from snapping any stems.
He hid in the tall bean plants until the killers gave up and left.
He flung beans at the men to slow their charge across the field.
context: An ancient legend (Diogenes Laertius, 3rd c. AD; also Iamblichus) says Pythagoras (~495 BC) refused to escape across a bean field because of his brotherhood's taboo, and his pursuers caught and killed him there. True or not, the story survived because it shows a thinker who would not break his vow even to save his own life.

question: Thales studied the night sky so closely while walking that he tumbled into a well. A servant girl laughed: he longed to know the heavens but missed the ground. Her point?
answer: Watch the world right at your feet, not only the far-off and grand.
choices: Watch the world right at your feet, not only the far-off and grand.
Never go walking outside alone once the sky has grown fully dark.
The stars hold no secrets worth a wise person's time at all.
A clumsy person can never learn the deep truths of the sky.
context: Plato tells this story (Theaetetus, ~369 BC) about Thales of Miletus (~600 BC), often called the first Greek philosopher. A Thracian servant girl mocked him for chasing the stars while blind to what lay at his feet, an old warning that wonder about the grand should not blind us to the plain things nearby.

question: Asked for one word to live by his whole life, Confucius gave the idea of reciprocity: 'Do not impose on others what you would not choose for yourself.' How does this differ from the later Golden Rule?
answer: It is stated as a restraint — what NOT to do — rather than a command to act.
choices: It is stated as a restraint — what NOT to do — rather than a command to act.
It tells you to treat strangers far better than you treat your own family.
It applies only to rulers and their ministers, never to ordinary people.
It promises a reward in the next life for everyone who keeps it well.
context: Confucius (~500 BC), Analects 15.23, names the principle 'shu' (reciprocity). His negative form bars the harm you would resent; the later positive 'do unto others' commands action. The two overlap but are not identical.

question: Old Lao Tzu rode an ox west to flee a corrupt world for good. The gatekeeper let him pass only on one demand: write your wisdom down. That writing became the Tao Te Ching. Why did that demand matter so much?
answer: Without it, his wisdom would have vanished west with him, unwritten and lost.
choices: Without it, his wisdom would have vanished west with him, unwritten and lost.
Because a gatekeeper outranked a sage and could lawfully command him.
Because the ox he rode was worth far more to him than any book.
Because the lands west of the gate were the true source of his ideas.
context: The story (Sima Qian, ~100 BC) explains how Daoism's founding text survived: the border official Yin Xi refused Lao Tzu passage until he set down the roughly 5,000 characters of the Tao Te Ching. Then he rode west and was never seen again. Spoken wisdom that nobody writes down dies with the speaker.

question: Two ancient Greeks made a famous pair: one always wept at human folly, the other always laughed at it. The laughing one also founded a huge scientific idea. Which man, and what idea?
answer: Democritus, who taught that everything is built from tiny pieces called atoms.
choices: Democritus, who taught that everything is built from tiny pieces called atoms.
Heraclitus, who taught that you can never step into the same river twice.
Democritus, who first mapped the planets circling the central sun.
Heraclitus, who proved the earth is just one wandering body in the sky.
context: Democritus 'the laughing philosopher' (~400 BC) founded atomism (with his teacher Leucippus); the gloomy Heraclitus was the weeping one. Later writers (Seneca, Montaigne) made the two a stock pair — never rivals who met, but two temperaments facing the same folly, one with tears and one with a smile.

question: Democritus argued that everything — stone, water, even the soul — is built from tiny indestructible bits in empty space, far too small to see. He never observed them. Why did he believe they must exist?
answer: Reason demanded it: keep cutting matter and you reach a bit that cannot split.
choices: Reason demanded it: keep cutting matter and you reach a bit that cannot split.
An oracle at Delphi had revealed their existence to him in a vision.
He had built a lens fine enough to glimpse the smallest specks of dust.
Priests had taught it as a sacred secret he was sworn never to share.
context: Democritus (~400 BC) and his teacher Leucippus reasoned to 'atomos' ('uncuttable') by pure argument, two millennia before instruments could test it: cut matter far enough and you must hit an indivisible part, or it could be divided away into nothing at all.

question: A disciple told Confucius that some sages taught repaying injury with kindness. Confucius shot back: 'Then with what will you repay kindness?' What did he say to do instead?
answer: Repay injury with justice, and kindness with kindness.
choices: Repay injury with justice, and kindness with kindness.
Repay every injury with a far greater injury in return.
Repay injury with silence and simply forget the wrong.
Repay both injury and kindness with the very same kindness.
context: Analects 14.34 (~500 BC). His retort exposes the lever: if kindness already answers injury, nothing distinctive is left to answer kindness with. Meeting wrong with fairness and good with good keeps justice from being spent cheaply on the undeserving.

question: Epictetus, born a slave in Rome, once warned his master the leg would break as it was twisted — then, when it snapped, said only 'There, I told you so.' He became a famed Stoic. What rule did he put first?
answer: Sort what you can control from what you cannot, and care only about the first.
choices: Sort what you can control from what you cannot, and care only about the first.
Endure every cruelty in silence, since complaint only doubles the pain.
Obey your master in all things, for a good slave will earn his freedom.
Fate is fixed, so striving to change anything at all is wasted effort.
context: Epictetus (c. 50-135 AD), enslaved to Epaphroditus before being freed, taught at Nicopolis. His Enchiridion opens with exactly this dichotomy of control: 'Some things are up to us and some are not.' Peace comes from wanting only what is up to us. His pupil Arrian wrote it down.

question: In Alexandria around 400 AD, Hypatia — a pagan woman — ran the city's most renowned school, lecturing on geometry and the heavens to packed halls of Christians and pagans alike. What about her position was extraordinary for her age?
answer: A woman led the city's foremost school of philosophy and mathematics, honored across faiths.
choices: A woman led the city's foremost school of philosophy and mathematics, honored across faiths.
She proved the earth circles the sun, centuries before any other thinker dared.
She alone was allowed to teach, for the city had banned every rival school.
She turned away each student who could not first solve her hardest proof.
context: Hypatia (c. 355-415 AD), daughter of the mathematician Theon, taught Neoplatonist philosophy, astronomy, and geometry. A pagan woman heading a renowned school and respected across religious lines, she was murdered by a mob in 415 amid the city's political strife.

question: The mathematician Blaise Pascal, who helped invent probability theory, treated belief in God as a bet. You cannot know if God exists, he said, but you must wager either way. On what grounds did he say to bet on God?
answer: A small finite cost risked against an infinite prize makes the bet worth taking.
choices: A small finite cost risked against an infinite prize makes the bet worth taking.
Reason alone can prove God exists, so betting against is plainly irrational.
Most people across history have believed, so the safe bet follows the crowd.
The beauty and order of nature leave no honest room to doubt a creator.
context: Pascal's Wager (Pensees, published 1670) frames faith as a decision under uncertainty, not a proof. If God exists the gain is infinite and the loss if wrong is small, so any nonzero chance makes belief the rational wager. It was an early use of expected-value reasoning.

question: Critics mocked the logician Jean Buridan with a donkey: set exactly halfway between two identical, equal piles of hay, the beast has no reason to prefer one over the other, and so it starves. What puzzle about choice does the tale pose?
answer: Pure reason facing two equal options gives no ground to pick, yet real choosers still pick.
choices: Pure reason facing two equal options gives no ground to pick, yet real choosers still pick.
Animals lack the reason to choose at all, so only humans truly face the problem.
Hunger always decides for us in the end, so deliberation changes nothing.
Two goods of equal worth must really differ, since nothing is ever truly equal.
context: Buridan's ass satirizes Jean Buridan (c. 1300-1361), who held the will must suspend choice between perfectly equal goods. He never used the donkey; critics added it to mock him. The real puzzle: a purely rational agent needs a tie-breaker, yet we break ties constantly.

question: Epictetus, the slave who won his freedom and opened a Stoic school, taught that being insulted, thrown in jail, or robbed of someone you love is never itself what wounds you. Then what, in his teaching, does the real harm?
answer: Your own judgment that the event is bad, which you could choose to withhold.
choices: Your own judgment that the event is bad, which you could choose to withhold.
The cruelty of the person who wronged you, which you are right to resent.
The loss itself, which no amount of clear thinking can ever soften.
The gods, who send hardship to test whether your faith will hold.
context: Epictetus (c. 50-135 AD) taught that 'it is not things that disturb us, but our judgments about things' (Enchiridion 5). Since the judgment is up to us, so is much of our suffering. This reframing became a root of modern cognitive therapy.

question: In 1600 Rome, after eight years in the Inquisition's cells, Giordano Bruno was burned at the stake. Among the heresies charged against him was a startling picture of the cosmos that shattered the closed medieval sky. What did he claim?
answer: The universe is infinite, the stars are distant suns, and countless other worlds may circle them.
choices: The universe is infinite, the stars are distant suns, and countless other worlds may circle them.
The Earth, not the Sun, sits unmoving at the exact center of a finite cosmos.
The heavens are perfect and changeless, while only the Earth below knows decay.
The stars are tiny lamps fixed to a crystal shell a short way past the Moon.
context: Bruno (burned Feb 17, 1600, Campo de' Fiori) was condemned for several theological heresies - he denied the Trinity and Christ's divinity, among others - and in 1600 the Church had no official ruling making the Copernican system itself a heresy. But his vision of an infinite universe filled with countless inhabited worlds is what history remembers.

question: Kant wrote that David Hume 'first interrupted my dogmatic slumber.' Hume's jolt was a question about cause and effect: when one billiard ball strikes another, what, Hume insisted, do we NEVER actually observe?
answer: Any hidden force itself - we see one event follow another, never the link joining them.
choices: Any hidden force itself - we see one event follow another, never the link joining them.
The motion of the balls, since the senses can never report such things truly.
The mathematics of it, which reason alone is said to supply before any sight.
The first ball at all, since a past event leaves no real trace in the present.
context: Hume's problem of causation: we observe only constant conjunction, one event reliably following another, never a necessary connection binding them; the 'cause' is a habit of the mind. Kant credited the jolt (Prolegomena, 1783) with launching his entire critical philosophy.

question: Augustine spent his youth chasing pleasure, fame, and rival philosophies, yet found peace in none of them. Looking back in his Confessions, he opened with one line naming why nothing he had tried could ever satisfy him. What did he write?
answer: You made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in You.
choices: You made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in You.
The heart finds its rest at last in mastering every pleasure the world offers.
The heart can never know peace, since longing is simply the human condition.
The heart is calmed by reason alone, once philosophy has silenced the passions.
context: Augustine's Confessions (c. AD 397) opens by addressing God: 'You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in You.' The whole book frames his wandering as a search whose true object he had not yet recognized.

question: Classmates mocked the large, silent Thomas Aquinas as 'the dumb ox,' yet his teacher Albert foretold this ox would one day bellow across the world. Aquinas held that faith and reason can never truly clash. On what ground?
answer: Both flow from one source of truth, so a real finding of reason cannot contradict a real truth of faith.
choices: Both flow from one source of truth, so a real finding of reason cannot contradict a real truth of faith.
Reason must always fall silent and humbly bow whenever it seems to collide with the claims of faith.
Faith is merely a temporary stopgap, filling the gaps that reason has not yet managed to reach.
They are two wholly separate truths that live apart and are under no need ever to agree at all.
context: Albert the Great's reported reply to the boy's mockers - that this ox's bellowing in doctrine would resound throughout the world - proved right. Aquinas argued (Summa Contra Gentiles, c. 1259-65) that faith and reason cannot contradict, since both derive from God as the single author of all truth; a genuine truth can never overthrow another genuine truth.

question: Descartes resolved to doubt everything he could: the world, his body, even mathematics, in case a powerful demon deceived him at every turn. Yet one thing survived the doubt. What did he conclude could not be doubted?
answer: That he was thinking - for doubting is itself a thought, so a deceiver cannot make him wrong about thinking.
choices: That he was thinking - for doubting is itself a thought, so a deceiver cannot make him wrong about thinking.
That the outside world exists, since so vivid an illusion would be pointless for a demon to bother staging.
That mathematics holds, because its truths feel far too clear and certain for any trickster to fake.
That his own body is real, for he can feel its weight and warmth directly whenever he attends to it.
context: Descartes' Meditations (1641): 'I think, therefore I am' (cogito ergo sum). The demon could deceive him about everything external, but the very act of being deceived proves a thinker is there to be deceived - making his own existence the first certainty he could not doubt away.

question: In Nietzsche's parable, a madman lights a lantern in bright morning, runs to the market crying 'I seek God!', and is mocked by the unbelievers there. He whirls on them: 'God is dead, and we have killed him!' What was he really telling the crowd?
answer: That they had torn out the root of their own morals and did not yet grasp the abyss they now faced.
choices: That they had torn out the root of their own morals and did not yet grasp the abyss they now faced.
That he had proven by clean argument that no god had ever existed anywhere in the first place.
That a cruel god had perished and humankind was now free to rejoice without any shadow of guilt.
That the church alone had died, while private faith in the heart could carry on entirely untouched.
context: The Gay Science (1882), section 125. Often misread as an atheist's boast, the parable is a warning: Europe had abandoned the faith that grounded its values yet kept living as if nothing had changed. The madman grieves the coming crisis of meaning - he even says he has come too soon.

question: Camus ends his essay on the gods condemning Sisyphus to roll a boulder uphill forever, only to watch it crash down each time. Rejecting both suicide and false hope, Camus makes a startling claim about that endless, pointless labor. What does he conclude?
answer: One must imagine Sisyphus happy - meaning is forged in the struggle itself, not handed down from above.
choices: One must imagine Sisyphus happy - meaning is forged in the struggle itself, not handed down from above.
One must pity Sisyphus deeply - a life without final purpose can only ever be pure suffering.
One must trust that the gods will relent in time and grant his ordeal some hidden reward.
One must conclude he should stop - a task with no end at all is never worth beginning.
context: The Myth of Sisyphus (1942). Facing the 'absurd' - our hunger for meaning meeting a silent universe - Camus refuses both despair and comforting illusion. His answer is lucid revolt: own the struggle as your own, and the scorn of fate becomes a kind of freedom.

question: After one book he thought had solved philosophy, Wittgenstein quit it to teach children in remote Austrian villages. Years later he returned to Cambridge — to overturn that very book. His new view rejected its core idea that words work by naming things. What replaced it?
answer: A word's meaning is its use in the flow of life — like a move in a game, not a label pinned on an object.
choices: A word's meaning is its use in the flow of life — like a move in a game, not a label pinned on an object.
A word's meaning is the private mental image it stirs up, locked inside each speaker's own head.
A word's meaning is fixed once and for all by the dictionary that the wider community agrees upon.
A word's meaning is the hidden logical form beneath it, which careful analysis can lay fully bare.
context: The Tractatus (1921) held that language pictures the world by naming. In Philosophical Investigations (published 1953), Wittgenstein replaced this with 'language-games': meaning lives in how words are actually used among people. 'A picture held us captive,' he wrote of the view he had himself once drawn.
